The Master said, "Falling. The monk asked, "What is the third phrase? The Master said, "Go. The monk bowed and the Master said, "The ancient style was truly magnificent.
Originally there were no Buddhas, patriarchs, Chan, or the Way; one simply followed conditions with ease and wandered freely according to one's nature.
At such a time, it cannot be said that you are strong and I am weak. To see is to see directly; not to see is to not see directly. Know this!"
If you know, speak directly; if you do not know, speak directly that you do not know. From where could one obtain all these reports regarding east, west, south, and north;

yin and yang, cold and heat; high and low, noble and base; right and wrong, self and other? As soon as one distinguishes the four sages from the six classes of ordinary beings, one immediately encounters errors and mistakes.
To speak of Buddhas and patriarchs, of Chan and the Way—it overturns the seas and mountains and tosses the heavens into chaos.
Kun. Even if Deshan’s staff falls like raindrops, he cannot be struck down; even if Linji’s shout rushes like thunder, he cannot be restrained.
Here at Shoushan, there is only a single sword; both Buddhas and demons are cut in two with one stroke, so that peace may prevail throughout the world.
You all need only attend to opening your bowls when hungry and resting when weary.
Close your eyes. Furthermore, what else is there? On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, it is merely ordinary.

Without giving rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation or study, one is eternally at ease within the light of formlessness. (He lets out a shout. Again, he cites a monk who asked Master Jiufeng Qian:
"The patriarchs have transmitted from one to another; what exactly is being transmitted? Jiufeng said, "Śākyamuni was stingy; Kāśyapa was wealthy. The monk said: [What about that?]
"What about the matter of the ultimate transmission? Feng said, "An old man of the same age divides the night lamp.
The Master composed a verse: "An old man of the same age divides the night lamp; Lighting this end, that end becomes bright. From the beginning, he has never borrowed another's mouth;
One must strictly avoid asking, 'How? What is it like?'"
Ascending the hall on the first day of the year, he held up his staff and said: "This mountain monk’s single staff has never been used to strike people indiscriminately.
Today, as the New Year begins, I am opening the seal; Śākyamuni Buddha and Master Bodhidharma cannot be let off."
As for the rest of their kind, they could be measured by cartloads or bushels. A sharp sword does not slay those already dead. Suddenly, if someone comes forward and says, "What about the Elder?

one must strike them across the back with the staff. It is not that one wishes to make it difficult for others to dwell together; rather, it is because, in general, the distinction between the ordained and the laity must be clear.
Relying on his staff, he descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The flavor of salt in water; the clarity of glue within color. It is certainly there, yet its form is not seen.
Even Great Master Fu was merely clear-headed in a dream and sober within a drunken stupor. If you wish to recognize the Mind-King, you still lack true awakening."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Above the head, vast and boundless; beneath the feet, vast and boundless. The *śakrāloka* eye cannot peer into it;

the body of Vairocana is fully manifest. Even if Mount Sumeru were to shatter and the waters of the ocean boil over, and the forests of the great earth were all to burst into flame at once, not a single hair would ever be moved.
There is no path for devas and humans to accompany him; there is no way for demons or outsiders to enter."
I have established no gate; let everyone under heaven follow their own joy as they please. I alone am unwilling. Have you not heard it said:
"A man-child, unstained amidst the dust"? (He lets out a shout.)
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "One tree, two trees of peach blossoms; three stalks, four stalks of tall bamboo.

In years past, one spoke in vain of Lingyun; today, let us cease talking of Duofu. The red is naturally red; the green is naturally green. The slanting is naturally slanting; the curved is naturally curved.
You students from north, south, east, and west—whoever you may be—often add extra legs to a painted snake. Do not add legs! Six."
Six originally become thirty-six.
When the Buddha ascended the hall for the discourse on his *nirvāṇa*, he said: "In the age of the Final Dharma, monks have three kinds of attachments. One person says: 'The Tathāgata is fixed.'"
One person says: "He entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees. To hold this as real is to burden the Elder Śākyamuni;
he has died and cannot be brought back to life. Another person says: "He is always on Vulture Peak Mountain and in all other dwelling places.
To hold this as real is to burden the Elder Śākyamuni; he is alive and cannot be made to die. Yet another says: "All dharmas are..."
Arising. All phenomena are unextinguished. If one can understand in this way, the Buddhas are ever present before one.
The living Śākyamuni is the dead Śākyamuni; the dead Śākyamuni is the living Śākyamuni.
To grasp this as being real is precisely a great illness. The worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness; none of them act in such a manner.
At that time, in what place did one meet the Old Man Śākyamuni? The wind is warm and the birds’ songs shatter; the sun is high and the flower shadows deepen.
When bathing the Buddha and ascending the hall, there was this nature even before the world existed; when the world perishes, this nature does not perish.
Whether appearing in the world or not appearing in the world, whether attaining Buddhahood or not attaining Buddhahood—all these are merely idle words.

The body of the pure Dharma-realm fundamentally has no coming or going; it is through the power of great compassionate vows that it manifests birth. To speak in such a manner is precisely because one has not eliminated worldly vulgarity.
Now tell me: do you call this the Old Man Śākyamuni, or do you not? One mention [of his name] encompasses forty [aspects].
9. Small Sermon on the Summer Retreat. A monk asked, "Majestic and dignified, brilliant and resplendent—prior to sound it is not sound; following form it is not form.
I wonder, what is this? The Master said, "A faceless fellow. The monk pressed further, "What is he right now?"

[The student] asked, "Where [is he]? The Master said, "His eyes see as if he were blind; his mouth speaks as if he were mute. [The student] asked further, "Has this person ever observed the *jinzu* (retreat)?
The Master said, "His feet do not leave the ground as he runs. [The student] asked, "Tell me, would this person consent to become a Buddha? The Master said, "Do not slander him.
[The student] asked, "If he does not become a Buddha, then whom will he teach to deliver sentient beings? The Master said, "There is."

“Sentient beings must be delivered. If there are no sentient beings, what is there to deliver? The student asked, “Right now, throughout the twenty-five realms of existence within the triple world, everything is vast and expansive.
Can one call this ‘no sentient beings’? The Master said, “One must not speak of dreams before a fool.
He then continued, “All you practitioners of Chan: you have cast off the external world and escaped from the internal body and mind. Your mind is no longer bound to your body.”
The body is like empty space; the body is not bound to the mind, and the mind is like the *dharmadhātu*. To observe the *kaṭhina* precept in this way, there is no foot to be restrained.
To observe the summer retreat (*vassa*) in this way, there is no dwelling that is not peaceful. Yet even this is not yet the place where the patch-robed monks (*śramaṇera*) tread.

Only when Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra sweep the beds and fold the blankets, and the two Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Equal and Wondrous, follow the donkey and hold the horse—when one reaches such a state, day by day...
This would consume ten thousand taels of gold. Even so, there are still people in the Western Heavens who are not yet willing to concede.

Again, he cites what is said in the teachings: "All various acts of grasping and rejecting are the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). To attempt to discern Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) without having escaped the cycle of rebirth—that nature of Perfect Enlightenment would itself be subject to the same flux.
There is no possibility of avoiding the cycle of rebirth in such a manner. O virtuous practitioners of meditation, what do you call this?

"Perfect Enlightenment—how can one avoid the cycle of birth and death? The stream flows from the eastern ravine to the western ravine; clouds rise on the southern mountain and drift over the northern mountain.

He ascended the hall and said: "After the rain, the bridge is level and the waters are full; before the mountains, the wheat is ripe and the birds sing. The willows by the bank are lush and drooping; the flowers in the forest—"
Brilliant! The light of the stream is deep and clear; the color of the grass is lush and green. Is this mind or is it the environment? Is it delusion or is it awakening?

I observe the trichiliocosm and find that there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where a Bodhisattva has not sacrificed their body and life. If you can understand this, let old Śākyamuni pass to one side.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Transverse and vertical, there is no obstruction. Within the ocean of the Flower Treasury, there is but a single mote of dust.

Whether moving with or against the current, what constraints can there be? Upon the top of the banner-pole, one performs a somersault. There is no principle outside of phenomena; there are no phenomena outside of principle.
There is no object outside of mind; there is no mind outside of objects. As a pearl within an oyster, as a prognostic mark on a tortoise shell, as horns on an ox, and as hooves on a horse."

Each and every one interpenetrates; layer upon layer they are subsumed. Although Śākyamuni and Maitreya have the *svastika* emblazoned upon their chests, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra likewise have their noses pointing downward.
You all are fortunately without concern; why must you insist on a talisman for protecting the body?
(He lets out a shout.)

Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are much like a cesspool. Why do you, for no reason, thrust your head into such a place?

Come, come! I shall engage you in this tangle. He took up his staff and said, "As for the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and the elder monks throughout the land—when they arrive here, their wits fail them and their tongues are tied. Try to speak out! The assembly was at a loss. The Master [continued]:
"It is said: 'It deceives people to death.

[He] ascended the hall and said: "When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents. When the Great Matter is already clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents.
You say there is a difference between these two? It is because of the place where I used to see guests off that I remember the time of leaving my own home."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When you hear the tea board, go drink tea; when you hear the bath board, go take a bath.
When you hear Shoushan’s way, you all should simply stop and rest. Why is it that you are unwilling to go in this manner?
If someone were suddenly to come forward and say, 'Venerable Master, I cannot blame you,' you should tell him: 'Before you reached Shoushan, I have already given you thirty blows!'"
Small General Assembly for the End of the Summer Retreat. A monk asked, "When one has an iron backbone and a heart forged of solid gold, what then?
The Master said, "It is not far from here to Qiantang. The monk pressed further, "If such a person were at the gate of Shoushan, how would you treat them?
The Master said, "I would send them off with great courtesy beyond the desolate fields. The monk said, "Thank you, Preceptor, for your testimony. The Master [nodded].
He then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master then said: "Heaven and earth share the same root; the myriad things are one body.
Filling the valleys when in the valleys, filling the pits when in the pits. Its capacity exceeds that of empty space, yet empty space still has its name and designation.
Its clarity surpasses that of the sun and moon, yet the sun and moon still possess their radiance. Every monkey wears an ancient rhombus-shaped mirror; every tree utters the lion’s roar."
In every atom and in every land, they are dense and majestic. Thus it is said: "The Dharma-King’s power of Dharma transcends all living beings;
he constantly bestows the wealth of Dharma upon all. Having long accumulated pure karma, his renown is immeasurable; he leads the multitudes through tranquility.

I prostrate to those who possess such wonders and such numinous clarity. Yet, because sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects, the various sages respond.

Illness and medicine; sometimes establishing the retreat (*kṣetra-bandha*), sometimes establishing the conclusion of the retreat (*kṣetra-mokṣa*); sometimes manifesting the entire body, sometimes manifesting half the body—this is solely for the sake of the noble Dharma’s circulation.
One must not allow arbitrary or forced interpretations. Fire does not wait for the sun to be hot; water does not wait for the moon to be cool.
The crane is white and the crow is black; the pine is straight and the thornbush is crooked. Under the clear breeze and the moonlight, the man who waits by the stump [sees] the cool hare.
Gradually, as the distance grew, the spring grass turned green. Again, it is recounted that on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreat in three places.
Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel him, but just as he was about to lift it, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs.
Although Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers, he could not raise the gavel. The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel?"
Mañjuśrī. Kāśyapa was speechless. The Master said, "Kāśyapa is no true man of honor! Do not speak only of Mañjuśrīs numbering in the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, or millions;

even if they were hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, or millions of World-Honored Ones, I would strike them down with a single blow and expel them. Have you not heard it said: 'Under the staff, there is the patience of non-arising;
when facing the critical moment, one sees no teacher'?"
When Master Liaoyuan retired from Lingyan and returned to express his gratitude, he ascended the hall and said: "Now, those who act as spiritual friends drive away the plow and snatch away the food;
they transform the ordinary into the holy. Those who behold such a spiritual friend are like those who see a blue lotus—their faculty of sight becomes pure.
Those who hear the spiritual friend’s preaching of the Dharma are like those who eat the food of the Land of Fragrant Accumulation—their pores all become fragrant. Ling... [text continues]

This is what Master Yan meant. Your return to the Ju and Li families deeply accords with my humble wishes. It is my good fortune that you are accompanied by such eminent disciples (nāgas and elephants); I hope you will continue to cherish yourself.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Above heaven and below heaven, from head to tail, arranged horizontally and vertically—this is what I constantly employ.
You all may only look on from the side. Do not accept anything learned from other quarters. Sometimes I instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink;
sometimes I do not instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink; sometimes I instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink."
This is so. Sometimes teaching involves raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye; at other times it is not so. When the wise hear even a slight word, they should seize it with vigor;
do not wait for daybreak and lose the rooster.
Upon returning from inspecting the fields, he ascended the hall and related: Guishan asked Yangshan, "Where have you come from? Yangshan replied, "From the fields."
Miaoyan asked, "How many people are there in the field? Yangshan stood with his spade thrust into the ground and his hands folded.

Miaoyan said, "Today on South Mountain, there are many people cutting thatch. Yangshan pulled the spade and walked away. Xuedou said, "Everywhere it is said that the 'spade stuck in the ground' story is extraordinary;
this is much like following the heterodox and pursuing the evil. According to Xuedou’s own view, Yangshan was caught by Miaoyan..."
Question: "I have simply managed to bind myself with a rope of grass; I am ten parts closer to death. Miaoxi said, "The benevolent see it and call it benevolence;
the wise see it and call it wisdom. The common people use it daily yet do not know it; therefore, the Way of the superior man is rare.
The Master said, "Fortunately, there is no trouble. That old fellow Miaoxi has recited a mantra, which has directly caused [this result]."
The heavens rotate to the left and the earth turns to the right.

On the occasion of the opening session for the newly acquired Tripitaka, [the Master] cited an instance from Xuefeng: One day, while leading the community in a communal labor of carrying firewood, he encountered a monk on the road.
He then threw down a piece of wood and said, "The entire Great Tripitaka speaks only of this. Later, Zhenru Zhe...
[The monk] said, "The entire Great Canon of Teachings does not speak of this. The Master asked, "What is this very thing?
Whether it is spoken of or not, where do you all see these two great elders? Zhongyue Neng then held up his whisk.
To raise it up is "Thus have I heard"; to let it go is "faithfully receive and practice. The Master said, "If you deliberate upon this as if it were the Buddha-dharma, your eyebrows must fall off."

Ascending the hall at the consecration of the Ten Thousand Buddhas Pavilion, a monk asked: "When it fills the void of space, it is not a decorated pavilion; when its true face is manifest, it is also not ten thousand Tathāgatas.
I venture to ask, upon what does Mount Shou rely for its establishment? The Master said: "Carpenter Lu Ban’s measuring line. The monk stepped forward and said:
"When an object meets its master, the eyes stand upright. The Master said: "The hook is in a place beyond doubt. The monk stepped forward again.
"If one does not ascend the tower to look out, how can one know the depth of the vast ocean? The Master said, "Why run about so wildly? He then continued: "One drags stones; two carry earth.
To trigger the mechanism, one need not use a crossbow of a thousand *qun*. Boundless pavilions fill the void; since the beginning of the vast eon, who has been the master?
You must discern who is the master! Best of all, one beam matches one pillar. [He then descended.]
The Seat Master bows to thank the Head Seat for holding the whisk. The Abbot prepares a vegetarian feast and ascends the hall to preach. Zen is not a matter of conceptual thought;
to seek it through conceptual thought is to deviate from it. The Way is devoid of merit; to measure it by means of merit is to err. Where can one establish "right" and set up "wrong"? To abandon...
One delusion leads directly to enlightenment. It becomes increasingly urgent and increasingly relaxed; it becomes increasingly intimate and increasingly distant.
Failing to penetrate through to that other side, most remain stuck right here. To advance is like ten thousand layers of silver mountains; to retreat is like a thousand fathoms of iron walls.
When pressed until a single path opens, and pushed until a single thread enters, one realizes that one's own self is precisely these silver mountains and iron walls. Upon reaching such a state...
"A field of land—what is so extraordinary about it? With its three virtues and six flavors, its taste exceeds all else. A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds.
He ascended the hall and said: "In every place, there is one's own steamed bun. Is this so, or not? Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still..."
There was no second person present. Under the eastern corridor and the western corridor, they chattered away like water pouring from a jar.
Suddenly, when asked by someone, "What is the self of the Venerable One? he could not answer. Although he could not answer, [the matter remained].
"Essentially, it has never been lost. *Heh heh!* He descends from the seat.

On the first day of the year, he ascends the hall, holds up his staff, and says: "As for having the Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the new year—this staff does not even dare to grant permission for that.

As for having no Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the new year—this staff does not even dare to grant permission for that either. It transcends the four propositions and is beyond all conceptualization."
The "one hundred negations" are all but old stories from various quarters; even the staff does not dare to grant them approval. (He draws a line.
At the commencement of the New Year, all things are renewed.
Ascending the hall: "The Tathāgatas of the past, stay outside the gate for now. The Bodhisattvas of the present, do not hesitate further.
Those who practice and study in the future, you must walk fast before it is too late! The empty space of the ten directions collapses onto the ground;
a fire breaks out from the bottom of the great ocean and burns the eyebrows of Śakra. The Dragon King of the Eastern Sea lets loose a single thunderclap—*Xinluo*!"
Inside the temple, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly. At the mountain gate, the Vajra Guardian raised his fist, and Huaguang, the Protector Deity, said:
"Exhausting one's own mind, one breaks the mouths of others. He let out a shout.
Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat. A monk asked, "What is it like when a single word expresses everything? The Master said, "Once the mouth is opened, it cannot be closed.
The monk pressed further, "What is it like when one does not rely on a single word? The Master said, "Once the mouth is closed, it cannot be opened. The monk pressed further.
"When it is not at all like this, how is it? The Master said, "Seven blows for thirteen. He then continued: "The moment you raise your eyebrows, you have already missed it;
once the mouth opens, one has already fallen into discourse. Few know the pivot of the Patriarchs' gate; the entire world is vast and empty, yet everyone treads upon fire.
To unfold [the teaching] before the sound deceives you, O *śrāmaṇera*; to deliberate after the phrase merely turns it into a track."
One kick overturns the waters of the great ocean; one punch topples Mount Sumeru. Yet even this is still the act of a restless, impulsive fellow.
How much more so for those who set up patterns and models, feigning muteness and deafness, severing false攀緣 (pān-yuan / clinging to objects), and seeking true liberation!
This is very much like mistaking a skull for water, or buying cinnabar to paint the moon. When will such people ever find rest? Shoushan does not...
I regret my verbal karma for you all; let me break it open for you. Holding up his whisk, he said: "Do you see this? This is the gate of Mañjuśrī.
If one enters through the gate of Mañjuśrī, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, walls, and tiles and pebbles will cause you to turn your back on the dust of delusion and unite with awakening.
Striking the whisk, he said: "Do you hear this? This is the gate of Avalokiteśvara. If one enters through the gate of Avalokiteśvara..."

As for those who enter through the gate: the pines rustle in the breeze, the mountain stream resounds, the crows cry and the magpies chatter—these teach you to return to the root and restore the source.

Upon reaching this state, you realize the Immovable Honored One and achieve supreme enlightenment. Yet, you must further know that there is a single aperture at the crown of the head. Do you understand this thoroughly?
The morning air is moist at the harvest of wheat; the midday shade is cool beneath the locust trees. Again, he raised the case of Layman Pang, who asked Great Master Ma:
"Who is it that does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas? The Master said: "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single draught, and then I will tell you.
The Master [Zhaozhou] offered this verse: "A phrase that covers heaven and covers earth— Master Ma has exerted his full strength to bring it forth."
[The Master] did not rise. [He said: "How amusing that Qingyuan received Shitou! Whenever you meet someone, simply ask about the rice of Luling. He ascended the hall and said:
"An ancient said, 'I intend to swallow you down,' but it was only because my front teeth were in the way. Now they are no longer in the way—can you be swallowed?
'I intend to spit you out,' but I feared my throat was too small. Now it is not small—let me spit you out!"
Can you? If you can swallow it, swallow it; if you can spit it out, spit it out. Even if you could swallow it and spit it out, I would still ask you: what is this dry piece of dung?
Ascending the hall, he said: "Ordinary and holy are half-closed and half-open; neither Buddha nor mind is entirely life-giving or entirely killing.
It is like a powerful wing sweeping through the void, soaring ten thousand miles across; like a golden-scaled fish that has passed the net, with not a single thread clinging to it.
How spirited and swift such a monk is! Sometimes the words reach him but the meaning does not; sometimes the meaning reaches him but the words do not; sometimes both the meaning and the words..."
Both arrive. Sometimes neither mind nor words arrive. If both mind and words arrive, how do you deliberate?
If neither mind nor words arrive, where do you then peck and probe? How is it when a person of the highest caliber arrives? A dot.
At Zhongxia, he ascended the hall and raised the case of Layman Pang, who said: "To protect life, one must kill; Ginger does not change its pungency.
Only when all are killed does one dwell in peace; Everywhere one goes, one encounters him. If you wish to know the meaning herein, There are thorns in the soft mud.
An iron boat floats upon the water; The bearded man has no whiskers. Some, upon hearing him say "kill," also immediately say, "Kill the Buddha!"
"Killing the Patriarch. What is there to choose? With such a view, it is better to simply stop and rest—to let go—than to be like one from Zhengzhou coming out through the Cao gate.
Suddenly, if you strike the bridge of your nose, an iron boat will float upon the water; these are words of truth.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Great Way is right before your eyes, yet it is difficult to behold within those very eyes.

If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way, it is not separate from sound, form, and speech. O virtuous ones, the incense burner in the Buddha Hall and the tally-sticks at the latrine have already spoken for you.
Venerable Kauṇḍinya, having drunk his fill, adds another cup and comes here to listen; he hears it all."

This is a footnote. At first, I thought it was merely a matter of the length of the thatch; once burned away, I found the ground was originally uneven. Entering the hall, he snapped his fingers once and said:
"If you hear this here, once a single faculty returns to its source, all six sense-bases are stilled and restored.

The sense-base of the eye performs the Buddha-work of the sense-base of the ear; the sense-base of the ear performs the Buddha-work of the sense-base of the nose; the sense-base of the nose performs the Buddha-work of the sense-base of the tongue..."
The Buddha’s work: the sense-base of the tongue performs the Buddha’s work of the sense-base of the body; the sense-base of the body performs the Buddha’s work of the sense-base of the mind;
the sense-base of the mind performs the Buddha’s work of all sense-bases. Are they ultimately one? Or are they six?
As soon as there is one, there are six; as soon as there are six, there is one. This is the meaning of "one and six. One cannot say they do not exist. Yet, there are no eyes, ears, or noses.
The tongue, body, and mind; formlessness, soundlessness, odorlessness, tastelessness, touchlessness, and non-existence of dharmas—furthermore, these cannot be recognized as having existence.
This is the meaning of the Teachings; what is the meaning of the Patriarchs? (He lets out a shout.)

A small *sǎn* (general discourse) for the end of the summer retreat. A monk asked, "The nine months of summer have been spent in labor; how do you speak of 'offering' [the fruit]? The Master said, "Layer upon layer, mountain passes and roads.
The monk pressed, "What is it like when one goes forth just so? The Master said, "Scarcely found south of the Yangtze; utterly non-existent north of the river."
It is then said: "For several days past, it may be called extreme heat; when rain falls in the evening, one immediately feels cool.

Since the heat does not come from without and the coolness does not emerge from within, yet manifests expansively right where one is without departing that place, then the ancient Śākyamuni was not first and the present Maitreya is not later.
Why wait until one has perfected the six pāramitās to finally reach the Dharma-cloud stage? Far...

Only after traversing the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* does one finally ascend to the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, one may manifest a Jewel-King Land upon the tip of a single hair, or sit within a mote of dust and turn the Great Dharma Wheel.
At times, one takes up a single blade of grass and uses it as the sixteen-foot golden body; at other times, one takes up the sixteen-foot golden body and uses it as a single blade of grass.
To observe the summer retreat in such a manner ensures that one’s efforts are not exerted in vain; this is truly the essence of the "wax."
People are like ice. When it has completely turned into iron pellets, the function is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.

How do you say it in a single phrase? "A single moon rises over the sea; how many families ascend the tower? Again, he raised the case of a monk taking leave of Guizong. Guizong asked, "Where are you going?
The monk said, "I am going to study the 'five flavors' of Chan in various quarters. Guizong said, "In my place, there is the 'one flavor' of Chan. The monk said, "What is it like?"
"What is 'single-flavor Chan'? Mazu struck him. The monk said, "I understand! I understand! Mazu said, "Speak! Speak!
As the monk was about to open his mouth, Mazu struck him again. Huangbo said, "Master Mazu produced eighty-four *kalyāṇamitra*s (spiritual friends);
when questioned, each one was dripping wet. Only Guizong was slightly better. The Master [Baizhang] said, "What are you talking about?"
It is not even slightly better; it is truly not yet there. Here, I have a single flavor of Chan, and I would immediately overturn the meditation seat for you.
If you do not seize it upon seeing it, thinking of it will leave you a thousand miles away.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To awaken to the Way upon hearing a sound—this would block your ears. To clarify the mind upon seeing form—this would change your eyes.
Sitting upright upon the meditation cushion, threading a needle with a thread: when a gust of west wind arrives, two or three leaves fall."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In Pūrvavideha, everyone is being pressed into service to carry firewood. In Aparagoyānī, they offer greetings and inquire after one's health.
In Jambudvīpa, what are you doing? He then added: "I still remember what happened just a moment ago."

[The Master] carved an image of the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands and a thousand eyes. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "For what purpose does the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion employ so many hands and eyes?
The Master said: "The spring breeze does not wrap itself in a turban. He then cited the story of Nanquan calling for the courtyard steward; when the steward responded, Nanquan said:
"In the past, for ninety days, the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother. At that time, King Udayana..."
He thought of the Buddha. He requested Maudgalyāyana to exercise his supernatural powers three times over;
they brought the craftsmen there to carve a Buddha image. They managed to carve only thirty-one of the marks. Why was this? It was because the mark of the Brahma-voice could not be carved.

The Abbot of the Monastery asked, "What is the mark of the Brahma-voice? Master Xuefeng called out to the Abbot, who responded. Xuefeng said, "This will ruin people! The Master then called to the assembly.
If he perceives the characteristics of the Brahma voice, for those who are to be delivered by a Buddha-body,
he immediately manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them. Even for those who are to be delivered by the bodies of devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, he immediately manifests all such forms and preaches the Dharma for them.
“The Dharma. He then asked, “Speak, then, what Dharma do you speak? and immediately descended from his seat.
When the letter from Master Tánfāng of Lóngxiáng arrived, he ascended the hall and said: “The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests the Dharma equal to empty space.
When one realizes empty space, There is neither ‘is’ nor ‘is not. Since there is neither this Dharma nor that which is not Dharma, then...
The Buddhas’ attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, their turning of the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and their entry into parinirvāṇa are all like dreams.

Master Tánfāng, the Chan Master Fóhǎi, repeatedly presided over famous monasteries and personally received imperial favor; yet, upon taking his leave of Jìngfǔ, he immediately took up residence at Lóngxiáng.
His final radiance and his bodily relics—eight *hú* and four *dǒu*—are not to be considered many. Let us briefly examine this.
"A single grain. Let everyone look at it. He held up the whisk and said, "The Sea God knows its nobility but not its price;
he leaves it for the human world to illuminate the night. He then threw down the whisk.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The phrase that encompasses heaven and earth; the phrase that follows the waves and drifts with the current;
the phrase that cuts off all streams—what would you call the one further phrase? Do not speak before a fool; it would break your head and split your forehead."
Ascending the hall, he said: "From where does this fine snow come? Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all white and vast.
Ultimately, where does it go? After the sun rises, it is revealed all at once."
Ascending the hall on the first day of the year: This year’s year is last year’s year; how many years have passed as the old year went and the new came?
Yesterday’s day is today’s day; the rising and setting of the sun do not occur on but a single day. This very thing is without coming or going, without entering or exiting.
"Every year is a good year; every day is a good day. The four oceans flow toward the East Sea—this is the Prajñāpāramitā.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the *Lotus Sūtra*, which says: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.

Those with overweening pride, upon hearing it, will certainly not respect or believe it. The Master said: "It has already been spoken. Can it be stopped? The Old Man with the Yellow Face [the Buddha] has already made his distinction."
He did not descend. Zhuo leaned on his staff and said, "Sometimes it is held aloft at the peak of a thousand peaks; it cuts through the celestial clouds, refusing to let them rise higher.
Entering the hall, he held up his whisk and said, "Those who know it call this thing a whisk; those who do not know it also call this thing a whisk.
How do you distinguish between them? What is difficult to distinguish? Among them, those who know it take hold of—"
It is used as soon as it arrives; those who do not realize its presence cannot employ it.
Now that it is in the hands of Shoushan, whether you realize it or not, from where have you obtained this news? [He] threw down his whisk and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The white peony and the red peony—when they bloom, it is the spring wind that causes them to bloom; when they fall, it is the spring wind that causes them to fall.
Yet the spring wind knows nothing of their blooming and falling. That it knows nothing is already a matter of calculation. He shook his hand and said, "No, no!"
Lan Hua-yan ascends the hall: "Good Wealth traveled through one hundred and ten cities and attended fifty-three spiritual friends;
only at the very end, upon seeing Mañjuśrī again, did he finally complete the Great Matter.
An ancient said, "There is yet another person—why did Good Wealth not attend him? Tell me, who is this person? *Duḥ!* (A shout).
Ascending the hall: The crow caws, "ya ya"; the magpie calls, "que que. The cuckoo cries, "guo gong"; the osprey shrieks, "gu e.
Why must one lengthen the ducks or shorten the cranes, or level the mountains to fill the valleys? Zen students join together as the moon sets behind the western peaks.
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: Before entering the womb, there is a turning word that this mountain monk has never uttered while dwelling in mountains at various places.
Today, on the anniversary of the Tathāgata’s birth, I cannot help but present it to you all. Having said this, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall at the beginning of the summer retreat: You people, seeing Shoushan move his lips and flap his tongue, immediately intend to huddle together and peck at him;

you try to calculate and measure it within the root of your own minds. Yet, when he lets fly the diamond circle and casts down the chestnut thorn, ten out of ten or five pairs cannot swallow or leap over it.
This is for no other reason than that, from the past until now, you have been accustomed to wandering thoughts within the skull. Furthermore...
Within the inner chambers, while soft and warm things have not yet been removed, one suddenly encounters harsh tongs and hammers and immediately feels discouraged.
I tell you clearly: this matter does not reside in words. Though there are thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises, they may indeed be devoid of words;
yet can they still allow the thieving mind to function? If you truly wish to put an end to the thieving mind, do not rely on them. Examine this within these ninety days.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Aṅgulimāla said, 'For immeasurable kalpas, I have never killed a living being.
How do you all understand this? You must not understand it as a discourse on non-arising. If you understand it in such a way, you will fall alive into hell."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ten directions of the world are a tumultuous clamor; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are but a single pinch of dust.
Right and wrong, long and short—none are spoken. How does this compare to the broad and long tongue of Mount Shou? Since it is a broad and long tongue, why does it not speak?"
"Coral branches support the moon branch by branch.

Entering the hall, [the Master said: "To face the wall all along is for the Way to be cut off and the people to be desolate. To focus solely on the journey ahead is to have one's eyes squinting and ears burning.
There has never been one who travels far without stopping, nor one who stays long without traveling. At times, at the crossroads of the street, he picks up..."
Holding the staff, he shares in the light and shares in the dust; it is vividly manifest in every place as radiance blazes forth.
At times, atop a solitary peak, he sets down his alms-bag, blocking the ravines and sealing the caves; it is vividly manifest in every place as he departs into withered stillness.
To say "this very mind is Buddha" is not permitted; to say "neither mind nor Buddha" is also not permitted. It is not the mind. It is not...
"This is the Buddha. It is not a thing, nor can it be attained. I see two clay oxen fighting as they enter the sea;
even until now, there has been no news. (He lets out a shout.)
Ascending the hall, he said: "To attain it in the mind, even *eranda* grass becomes a sandalwood tree; to lose it in its essential meaning, even nectar becomes a garden of thorns.

The Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally the same—why, then, is there attainment and loss? If you say there is a distinction between the holy and the ordinary, this is because your realization and cultivation are not authentic, and thus the mind and its essential meaning appear different.
To speak in such a way is to call one a blind old woman from a village of three households."

I speak. I have never even dreamed that there is so much as a single hair upon the feet of my monks. There are a certain sort of fellows who say: "Those who attain this matter originally did not attain it;
those who do not attain it likewise do not lose it. These are all nothing but wild fox spirits, bewitching the men and women of households;
they will never reach the end of their delusions. Furthermore, they run into old bald slaves on the meditation platform who do not recognize what is good.
Evil! Three hundred or five hundred of them gather their heads together and deliberate, saying: "I have opened the eyes of the human and celestial realms; for what reason should I do so?
Not even a drop of water or a thread of silk must go unpaid. Only then will they be satisfied.
Small *sǎn* (informal discourse) on the conclusion of the summer retreat. A monk asked, "One person attained awakening because of a teaching;
one person attained awakening because of inquiry; one person attained self-awakening without a teacher. When these three arrive at Shoushan, which one will you receive?
The Master said, "A lion bites a man; a hunting dog chases a clod of earth. The monk pressed further, "In that case, shall we all go together to the hall for practice? The Master said, "Go! You!"
[The Master] would not accept his words. The student continued, "If one does not come in this way at all, what then? The Master said, "That would be somewhat better.
The student continued, "Under the gate of Shoushan, the wind cannot enter and the water cannot touch it. The Master said, "Rare is the guest who comes with pierced ears;
many are those who mark the boat after the sword has been lost. The student continued, "The Master has only the heart to receive the jade; you lack the resolve to cut off the city."

[The monk] expressed this intention. The Master said, "Do not wrongly blame this old monk. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "The Yellow-Faced Old Man contemplated such matters during the three seven-day periods.
What are these 'such matters'? Is it that the past and future limits are severed? Is that what these 'such matters' are?
Is it that having finished saving sentient beings, he entered parinirvāṇa? Is that what these 'such matters' are?"
What is it? If you call this "such-and-such a thing," you are precisely like a water jelly using a shrimp for eyes;
you have no autonomy and slander the Yellow-Faced Old Man. You will surely have a day when you eat iron rods. All of you:
what exactly have you been contemplating within these ninety days? I say that the Yellow-Faced Old Man and you see with the same eye.
The same ear hears; the same nose smells; the same tongue tastes; the same body touches; the same mind knows.
The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure, non-dual, indivisible, without distinction, and uninterrupted.
Yunmen’s hand-fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra, and seizes the carp of the Eastern Sea.
A blow with a staff. Rain pouring down like a basin being overturned. And what about this? "In years past, I searched in vain along the road;
today, I see it as ice within fire. Again, Master Baoning Yong addressed the assembly, citing Dongshan: "On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice;
before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is 'dog-urine-day' (a chaotic, muddy day). At the top of the banner-pole, a *jiu-zui* is being fried. Three!"
The monkey winnows coins at night. Shishuang said: "The wind blows through the stone mortar, vying in its roar;
a clay-formed Vajrapāṇi runs through the void. He kicks over the moon in the sea, and chaotic waves arise; he startles the Earth Star, which invades the Southern Dipper.
Daowu said: "A three-faced cat treads upon the moon; a two-headed white ox grasps smoke in its paws. A crowned green hare stands atop the courtyard cypress."

"A turtle shedding its shell flies up into the sky. These three verses serve three purposes: first, they act as teachers for the ancestral Buddhas; second, they test the eyes of the patch-robed monks;
third, they provide a model for all people under heaven. If one can definitively resolve them, it may be granted that they possess a single eye. The Master said:
"Baoning’s critique of these three verses is easy to distinguish as snow-dust, yet difficult to discern as soot within ink."
Shoushan, not sparing his own eyebrows, has commented on this from beginning to end: first, it serves as a teacher for the patriarchs and Buddhas, yet it is not worth a single coin;
second, it tests the eyes of the monks—what a mere clay pellet! Third, it serves as a model for all people under heaven; do not misunderstand it.
Even if you were to understand it, ten thousand miles away you would still be looking toward your hometown.

At the consecration ceremony for the Ten Thousand Buddhas, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Master Guishan said: 'When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the essence reveals the true permanence;
when phenomena and principle are non-dual, that is the Buddha of Suchness. Where is the Buddha right now? The Master said, "Bamboo in the south, wood in the north.
The monk pressed further, "Does this Buddha have form and appearance, or not? The Master said, "A foreigner drinking milk returns [empty-handed]."
Xuefeng remarked, “What a strange good physician! Jianyun asked, “Why, Master, do you go to such lengths to set up a model and draw a pattern?
The Master said, “I beat the grass only to startle the snake. Jianyun asked, “I wonder, does this have merit or not? The Master said, “Let it cool down first, then come look.
Jianyun said, “I only wish that the east wind would exert its full force and blow everything at once into my gate. The Master said, “And again...”
"Going thus," he said, "Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep; what do you call 'Buddha'? Morning after morning one rises together with him;
do not mistake the zero-point on the scale. Rising and sitting, he is ever present; in the end, who is he?
Speaking and remaining silent, we dwell together; neither one nor two. Not a hair’s breadth separates us; they are like a shadow and its form. To know this—"
Segment. How many people are there in empty space? One cannot grasp them by groping. Even with a hundred refinements of pure gold and a thousand clever schemes, one cannot cast it into form;

one cannot carve it into shape. As soon as Master Fatai opened his bellows, its spirit was revealed—it truly shines upon the earth and dazzles the heavens, soaring through the present and illuminating the past. Nevertheless, even so, he has only written half of it. You—

All you people, from morning until evening—whether ascending the hall, entering a room, opening your sitting mat, or unfolding your alms bowl—where is there any place for your original face to be hidden?
Do you see it? If you do not investigate the source now, you will have to wait until that year to ask Maitreya.
Ascending the hall on the first day of the eighth month: Mountains and rivers have no obstruction; radiance penetrates everywhere.

The people of the four continents are right now in this courtyard, clamoring over the Buddha-dharma with great noise. Suddenly, someone might come forth and say: "All you people are fortunately at peace;
for no reason, you have been smeared on the beaks by the saliva of wild foxes. Seeing others, you immediately wish to contend over the Buddha."
"Quarreling over the Dharma. Quarreling over this, quarreling over that—quarreling until the year of the donkey, it still will not cease.
[The Master] snaps his fingers and says, "How unfortunate! Śakra Devendra, having heard this, descended from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and shouted, "You pack of demonic sons!
What are you quarreling about here? He struck each of them twenty blows and banished them to other directions. —From *Shou* (Longevity).

Master Shanbu could not help but dance with his hands and stamp with his feet. After the fiery clouds have first dispersed, when the metallic energy of autumn is about to bring coolness—ascending the hall:
"The wild geese pass through the vast sky; their shadows sink into the cold waters. Insects chirp upon the ancient steps; their echoes answer within the empty hall. All is luminously clear."
Before the birth of the Buddha, the true mechanism was revealed in its solitude; it is clearly beyond the reach of seeing and hearing, manifesting itself without partiality.
It cuts off all manifold differences and gathers them back into the single principle. How would you say it? "The staff intends to swallow the Buddhas of the three ages;
the lantern pours forth a hundred bushels of bright pearls."
The Dharma Master Yunkxi ascended the hall for the formal lecture. "Ordinary people see form as form and see emptiness as emptiness;
the sages see form as emptiness and see emptiness as form. How do you all understand this?
If you see form as form and see emptiness as emptiness, you are the same as ordinary people. If you see form as emptiness and see emptiness as form, you are the same as the sages."
As soon as there is the dualistic view of ordinary and sage, this person falls into the attachment to views; they are no different from the non-Buddhist outsider Śreṇika.
[The Master] suddenly brandishes his staff and says: "This thing is definitely neither form nor emptiness. How do you see it? This makes one long remember General Li:
"Ten thousand miles away at the edge of heaven, a falcon soars."
Chongyang ascends the hall: Yesterday was the Mid-Autumn Festival; today is again the Double Ninth. I am close to the purple *yū* tea;

I am distant from the yellow chrysanthemum wine. Yet the purple *yū* and the yellow chrysanthemum are inherently neither close nor distant. Acquaintances fill the world, but how many can truly know one’s heart?
At Yiyunwu (House of Pleasing Clouds), having completed the construction of a stone Buddha stupa, he ascended the hall and cited the Middle Way from the Teachings:

"If a person were to give hundreds of thousands of taels of pure gold every day, it would not equal briefly entering a temple and sincerely performing a single prostration before the stupa. Regarding the partiality and deficiency of principle:
"If a person sits in stillness for even a brief moment, it surpasses the construction of eighty-four thousand stupas; for a precious stupa will ultimately turn to dust."
To achieve perfect enlightenment with a single thought of sincere mind is a partiality toward phenomena.

Even if you were to transcend both principle and phenomena, and neither the "correct" nor the "partial" were established, you still could not yet see Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni. Do you understand this thoroughly? When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, the entire body is revealed;
where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huibian Chushi,
