“The Buddha-Sun Shining Everywhere,” Volume Six*
Recorded at Enkō Kōzen-ji Temple on Kajikōji Road;
compiled by the bhikṣus studying under the Master, Keihō, and others.
On the first day of the eighth month in the seventeenth year of the Zhizheng era, the Master entered the temple.
The Mountain Gate: the gate of no gate. To enter it, one must enter without entering. Clouds hang low over the four fields; waters fill the twin lakes.
If you wish to traverse the world with ease, you must arrive here in person at least once.
Buddha Hall: Do you still recognize the Buddha? His face is like the full moon; his eyes are like lotuses. Heaven and earth alike pay him reverence. Ancestral Hall:
One flower and five petals—there must be a cause for their arising. But tell me, from what place did they arise?
On the bank, hoof meets hoof; in the water, beak faces beak.
Occupying the hall, it is one zhang wide and ten chi high. Why is it that you all cannot enter and act within it?
An iron wall, an iron wall!

[The Master] takes up the memorial from the Xuanzheng Yuan: "Harmonizing yin and yang, penetrating the workings of transformation, illuminating the sun of the Buddha, and spreading its influence everywhere."
The True Wind. It belongs to those of great power who accomplish such deeds of great power. He calls to the assembly, saying: "Lift up your eyes!
Holding up the letters from the various mountains: "From Jiangnan and Jiangbei to Zhejiang, east and west—within the same there is difference;
within the different there is sameness. The wild landscape is no longer severed by mountains; the light of heaven directly communicates with the water. Do you understand? If not, then look!
The footnote below refers to the Dharma-seat.
All dharmas take emptiness as their seat; since even emptiness does not exist, what can be said of all dharmas?
Thus they disperse. Are you not a man of stature? Why wait for "how" or "what"? For now, listen while I change five into six. Thereupon—
The Master ascends the seat. Having finished offering incense and making prayers for the Emperor, he says: "The emergence of words and traces is the source from which divergent paths arise.
Those who directly penetrate the root—come forward and meet me. A monk asks: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil."
"The Sage attains the One and thereby governs the world. How is it that Heaven attains the One and thereby becomes clear? The Master said, "All stars bow toward the North.
[The student] asked further, "How is it that Earth attains the One and thereby becomes tranquil? The Master said, "There is no water that does not flow toward the East."
Jin asked, "What is it like for a sage who attains the One to govern the world? The Master said, "When one person has cause for celebration, the myriad people depend upon it.
Jin asked, "And what about a patch-robed monk who attains the One? The Master said, "Cutting the grass, the snake’s head falls off."

The monk stepped forward and said, “Today the Master opens the hall to expound the Dharma; civil and military officials are present at the assembly, and all beings of the human and celestial realms surround you.
I wonder, is this one person or all people? The Master replied, “All. The monk continued, “An inch of brush tip is a three-foot sword;
all are those who stabilize the nation and bring peace to the people. The Master said, “No more need be said. The monk bowed, and the Master then spoke:
Solitary and towering, steep and majestic—sages and worthies have no recourse. Vividly surging and luminously clear, it pervades everywhere without remainder.
There are worlds where light constitutes the Buddha-work; there are worlds where adornment constitutes the Buddha-work;
there are worlds where fragrant food constitutes the Buddha-work; there are worlds where sound constitutes the Buddha-work; there are worlds where...
Silent stillness constitutes the Buddha’s work. Now tell me: here at Ba’en, what constitutes the Buddha’s work? It is the inconceivable that constitutes the Buddha’s work.
That is to say: the appearance of the Buddhas is inconceivable; the karmic fruits of sentient beings are inconceivable;
the formation and destruction of worlds are inconceivable; and even this inconceivability itself is inconceivable.
Therefore, the one becomes the immeasurable, and the immeasurable becomes the one. Within the great, the small appears; within the small, the great appears.
Upon the tip of a single hair, the Jewel-King Buddha-land is manifested; seated within a mote of dust, the Great Dharma-Wheel is turned. Ultimately, by whose power of grace is this sustained?
[The Master] lets out a shout. He then cites Nan Tang Jing Heshang, who said: "The sovereign is clear-sighted; the generals are alert.
Once victory is won, the six states are at peace. The Master says: "Even so, even the sovereigns Yao and Shun still had their transformative influence.
When great merit is not rewarded, how can one speak of a single phrase? Autumn wind blows across the Wei River; fallen leaves fill the Chang'an road."
Peace. That evening, there was a small formal discourse (*xiaochan*). [The Master] raised the words of Great Master Linji: "Sometimes a single shout is like the Vajra King’s precious sword;
sometimes a single shout is like a crouching lion; sometimes a single shout is like a probing pole and a blade of grass. Sometimes...
A shout. It does not function as a single shout. The Master then shouted and said: "Tell me, where does this shout land?
Is it the Vajra King’s Precious Sword? Is it the Crouching Lion? Is it the Probing Pole and Shadow-Grass?
Or is it a single shout that does not function as a single shout? Try to discern this! If you cannot discern it..."
Requiting your debt of gratitude, I have annotated and shattered [your delusions] for you. The Vajra King Sword can be verified before one's very eyes;
if you hesitate or deliberate, you will fall into pits and ravines. The lion crouching on the ground is right here and now. Smash the skull and pull out the teeth.
Whether the probing pole and shadow-grass are "good" or "not good," sometimes raise with the left hand and push down with the right. At times, a single shout does not even act as such.
"The function of the single shout! Masters Linji, great and small, have been nothing but talking in their dreams. To understand it in such a way is still lacking one shout. [He lets out a shout.

On the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall and said: "Before heaven and earth were divided, where was the high and the low, the covering and the supporting? Where the sun and moon do not reach—"
The radiance shines and illuminates without partiality; truly, it cannot be sketched nor can it be painted. Last night at the third watch, it was as bright as day.
[He] ascended the hall, took up his staff, and called to the assembly, saying: "Do you recognize this staff? It turns heaven and shifts earth. Furthermore—

Who is it that beats the rain and knocks the wind? Without borrowing the power of another, if you can recognize this, you will be able to manifest all manner of dignified postures without arising from the samādhi of cessation, and achieve all-encompassing wisdom without passing through kalpas of monastic training, without severing the afflictions.
Thus one realizes nirvana. Śrāvakas sever afflictions; Bodhisattvas realize that the essence of afflictions is empty. When there is anger, there is no characteristic of anger;

when there is joy, there is no characteristic of joy. Anger and joy are not interconnected; they have been devoid of essence and characteristics from the beginning. [The Master] threw down his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The whole body is eyes—why cannot you see? The whole body is ears—why cannot you hear?
The whole body is the mouth—why cannot it speak? The whole body is the mind—why cannot it discern?
Bao'en has a clever and divine incantation; I shall bestow it upon you all. He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised the teaching: "In the scriptures it is said that the bhikṣu Yaśodā attained liberation of mind by gazing at the ground;
the bhikṣu Bhadrika attained liberation of mind by gazing at a blade of grass. Holding up his whisk, he said: "To repay his debt of gratitude, I raise this whisk.
Have you all attained liberation? If you say, 'I have attained liberation,' you have not yet seen the whisk being raised."
At that time, who bound you?
A small-scale *sǎn* (sermon) for the Winter Solstice. A monk asked: "Last year at the winter solstice, the eyes were filled with banners and flags;

this year the winter solstice has arrived, and by virtue of this, one is spared from turmoil and separation. Ultimately, there are no weapons or armor here. The Master said: "Just so. [The monk] stepped forward and said: "A thousand..."
"Soldiers are easy to find; a single general is difficult to seek. "What kind of general is difficult to seek? The Master said, "Lower your voice, lower your voice.
[The student] asked, "If one suddenly encounters an urgent military emergency, what then? The Master said, "There is naturally someone to maintain order. [The student] asked again.
"In this way, no one has recognized his past labors on the battlefield; he simply wishes to re-discuss his merit that covers the age. The Master said, "Where does it fall?
The student replied, "The official decree is kept within a purple silk bag; his name is inscribed upon the golden scroll, and the fame spreads throughout the world.
The Master said, "Now, proceed slowly. He then said, "The accomplishment of all things does not depend on another; the destruction of all things is likewise [not dependent on another]."
A distinct dharma. Attaining mastery over heaven and humanity, it traverses and encompasses the worlds of the ten directions.
To understand it in such a way is called "relying on supernatural powers" (abhijñā); one's own eye is not yet open, and one lacks the capacity for true freedom.

You must directly recognize its true face, exhaust all thieving thoughts, and undergo a resurrection after death; only then are you fit to advance. There are immeasurable mundane dharmas and immeasurable supramundane dharmas.

The Dharma. Immeasurable supernatural powers and wondrous functions; immeasurable, sublime adornments—each one manifests before us, each one is liberation, each one is luminous and subtle, each one is naturally authentic. Thus it is said:
"The treasury of the true nature within the mind has neither head nor tail; responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom. Is there still something beyond this? Yes."
Today is the fifteenth; tomorrow is the sixteenth. Again, he raises the Way of Yanguan:
"Taking empty space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the drumstick—what kind of person can strike it? Nanquan said, "Old Teacher Wang does not strike this broken drum. Fayan said:
"Master Wang does not strike. Naturally, he is a broken drum. The Master said, "But tell me, where exactly is the place that is broken?
When will you ever dream of it, even in a donkey's year?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Chan Master Chengtian Song showing the assembly: "First, the single spear and armored horse; second, the armored horse and single spear;
third, scattering stars and arraying the ranks; fourth, returning home in brocade. A monk then asked, "What is the single spear and armored horse?
Song said, "Were it not for a jaw made of gold, how could one shoot down Wei Chi? The monk said, "If so..."
The monk asked, "What is 'clad in armor with a single spear'? Sung said, "A golden arrow falls before the horse; Loufan loses his soul.
The monk asked, "What is 'scattering stars and arraying ranks'? Sung said, "Battle clouds stretch across the sea; the Sage and Wise Ruler remains unrecognized.
The monk asked, "What is 'returning home in brocade'? Sung said, "Throughout the four seas there is no news; returning to serve the Sage and Wise Ruler."
The Master said: "At Chengtian, we are fortunate to be in a time of peace; why should we meet with one another with spears and shields?
Today at Baen, we do not require single spears or armored cavalry, nor do we require armored cavalry or single spears.

We do not require the scattering of stars or the arraying of battle formations, nor do we require returning home in brocade robes. When cold comes, we turn toward the fire; when heat comes, we enjoy the cool breeze. Thus, casting off our hands, we arrive home."
People do not recognize this; there is not a single thing they can offer to the Honored Hall.
When the Buddha attained the Way, he ascended the hall [and said]: "When the Tathāgata appeared under the morning star, he attained the Way. You say that at midnight one is drowsy from exhaustion;
do you still see the morning star?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Nanquan said, 'At eighteen, I understood how to manage a livelihood.
Zhaozhou said, 'At eighteen, I understood how to break up the family and scatter the household. Where do you all see these two great elders?
If you see Nanquan in the place where he manages a livelihood, you do not see Zhaozhou. If you see Zhaozhou in the place where he breaks up the family and scatters the household, again..."
If one does not see Nanquan, it is better to harmonize the various houses so as to avoid mutual contradiction;
otherwise, those who are trying to make a living will end up ruining their homes and scattering their households. To be utterly naked and starkly bare, with nothing to grasp—how joyful!
Those who have ruined their homes and scattered their households can now make a living by seizing all seven treasures and eight jewels at once, with nothing lacking—how joyful!
Alive! Then repay your kindness by sitting and watching Yangzhou. "All that was gathered through war is now destroyed by song and dance.
On this New Year’s Eve small *chan* talk:
This day has passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly; like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be?
Those who dwell on land find joy in dwelling on land; those who dwell in water find joy in dwelling in water; those who dwell in market towns find joy in dwelling in market towns;

those who dwell in the suburbs find joy in dwelling in the suburbs. Even down to the tiny insects that fly and crawl—all sentient beings—there is none whose movement and coming and going is not accompanied by joy.
When the World-Honored One Śākyamuni spoke thus, what was his intention? Can you say?
"Come into the white clouds; I shall teach you the song of the purple mushrooms. He then raised up the case of Master Xinghua, who said:
"I have heard that one can shout in the long corridors and shout in the rear quarters. You disciples must not shout blindly or shout recklessly.
Even if you could shout so as to make Xinghua stay in mid-air, he would then fall down with not a breath of life left, and only after slowly regaining consciousness would he rise again."
"I tell you, it is not yet so. Why? Because I have never scattered real pearls inside a purple silk curtain for you people.
The Master said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have simply told him: 'Why must you wait for this old fellow?'"
He looked east and west, then let out a shout. To startle the multitude, one must be a man of heroic spirit; to defeat the enemy, one must be a lion’s cub.

On the occasion of the New Year, he ascended the hall: the beginning of the three hundred and sixty days, the start of the twenty-four solar energies, as the handle of the Great Dipper turns toward spring.
The scenery is dazzling to the eye. Sometimes the days are short and the nights long; sometimes the nights are short and the days long.
Sometimes the heat departs and the cold arrives; sometimes the heat arrives and the cold departs. The root of the flower is inherently brilliant; the tiger’s coat is originally striped.
Although one does not change from who they were in former times, it cannot be avoided that everyone adds another year. He called the assembly and said: "Just this single year—add it until the end."

The future limit—where does it reside? On the night of the Lantern Festival, he ascended the hall and said: "From within the furnace of blazing flames, one plucks the moon; this moon is entirely without waxing or waning.
From the bottom of the great ocean, one strikes the golden lamp; this lamp is not subject to darkness or light. It is precisely on the fifteenth day of the first month that the heavens and humans..."
The intermediate sign does not emerge; it is black as lacquer and bright as the sun. From antiquity to the present, who has gained and who has lost?
All is the constant portion of my own mind; it does not depend on any external artifice. (He lets out a shout.)
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Before Baen (Bao'en) ascended the curved wooden seat, he was a fellow student with this staff.
For forty years, while residing in mountains at five different places, he has shared in joy with this staff.
But ultimately, how does one study? And what joy is there? It is easy to make this staff speak; it is difficult to make Baen speak."
[The Master] immediately raised an objection: "Why is this? The mouth born of one's parents will never speak for you. Now, listen while this staff speaks.
He struck [the floor] once and said, "These are words that cut through iron."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In the deepest depths of the ocean's floor, one stirs up a spark of fire; atop the highest peak of a mountain, one catches a pair of fish.
With this fire, one cooks these fish; summon the wooden man to open the alms bowl. The stone man hears this and sighs in silent lament."
Do not sigh in lamentation. To strive for it is insufficient; to yield is more than enough.
At the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, as he ascended the seat, a monk asked: "When a single mote of dust contains the boundless Dharma-realm, what then? The Master said:
"At the third watch, he does not close his door. The student asked, "Why did Sudhana go to the south? The Master said, "He never moved a single step.
The student asked, "The fifty-three spiritual friends each spoke of the essentials of the Dharma; could it be that they were speaking falsely?
The Master said, "When one family has trouble, a hundred families are busy. The student asked, "What is Universal Radiance?"
The Master said, "Rolling in the grass. [The student] asked, "What is the body of Vairocana? The Master said, "Above is heaven; below is earth.
[The student] said, "Bamboo shadows sweep the steps, yet the dust does not stir; the moon pierces the depths of the waves, yet the water leaves no trace.
The Master said, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its basket. [The student] said, "Today, the Marshal respectfully invites the entire assembly of this mountain to read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*."

[The student asked: "In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in eighty-one fascicles, which single phrase is most intimate? The Master said: "Closing one's eyes and leaping over the Yellow River. The student further said:
"If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand; only by hearing sound through the faculty of sight can one truly know. The Master said: [Silence].
"Leave it to the tortoise to be drilled and the tile to be struck. He then said: "Whether speaking of the real or the unreal, both reality and unreality are fundamentally empty.

Whether according to principle or phenomena, both principle and phenomena are eternally quiescent. In his questioning, every word transcends all dependencies; in his responding, every phrase penetrates the source. As the Sūtra says:
"Within every single atom of the Flower Treasury World, the entire Dharma-realm is manifested; jewel-radiance and transformation Buddhas gather like clouds."
"This is the Tathāgata’s mastery over buddha-fields (*kṣetra-vaśitā*). Because of this mastery over buddha-fields, one realizes the Buddha-body within the ordinary body;

because of manifesting the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one dwells in a defiled land while it is identical to a pure land. The Son of Heaven in the bustling marketplace; the old monk at the tips of the hundred grasses;
'three by three before, three by three after'—how do you understand this? [He] lets out a shout. He then cites a monk asking Shanglan:
Master Chao asked: "Once Sudhana had already seen Mañjuśrī, why did he then go south?

What is the meaning of this? Lan said: "Learning relies on entering the chamber; knowledge enables one to traverse all quarters. The monk asked: "After arriving at the city of Sumāgadhā, why did Maitreya send him to see Mañjuśrī?
Lan said: "The Way is vast and boundless; there is no end to meeting people along the way. The Master said: "How extraordinary!"
Most extraordinary among the extraordinary; most profound among the profound. To penetrate the source of the Dharma, one must be Shanglan before it can be attained.
Under the gate of the Patriarchs, this is still not yet sufficient.
Small Sermon at the Beginning of the Summer Retreat. A monk asked, "What is Chan in the mountains? The Master said, "A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind.
The monk pressed further, "What is Chan in the city? The Master said, "A single brick on a crossroads. The monk pressed again.
"What is Chan in the village? The Master said, "A man from Fusang plants fields in Shaanxi.
The student replied, "Thank you for your answer, Master. The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! Then he continued: "Food and clothing sustain one's life; not even a single day can do without them.
A broom and rag robe withstand cold and heat; coarse food heals the withered body. Yesterday was the third spring month; today is the ninth summer month. Why not take advantage of it?"
When the physical body is strong and healthy, one brushes aside the teachings and the path of birth and death becomes clear.
When you wish to go, you go; when you wish to stay, you stay. Who can obstruct you? Who can hinder you? How magnificent! How joyful! But tell me:
how do you brush aside the path of birth and death? "Empty-handed, holding a hoe; walking, riding a water buffalo. A person comes across a bridge...
The one above has already passed. The bridge flows, yet the water does not flow. If you do not understand, I shall provide you with a commentary:
Empty-handed, grasping a hoe; Riding a galloping horse up a high tower. Walking while riding a water buffalo; In the midst of clamor, cold and still.
A person passes over the bridge, Yet the rice basket remains hungry. The bridge flows, yet the water does not flow; Stirring the fire to seek a bubble. Time does not wait for man.

"San. He then cited the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*: "Abiding at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. Do not attempt to extinguish the various deluded minds.
Abiding in the realm of deluded thoughts, do not apply analytical knowledge. In the absence of such analytical knowledge, do not discriminate as to what is real. The Master said:
"If this were so, one could say 'it exists,' and one could also say 'it does not exist. One could go upward, and one could also go downward."
To attain it is to attain it; not to attain it is also to attain it. A few wisps of white cloud enshroud the ancient temple; a single ribbon of green water winds around the green mountains.

Entering the hall: The myriad flowers have already faded; the hundred grains are flourishing. Green trees resound with the song of orioles; carved beams echo the chatter of swallows. The vast wilds...
The cool breeze rustles; the vast sky is shrouded in fine, misty rain. There is but one firm and dense body, manifesting within all atoms of dust.
Is there ever a moment when it is not manifest? (He strikes the meditation staff once.)

Ascending the hall, he said: "When a hawk transforms into a dove, its eyes remain; when a fish transforms into a dragon, its scales remain; when an ordinary person transforms into a sage, their mind remains.
Which of these is your own mind? He let out a shout.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Heaven cannot cover it; who is able to cover it? Earth cannot support it; who is able to support it?
The sun and moon cannot illuminate it; who is able to illuminate it? Parents cannot give birth to it; who is able to give birth to it?"
This single phrase can delude the people of the world, and it can also awaken the people of the world. Holding up his whisk, he said:
"It is right when the eyes are open; it is right when the eyes are closed. Throwing down the whisk, he asked: "What is this?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "When cognitive vision establishes cognition, that is the root of ignorance. When cognitive vision is without seeing, that is nirvana.
How far apart are ignorance and nirvana? After a long silence, he said: "Walking until the end of the water, sitting to watch the clouds arise."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), there are the metaphors of the goose in the bottle, the person in the well, and the mountain in the window.

In the Vehicle of the Teachings (Jiaocheng), there are the metaphors of the moon in the water, the image in the mirror, the sword in the treasury, the gold in the cauldron, and the space within the vase."
Those who possess wisdom must rely on parables to achieve understanding. After thirty years, you shall realize it;
do not let the old monk down.
*Note on the Unceasing Rain* (Zhàshàngtáng): "The great sun floods the eyes; ten thousand miles, not a single speck of cloud. As the ancients said:
Even the blue sky must receive a blow of the staff. Take this intention of not yet returning and speak it to those who are traveling toward desire.

[He ascends the hall. Raising his hand, he says: "When opened, it becomes a palm; the five fingers are distinct from one another. In the Linji school, these are the Three Essentials and Three Mysteries.
In the Dongshan school, they are the Interchange of Orthodoxy and Deviation. In the Yunmen school, they are the Three Statements for Lifting Up and Recommending. In the Guiyang school...
Thus, father and son sing and respond to one another. In the Dharma-eye, there is only mind and only consciousness. Among the five schools of the Chan gate, there is contraction and expansion;
then, clenching his fist, he said: "Right now it is a fist—there is certainly no high or low. Since there is no high or low, it cuts off past and present.
He takes the lantern into the Buddha hall; he brings the triple-gate to the lantern."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "At the hour of the rat in the dead of night, when the mind abides in the unborn, that is itself birth and death.
Holding up his staff, he said, "This here is not the unborn. He struck it once and set it down, saying, "Where has birth and death gone?
Last night at the third watch, while in the abbot’s quarters, I happened to step upon something; I did not know whether it was a tile or a stone. Looking at it this morning at dawn—
Originally it was a rotten peach. One moment one doubts it is a tile, yet it is not; one moment one doubts it is a stone, yet it is not.
At daybreak, looking at it, it is indeed a rotten peach. From where does this doubting mind arise? It is neither spirit nor ghost.
Consider it carefully: it was you all along. Long ago, when Xuansha entered the mountains with a monk and saw a tiger, the monk said, "The tiger, Master!
Xuansha said, "It is you, tiger! and clapped his hands three times before descending from his seat.
Small-scale *chanshi* (general address) for the end of the summer retreat. A monk asked, "The Buddhas hand over to one another, and the patriarchs transmit to one another.

I wonder, is this the transmission of the robe, or the transmission of the Dharma? The student has come forward; I pray the Master will provide instruction. The Master said, "The Yellow River has nine bends.
The monk stepped forward and asked, "In the past, when Master Dahui resided at Yangyu Hermitage, he sent thirteen people forth in a single summer. Ultimately, was it..."
[The student asked: "Is there transmission or no transmission? The Master said: "Scratching one's forehead while gazing toward the Fusang tree. [The student] further asked:

"Among the assembly at Baen, is there anyone who has attained the Way? The Master said: "Blue sky and bright sun. [The student] further asked: "I, this student, have not yet found the point of entry."
"Please, Master, do not withhold your compassion. The Master said, "Do not speak like a ghost. He stepped forward and said, "Carrying poems and books, one returns to one's old retreat;
wildflowers and singing birds share the same spring. The Master said, "Taking it as it is. Then he said:

"What has been spoken by Baoen during this summer retreat, and what has been investigated by you all during this summer retreat—you must know that in what was spoken not a single word was uttered, and in what was investigated not a single dharma was employed."

The Way is a single word; it is spoken yet there is no speaking. It does not rely upon a single dharma. To participate is to have no participation; this "no-participation" is true participation. To speak is to have no speaking;
this "no-speaking" is true speaking. Therefore it is said: "In the ten directions they gather together as one; each and every one studies non-action."
This is the field for selecting Buddhas; one returns having passed the examination with an empty mind. A great man cannot be subject to another’s direction.
To "pass the examination with an empty mind" is to degrade the worthy and make them base; to "become a Buddha or a Patriarch" is to love the holy and hate the ordinary—none of these apply here.
To bind oneself when there is no rope is like a lion cub leaping straight down and letting out a single roar;
foxes, wolves, and jackals all vanish at once. It is like a drum smeared with poison: those who hear it, whether far or near, all perish. When the ninety-day retreat is completed, what then?
Ordinarily, it is just as when the autumn wind arrives: without intending to cool others, people cool themselves. Again, he cites Dongshan:
Together with his uncle, the Master Miji, he went to visit Chan Master Zhe of Ezhou. Zhe asked, "Where have you recently come from, Ācārya? Shishuang replied, "Hunan.
Zhe asked, "What is the surname of the Regional Inspector? Shishuang said, "I do not know his surname. Zhe asked, "What is his name?
Shishuang said, "I am not informed of his name. Zhe asked, "Does he still attend to official affairs? Shishuang said, "He has his own hallways."

The curtain was still drawn. Zhe asked, "Does it still come in and go out? Shanshan replied, "It does not come in or go out. Zhe said, "How can it not come in and go out? Shanshan shook his sleeves and departed.
The next day, Zhe entered the Sangha Hall and said, "Yesterday, regarding the two *jiaoluo*, one phrase was not yet refined.
I now ask you both to speak it. If you can speak it, I will provide gruel for you and wait for you to complete your summer retreat. Speak quickly!"
Sudao said, "The mountain says, 'He is born too noble. The Master said, "If you wish to understand his nobility, Baen would not open these two flaps of skin. Where, then, will you all search?"
Ascending the hall: The autumn wind is cool; the autumn night is long. The Milky Way stirs no waves; the moon-orchid emits no fragrance.
When the ear reaches the limit of sound and sound reaches the ear, let the dewy grasses weep for the autumn crickets.
On the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall and cited the following: Once, while Yunyan was sweeping the floor, Daowu said, "Why are you being so preoccupied?
Yunyan replied, "You must know that there is one who is not preoccupied. Daowu said, "If that is so, then it is the 'second moon'.
Yunyan held up his broom and asked, "Which month is this? Daowu shook out his sleeves and walked out. Yunmen remarked, "The servant sees through the mistress."
Qin asked, "The Master said, 'Yunyan held up a broom,' and Daowu immediately went out. These are all the 'second moon.
Which one is not so preoccupied? This night, the single orb is full; where is its clear light not present?"

The General-in-Chief returns from his reconnaissance; ascending the hall, he speaks: "The army follows the seal’s turn; Ji Xin ascends the nine-dragon carriage. The general pursues the talisman’s movement;
Huo Guang sells the city of counterfeit silver. Thus, where there is a talisman, there must be a general; where there is a seal, there must be an army."
"The soldiers are here; where is the seal? After a long silence, he said, "Today at Baoen, a small emergence meets a great encounter.
He ascended the hall and said: "If I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; if you momentarily raise your mind, worldly toil arises first. The Master said:
I am not like that "yellow-faced old man" who smashed everything into such a mess. What could he call the "Ocean Seal"? What could he take to be "worldly toil"?
Even if one sought for it as much as the point of a needle, it would be utterly unfindable.
The various mountains ascended to the Upper Hall. A monk asked, "What is the lion in its cave? The Master said, "Its head touches the heavens.
The monk followed up, "What is the lion emerging from its cave? The Master said, "Its paws tread upon the earth. The monk followed up, "What is the roaring lion?
The Master said, "Do you hear it? The monk replied, "I am hearing it right now. [The Master asked,] "How so? The Master said, "Prostrate obeisance, sir."

The Master said: "A single flower blooms and the whole earth is spring; a single leaf falls and the world is autumn. When the strings are moved, the melody differs—only those who know the sound can appreciate it.
To blink an eye or raise an eyebrow is already to have missed the mark. Thus, he issues a command that leaves no room for transgression and seizes the vital passageways;
he offers a flavorless discourse that blocks the mouths of men. This is the staff of Deshan, the shout of Linji, the raised finger of Guizong, and the face of Luzu.
The Wall; Guizong cutting the snake; Da Sui burning the slash-and-burn fields; Shigong drawing his bow; Zihu looking at the dog.
Sometimes it is level fields and shallow grass; sometimes it is iron walls and silver mountains; sometimes it is flashing lightning and rolling thunder; sometimes it is mixing mud and blending water.
Fully upholding the True Seal and alone shaking the great guiding cord—yet when examined closely, there is no lack of leakage. Therefore, immediately...
"The mind is itself the Buddha. At present, you have not yet entered the profound mystery; thus, "neither mind nor Buddha" remains merely the ultimate point for following tracks.
The path that points upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages; students exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections.
Is there still a portion of seeking and aspiring? When the level marshes end, there are green mountains; the traveler stands even beyond those green mountains. Again, it is cited: A monk asked—
Master Huanglong Ji said, "What is the meaning of Chan? Ji replied, "Its meaning is slander.
The Master said, "If someone were to ask Nanhu, 'What is the meaning of Chan? I would tell him, 'Its meaning is praise. Now tell me, which is it—slander or praise?
To see it with the eyes is blindness; to hear it with the ears is deafness; to speak it with the mouth is dumbness; to contemplate it with the mind is..."
Exhausted. Snow buries stones a thousand fathoms deep at the edge of the sky; frost has broken several pines at the cave entrance.
Returning to the temple on an early winter day, he ascends the hall. A monk asks: "In the past, a monk asked Da-sui:

'When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, I wonder, will this [reality] be destroyed? Sui said, 'It is destroyed. The monk said, 'If that is so, then it follows him...'"
"He goes. Suí said, "He follows him. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "If you have doubts, seek instruction elsewhere.
[The student] advanced and said, "Later, Xuedou’s verse says: 'Standing amidst the conflagration at the end of an eon, the patch-robed monk still lingers within two layers of barriers.'"
"Pitifully, he followed him with a single phrase; ten thousand miles of weary toil, traveling alone to and fro.

"What is this 'double barrier'? The Master said, "There are even ten layers. [The student] asked, "For what reason did this monk have doubts? The Master said, "Torn asunder. [The student] asked, "I do not understand;
what was the meaning of Da-sui? The Master said, "Before, it did not reach the village; behind, it did not connect to the shop. [The student] entered [the discussion].
[The Master] said: "White clouds may briefly leave the green peaks, but the bright moon cannot be made to descend from the blue heavens. The Teacher said: "You are still drunk. He then said:
"It is easy for a single hair to swallow up the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; it is difficult for the mountains, rivers, and the great earth to swallow up a single hair.
It is neither difficult nor easy. Spread out a tattered mat and sleep in the daylight; I imagine this is what the 'Upper Regions' (the heavens) are like."
In the Tuṣita Palace, there is likewise no such thing as one’s back being scorched by the sun. Again, consider how the green ivy winds its way straight up to the summit of the cold pine tree;
the white clouds are limpid and vast, appearing and disappearing within the great void. All phenomena are fundamentally tranquil, yet it is people themselves who create the clamor.
Huanglong said, "What is all this fuss about? The Master replied, "It would be better not to say there is nothing.
*Furitsu Fushō Eben Shosoku Zenji Goroku*, Volume Six, Phonetic Transcriptions.
Huán (hú guān qiè) Tí (tú xī qiè) Xiè (sū xié qiè) Lè (lì gé qiè) Jiāng (jí zhǎng qiè) Shē (yǔ jū qiè) Nìng (zhí yǔ qiè) The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fúrì Pǔzhào Huìbiàn Chǔshí, Volume Seven.
Record of the Sermons at Tianning Yongzuo Chan Monastery in Haian Prefecture, compiled by the attendants Liangyan and others. Addressing the assembly:
"The words and phrases of the Patriarchs leave you with no place to chew or swallow. Now, you brothers who travel on pilgrimage are knocking at the gates of others."
Householder, you eat his leftover soup and rancid rice; how unawake you are! You merely gnaw at it crosswise and lengthwise, refusing to let go, like a fly on a pile of dung.
As soon as you are brushed away, you instead give rise to resentment. Sentient beings are so inverted that they take contact for purity.
Do not wait until a feverish illness strikes, when you will seek life but cannot find it, and seek death but cannot find it.
Reflecting back on what you have done in the past, it remains entirely incomplete. These words are not spoken by me to deceive or mislead you.
Look at how the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old benefited beings: Nanquan said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
Furthermore, when a monk asked Dongshan, "What is the Buddha? Dongshan replied, "Three pounds of flax."
I allow you to taste it. I will never let you engage in intellectual speculation with the faculty of thought;
rather, from the very crown of a thousand sages, I draw forth a long sword leaning against the heavens and strike a single blow upon your eighth consciousness.
Only when you have cast off your body and surrendered your life, finding life within death, will you be fit to open your mouth wide and say, "I am a monk. If you yourself already understand this...

It removes stickiness and unties bonds; it can also bestow upon others the release from stickiness and the untying of bonds. Having already attained Buddhahood oneself, one also causes all sentient beings on this great earth to become Buddhas—do you understand this well?
Addressing the assembly: "If, throughout the twelve periods of the day, you do not rely upon or depend on a single thing, you have not yet attained the status of a true master.
In our school, we are not like the masters of the Three Canons and Five Treatises who bury themselves within the entanglements of words. Brothers, as soon as you open your mouths, you speak thus."
I am a Chan practitioner. Yet when asked what Chan is, one looks east and looks west, with a face like a flat carrying-pole.
How bitter! How grievous! The school of Bodhidharma—look at it, and it is about to fall to the ground.
Having consumed the food of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one does not attend to the fundamental matter, but instead clutches at literary phrases and worldly sayings, speaking in loud voices. Alas!

They have no sense of restraint and are utterly shameless. There is a certain type who does not sit upon their meditation cushions to investigate and clarify their original face prior to the birth of their parents;
instead, they coldly practice the "guest's pounding" in hopes of seeking blessings and eradicating karmic obstructions.
They are far removed from the Way. Have you not heard it said: "If you would rest now, then rest; if you wish to seek realization..."
At that time, there was no awareness of time.

He addressed the assembly: "In a single day, one becomes the head of a village monastery; for ten thousand kalpas, it will be difficult to emerge from this. A great difficulty! A great difficulty! If you are such a man,"

The words of the Buddhas and the words of the Patriarchs are not meant to be stored away in one’s breast; they leap forth toward other worlds. How much more so regarding the shallow and mundane studies of this world?
Even if one can recite the four Vedas, it only increases delusive thoughts—what can such things accomplish?
One merely consumes the saliva and spittle of others with no end in sight; it is better to remain free from affairs. When you see me say "no affairs," do not simply take it to mean being idle.
This is the convergence of circumstances. Furthermore, it can be attained through striving. If you wish to truly be without affairs, you must apply yourself with desperate effort;

you must undergo a "great death" once, and by finding life within death, you will be able to transcend Vairocana and Śākyamuni, passing through hundreds of enclosures and thousands of layers, reaching everywhere with total penetration.
The patriarchal nose and the supreme vehicle of the lineage have been entirely swept away; there is no need to bring them forth. Yunmen said:
"Today I shall talk with you of this entanglement: excrement and ash, urine and fire, mired pigs and scabby dogs—ignorant of good and evil, making their livelihood in a pit of filth.
If you can leap out of that pit of filth, then come to this mountain monk’s hand and ask for a blow."
Addressing the assembly: Look at such a time as this! You brothers who have the aspiration to study the Way—where have you been putting down your packs?

Since the beginning of time, why was the lineage established? It was certainly not merely for the sake of a few fellow countrymen or Dharma relatives, nor to provide for the mouth and belly while indulging in ignorance.
Yet you form groups and bands, creating the karma of hell, while pushing the Buddha-dharma and the Way of Chan to one side.

Who would have known that karmic retribution would arrive so suddenly that one could not avoid it? Amidst the mountains of blades and trees of swords, the boiling cauldrons and burning coals, there is no one who can take one’s place.
Why is it that nowadays, throughout the great monasteries and forest retreats, from north to south and east to west, there is not one person in ten thousand?
It is because their evil deeds have reached their full measure and the fruits of their karma have ripened; they must suffer what they themselves have created. Furthermore, let me...
Who will take this up? The Patriarch urged you to leave the household life not merely for the sake of food, clothing, fame, or profit, nor simply to abandon your hometown and leave your well;
it was solely because the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift. You must seek out teachers and visit friends, investigating with the utmost urgency until clarity is attained.
With a single burst of energy, he departs to become a Buddha and a Patriarch; he departs to repay the profound kindness of his parents; he departs to deliver all people across the world.
Since this is not so, for what reason did he leave the home life? Coldly reflecting, the ancient style is truly magnificent: when hungry, he begs for food; when cold, he mends his robes;
he eats one meal at midday and stays one night under a tree. Lodging as a traveler within the triple world, he demonstrates the way of a single journey.
One must return, completely sever ignorance, and only then attain the Buddha-way. Have you not seen how National Teacher Wuye addressed the assembly? He said:
"After the ancients had attained the Way, they lived in thatched huts or stone chambers, eating rice cooked in broken-legged cauldrons for twenty or thirty years.
Fame and profit did not trouble their minds; wealth and treasure were not on their thoughts. They utterly forgot the ways of the world and concealed their traces among the mountain crags."
"The sovereign issues the command yet they do not come; the feudal lords send invitations yet they do not arrive.
How can this be the same as our own kind, who crave fame and profit, wallowing in the ways of the world like petty peddlers? Having small desires, we forget the great fruit. Thus he pointed it out.
How perfectly clear! Cultivating merit is not as good as avoiding transgression; much emptiness is not as good as a little reality.
Within this "line of the robe," there is a single circle of perfect light—whom does it not belong? Do not let this human body be lost;
you must grasp it directly, and then you will stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you say my words are false, I am willing to enter the Hell of the Plucked Tongue.

Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the teaching that there are six recollections: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṃgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of heaven, and mindfulness of giving.

Within the gate of the patch-robed monks, what is it that you should be mindful of? If you say you are mindful of the Buddha, the moment you utter the word "Buddha," you must rinse your mouth for three years;
this cannot be called mindfulness of the Buddha. If you say you are mindful of the Dharma, even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma. Not...
However, one who contemplates the Dharma is a practitioner of purity; such a person does not enter nirvana. A bhikṣu who violates the precepts does not enter hell.

This cannot be the contemplation of the Saṅgha. Upholding or violating the precepts merely binds the body; if there were no body, there would be nothing to bind. This cannot be the contemplation of the precepts.
There is no peace within the three realms; they are like a house on fire. This cannot be the contemplation of the heavens. As for the giver... the recipient.

As for this, both the recipient and the object given are empty and quiescent within the three wheels; none of them can be apprehended. One must not harbor the thought that "this is giving. Is it then non-thought?
The very moment there is non-thought, it is already thought. To avoid drowning only to throw oneself into fire—your illness becomes even more profound.
Even if you were to be uniquely liberated and without dependence, you would still not be fit to be a servant to a monk. Do you wish to understand?
It is the shadowless tree of a thousand years; it is the bottomless boot of the present age.
Addressing the assembly: Coming up and going down—everyone here appears to be a patch-robed monk.

Yet, if one examines them closely, this very act of coming up and going down is entirely devoid of the true scent of a patch-robed monk. Is it that those who neither come up nor go down are the patch-robed monks? No.
Even an oil lamp or a pillar cannot be anything other than an inconceivable person; yet the Buddha-dharma is not a matter of this sort.
In the end, it does not prohibit you from coming up or going down. Whether you come up or go down, there is no dharma that can harbor resentment toward you;
I only fear that there is doubt within your own mind. Even if you sit upon the meditation seat with eyes closed and brows knit, you cannot escape the proliferation of mental discursive thoughts.
He flew away. While walking back and forth in the corridor, he remained as before, stumbling and falling in all directions.

Seeing you in such a state, the Patriarch set up this hitching post for donkeys. A monk who has settled his affairs simply pulls it out and goes; coming up and going down—what business is there in that?
Master Fayan said: "Last night when the bell rang, everyone came here. Tonight when the bell rings, come again."
"What matter is there? What matter is there? Not a single matter. For one who has no matter, even the Buddha can do nothing for him.

Master Dongshan said: "In my place here, it is not as it is in other quarters, where one person comes up and another goes down, chirping and chattering in private about Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma; all of these are merely directed toward you."
In the presence of his brothers, he spoke with his whole mouth, uttered with his whole mouth, brought up with his whole mouth, and selected with his whole mouth.
There was no place for you to shield on the left or conceal on the right. These words were spoken because there was no other way; they were all poured out together at once.
To call this "a physician for dead horses. According to my own understanding, there are no Buddhas and no patriarchs; there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
I only require that you be directly free from concerns. To ask further, "How is it?"—what misery! O Buddha! What a pity!
Addressing the assembly: You may study the Way within this school, yet most only recognize that which is "bright and alert.
Little do they realize that this very brightness and alertness is the root of birth and death. As Master Changsha said: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real."
It is simply because one has recognized the Buddha from of old. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, this has been the very root of birth and death;
yet foolish people call it the "original person. At the Śūraṅgama Assembly, the Elder Śākyamuni spoke to Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions.
The seeds of karma arise spontaneously, like a cluster of akṣa fruits. Those who practice cultivation cannot attain [liberation]..."
They may achieve unexcelled Bodhi, or alternatively become Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
they may even become non-Buddhist deities, Māras, or the retinues of Māras—all because they do not know the two kinds of fundamental roots and practice in a confused manner.
It is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal; even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never succeed. What are these two? Ānanda, the first is...
First is the root of beginningless birth and death; this is that which you, along with all sentient beings, now take as your own nature—the mind that clings to objects.
Second is the fundamentally pure essence of beginningless bodhi and nirvana;

this is your current essential brightness of consciousness, capable of giving rise to all conditions, yet that which is lost amidst those conditions. Because all sentient beings have lost this original brightness, although...
One acts all day long without being aware of it. O worthy ones, tell me: are the root of birth and death and Bodhi-Nirvana the same or different?
If you say they are the same, then birth and death are one thing and Nirvana is another.
If you say they are different, then Ānanda’s single body would become two Buddhas; why does he not come forth to deliver a message? Do not merely...

Behind one's back, they flaunt their slave-like lips and maid-like tongues; yet on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, when Old Yama demands payment for your straw sandals, can anyone else pay it for you?
Addressing the assembly: "O virtuous ones! The entire being of the sage is precisely the ordinary person, yet the ordinary person does not know this.
The entire being of the ordinary person is precisely the sage, yet the sage does not recognize this. Because they do not recognize it, every thought is purely true;

because they do not know it, every situation belongs to delusion. When the Buddhas appear in the world and the Patriarchs come from the West, the entirety of delusion is precisely truth, and the entirety of the ordinary is precisely the sage."
O Sage! Who has no blood beneath their skin? In whose hearth is there no smoke? Sometimes he kicks out his toes, revealing them starkly; a needle cannot pierce them.
Sometimes he spreads open the palms of his hands, blowing with a whistling breeze; water cannot wet them.
There is not a single speck of dust they do not encompass, not a single kṣetra they do not pervade, not a single entity they do not include. Not one...
The faculties are not complete; it can be skillful or clumsy, hidden or manifest, great or small, closed or open.
Tell me, what kind of thing is so extraordinary? (He lets out a shout.)
Addressing the assembly: From the very beginning, there has been no dharma to transmit, nor has there been anyone to receive it. If one seeks a teacher or a disciple, neither can be found.
Within this, a single phrase is borrowed, like the signal flag of a military commander; when needed, it is used; when not needed, it is set aside. Originally, there is no substantial dharma.
The entire Great Canon of the Teachings and the separate transmission outside the teachings are both upon the stone.

To plant a gourd vine and then laboriously seek out its branches and leaves—this is what the Buddhas of the three periods have been doing in their dreams; this is what the patriarchs of the six generations have been doing in their dreams;
this is what the old monks of the world have been doing in their dreams; this is what this mountain monk has been doing in his dreams;
and this is what all of you have been doing in your dreams. This great dream will continue until the very end of the future, and it remains forever unawakened.
"You wish to transcend birth and death, yet you are bound by birth and death. You wish to sever ignorance, yet you are entangled by ignorance.
Some say: 'Ignorance is itself great wisdom; what need is there to sever it? Birth and death are themselves nirvana;
what need is there to transcend them? You fools! Who is within the three realms, and who is outside the three realms?"
Understand it directly. The mouth is the gate of calamity. Addressing the assembly:
The ancient Śākyamuni did not come before; the present Maitreya does not follow after. Right at this very moment, the sentiments of both ordinary beings and sages are exhausted.

The essence reveals true permanence; phenomena and principle are non-dual. This is the Buddha of Suchness. Within this assembly, every person is fundamentally endowed with it, and each individual has fully realized it.
In the great monastery of Perfect Enlightenment, one understands the fundamental task of a monk.

Thus, one may serve as eyes for devas and humans, yet devas and humans have no way to peer into them; one may serve as a teacher for Buddhas and patriarchs, and Buddhas and patriarchs have grounds to offer praise.

Even if you had eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms, lifting them high as high as the Brahma-heaven and lowering them slowly and deliberately, you would never have moved a single hair on the soles of his feet. Why is this so?

Because he did not establish a single dharma nor maintain a single mystery; he penetrated both the source and the path, and having reached the very top and bottom, attained great liberation and dwelt in non-abiding.
It is inconceivable. Only by dwelling in such a manner of *an-gu* (sitting in meditation) is one fit to uphold the treatises.
Addressing the assembly: According to what is said, this Sahā world consists of pits and hollows, mounds and hills, tiles, rubble, thorns, and mountains of earth and stone.
There are heights and depths, and unevenness. In the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), the ground is as level as the palm of a hand;

its palaces and towers are adorned with rare jewels; and the water-birds and forest trees constantly proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Nevertheless, there are those who die young and those who live long, and there is suffering as well as joy.
If one discusses this "little bit" [of reality], it is eight *liang* over there and half a *jin* here—it is neither pure nor defiled, neither born nor a Buddha. It is not...

To loathe this and rejoice in that, to love the holy and hate the ordinary—since one possesses neither such feelings of loathing or rejoicing nor such views of holy or ordinary, one may follow conditions with ease and expansiveness, acting freely and spontaneously.

To transform the great earth into gold, churn the long river into cream and curd, change rice stalks into millet stems, and alter a short life into a long one—all these are the constant domain of my mind; they are not... [extraordinary].
There is one who borrows another’s artifice; picking up his staff, he says: "The ten directions of the world are right before your eyes. He addresses the assembly:
"Within the teachings of the Buddhist scriptures, there is also that which is most terrifying. There are thorns within the soft mud;

only when you step upon them do you know it. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'There is a great scripture within a mote of dust, its volume equal to the three-thousandfold world system, written in full.'"
Within the trichiliocosm, there is nothing that is not fully encompassed. There is a wise person who breaks open a mote of dust to reveal a sutra;
if you can realize this, how would Śākyamuni differ from him? A wise person takes up a single blade of grass and uses it as a sixteen-foot golden body;
at other times, they take that sixteen-foot golden body and use it as a single blade of grass. The entire trichiliocosm resides within a single [particle].
At the tip of a single hair: within the space of a single hair-tip, one gathers and encompasses the three thousandfold world-system.

Whether you employ it or do not employ it, where else could there be such names as "nirvana" or "birth-and-death"? Nor does one see the existence of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or the sequential stages of the Three Vehicles;
all of these are merely what people have carried along with them. I fear only that you cannot recognize them for what they are. Once you have recognized them, however—
"What matters is this: when hungry, one eats; when cold, one puts on clothes. He addressed the assembly:
"When one person attains the Way, the Earth Deity informs the Space Deity, and the Space Deity informs the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, successively announcing:
'In the lower realms, there is one who has attained the Way and possesses the capacity to save others. If one were to rely upon..."
This statement is certainly not false. We śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya, fill the great earth; there cannot be a single one among us who is not so.
Truly, we dare not deceive you, brothers. Let us speak as one: when I sought teachers and chose friends, traveling on foot to study Zen, I went far as three thousand *li* and near as five hundred.
How many teachers have I sought? How many friends have I chosen? How much have I practiced?
"You have not yet attained much. How much Chan have you mastered? Have you ultimately realized the Way or not?
An ancient said, 'Just as when a person drinks water, they know for themselves whether it is cold or warm. It is also said, 'Seeing smoke from across a mountain, one knows it is fire;
seeing a horn over a wall, one knows it is an ox. I only fear that you have not attained it. Where is there anything that cannot be known? For now, what do you call the Way?"
Let me try to reveal it to you: is this empty or is it real? Is there such a thing? Is there? If not, the day will come when you must carry an iron bit in your mouth and bear a saddle upon your back.
Addressing the assembly: "There is nothing; take care. The assembly remained for a long time without dispersing. The Master then said, "What matter is there? Come forward and let us resolve it.
Now, when one speaks of "nothing," so many people misunderstand it, saying, "Nothing is good.
Compared to coarse afflictions, although these are difficult to sever, they are light; yet the illness of being addicted to "nothing" is difficult to cure and is heavy. Have you not seen?
The Way belongs to those who are non-active and without affairs; even so, it remains difficult as a golden chain.

As for the two vehicles, having severed their fetters and realized the state of an Arhat, they immediately claim that everything is finished and settled, dwelling in great liberation and no longer advancing.
Viewed with the True Eye, this is like being in a deep pit; one must simply turn the mind toward the Great Vehicle and reach fulfillment at the tenth stage before seeing one's nature.
It remains veiled by a fine gauze. Thus, even worlds such as those of Maitreya, Akṣobhya, and Sukhāvatī are still called "shameless and indolent bodhisattvas" by those superior beings.
To study the Way within this [world] is truly difficult, truly difficult.
Not sitting in the Palace of the Empty King, not donning the garment of original nature—why must one remain thus? One must strictly avoid the state prior to birth.
Only when reaching this stage does one possess even a trace of the true breath of a monk.
Addressing the assembly: When you see the Old Monk ascend the hall and raise his whisk, he immediately says, "I am pointing this out to you students:
while you are on your long benches, opening your mats and unfolding your bowls to eat porridge and rice—why do you not awaken right here?
When your delusive thoughts arise, there is Chan; when your delusive thoughts do not arise, there is no Chan. Chan is not your delusive thoughts."

This is something to be realized through contemplation. As I, this mountain monk, usually say: whether in speech or silence, movement or stillness, in every turn of the body or every bow and gesture, each and every thing is luminous and wondrous;
each and every thing is authentically true. If one can see it directly without relying on the staff or the shout—just as Deshan and Linji did—it is most clearly evident.
It is precisely these few things that you cannot penetrate. What is obstructing you? Why not bring it to an end this very moment?
Nevertheless, when there is complete clarity, there is nothing to be clarified; in the realm of profound mystery, one must directly revile it. Do you understand?
Addressing the assembly: If you wish to see your own mind right now, how do you see it? First, what is this mind?
If you say that it is simply this very act of investigation and pursuit, you will again incur the Buddha’s rebuke. That which investigates and pursues is definitely not the mind;
this is merely deluded consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness has arising and ceasing, whereas the mind has no arising or ceasing. Arising and ceasing belong to consciousness, not to the mind.
It pertains to the mind. Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings who have not attained the Way have been deluded by false consciousness and thus wander through birth and death.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having awakened to the true mind, are not subject to the wandering of birth and death.
The true mind is not defiled when in a state of defilement, nor is it pure when in a state of purity; it does not arise when arising, nor does it cease when ceasing. It is, for example, like a...
The *rūpa-maṇi* jewel: if a person obtains it, there is none who does not attain Buddhahood.
[He] showed this to the assembly. Xuansha said: "Where the man of the Way proceeds, it is like fire melting ice; once the arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return.
Therefore, it refuses to dwell within the cage of constraints, and though called, it does not turn its head back. The ancient sages made no arrangements. To the ultimate...
Now there is no place [for it] to abide. Furthermore, it is said: "The practitioner does not awaken, yet delusively involves himself in the dust of the world;

he is struck at every turn and bound at every point. He further intends to concentrate his mind and withdraw his thoughts, seeking to subsume all phenomena into emptiness; yet as soon as a thought arises, he attempts to break it down and eliminate it."
The moment a subtle thought arises, one immediately suppresses it. Such a view is that of an externalist who has fallen into nihilism—a dead man whose soul will not return.
Obscure and indistinct, devoid of awareness or cognition, it is like stuffing one's ears while stealing a bell; it is merely self-deception.
Lately, many of such types have flourished in the world. Furthermore, there is another class who follow like donkeys and horses behind others.

In China, they have been transmitted from one to another in succession. People falsely identify with these illusory dream-companions—the capacity to be angry and to rejoice, the capacity to see and to hear—and take this to be the great matter of transcending the world.
They teach others that once this is clearly recognized, the task of a lifetime of study is finished.
To them, I, this mountain monk, say: "This is not the ancient sages; it is called the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*), the very root of birth and death. Now, let me ask you: [is this truly so?]
When this original person reaches the time of impermanence and is burned into a heap of ashes, tell me:
where has that which can be angry and can be joyful, that which can see and can hear, gone? To investigate in such a manner is the "quicksilver-silver" of Chan.
"This silver is not genuine; it flows away as soon as it is once smelted. It is like donkey's milk: when you try to milk it, it produces nothing but excrement and urine.

If one wishes to make butter or curd, it is truly difficult; how much less can one hope for clarified butter (ghṛta)? Because he asked about the ground, [the master] said, "Who do you usually consult?
He replied, 'There is someone who taught me to investigate only: "All phenomena return to One; where does the One return? Furthermore, he taught me to understand it in this way. "
"Only today do I realize it was not right. I went to the Master and requested a *huatou*. I said, 'In the ancient public cases, what is there that is not right?
My eyes were originally straight; it is because of you, Master, that they have become crooked. After I had pleaded with him repeatedly, he spoke to me."
Go. Study the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature. When you suddenly smash the lacquer bucket, come to this mountain monk’s hand and ask for a blow of the staff.
Addressing the assembly: One who sits atop a hundred-foot pole, though they have gained entry, has not yet attained the truth. One must advance further from the top of that hundred-foot pole;
only then will one manifest their entire body throughout the worlds of the ten directions. But how does one advance from the top of that hundred-foot pole?
The moment you conceive a thought, you have already fallen to the ground. To remain unmoving for even a speck of dust is like a dull bird flying against the wind;
how does this differ from sitting idly? Is there anyone who can grasp this? Like a spark struck from stone or a flash of lightning, there is no time to blink.
Be swift! Be swift! Time does not wait for man. Those with the resolve to study Chan must never consider a small achievement sufficient. Ascend!
One must reach the summit of the mountain; one must reach the bottom of the sea. If you climb a mountain but do not reach the summit, you will not know the vastness of the universe.
If you enter the sea but do not reach the bottom, you will not know the depth of the blue ocean.
Having already reached the top of the hundred-foot pole, you must advance further before you can succeed. Here, I have no path to lead you in, nor any phrase with which to deliberate with you.
The measure is one of singular, simple sincerity—like two horses locking horns in a head-to-head struggle; there is no further deliberation. One falls to the ground and that is the end.

It is not like the old masters of various quarters who speak within their private chambers about Zen, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma, as if there were something to be grasped or sought after, passing it from mouth to mouth and person to person, taking this to be the upward-holding of the lineage and the life-vein of the School. [This is cold.]
Dì looked upon it and saw that it was no different from boiling cauldrons and glowing coals. To gain an advantage is to suffer a loss.
If one were a true seeker of the Way, how could they ever be willing to consume such food? One must urgently spit it out.
Addressing the assembly: The entire Tripitaka is merely an account book for selling fields.

It clearly delineates the boundaries in each direction—east, west, north, and south—and the length and breadth of every mou and bu, without any increase or decrease. Yet the buyer must personally go to the site itself.

Fifty years ago, someone took Baolangpu as a field and sold it to the residence of Governor Yang. When the verification was finally conducted, it turned out to be... [the rest of the text is missing].
These are empty words. Among the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist paths in India, they have been passed down through successive errors.
Only the Buddha alone speaks words of truth. Bodhidharma did not establish written texts; he pointed directly at the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha.
This was merely to provide a witness for those who purchase fields. Have you all ever reached this ground? You must know that it is entirely...

Throughout the ten directions, across heaven and earth, from humans and beasts to grass and shrubs—whether high or low, broad or narrow—there is not a single empty space that is not within one’s own house.
Therefore it is said: "A plot of vacant land before the mountain, I join my palms and earnestly ask the patriarch:
How many times have you sold it only to buy it back? Out of love for the pines and bamboos, it draws in the pure breeze. —The Elder of the Fifth Patriarch.
To speak in such a manner is much like someone who assumes another’s surname to farm the government fields, yet refuses to pay rent or taxes;
there is no other way to settle this than to act according to precedent. (He raises his staff and says: “Hūṃ! Hūṃ!”

Addressing the assembly: Those who travel as seekers all say, "I have crossed through clouds and traversed waters, carrying my bag and bearing my bowl, because the matter of birth and death is great, and thus I have come to consult with a spiritual friend.
Yet, when asked which one is the spiritual friend you are consulting, they are at a loss.
"Where are you right now? [The Master] replied, "I am in various places, sitting upon a curved wooden chair, holding the handle of a whisk, and discussing the profound and the subtle.
[The Master] said, "I say you have misunderstood. This is merely a 'name-knowledgeable friend' (nāma-kalyāṇamitra)."
You must know that true spiritual friends do not sit upon curved wooden couches, nor do they grasp the handles of fly-whisks; they do not discourse on the profound, nor speak of the wondrous.
Before you left the household life, your enemies, relatives, and kin, as well as your notions of self and other and right and wrong—these were your true spiritual friends.
Now that you have left the household life, the lanterns, the pillars, the incense burners, the chairs, the alms-bag, and the shoe-bag—these are your [true spiritual friends].
True spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). Thus, whether heard or seen—whether it be bells, fish-bells, drums, or wooden clappers;

waterfowl or forest trees; this side or that; quietude or clamor—they are all your true spiritual friends. Without needing to give rise to a single thought or stir a single speck of dust, you should awaken directly.
This allows you to transcend conceptualization and intellectual understanding; within the field of the five aggregates (skandha), you have completed a lifetime of study.

When the task is completed— sitting beneath the three-fold causal conditions and before the seven-foot single mat, practicing the *ziluodu* (the *jiaolu* or *kṣānti* of the *dharmadhātu*) three times by day and three times by night—
it is only then that one may be said to have reached the ultimate realization.
Addressing the assembly: A guest in the lineage of the Patriarchs has a primary matter of inquiry that they ought to investigate.
To do nothing but pore over the sutras and treatises is utterly inappropriate. The sutras have their own masters, and the treatises have their own masters;

since you call yourself a Chan Master, why are you poking your head into a heap of old paper? The Buddha himself taught the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings—these are like empty fists.
To deceive children is called ignorance because of this lack of understanding. If you wish to become a man of immeasurable capacity, you must engage in genuine inquiry and attain true realization;
only then will you not be fettered by birth and death in the future, and be free to go or stay as you please. Otherwise, you will be led astray.
Have you not seen how National Teacher Yan said: "The entire matter of the Western Heaven has been completely buried by people of the present day"?
They are extinguished; one cannot find a way out. Furthermore, there was an old master who said: "Throughout the land of the Great Tang, all are thieves who exterminate the Hu race.
When the sons and daughters of common households first enter the monastic groves, how have they ever attained realization?

Upon hearing the sutras or the śāstras cited, they immediately thrust their heads into the midst of them, reciting mantras and repeating words, thereby deceiving how many people for ten births and through kalpas!"
