Their appearing is not non-existent; how do you gather them back? [The Master] replied, "Hiding the head and exposing the tail. He also said, "Not even a pinch is required. He also said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are separated. No hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are separated.
Even if you were to understand this clearly, it is still merely poking one's head out from within a toad’s den. [The Master] spoke on behalf [of the student], saying:
"Seeing the cheek behind the head. He also said: "One gain and one loss. He also said: "Do not show off too much. At other times he said: "Baofu had a vow not to scatter sand; for what reason?"

[The Master] throws it away. A substitute says: "Sweet mouth, bitter heart. He also says: "Look, look! It has fallen right upon your eyes. He also says: "One does not notice the stench of one's own excrement.
Or he says: "The entire earth is the light of Prajñā. Before the light has even arisen, where would you search for it?
A substitute says: "Stars in the sky, wood on the ground. He also says: "This lacquer bucket. He also says: "Ice melting, tiles [shattered]."
The Master ascended the hall and said: "To rest now is to rest immediately. If you seek the moment of realization, there is no such moment.
Have you all attained it yet? He spoke on behalf of them, saying: "When meeting food, eat; when meeting tea, drink. He also said: "The bright moon shines upon the night."
The practitioner further said: "In a *hūbǐng* (a type of cake), what juice can one seek? Or he said: "Movement is like drifting clouds; stillness is like the valley-spirit (*gushén*).
Being neither moving nor still—how do you discern this? On his behalf, [the Master] said: "A wild fox crossing water. He also said: "He follows along."
It is also said: "A single arrowhead pierces three barriers.

Entering the hall, he said: "That which is not received is the eye. That which you bring forward must surely be blind. Tell me, when the Old Barbarian came ten thousand miles from the West, what did he bring with him?
Since he brought nothing, there is likewise no one here in this land to receive it. Is it not so?
To say, "Since he was already a great man, so am I," is already to slander the Patriarch.
How can one avoid this fault? [The Master] provides these substitutions: "Thank you, Third Lady; you do not recognize the four characters. Or: "Exerting effort without merit. Or:
"Standing before the furnace, one does not avoid the flying sparks. Or: "The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. You, in your daily life...
Seeing a pillar, one asks: "What do you call this? If you call it a pillar, that is still the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).
If you call it the mind-consciousness, that is still the pillar. Ultimately, what do you call it? On his behalf, [the Master] says:
"It cuts off the tongues of everyone under heaven. He also says: "A great axe cannot split it open. He also says: "It strikes right into the nostrils."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The secret intent of Vulture Peak was personally heard by Kāśyapa; the single transmission of Shaoshi was silently realized by Shen Guang.
You people who come here—do you know that Tianning has a taboo name? He spoke on behalf [of the assembly], saying: "It is not even necessary. He spoke again, saying:

"Truly, it is rarely heard. He spoke yet again, saying: "Muddying the clay and mixing the water. At other times he said: "The great sun overflows the eyes; ten thousand miles away, not a single speck hangs."
Yun said, "Set aside the blue sky and take the blow. What phrase could he have offered as a substitute? [The Master] provided: "Adding a point to an arrowhead. He also said:
"Let him leap and skip as he pleases. Or he said: "Luo-luo li-luo-luo-li. Or he said: "Right here! Right here! [The Master asked:
"What is right here? [The Master] provided: "An iron snake lies across the ancient road. He also said: "How many people have trodden upon it?"
"Non-attachment. He further said, "I will pick it up for you; come and look.

Upon ascending the hall, he raised his eyebrows, blinked his eyes, struck the meditation seat, and held up his whisk. Whether pointing upward or downward, speaking of mind or nature—all these are merely spirits clinging to grass and wood.
To provide instruction beyond the ordinary, he washes clods of earth in the mud. Is there still a way to benefit others?
There is none. A master of the school (daishu) says: "It is still somewhat lacking. Another says: "Hauling in the cable to let the boat go. Another says: "A tortoise entering the water. Or he says:
"Rabbits and horses have horns; oxen and sheep have no horns. How do you deliberate upon this? The master of the school says: "In accordance with principle, in accordance with fact.
Another says: "A staff strikes the head of a stone man. Another says: "Retreating three thousand li."
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The veteran elders from all quarters all claim, 'I am here to receive beings and benefit living things.

But when one examines them closely, they are much like a net cast across the heavens; nineteen out of twenty fall right into it. A monk who has finished his business will never accept such confinement.
Is there anyone such? Is there? A monk stepped forward and bowed. The Master said, "On a day like today, what kind of season is this?"

[The Master] stepped forward. The monk was speechless. [The Master] spoke on his behalf, saying: "I, this humble one, am at fault. Or he said: "The sun may grow cold, and the moon may grow hot; no demons can destroy the True Teaching.
Furthermore, he asked: "And what is the True Teaching? He spoke on his behalf, saying: "I fear it will rot away! He also said:
"Receive this one question with care! He also said: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Yesterday it was clear and dry, and the magpies sang; today it rains, and the cuckoos cry. The Zhao jade was originally without flaw, yet Sima Xiangru deceived the Qin ruler.
Regarding this phrase 'acting in accordance with the time and reaching the season,' how would you speak? [The Master] provides the response: 'Every day is a good day. He also says:
'A gentleman may be eight. Or again: 'A gourd hangs on the eastern wall. Or he says: 'Even with eyes open, one is caught.'"

Even when closing one's eyes, it is still there. What is the Buddha and the Patriarchs coming forth for? On their behalf, it is said: "If one attempts to break through it with clarity, it is inadequate.
It is also said: "Fleeing from one's shadow at midday. And it is also said: "The goddess of merit and the woman of darkness."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To reach the point where not a single dharma can be grasped by the mind—even this is not yet the place where a patch-robed monk walks.
What, then, is the place where a patch-robed monk walks? He answered on their behalf: "The talk has fallen. Again he said: "The verification is right before your eyes. Again he said: [Silence].
The mud beneath one’s feet is three feet deep. At times he said: "Awakening occurs in a single instant, yet practice must endure for a long time.
Above, there is nothing to grasp at or look up to; below, one cuts off all personal selfhood. To call this a 'path of the man of the Way' is merely a temporary crossroads.

Do not misunderstand this. It is also said: "The tongue has no bone. It is also said: "At the top of the *kṣa* pole, the lotus heart points upward.
In the master’s room, he addressed the assembly, saying: "When the mouth opens, it is not on the tongue.
How do you ask? Six dice, all red in the bowl. How do you win? A ten-thousand-jin bell is covered by the crown. How do you emerge? Do you know?
It arises from the mind. Why? Because the mind does not know the mind. Seeing arises from the eye. Why? Because the eye does not see the eye.
Sentient beings are themselves the Buddhas; from where does delusion come? The Buddhas are themselves sentient beings;
from where does awakening issue? All-encompassing wisdom is pervasive. Why? Because it illuminates what is before but not what is behind. Boundless practice.
[The world] is full. Why? Because [the treatise] discusses the fruit, not the cause. The sun and moon traverse the four continents;
why do they not reach everywhere? A world exists within a single atom; why is it not large?
One day, as the Master went out of the city, he encountered a monk begging for alms. The Master held up his bowl and asked, "In a bowl as large as this, how much rice can be contained?
The monk said, "What do you have to offer? Quickly take it down and give it here! The Master said, "You are truly insatiable. The monk was speechless.
[The Master] spoke on his behalf, saying, "To feed the donkeys and nourish the horses. One day, as the Master was going out the gate to receive guests...
A monk asked, "Opening the gate to wait for a true friend (jñānin), yet the true friend does not come by. What kind of true friend is one who does not come by?
The Master simply said, "I do not understand. The monk said, "What have you seen, Master? The Master said, "Good intentions do not meet with good rewards.
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "This case is fully acknowledged. One day, while escorting a deceased monk, a monk asked:
When a deceased monk has passed away, to what place does he go? The Master said, "If you recognize the place from which he came, you will know the place to which he goes.
The monk asked, "Ultimately, from what place did he come? The Master said, "A stone ox runs along the river; one horse gives birth to three tigers."
The monk said, "In that case, there is no place from which it comes. The Master asked, "What were you just now asking? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
One day, while the Buddha Hall was being renovated, the Master asked the administrative monk in charge, "In what year was this hall built?
The monk struck the pillar and said, "Why do you not answer the Master? The Master said, "How dare you!"

A monk asked, "Grass with roots, you, the Master, may remove at will; but as for rootless grass, how do you remove it?

The Master struck the ground once with his hoe, and the monk immediately threw himself down. The Master said, "In other places they burn the dead; here, we bury them alive. The monk rose and ran away.
The Master laughed heartily. While the Master was at Fengshan, one day during an audience with the Chancellor Gao, the Chancellor asked:

"In Zen there are five schools, and in the Teachings there are three vehicles. I do not ask about the Teachings; what is Zen? The Master replied: "It is precisely the time for the New Year’s official banquet. Gao said:
"Bodhidharma came from the West not to establish written texts, but to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha."
"Buddha. "Where is the Buddha? The Master said, "The strings and pipes are intermingled; the crimson and purple robes shine brilliantly.
Dongguo said, "Is this not your realization, Elder? The Master said, "I dare not say so. Dongguo said, "We shall discuss this on another day. The Master said, "Very well."
"Yes, yes," he replied, and then withdrew. While the Master was at Shoushan, one day while he was planting pine trees, a monk asked, "How many pine trees do you intend to plant on this mountain?
The Master said, "Three hundred thousand. The monk said, "Is that not too many?
The Master said, "I shall teach each and every one of them to cover heaven and earth. The monk said, "In the past it was Linji; today it is Shoushan. The Master said, [Yes].
Furthermore, he obtained the certification of the *ācārya*. The monk said, "As for Linji, who struck the ground three times with his hoe, Huangbo said, 'My school has reached you;
it shall flourish greatly in the world. Does this refer only to Linji alone, or does it extend as an entrustment to all future descendants?
The Master said, "A single drop of ink forms two dragons. The monk said, "One [dragon] belongs to the Mountain Gate..."
"It serves as a model for future generations and acts as a banner for those who come after. "How about you, Preceptor? The Master held up his hoe.
The monk said, "In that case, you have transcended the ancients. The Master threw down the hoe and returned to his quarters.
One day, the Master suddenly heard the sound of a bell. He stood up, joined his palms, and said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva!
Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattva! A monk asked, "Where are you now? The Master replied, "I am returning to the South Sea.
On another day, a master of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* visited him. The Master asked the master, "How many kinds of dharmadhātu are there in the *Avataṃsaka*? The master—
[The Master] said, "There are four kinds of dharma-realms. The host asked, "In which of these dharma-realms are you currently situated? The Master was at a loss for words.
The Master said, "You do not even understand the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena. The host said, "I understand. The Master said, "A Cao-Dynasty man from Zhengzhou!"
One day, while the Master was with the assembly observing the snow, he asked a monk, "Is this fine snow? The monk said, "In what way is it fine? The Master pointed at the snow.
After a long silence, he asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "There is no fire; you will freeze to death. How many such people are there?
One night, while the Master was in the central courtyard with a monk gazing at the moon, the monk pointed at the moon and asked the Master about it.
[The monk asked: "What clarity is attained by that one half? What darkness is attained by this one half? The Master said: "As for clarity, it follows its own clarity;
as for darkness, it follows its own darkness. The monk asked: "When it is full on the fifteenth night, where does the darkness go? The Master said:
"I would give you thirty blows, and that would not be considered too much. The monk said: "In that case, there is neither clarity nor darkness at all. The Master said: [Silence].
"Do you see the true moon? The monk asked, "What is the true moon? The Master said, "It does not illuminate. The monk asked, "When it does not illuminate, what then?
The Master said, "How many people are groping in the sky and feeling about on the ground!

The monk asked, "Is this not just that very thing? The Master said, "It is still but a shadow. As the monk was about to offer further words, the Master gave a shout. One day, the Master went to attend...
A donor was hosting a vegetarian feast. He asked the monks, "I borrowed my seat from King of Lamps and took my food from Fragrant Accumulation;
how does today’s offering compare to those? The monks replied, "It is difficult to digest. The Master said, "You must quickly vomit it up. The monk asked, "With what shall we repay the donor?
The Master picked up his alms bowl and said, "You too have received your share of rice according to the custom. The monk was speechless. The Master said, "How bitter! The Buddha!"
One day, when the Dharma Master came to visit Master Daye, the Master asked, "What sutra are you lecturing on? The Master replied, "The Lotus Sutra.
The Master [Daye] asked, "Does the sutra not say, 'This is true diligence; this is called the true dharma-offering to the Tathāgata'? Is that so? The Master replied, "It is.
The Master [Daye] said, "That there is an offering is not in doubt; but what is the true dharma? The Master replied, "It is fully contained therein."
In the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," the Master said, "I thought this was a golden-maned lion;
it turns out, however, to be but a member of the jackal clan. The student asked, "What is the True Dharma? I hope the Master will compassionately instruct me.
The Master replied, "Have you not come from Mount Tiantai? The student replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Mount Tiantai is eighteen thousand *zhang* high. At its summit—"
"How many people can sit on top? The host had no reply. The Master said, "Go drink tea.

One day, while the Master was receiving a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*), the masters from various mountains arrived and all manner of entertainments were assembled. When the meal was finished, an elder asked, "Just now there was such a great commotion."

"Now it is quiet and still; where has all that clamor gone? The Master said, "Everyone is right here. The Elder said, "Originally there was not a single thing; yet it manifests in a hundred thousand ways. The Master said, "We are both monastics; let us loosen our belts and broaden our stomachs. Dongshan asked, "Is there such a principle as this? The Master said, "I see that the lamp-light Buddha’s original radiance is auspicious in this way.
The Elder then gave a shout; the Master also shouted. He added, "Blowing on fire because of the wind requires little effort," and then struck him.
The Elder said, "Do not mete out blind floggings and blind blows. The Master said, "You simply take the blow; I want these words to circulate."
One day the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "In the first year of the Taiding era, on the eleventh day of the first month, there was a decorated tower outside the Chongtian Gate.
At that time, at the fifth watch, an arrow was shot from atop the tower and pierced through twenty-four golden drums.
From this moment on, the world enjoyed peace. A monk then asked, "What is the arrow? The Master replied, "At the crossroads."
While breaking a chopstick stem, there was a Dharma Master named Yanfurun who asked, "I have heard that the Master’s verse on 'meeting the opportunity' says:
'The drums thunder outside the Chongtian Gate; Suddenly, empty space collapses to the ground.
Picking up a single snowflake from a red furnace— It is, however, the Yellow River ice in the sixth month. Where is this 'sixth-month ice'? The Master spread his two hands. Fa-...
The Master remained silent. He said, "The subsequent text is long; we shall attend to it on another day.

One day, because a donor had presented him with *yángméi* (southern hawthorn) fruits, a monk picked one up from the box and asked the Master, "These *yángméi* are all the same; why are some red and some white?
The Master closed the lid of the box and said, "What do you see? The monk was speechless. The Master then opened the lid again.
Xuedou said, "Huh? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "You are simply a fellow who knows nothing of opening and closing.
One day, as the Master entered the sutra hall, he saw a monk reading a scripture and asked, "What sutra are you reading? The monk replied, "The Diamond Sutra.
The Master said, "I am not asking about the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; what sutra are you actually reading? The monk had no reply. The Master [said]: "..."
He summoned the heads of the various offices and instructed them: "Tomorrow, none of you shall come to my desk. One day, while the Master was observing the rice fields with a monk, the monk asked:
"A single grain of seed is sown in spring, and ten thousand grains are harvested in autumn. There are no idle fields throughout the four seas, yet farmers still die of hunger."

"Is it that the roots and sprouts are different, or is it that the heavenly dew is not evenly distributed? The Master said, "A field with wide furrows does not hold water; do not begrudge the dragon in the emerald pool.
The monk said, "If that is so, then people of this age will be disappointed. The Master said, "What have you been eating all along, you fellow?
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "This ungrateful and undutiful fellow! He then struck him. Because of Yuan... [The Master]... [The text ends here].
One night, while the lamps were being lit in the hall, a monk asked, "What is the lamp of original nature? The Master said, "That is still a matter of today.
The monk said, "How does a matter of today relate to the lamp of original nature? The Master pointed to the lamp and said, "One, two, three, four, five.
The monk said, "Thank you for the Master’s instruction. The Master said, "Though the road to Jian’ge is perilous, travelers pass through it at night."
[The monk] said more, but the monk remained silent. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying: "Be careful not to bore through the tortoise shell or strike the roof tiles.
One day, because a monk presented him with a staff, the Master asked: "Did you get this from Tiantai? The monk said: "I did not get it from Tiantai. The Master said: [Silence].
"Did you not obtain it from Mount Nanyue? The monk said, "I did not obtain it from Mount Nanyue. The Master asked, "From where did you obtain it? The monk passed him his staff.
The Master held it up and asked, "Is this the essence or the function? The monk said, "When it is wielded, it arises as function from the essence."
"Releasing [the function] means gathering the function back into the essence. The Master said, "If you come in this manner, you obtain the essence, but not the function.

The monk said, "When the Master speaks in this manner, I obtain the function, but not the essence. The Master struck once, leaned on his staff, and said, "Essence and function are gathered up at once.
When the Master responded to the imperial summons and went to the capital to transcribe the Golden-Lettered Tripitaka, one—
The Master entered the inner palace and presented the scroll. A scholar asked, "It is not formed by the individual strokes; it is not the character 'eight. What character is this?
The Master held up his brush and said, "Gold dripping everywhere. The scholar said, "I shall faithfully accept and practice this."

The Master said, "Scholar, you must not be careless. The scholar then bowed in thanks. One day, while the Master was wandering the mountains, he saw a forked path and asked a monk, "Which way goes to the east?
Which way goes to the west? The monk said, "I pray the Master examine this for us. The Master then walked on.

Reaching the midpoint of the road, he asked the monk, "How many *li* is it from here to the mountain peak? The monk said, "Three *li*. The Master said, "When you encounter a fierce tiger on the road—"
"How is it? The monk made the sound of a tiger. The Master struck him and said, "Today, quite casually, I have struck a tiger.
The monk did not accept this. The Master said, "Remember this clearly and show it to a master. One day, several monks came to pay their respects to the Master.
The Master asked the head monk, "What is your name? The monk replied, "Pǔtōng. The Master said, "I do not ask about 'Pǔ' (Universal). What is 'Tōng' (Penetrating)?
The monk stood with his body turned slightly and his hands clasped. The Master said, "You intend to face me through the nostrils.
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "A second or third time is unnecessary; there is no different soil in the same pit," and he struck him. The Master.
One day, after returning from entering the city to visit the palace, a monk asked, "It must have been difficult for you, Master, to go in and out.

The Master said, "Last night there was a fine wind. The monk said, "Last night there was a fine wind. The Master said, "Tomorrow there will certainly be rain. The monk was speechless. The Master sighed, "Heh heh.
On another day, the Master entered the garden and asked the head gardener, "Is the melon ripe yet? The gardener replied, "It has been ripe for a long time."
The Master said, "Bring me a slice of sweet melon. The Head fetched a melon and presented it to the Master, who said, "Thirty large knives.
The Master said, "The monastic community is satiated. One day, while the Master was asking for noodles, a monk came to pay his respects. The Master drew out some noodles and showed them to him.
The monk bowed respectfully and departed. The Master called to the monk; the monk turned his head. The Master said, "Many have mouths but cannot eat flour.
One day, while gathering *bottle-millet* (*yǐngsù*), the Master asked a monk, "How many grains of millet are in this bottle?

The monk split the millet and poured it out. The Master said, "Do not pour it out in such disorder. The monk asked, "What is it like when one does not pour it out in disorder? The Master replied, "You will understand it in the year of the donkey."
One day, while the Master was viewing the sea with several monks, a monk asked, "It is just a single expanse of water;
why do you call it 'sea'? The Master said, "It is just a single expanse of sea; why do you call it 'water'? "Now tell me," he continued.
“Where does the source come from? The monk said, “It comes from a single drop. The Master said, “And where does that single drop come from?
The monk was speechless. The Master said, “This fellow has no foothold; if I do not beat him, when shall I? He struck him several times.
Then he called another monk forward and said, “Please, Upasaka, offer a substitute phrase for him. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him as well. Again—
A monk came forward and said, "I can say it. The Master asked, "How would you say it? The monk bowed respectfully (*zhēnzhòng*) and departed.
The Master struck him as well. One day, while a monk was serving tea, the Master asked, "For whom is the tea being served today?
The monk replied, "Specifically for the Master. The Master said, "It happens that the old monk is not here. The monk then departed.
"Tea," the Master said, withdrawing his hand. The monk hesitated; the Master smashed the bowl and immediately returned to his quarters.
One day, the Master visited a neighboring hermitage and asked a monk, "What kind of flower is this in the courtyard? The monk replied, "The 'itchy' flower. The Master asked, "Why is the flower itchy?
The monk replied, "When one house has trouble, a hundred houses are busy. The Master remarked, "The drums and horns have sounded."
One night, the Master sat in the dark with a monk. A lad came along carrying a lamp. The Master asked, "These two look alike;
one is a shadow—what is the other? The monk was speechless. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying, "Ask anyone else."
Asuṅga and Mañjuśrī were sitting together in succession. Mañjuśrī picked up a crystal cup and asked, "Is there such a thing as this in the South?
Asuṅga replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said, "What do you usually use to drink tea with? Asuṅga was speechless. [If one were to] provide a substitute response for him, one would say:
"The pointing is not yet reached. King Aśoka asked Piṇḍola: "I have heard that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha. Is this true or not?"
Lu brushed his eyebrows aside with his hand and said, "I have personally seen the Buddha come. The King had no reply. [The Master] provided this on his behalf: "In a previous life, I was fortunate.
There was a hut-dweller in the Han kingdom who encountered the Emperor while out on a tour. When someone reported, 'The Great King is coming;
please rise,' the Master said, 'Not only would I not rise for the King, I would not even rise for the Buddha. The Emperor proclaimed and asked, 'Is the Buddha not your teacher? The Master replied:"
[The Master] said, "It is so. The Emperor said, "When a disciple sees his teacher, why do you not rise? The Master was speechless. [A master] provided this substitute reply:
"If one wishes to observe the teacher, first observe the disciple. After Kāśyapa had finished treading mud, a venerable one asked him, "Why do you do this yourself?
Kāśyapa said, "If I do not do it myself, who will do it for me? The venerable one was speechless. [A master] provided this substitute reply: "This leaves people in doubt."
[The Emperor] was attached [to his own views]. Emperor Wu asked Bodhidharma, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?

Dharma said, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor said, "Who is it that stands before me? Dharma said, "I do not know. A later master provided this commentary: "When did the Great Master leave Western India?"

Compiled by the Attendants at the Chief Seat’s Quarters of Mount Jing. On the occasion of the summer retreat, the Master took up his whisk and held the formal address. He brandished his staff and said:
"This is the staff of Mount Jing. Why is it in the hands of Elder Qi? You already know its origin; what need is there for further words? He then dropped it.
Perhaps you do not yet know; let me not fail to reveal a bit of news. At the summit of Lingxiao Peak, the field for selecting Buddhas is opened.

A single phrase facing the sun cuts off the ten directions. If you truly cut them off, then even those of long-standing study under former masters need not refrain from their practice or protect life.
For those of later learning and beginners, who would dare to violate the rules or establish precedents? Above, there is nothing to grasp or look up to; below, all personal effort is severed.
In every person, the eternal light manifests before them; each individual stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. The Buddhas of the three periods have tongues that possess no bones;
the Patriarchs of the six generations have eyebrows placed above their eyes. When Deshan saw a monk enter the gate, he struck him immediately—like using a painted cake to satisfy hunger. Linji...
Seeing a monk enter the gate, [Zhaozhou] immediately shouted—this is like hoping to quench one's thirst by looking at a plum. When Old Miaoxi saw a monk enter the gate, he would say:
"To call it a bamboo whisk is to encounter resistance; not to call it a bamboo whisk is to turn one's back. You may not utter a word, nor may you remain silent."
The story of carving sand lacks the discourse on engraving jade; the tale of binding grasses contradicts the intention of the Way-man.
Since one cannot offer a word, yet one cannot remain without a word, he takes what is presented and breaks it into two pieces. Look at what kind of trickery he can perform!
The Dragon King of the Vast Marsh, unable to restrain his amusement, strikes Mount Sumeru with a single blow until it shatters into a hundred fragments, and leaps up to the Brahma Heaven.
The Master departed. He called to the assembly, saying, "Tell me, does this present period of Buddhist service have any way of benefiting others?
With his staff, he struck three times in succession. He then cited the case of National Teacher Nanyue Huairang, who sent a monk to Jiangxi.
The Master of the Probing Horse (Tánmǎ Dàshī) waited for the Master to ascend the hall and stepped forward to ask, "What is it?
The Master said, "Since the time of chaos, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce.

The Master [Yunmen] said, "When the Master of the Horse said that for thirty years he had never lacked salt and sauce, he had already consumed a great deal of salt and sauce. Had I been the Master of the Horse..."
As soon as the Master saw this monk emerge, he descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and gave him a severe beating before sending him back.
He then recounted the incident to Nanyue to demonstrate that his lineage had a firm foundation and that his own insight was clear and discerning;
thus, he ensured that the tongues of all people under heaven would be silenced, and the single stream of Caoxi would not fall into desolation.
At the Liang Wang Repentance Assembly, Chan Master Guan was requested to give a small discourse (*xiaocan*). The Master said:

"If you can understand this very thing, it does not diminish in the state of an ordinary person, nor does it increase in the state of a sage. It transcends the radiance of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of suns and moons;
it pervades the entirety of inconceivable space. There is not a single principle that is not revealed, not a single event that is not encompassed, and not a single thing that is not profound."
The earth is not ultimately real. Ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; afflictions are themselves bodhi; birth and death are themselves nirvana;

and worldly toil is itself liberation. It is like the nature of empty space, which is not composed of manifold characteristics, yet does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics.
However, blue is not blue by itself; yellow is not yellow by itself; red is not red by itself; white is not white by itself.
[The Master] said: "It is simply the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that, within this, grasps and measures, [discriminating] 'this is blue,' 'this is yellow,' 'this is red,' or 'this is white.

When the mental consciousness does not arise, the faculties and their objects are serene and still. Water and its waves, the fist and the palm—whether rolling up or unfolding, closing or opening, how could there be two different things?
Movement and stillness, coming and going, have never been of two natures. Churning the butter until the *sarpis* and *ghṛta* become a single flavor; melting the vase and the platter."
To treat hairpins and bracelets as one piece of gold; to regard the union of yin and yang and the cycles of cold and heat as one season;

to blend the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Ji Rivers into one body of water—this is for a single seal to be all seals, a single gate to be all gates, a single accomplishment to be all accomplishments, and a single destruction to be all destructions.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddha taught all dharmas to cure all minds. Since I have no mind at all, what [is there to cure]?"
To employ all dharmas in this manner means that for one who gathers an assembly, there is no assembly to be gathered; for one who preaches the Dharma, there is no dharma to be preached;
for one who delivers sentient beings, there are no sentient beings to be delivered; and for one who repents of offenses, there is no offense to be repented.

Have you not seen how the Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, asked the Second Patriarch: "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind ailment; I pray that the Master will repent my offenses for me. The Second Patriarch—
He said, "Bring forth your sin so that I may repent it for you. The Third Patriarch said, "I have sought my sin, but it is utterly unattainable.

The Second Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting your sin for you. O virtuous ones, do you understand this clearly? Had he not shot the stone tiger at Lan-tien, he would have nearly killed General Li by mistake.

At the assembly of the *Sūtra of the Flower Adornment of True Thusness*, the Venerable Luoyi invited the Master for a small discourse. The Master said: "To read the sūtras, one must possess the eye for reading sūtras;
to see the ground, one must obtain the phrase that sees the ground. At the hour of midnight before Mount Zhengjue, the Elder Śākyamuni..."
The morning star appeared, and he suddenly attained great enlightenment; this is the second phrase.
The three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teachings, the provisional and the real, the sudden and the gradual, the half and the full, the partial and the complete—these are the third phrase.

All the Buddhas of the three periods, the six generations of patriarchs, and the old monks of the world, even if they exerted their utmost strength, could only speak of the third phrase. At the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra...
The Venerable One, along with the forty-two ranks of Dharma-body Mahāsattvas and the fifty-three ranks of spiritual friends, each expounded inexhaustible Dharma gates;

yet when has he ever uttered the First Phrase? If there were a single person who could utter the First Phrase, Mount Sumeru must be ground to powder, the waters of the ocean must be dried up, and the empty space of the ten directions must be struck down.
It falls to the ground. Why is this so? This Dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to understand has rarely been heard of in antiquity or today.
Do you all know it? Right now, before your very eyes, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the myriad phenomena of the universe; the grasses, trees, and forests;
the walls, tiles, and rubble—all these speak day and night with blazing intensity, without ceasing. Yet, it is they who speak most intimately; they speak...
Since the speaker does not open their mouth, the listener likewise has no need for ears. It is vividly clear and distinct, without a single hair’s breadth of concealment;
the True Sutra is manifest before one, saving so much effort. Why wait until incense is offered and the scroll is unfurled before the Wheel of Dharma is turned?

It would be better to head straight for the Flower Treasury Ocean (Huazang Hai), exiting from the left and entering from the right, lying prostrate and sleeping crosswise atop the crown of Vairocana’s head.
What more need be said of Bodhi and Nirvana, True Suchness and Liberation? All names—what are they but the rattling of a hot bowl?
All words and speech—what are they but the tethering stake for a donkey? Therefore, the Great Master Linji said:
All that exists as sound, name, and phrase is entirely dependent and transformative. It is stirred up from the ocean of vital energy within the navel-cakra;

through the clashing of teeth, the meaning of phrases is formed. Clearly understand that these are illusory transformations. Externally, they manifest as the karmic activity of vocal expression; internally, they represent mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
With volition and recollection, all are merely dependent manifestations. To simply recognize these external attachments and take them as real understanding is a mistake.
Even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it would still be but a mere supernatural power; I call it the "True Sutra," yet even that is but a provisional teaching.
After all, what is it? The Compassionate Boat does not sail upon the vast blue waves; at Jiantuo Pass, the wooden goose is released in vain.
At the Huayan Sutra Assembly of Eimei-in, the repository keeper Tsukushi requested a small discourse.
The Master said: "True everywhere, true everywhere; in every speck of dust is the original person. When the truth is spoken, the voice does not appear;
the majestic, upright essence has caused the body to vanish. O worthy ones, do you see this majestic, upright essence? It is the great earth and sky, the sun, moon, and stars."
Throughout the myriad phenomena of the universe—the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas; humans, devas, ghosts, and animals;

and all sentient beings with moving life—there is nowhere that does not contain Vairocana, who sits serenely therein, attains equal and perfect enlightenment, and turns the Great Wheel of Dharma for the sake of all living beings.
Nevertheless, within the realm of sentient beings, one neither grasps at a single dharma nor rejects a single dharma. Thus it is said:
"The bodies of all Buddhas are but a single Dharma-body; their single mind and single wisdom, as well as their powers and fearlessnesses, are likewise so.
This does not preclude each individual from abiding in their own sphere, each realizing liberation for themselves, each performing Buddha-work for themselves, and each [attaining] for themselves...
Manifesting supernatural powers: when manifesting supernatural powers in the sphere of the eye, one performs buddha-work in the sphere of the ear;

when manifesting supernatural powers in the sphere of the ear, one performs buddha-work in the sphere of the nose; when manifesting supernatural powers in the sphere of the nose, one performs buddha-work in the sphere of the tongue;
when manifesting supernatural powers in the sphere of the tongue, one performs buddha-work in the sphere of the body. In the sphere of...
When manifesting supernatural powers within the sphere of the body (*kāyāyatana*), one performs the Buddha-work within the sphere of the mind (*manāyatana*).
When manifesting supernatural powers within the sphere of the mind, one performs the Buddha-work within all spheres. Since the sphere of the mind is inexhaustible, space is inexhaustible;
since space is inexhaustible, the worlds are inexhaustible; since the worlds are inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible. Since sentient beings are inexhaustible...
The Buddhas are inexhaustible. The Buddhas being inexhaustible, their vows and practices are inexhaustible.
Their vows and practices being inexhaustible, the ineffable, ineffable realms, liberations, spiritual powers, and Buddha-activities are inexhaustible, inexhaustible.
Nevertheless, these still remain within the measure of the Dharma-realm. As for that single phrase beyond measure—how can you speak it? Do you understand? Mountain flowers bloom like...
Jin. The waters of the mountain stream are as deep blue as indigo.
At the commencement of the retreat at Yuanming Monastery, the *zhangzhu* (steward) Mao requested a small lecture (*xiaocan*). The Master said: "Yongjia said: 'Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan;
whether speaking or silent, moving or still, the essence remains serene. Even if a sharp blade were constantly leveled before you, and even if lethal poison..."*
It is also tranquil and leisurely. As for Zen, it is not non-existent. What is this essence? Is it that "above is heaven and below is earth"?
Is it that "the monastic is a monastic and the layperson is a layperson"? Is that the essence?

Is it that "majestic and dignified, brilliant and radiant, prior to sound there is no sound, after form there is no form"? Is that the essence? Is it that "resting and ceasing, a single thought for ten thousand years"?
"Go! Go cold and still! Go like a single strand of white silk! Go like the incense burner in an ancient temple!
Go like cold ashes and withered wood—is this the essence? Is it that within suchness there is not-suchness, and within not-suchness there is yet suchness—is this the essence?
If you calculate and deliberate in this way, you are merely driving iron stakes into empty space. Do not take up the intellectual learning of the common crowd."
The mind of the Patriarchs is buried; it is simply a matter of sitting in meditation. You must first bring an end to your own "thieving mind" before you can succeed.
If you do not bring an end to your own thieving mind, what benefit is there in sitting in vain? Furthermore, what is this thieving mind? It is simply all that is not resolved:
every arising and ceasing of thought is, in its entirety, the thieving mind. To die to the thieving mind is to be one with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

There is no difference. The Buddhas and Patriarchs desire that people quickly realize the supreme, wondrous Way. Whether through long-term or short-term practice, they seek realization within a fixed period.
Ultimately, what is it that is realized? It is simply to teach you to exhaust all thieving minds and suddenly clarify your own nature.
During the time of silent sitting, one must employ skillful means. The Great Master Huineng said: "Do not think of good; do not think of evil. At this very moment—
At such a time, what is this original face? O worthy ones, right now before your eyes, what is this that stands out so vividly?
This original face of your own cannot be sought from another; if it were sought from another, it would not be your own.
From birth until old age, that which puts on clothes, eats food, and discharges excrement and urine—this is what is called [the original face].
This stinking skin-bag will suddenly reach its full term; when the four elements disperse, where will your own original face be?
Master Shitou said: "If you wish to know the immortal within the hermitage, it is not separate from this very skin-bag right now. Study this!

The period of sitting concluded with the distribution of offerings. Supervisor Cheng invited the Master for a small discourse (xiaocan). The Master said: "The Great Way transcends verbal explanation; the true mechanism has no front or back.
When even a speck of dust is not exhausted, Mount Sumeru suddenly emerges; as long as one's realization of the ground is not yet forgotten, there remains a five-colored rope beneath one’s feet."
One should know that this matter is fundamentally already manifest; there is no need to lower one's head. It is difficult to attain through deliberation. Therefore, Deshan said:
"A hair’s breadth of attachment is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion results in shackles for ten thousand kalpas. How can you remain sitting here?
You must turn toward the other side, and even further beyond that—where neither Buddha nor Patriarch is established. This is your own self.
Only when you treat [the Dharma] like a born enemy do you possess even a trace of the breath of a *śramaṇa*. If you merely stand with hands folded behind the thousand sages, what are you good for?
Relying on their gateways and leaning against their walls, you are stubbornly called "Master" by people of the age. Yantou said:
"When I was traveling as a pilgrim in the past, I saw one or two venerable elders who did nothing but instruct me to manage things day and night."
My buttocks grew calluses from sitting, and my mouth was dripping with saliva as I sat in meditation to maintain my vigilance.
Even at such a time, desire still remained. To be without dependence and without desire is to be a Capable Sage (Śākyamuni).
O virtuous ones, among those who study the Way today, who is without dependence? Who is without desire? Those who have dependence and desire float within the sea of birth and death.

He hung a board on each bank; whenever someone came to cross, he would strike the board once and ask, "Who is it? If a person replied, "I want to go to the other side," he would ply his oars to welcome them. One day, there was a woman carrying a baby who asked him [the same question]. When he struck the board and asked, "Who is it? she replied, "I am going to the other side. He then raised his oars to meet her. At that moment, a monk happened to pass by and asked, "What is this woman doing? The ferryman said, "She is carrying her child across the river. The monk said, "How can you say that? Yantou said, "Now tell me, from where did this child in the old woman’s hand come? He then struck her.
The woman said, "I have given birth to seven sons; six of them did not meet with one who understands them. This one, too, is of no use."
He then cast it into the water. Only after the snow has fallen does one know the integrity of the pine and cypress; only when faced with difficulty does one see the heart of a true man.
Nevertheless, you must by no means mistake the bridge of a donkey’s saddle for your father’s chin. (A shout.)
The offerings were presented at Nanshan. The Master’s disciple, Yifang, requested a small-scale discourse (xiaocan). The Master said: "This matter is near at hand, right upon the surface of the lips;
yet it is far away, across the lands of the Ganges sands. It cannot be conjectured through existence or non-existence, nor can it be measured by ease or difficulty.
To be stalled by written characters and spoken language is to be bound by written characters and spoken language; to be mired in the meditation cushion [is likewise a hindrance]."
As for the meditation board, one is constrained by the *pútuán* (grass mat) and the meditation board. Generally, those who practice seated meditation rarely achieve complete penetration.

If you do not become attached to existence, you will immediately become attached to non-existence. If you are attached to existence, you try to eliminate it with non-existence; but when you are attached to non-existence, how can you eliminate it?
If you wish to become a disciple of the Empty King, do not let the disease of the mind remain, for it is the most difficult to cure. To speak according to reality:

since Śākyamuni appeared in the world and Bodhidharma came from the West, the torch has been passed down through successive generations. Yet, like waves rising in a windless sea, one suddenly pierces through [the veil of delusion), and the three realms sink into stillness.
Returning to observe the world, it is seen as nothing more than a dream. Only when one reaches this state is it truly well.
"Sitting in meditation. Who is this person sitting? What is this meditation? It has been thoroughly investigated and resolved. One may say it exists; one may say it does not exist.
One may say it is difficult; one may say it is easy. One may say it is attained; one may say it is not attained. If it is not attained, how is it attained?
From where does life come? "An iron saw dances on the three stages. From where does death go? "Ox-hide drums cover the pillar. This was the former Taizhou Fu.
The Elder asked Gushan, "Where were your nostrils before your parents were born? Gushan replied, "They are right here now.
"Where are they now? the Elder asked. The Elder Fuzhao did not approve of this and said, "Ask me and I will tell you.
Gushan then asked, "Where were your nostrils before your parents were born? Fuzhao merely shook his fan.
[He] finished speaking. "At that time, had I been Mount Gu, I would have overturned his meditation seat for him. To see it is not to think; to think of it is to be a thousand li away.
You worthy ones, do you wish to know where the nostrils of Nanshan fall? [After a long silence: When the rhinoceros gazes at the moon, patterns form its horn;
when the elephant is startled by thunder, flowers enter its tusk."
The Elder Wuxue had previously prepared his disciples; the *gudu* and *weina* requested a small discourse (*xiaocan*). The Master said:

"The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally without mysterious subtlety or intellectual understanding. To speak of the Way, there is directly beneath it nothing to do. Rest! Cease! What a fine, liberated monk!"
If one steps forward with a distracted gait, then even a thousand or ten thousand *li* will not suffice. But if we discuss this matter:
coming from such a state, it has never been clouded or dulled; it cannot be shrouded by sound or form, nor can it be bound by birth and death.
It is free and at ease, without gain or loss, liberated in every place and complete in every place—pure and naked, utterly beyond all assumption, bare and vivid.
"Free and easy, beyond grasp; it pierces the nostrils of all people in the world. It relies entirely upon this one point.
If there were not this one point, why did the Old Barbarian (Bodhidharma) come from the West in the first place? Take, for instance, Shitou and Mazu."
Baizhang, Huangbo, Linji, Deshan, Yangshan, Dongshan, Yunmen, and Fayan—all these were ancestral masters of the highest caliber.
Yet even they could not have survived to this day. As the saying goes: "The hook is cast into the four seas, yet it is only the fierce dragon that is caught."
This is an exceptionally profound discourse for the purpose of seeking a kindred spirit. Have you not seen how one day Yangshan asked a fellow practitioner, "How is your realization these days?
The other replied, "In truth, there is not a single dharma that can be taken as an object of the mind.

Yangshan said, "Your understanding still remains within the realm of objects. The other asked, "Why is that? Yangshan replied, "Do you have no capacity to know that which could be taken as an object of the mind?"
The Venerable Yuanwu said: "Even when one has reached the point where not a single dharma can be taken as an object of the mind, one still encounters the scrutiny of Yangshan.
At this stage, there is neither a knower nor a known; there is not even a single dharma—nor is there 'no single dharma. One must be such a person before it can be attained.
If you wish to exhaust the view from a thousand li, you must ascend yet another story; you must know that for a person who has truly realized it, not a single word [is uttered]."
A vain shot. Now, there is no need to turn your head or shift your gaze; it is simply a matter of directly taking responsibility.

This can serve as a marvelous cause and manifest a sublime sign. It dries up the ocean of suffering, shatters the mountains of obstructions, severs the root-source of birth and death, and crushes the nesting place of ignorance.
At this very moment, how do you speak a single phrase to celebrate and praise the offering? Within the realm—
The sun and moon hang suspended, traversing all; a single expanse of clear sky, ten thousand ages of spring.
At the Huayan Sutra Assembly of Xinghua Monastery, Chief Administrator Kui requested a small-scale discourse (xiaocan). The Master said: "The ox of Huai Prefecture eats the grain."
The horse of Yizhou has a distended belly; the world seeks a physician. By applying moxibustion to the left flank of a pig, Vairocana Tathāgata laughs heartily and says:

"Within the ocean of the twenty-fold Flower Treasury World-System, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas therein—down to the beasts such as oxen and horses—when subjected to this single moxibustion by the Venerable Dushun, are unfailingly benefited in accordance with the occasion."

[He] paused. [The meaning] has been thoroughly penetrated to the very bone and marrow. He called to the assembly, saying: "Tell me, were those four lines of verse just now from the Teachings (Dharma) or from Chan?
If you say they are from the Teachings, which volume of the eighty-one fascicles of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra contains such words?
If you say they are from Chan, Master Dushun was himself a patriarch of the Xianshou school; why then..."

Speaking thus, is there anyone who can definitively settle this? If no one can settle it, this mountain monk will not begrudge his verbal efforts and shall provide an explanation for you all once over.
Master Zhao said: "When an ancient mirror reflects the essence, that essence naturally manifests its form;
when an ancient mirror reflects the mind, that mind naturally becomes clear. How has the Teaching ever been different from Chan? Thus spoke Master Niu-tou Guizong.
He said: "I now wish to speak of Chan. All you sons, draw near together. Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara, which skillfully responds to all places.
Has Chan ever been different from the Teaching? The Teaching is the Buddha’s mouth; Chan is the Buddha’s mind.

For those who have not yet understood, listen to these words: 'Right now, who is it that moves the mouth? If you can comprehend it within this very moment, you will cut off the tongues of all people in the world."
Tongue! Furthermore, what Chan is there to divide? What Teaching is there to select? To establish it is up to me;
to sweep it away is also up to me. I am the Dharma King; I am sovereign over the Dharma. If I establish it, there is Chan and there is Teaching.
If I sweep it away, both Chan and Teaching are eliminated. Since Chan and Teaching are eliminated, where would the twentyfold Flower Treasury World-Ocean be placed? Listen!

I have a verse that says: Suppose one were to travel through all the Buddha-fields of the eastern direction, taking the entire great earth and Mount Sumeru, grinding each and every part until they are reduced to fine dust.
With each particle of dust, one marks a single field; and so it is for the four intermediate directions, above, and below, until the entire realm of empty space is filled.
Then, using the number of these aforementioned particles of dust, one would manifest each one as a patch-robed monk. One...
A single monk manifests as many bodies as there are atoms; each body possesses as many mouths as there are atoms, and within each mouth are as many tongues as there are atoms.
Each tongue proclaims as many meanings as there are atoms, continuing through every single kalpa until the end of the future.
Thus, they deliver and liberate unspeakable numbers of sentient beings, with each attaining the rank of Vairocana, constantly expounding the Dharma for unspeakable kalpas. Such merit as this—

It can be said that there is no one in the world capable of measuring it. It is like a master illusionist who gathers a crowd of illusions and then teaches the dharma of illusion to that illusory crowd.
Having heard the dharma of illusion, they realize the illusory mind; having realized the illusory mind, they perfect illusory practice;

sitting at the illusory site of enlightenment, they become illusory Buddhas and deliver immeasurable illusory sentient beings. That successive attainment of Buddhahood is likewise so; ultimately, [it is all an illusion].
Not departing from illusory phenomena, the primordial reality (bhūtakoṭi) is eternally quiescent; it is like space, without increase or decrease.
If one can awaken to this true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), who is there that attains or fails to attain Buddhahood? Vairocana and I have realized this together.
Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, the wondrous Dharmakāya; the fifty-three spiritual friends—may they bear witness to these words for me.

As the period of repentance at Yanfuyuan has concluded, the Venerable Vinaya Master respectfully requests a small discourse. The Master says: "In a single thought, universally contemplate the immeasurable..."
The *kalpa* has no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus one understands the affairs of the three periods of time; transcending all expedient means, one accomplishes the Ten Powers.

[The Master] picks up his whisk and makes a circular gesture, saying: "Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, sentient and non-sentient beings—herein they realize equal and perfect enlightenment.
The entire mind is Buddha; the entire Buddha is mind. Since the mind is ultimately non-existent, the Buddha, too, is non-existent."
He does not stand. Thus it is said: "Clearly seeing that there is not a single thing—neither person nor Buddha.
The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble in the sea; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. In this way, one is liberated everywhere, yet does not fall into the deep pit of liberation.
One is radiant everywhere, yet does not become stuck in the superior marks of radiance. Whether walking or staying...

Whether sitting or reclining, one does not fasten on girdles or belts, yet remains constantly vivid and alert. Whether long or short, square or round, there is no need for artificial arrangement, yet one can remain continuous and dense.
All day long speaking, the tongue never stirs; all day long silent, one does not dwell within the realms of darkness.
All day long he eats rice, yet he has never chewed a single grain. All day long he wears clothes, yet not a single thread has ever been hung upon him.
Directly beneath, he is like a long sword leaning against the heavens; for a thousand days he shines simultaneously. The devas have no way to offer flowers;
the non-Buddhists have no door by which to peer. This is not done by force; it is because the Dharma is thus. To a Bodhisattva, this is called the six perfections and the myriad practices.
As for its practice: among śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is called the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
among devas, it is celestial adornment; among humans, it is human wealth and happiness; among asuras, it is the extinction of strife for asuras; among pretas, it is the removal of hunger for pretas;
among those in the hells, it is coolness for those in the hells; and among animals, it is intelligence for animals. This is merit.

There is nothing that is not gathered; there is no transgression that is not extinguished. Delivering the four modes of birth and serving as a bridge and vessel for the nine realms of existence—how do you express this single phrase regarding the gathering of causes and the ripening of results?
Within the sea of afflictions, they act as rain and dew; upon the Nameless Mountain, they become clouds and thunder.
The attendant Zhi requested a general discourse. The Master said: "Beneath the feet of every person lies a great matter, like a thousand suns rising at once;
it is like the sun shining without a cloud in the sky, or ten thousand mirrors facing a terrace—within the mirrors there are no images.

From the very beginning, before parents were even born, through to earth, water, fire, and wind, it is never distinguished as true or conventional, beautiful or ugly, nor does it carry the notions of self and other, right and wrong."
After it has been dispersed, there has never been so much as a hair’s breadth of appearance or even a single thread of separation.
It covers heaven and earth, spanning from antiquity to the present; Buddhas and patriarchs alike have realized and entered it together.
As when Master Shishi saw someone approaching, he would immediately pick up his staff and say: "The Buddhas of the past were like this; the Buddhas of the present are also like this."
"Ma! The Buddhas of the future will also be like this. Thus it was for thirty years—like a donkey urinating in search of a damp spot.
One day Changsha Chengyan, the Great Tiger, said to him, "Master, put down the staff in your hand and deliver another message.
Shishuang then desisted; "One is not, two is not"—this too was a lapse. Furthermore, Shushan addressed the assembly, saying, "I, the old monk..."
Before the Xiántóng era, one realizes the affairs of the *dharmakāya*; after the Xiántóng era, one realizes the matters above the *dharmakāya*.
Regarding these two layers of public cases, Yúnmén came forward and asked: "What are the affairs of the *dharmakāya*?
Shànshān said: "A withered stump. [Yúnmén said: "Wrong. Yúnmén asked: "What are the matters above the *dharmakāya*? Shànshān said: "Not a withered stump. [Yúnmén said: "Understood."
Mendun asked, "Do you permit a student to speak according to principle? Shanshan said, "I do. (This is like "inviting a thief to break into one's house.
Mendun said, "As for a withered stump—is that not a matter concerning the realm of the Dharma? Shanshan said, "It is. (If one explains it, it is no longer sufficient.)
Mendun said, "It is not a withered stump. Does this not clarify matters regarding the Dharma-body? Shanshan said, "Yes. [Mendun] fell into the seventh and eighth stages of confusion.
Mendun asked, "Does the Dharma-body encompass all things? Shanshan said, "The Dharma-body is all-pervasive; how could it not encompass them?

Long ago, when the Patriarch Nanyue Huairang saw Master Mazu sitting in meditation, he asked him one day, "Virtuous One, you sit in meditation—what do you hope to achieve? The Master replied, "I hope to become a Buddha."

The Patriarch then took the brick and began grinding it upon a stone in front of the Master’s hut. When the Master saw this, he asked, “What are you doing? The Patriarch replied, “I am grinding it into a mirror. The Master said, “How can grinding a brick produce a mirror? The Patriarch said, “How can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha? The Master asked, “What then is the way? The Patriarch said, “It is like a cow pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, would you strike the cart or strike the ox? The Master said, “I would strike the ox. The Patriarch said, “If that is so, why do you strike the cart? The Master was at a loss for words. The Patriarch then left. Later, when the Master was traveling through Mount Shao, he met the Patriarch again. The Master asked, “Since you left me, what have you been doing? The Patriarch replied, “I have been practicing the Way. The Master asked, “And what is the Way? The Patriarch said, “It is simply not being deluded. The Master said, “Who is it that is not deluded? The Patriarch said, “This is a question you should ask yourself. The Master remained silent. The Patriarch said, “Do not seek outside yourself; the Buddha-nature is right within you. Upon hearing these words, the Master attained great awakening. He then composed a verse: “Grinding a brick cannot make a mirror; Sitting in meditation cannot make a Buddha. The nature of the mind is originally clear and bright; The body of the Way is fundamentally perfect and complete. When the clouds disperse, the moon appears in the sky; When the wind ceases, the water becomes calm. The myriad phenomena are all empty and still; Only the True Mind is eternal. Having spoken this verse, the Master bowed and departed. The Patriarch called out to him, “Wait! The Master turned his head. The Patriarch said, “Have you forgotten the verse you just composed? The Master replied, “I have not forgotten it. The Patriarch said, “Then recite it once more. The Master recited it from beginning to end. The Patriarch said, “From here on, you must not speak of this verse to anyone else. The Master bowed and withdrew. That night, the Patriarch passed away. The Master then returned to Mount Huangmei and succeeded to the Dharma. This is known as the Fifth Patriarch, Great Master Hongren. The Master’s dharma heirs included Huineng, Daoxin, Puji, and others. His lineage flourished greatly. It is said that the Patriarch’s original name was Sengcan; he was a native of Xunyang in Nanjun. He was a descendant of the imperial clan of the Han dynasty. He entered the monastic order under the guidance of Master Tanyou of Mount Dongting. He received the full precepts at the age of twenty-five and studied the *Lotus Sūtra* extensively. Later, he traveled to Mount Shuangfeng in the province of Jingzhou, where he encountered the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin. The Patriarch recognized his potential and transmitted the Dharma to him. He resided at Mount Shuangfeng for thirty years, during which time he taught extensively and guided many disciples. He passed away in the year of the Jiazi cycle at the age of seventy-two. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Shuangfeng. His posthumous title was Great Master Dayi. His teachings were compiled into the *Record of the Transmission of the Lamp*. His legacy continues to this day.

The same applies to the Way and the formless samādhi. The Master asked again, "Is there arising and ceasing? The Patriarch said, "If one perceives the Way through arising and ceasing, that is incorrect.
Later, when Master Mazu appeared in the world, a monk asked him, "What is the cultivation of the Way?

He replied, "The Way does not belong to cultivation. If one says it is attained through cultivation, then what is cultivated will arise and subsequently perish; this is the same as [the aforementioned error]."
The Śrāvaka said, "If one does not practice, one is the same as an ordinary person. The Master asked, "What kind of understanding must one have to be called a practitioner of the Way?

The Master said, "These belong to the realm of conditioned activity. Furthermore, if you seek outwardly, you will only wander further astray."

This becomes increasingly remote; it merely exhausts the mental constructs (*cittamātra*) of the triple world. A single moment of deluded mind is itself the root of birth and death within the triple world.

He said, "I am no human being. In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once lived on this mountain.

Because a student asked me, 'Does one who practices great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect? I replied, 'It does not fall within cause and effect. Consequently, for five hundred lifetimes I have fallen into the body of a wild fox.
Now I beg the Elder Master to provide a turning word on my behalf, so that I may be released from this wild fox body. The Old Man [consented].
He then asked, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect? Zhaozhou replied, "They do not obscure cause and effect.
At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment and immediately cast off his wild fox body. Miaoxi said: "‘Not falling’ and ‘not obscuring’—half are bright and half are dark.
‘Not obscuring’ and ‘not falling’—both ends are empty and desolate. This was the very wild fox from five hundred lifetimes past."

The fox! Now, in this cold place, you vainly pursue and call out. [The Master] lets out a shout and says: "Since there are guests from Jiangnan among those seated here, do not sing the *zhègū* before the wine-cup.

People are also among the wild foxes. Tianning is not one who hammers in a stake while rocking a rudder, or who fixes the bridge-pins to tune the strings.

its body perishes beneath the blade. Although Yantou had a path for escape within the tiger’s pit and a mechanism for emerging upon the edge of the sword, if one examines this closely, he still lacked full awakening. It was merely...

He was about to change the eyes of all people under heaven, yet this monk, with a single broken fishing line, without raising a weapon, pierced his nostrils.

Thus, the 'Snow Melody of the Yangchun' is difficult for people of the age to harmonize; as for the songs of the village and the dances of the community, they are found everywhere."
When one attains harmony with others, Miaoxi said: "Old Man Shun is indeed so, yet he cannot avoid being caught in a tangle.
Upādao, you who do not spare your own eyebrows, shall explain it through for all of you: sound is not sound; form is not form.
"Behind the horse, ahead of the donkey; spirits appearing and ghosts vanishing. "The *xuequ* and *yangchun* melodies do not harmonize in equal measure;
village songs and communal dances are but a muddled jumble. [The Master] struck the meditation seat with his whisk and said, "This is certainly not sound. He then raised it again and said:

"This is definitely not form (*rūpa*). But what, after all, is it? [The Master] gave a shout and said, "If you do not investigate the source at this very moment, you must wait until the future to ask Maitreya.
The Master continued, "Benren, you have only managed to say that 'sound is not sound' and 'form is not form.
What extraordinary quality is there in that? Though it may be like the 'White Snow' and 'Yangchun' songs," [he added].
He can indeed sing it, yet how can people harmonize with it? Where does the mystery lie? Sound is not sound; form is not form.
To cite Xuefeng’s question to a monk: “Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, “Fuchuan. Xuefeng said, “You have not yet crossed the sea of birth and death.”
"Why did you overturn the boat? The monk remained silent. Upon returning, he recounted the incident to Fuchuan (Fushan).
Fuchuan said, "Why did you not say, 'He has neither birth nor death'? The monk went back to Xuefeng again. Xuefeng raised the previous conversation once more and asked the monk.
The monk said, "He has neither birth nor death. Xuefeng said, "These are not your words. The monk said, "Fuchuan spoke thus. Xuefeng said, "I have..."
"Twenty blows! I entrust them to Fushan; twenty blows the old monk shall eat himself.
In any case, it is none of your business, Ananda. Miaoxi said: "A master of the school—his natural brilliance still remains. Even so, it is like 'the heart of a thief being uneasy.
If that were the case, it would not be the monk's business at all; why then must he eat twenty blows himself? Simply add more!"
"Twenty blows! I shall simply strike him for concealing the boat and that will be the end of it. Tell me, where does his fault lie?
You are old and venerable, yet you ought not to speak on behalf of another. The Master said, "Fuchuan said, 'He has no birth-and-death.
Does he still understand Xuefeng’s meaning? If he had understood Xuefeng’s meaning, why did [Xuefeng] say, 'I have twenty blows to send with you'?"
"The overturned boat—twenty blows for the old monk myself to eat. Do you understand?
If you understand it here, then you will see that Miaoxi said, 'The heart of a thief is empty,' and thus he has thoroughly exposed Xuefeng. If that were so, it would not be the fault of this monk;
why then should twenty blows be eaten by himself? Simply add another twenty blows and strike the overturned boat, and that is all. What do you say, Miaoxi?"
Xī asked, "Is there still transgression? [The Master] placed a cangue upon his head and shackles upon his feet.

Jingqing said, "The first day of the year begins the reign; all things are renewed. The monk said, "Thank you."
The Master answered the question. Qing said, "Today the mountain monk has suffered a loss. Another monk asked Mingjiao, "Is there any Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the new year?
Mingjiao said, "No. The monk said, "Every year is a good year; every day is a good day."

this is like having a dragon's head but a snake's tail. The Master said, "Today the mountain monk has suffered a loss.
Miaoxi said, "These two venerable masters—one stands atop a high peak without revealing his crown; the other walks upon the bottom of a deep sea without getting his feet wet."

This is indeed so; yet it cannot entirely avoid some ambiguity. Tonight, if someone should ask me, Zhaojue Gaoseng, "Is there still any Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the New Year? I would simply tell them:
"Today, a troupe of servants in the tea hall is performing village songs and communal dances, playing with gods and ghosts, until the Venerable Dianxiong loses his temper and seizes his alms bowl."
He hurls the bowl-mountain with a single toss beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Startled, Kauṇḍinya becomes terrified and frantic;
he mounts a pillar upside down and leaps into the nostrils of a Chan practitioner carrying a wooden board.

He crashes into Tiantzhu Peak at Shuzhou, where the mountain deity of Anle Mountain, unable to restrain his amusement, comes forth, seizes him by the chest, and holds him fast, saying: "Venerable One, you..."

Overwhelmed by this single question and unable to bear his own embarrassment (*mala*), he turned back toward the Buddha Hall.
The third person sat in meditation. As before, he tapped his chest and ribs, saying, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
He said to himself, "Stop, stop! Upādhyāya Gao, when he asked about the Buddha-dharma at the beginning of the new year, why have you been performing somersaults in empty space all along?
You speak of liberation and deceive people with empty talk. After a long silence, he said, "Upādhyāya Gao, today you have lost ground."
