Amidst the golden auspicious clouds above the city battlements, he encountered the Sixth Patriarch on the road and immediately received his countenance. Holding a wine vessel, he chanted and whistled long;

dwelling within the city walls, he came and went as he pleased. Yet he spoke of the causes of his past offerings throughout immeasurable kalpas—one must know that the fruit of Buddhahood is not [attained through such means].
Related: At the time of his passing, he manifested the Samādhi of Compassion; he transformed fire to cremate his body with utter ease.
Eulogy for the Eighth Patriarch, Buddhanandi, of the kingdom of Kāmata:
"The small Gautama’s *uṣṇīṣa* is like a pearl emerging from the emerald mist; his discourses on meaning are praised as a wind that chills the boastful."
Ling! When the mind is clear, it does not dwell in the babbling of the mouth. Without words, how many blows of the staff can one endure? With words, one misses the mark by two or three.
Disciples of later generations merely exhaust their efforts; yet the myriad phenomena of the forested world can speak for themselves.
The Ninth Patriarch, Buddhamitra, while at the house of Viśāla, saw a white light arise; he immediately knew that a sage was hidden there.

Having passed the age of fifty, he remained mute and spoke no words, fearing that his parents’ affection for him might not yet have faded. Even the Buddhas said, "This is not my way"; where, then, shall future generations find it?
The Empty King (Śūnyarāja) came to China and India to transform beings according to their capacities; wherever he went, the green mountains became sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

The tenth patriarch, the Venerable Pārśva, was praised for remaining in his mother’s womb for sixty years, awaiting the white elephant who would bring him the jewel. In Central India, there was one named Durlabha.
The name [of this place] is so called because the *utpala* flower blooms here; its auspicious light flows through day and night without darkness.
Where once lay the dust upon the wakeful jeweled seats, now heavy carpets are laid over high pillows. How lamentable is the state of the Chan lineage in future generations!
The Eleventh Patriarch, Purnaśa, said:
"The nature of gold is impermanent and subject to change; sentient beings merely seek it outside themselves. The coming and going of the unsettled mind is not the Buddha;

through the free-flowing exchange of question and answer, one realizes that the Buddha is the mind. When the wondrous words of the teaching reveal the true nature, how could one who has dissolved their delusions still accept falsehood?"
The conditions for encroachment: the pure regulations of former sages and later saints remain; flower and leaf, layer upon layer, cover the ancestral grove.
Verse on the Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa:
Not recognizing is precisely recognizing the Buddha-body; The previous life was clearly that of a silkworm; With a great mind, one naturally suffices to encompass the dragon.
The treasury is deep; what prevents one from ferrying those who are like horses? The King of Vaiśālī is named Ajātaśatru; in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the transformation is newly underway.
Whether as being or non-being, his merit is preeminent; wherever he goes, he turns the wheel of Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
The thirteenth patriarch, Kāpimāla:
how extraordinary was his initial manifestation of supernatural powers! By transforming demons into Buddhas, he first opened their minds;

thereafter, three thousand followers took refuge, and five hundred divine monks arrived for the *karmavācanā*. Like the vast ocean containing the ocean of true nature, how could such a sage’s transformations not be so?
Ordinary talent. For sentient beings, there is no need to discuss whether they are ordinary or sage; it is but a single hair-tip that encompasses the nine extremities of the universe.
The fourteenth patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was praised thus:
"In the deep mountains, solitary and remote, human tracks are severed; beneath the great tree, five hundred dragons lie hidden. He constantly aspired to seek a teacher, yet found none."

Meeting by chance, we fortunately encounter one another through the conditions of hearing the Dharma. In the human world, people cherish only the blessings of rebirth in heaven; yet here on this seat, I suddenly behold your face like the full moon.
If one does not understand the principle of formlessness upon reaching this point, the clouds of delusion will still lock one in layer after layer.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Kanadeva, praised the Buddha-nature as being like the full moon:
"Majestic and signless, it is truly real. Having heard the Dharma from the Master, the ground of the mind was opened;
piercing water with a needle reveals the wise man. Meritorious karma is transformed into the karma of the Tamer; false causes are turned into Nirvana."
The *Bannin* [inscription] at the Long Banner Gate in Pāṭaliputra. One phrase concerning the color of the parasol and the sound of the horse.
The sixteenth patriarch, Rāhulabhadra, praised the preaching of the Dharma by insentient things;
there was a reason for this. The previous life of the wooden fungus was that of a bhikṣu; father and son ate together, yet it remains as it is today.

This concludes it. The retribution of causes and conditions shall be discussed later. The World-Honored One Śākyamuni has already prophesied the events of a thousand years. As the Teacher of the Doctrine, he should act as a peer among the assembly of sages.
Pointing toward the golden bowl meal in the Brahma Palace, both teacher and disciple have gained a full and contented slumber.
Hymn to the Seventeenth Patriarch Saṃghanandin:
He passed away from the presence of the Buddha Śālarāja, And returned to the world of dust to honor the multitude of deluded beings. Suddenly, at midnight, the light of heaven shone forth;
He went straight to a cave in a high cliff to dwell. The gold remained in the well, fundamentally unmoving; When food arrived from the heavens, it was for him alone.
Who carries [it]? Because there is neither self nor non-self, it is established for you. This matter is clearly presented face-to-face.

The eighteenth patriarch Gayasata praised the purple clouds like a canopy emerging from the mountain peak; the youth was just then holding a precious mirror while wandering. This is precisely the hundredth year of the Sage’s opportunity.

Throughout the years, he has simultaneously pursued the Way and its Virtue, continuing the practice of former masters. The wind-bells merely ring out from the mind; flowers and fruits are sought through planting in the earth.
When there is no flaw within or without, what need is there for outward display? Do not allow yourself to mistake them for bubbles on the water.
Eulogy on the Nineteenth Patriarch, Kumāralata:
The moment he heard the knocking at the door, doubt suddenly arose: "In this house there is no one; who is it that answers? A bright moon emerges from the clouds ten thousand miles away;
a *maṇi* jewel appears at the bottom of a thousand-fathom deep pool. Why do you rush about seeking Buddhas and patriarchs? Let go of body and mind—this is the right way.
At this moment, when not a single thought arises, the three periods of time are severed; from the beginning, the nostrils have hung down large.
The twentieth patriarch, Jayata, praised this mind as pure, without arising or ceasing—tranquil yet numinous, manifest before one. All who enter this gate are [thus enlightened].
The Buddha. Previously, the various patriarchs had no transmission. The double-tusked lion roars in the mountains; the broad-horned ox sleeps at the bottom of the water.
If you further weary yourself by discussing sin and merit, not only are you laughable, but you are also pitiable.
Hymn to the Twenty-first Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha:

This day we praise the one named Sarvāstivādin (Pervasive Practice), a *dhūta* ascetic. In his previous life, he was born in the kingdom of Changle; there, leaning on his staff, he personally performed repentance before a painted Buddha.

As a patriarch, he succeeded to the Way of the Emptiness School (*śūnyatā*), and his realization was already complete. Having illuminated the gate of the Dharma and completed his return-greeting, he shared a womb with the Bhikṣuṇī, a treasure.
Juzhuoming: To fully understand that past karma manifests through the mind, one must recognize the gravity of the offenses in the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules.
Verse 22: Eulogy of the Twenty-second Patriarch, Mañjuvara.
At the prime of his youth, he abandoned his father to follow a teacher; A solitary, towering lotus blooming amidst the flames. The royal palace was but a floating cloud to him.

Contemplation: Having personally inherited the ancestral seat transmitted by the successive sages, why would one ever disdain dwelling in a village while seated in meditation? Wandering about is merely for the purpose of transforming humans and devas.
Reflecting on this, I see that many in later generations are mediocre and reckless; who will board the Great Dharma-ship of the Tathāgata?
The Hymn for the Twenty-third Patriarch, Haklenā: In the fourth kalpa, he was a bhikṣu;
He attended the assembly at the Dragon Palace, leading the assembly of monastics. Now he comes with a flock of cranes flying in accompaniment;
This is all because his virtue was not cultivated at that time. The Golden Banner of the Seven Buddhas once received his prayers; The two individuals, the crimson and the plain, were originally...
His companions performed the cremation, and his remains once again appeared in the air; the śarīra were then gathered into a single stupa.
Verse for the Twenty-Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Siṃha:
"What need is there for a man of the Way to strive with the mind? Ultimately, being without mind is the true seeker of the Way. The younger brother Huìfāng sighed over the Dragon’s Son.

Tragically, the Master of the Crane could not escape the oppression of Māra’s grief; a white rainbow pierced straight through, a portent for our own faction, while black vapors split across the sky—surely there was a reason for this.
For now, let us pass on the *kāṣāya* to the legitimate successor; as one whose emptiness is profound, I shall no longer reckon with enmity or favor.
Hymn to the Twenty-fifth Patriarch, Vasubandhu:
Vasubandhu was one who underwent two births; as soon as that body perished, this body was formed.

Only when he opened his left fist did he first obtain the divine pearl that illuminated the seat with light. He subdued heterodox arguments on fifty-nine occasions and served as a patriarch for over a thousand years.
The wind is clear. Our late Master’s robe of verification is difficult to burn; it is enough to startle the celestial Māras and heterodox paths.

The twenty-sixth patriarch, Ramaputta, praised how he once suffered imprisonment for the sake of the Dharma, yet today returns to the Prince’s palace, intending to fulfill his original vow to leave the home-life and become a Buddha.

The matter requires that you come to succeed the Patriarch and revitalize the profound wind of the Dharma. Though the years have passed, your devotion as a śrāmaṇera has grown ever more earnest; you know all through the power of the *karmavācanā*, for the earth trembles at your every act.
What dharma do you intend to employ to deliver sentient beings? For now, let us first subdue the Brahmin through your supernormal powers.
Hymn to the Twenty-Seventh Patriarch Prajñātāra:
Without father and without name, he blends with the world; Were it not for the eye of wisdom, none could fathom him.

Know that the Great Power of the Buddha-land Is none other than the Child of the Royal Capital’s Garland. India did not remain outside this profound transformation; All of China is contained within this wondrous [truth].
In his heart, he transmitted the Way of the Buddha to his two sons in later years; one went west, and one went east.

The twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma, praised [the One Vehicle] with a single word that utterly shattered the delusions of the six schools. While in the kingdom, he eliminated heterodox views; when he first arrived in the land of Han, he was a sage of emptiness.

Truly, King Liang could not avoid being humbled by the celestial majesty. The merit of ordaining monks and building temples is difficult to discuss; though he severed his arm to find peace of mind, he did not yet enter the subtle.
Only the flowers and trees of Shaolin remain. With a pair of light sandals, he returned from the West on his own.
Hymn for the Twenty-ninth Patriarch, Grand Master Huìkě:
He read extensively across all books and possessed correct knowledge. The Great Being of Shaolin is my teacher. I pray that he may instruct me on the essential point heard beneath a single phrase.
When I came to stand in the courtyard amidst the falling snow, The entire world was empty, without a single thing. Sentient beings fail to realize this and wander in vain.

One who possesses great knowledge [knows that] the butcher’s shop and the wine tavern are fundamentally equal. If one is willing to relinquish the distinction between enemies and kin, compassion will arise spontaneously.
Verse for the Thirtieth Patriarch, Master Sengcan:
When contemplating and investigating the nature of sin, one finds it is empty. It dwells neither within nor without, nor does it abide in the middle. If we people wish to repent, how should we do so?
Confession. At the bottom, where the wind is hidden, there is yet more wind. For ten years wandering back and forth, there has been no fixed abode.
The devotion of donors from many quarters shares this same heart. In my life I have loved Mount Luofu most; in the end, I shall once again be buried at Mount Wangong.
Eulogy for the Thirty-first Patriarch, Master Daoxin:
"No one binds you—do not sigh in vain. Why do you come again seeking liberation? Upon reaching this point, let both body and mind be utterly relinquished;
thus, you shall be freed from the confinement of past suffering and joy. On Mount Poutou, the clouds are like a canopy; such were the events during the Wude era."
The tally has been struck. The Imperial Edict summons you; it is enough to provoke a smile. The myriad affairs of this floating life are all but trivial.
Eulogy for the Thirty-second Patriarch, Great Master Hongren:
Shide, that child on the road to Huangmei, Was able to speak of Buddha-nature long ago, no longer a fool. What was his body in a former, past life?

The limit has been reached. On this day, he returned home, yet his mother remained unaware. Only seven of the Tathāgata’s marks were lacking; a single horizontal branch split off from the ancestral trunk of faith.
At midnight, a guest took the robe and departed; when he no longer ascended the hall, the assembly first began to doubt.
Eulogy for the Thirty-third Patriarch, Master Huineng:
Originally from Xinzhou, he was a woodcutter by trade. Having happened to hear a merchant reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he immediately went to the Fifth Patriarch to study Chan.
He laughed at the haste of writing the verse at the third watch; through this, the debate over the wind and the banner was settled. Thus the robe and bowl were transmitted down to him.
Now, this collection deceives people; they claim to have come with no mouth, yet their talk of the *Platform Sūtra* is even longer.

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praised the northeast of Jambudvīpa as the most cool and refreshing; here resides Mañjuśrī, the Wondrous Auspicious One, who practices the Way amidst the mountains and rivers of the Purple Palace.
Abiding in a golden palace, he gathers the radiance of his own body; ten thousand bodhisattvas serve as his retinue, and five hundred nāgas protect the site of enlightenment.
Though he is indeed the Buddha Samantadarśin of the future, when one observes his skillful means, they are nonetheless quite ordinary.

A Praise of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the Eldest Son of the Tathāgata: The vows and practices of the Honored Samantabhadra are vast and profound, beyond the reach of speech. A single hue of shimmering silver blankets the world;
a six-tusked fragrant elephant shakes heaven and earth. As numerous as the atoms within the infinite oceans of lands, they are inconceivable and great.
In this Dharma gate, from beginning to end, how could one ever depart from the present moment? Ordinary people merely toy with their own spirits.

As for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, he praises the sacred mountains by the sea as abounding in sages and worthies; his power of compassionate vows is foremost among all. His countenance is like a precious moon, facing the three...

Five. His transformations are like clouds of oil covering the great trichiliocosm; amidst clusters of jeweled necklaces he constantly speaks of the wondrous, and within sandalwood groves he always discourses on the profound mystery.
When will there be a Buddha of Non-arising in this realm? I shall simply wait for the year when empty space falls to the ground (sitting upright).
The Tathāgata of the past, Zhengfaming (Vimalaprabhā), should be known to have already perfected the Buddha-way.

Yet he returns as a Bodhisattva to fulfill his profound vow, constantly delivering sentient beings within this Sahā world. He travels to the peak of Potalaka Rock to lead others back to birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Do you know how the six sense faculties function interchangeably? Green and yellow fill the ears, and sound fills the eyes—this is the manifestation at Potala.
To the east of the Great Ocean and west of the Southern Sea, in the depths of the Sea-Clouds, Sudhana went to pay his respects.

Upon the mountain peak, moonlight flows eternally; upon the surface of the water, where there is no wind, reflections remain in the pool. Having sought out the sound from afar, he first rescued those in suffering;

by hearing the Dharma and entering into its principle, he simultaneously eliminated greed. Within the realm of Jambudvīpa, his faculties are most excellent; day and night, incense and lamps share a single shrine (Sudhana and the Water-Moon).

The Avalokiteśvara of the past is the very same as the Avalokiteśvara of the future; not separate from the faith and understanding of sentient beings, he manifests thirty-two forms according to what is appropriate.
Through hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, he remains as if in the present moment. When the faculties and their objects are exhausted, one is liberated within the realm of sound;

when the ocean of karma is spent, all returns to the profound ocean of vows. Sooner or later, may we be rescued by his lotus-boat—the blind turtle meeting the floating log, like a mustard seed being pierced by a needle.
Fundamentally dwelling in stillness, the body does not move; according to conditions, he preaches the Dharma to transform devas and humans.

A solitary moon suddenly appears amidst the waves; ten thousand nations secretly experience spring within the snow. When deluded, sentient beings repay their karmic fruits; when awakened, there is no ear that clings to the dust of sound.
This majestic and subtle realm of perfect penetration—let the great earth, mountains, and rivers serve as its demonstration. (Devas and Humans / Water and Moon)
Mañjuśrī carefully selects the perfect penetration (*āyatana*), examining each faculty-door and its respective function. All the Sages unanimously extol the subtle principle of hearing;
yet when the six sense-objects reach their point of use, they are empty. A sound resonates through a wall without distinction of distance;

while the verbal expressions for entering the Way have a beginning and an end, one who has secured the wish-fulfilling jewel of radiant light brings benefit to self and others—what joy could ever be exhausted? (The Pearl Vase and Jewel Throne)
O Holy Master, do not debate the ancient and the modern; The True Teaching is difficult to divide into essence and function. The formless has never been separate from the formed;

What I have heard is ultimately no different from what others have heard. It relies entirely upon the power of a single thought of compassion, And is also aided by the熏 (perfuming) of samādhi and wisdom over many lifetimes.
Monks of the Dharma-ending age can all realize this; The Tathāgata’s words of truth do not deceive you. (A monk prostrated.)
Gazing afar at Mount Potalaka, the small white flowers are in full bloom, ready to be plucked. The sound of the tide crashing against the shore rolls on incessantly;
the birds chirping through the forest call out *guan-guan* all day long. Recite the "Universal Gate" chapter constantly; for sentient beings of meager merit, this may seem trivial.

Yet, through simply hearing, contemplating, and practicing it without confusion, one shall behold the Compassionate Countenance in every movement—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. (Flowers by the Shore, Rock Caves)
One night, the monk Jingqian of Donglin dreamed that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said to him, "I have bestowed three pearls upon this woman.
Arise, arise! The donor has arrived. The next day, a certain lady arrived. [Jingqian] wished to adorn the precious image;
consequently, they opened the belly of the statue and found therein a square-inch mirror, a scripture written in fine silver script, and a lapis lazuli bottle. Inside the bottle—
It was as large as a finger. Within it, three śarīras leaped about, emitting light. I tested them with an iron awl;
the awl penetrated, yet the śarīras remained unharmed. I happened to witness this and prostrated myself a hundred times, bowing my head to the ground, and composed a eulogy, saying:
The sounds of the world are all heard with the ears, yet this Great Being alone perceives them with his eyes.
Since his eyes perceive sound and his ears hear form, form is not inherently form and sound is not inherently sound. When the single mind does not arise, the six faculties are simultaneously stilled.
Because both are quiescent, he is able to give rise to great compassion; because of great compassion, he delivers all sentient beings.
Sometimes he acts as a painter and paints his own image; sometimes he acts as a carver and carves his own form; sometimes he manifests as an eagle’s nest; and sometimes he manifests as a clam’s egg.
And as for these various marks, this great compassion neither arises nor is there one who receives it. Regarding this, I say:
like the eye toward forms and the ear toward sounds, although they cannot be grasped, they are nonetheless indestructible, for all are like illusions.
Since all things are like dreams, I prostrate to the image that is like an illusion and like a dream; I prostrate to the sutra that is like an illusion and like a dream;
I prostrate to the jewel that is like an illusion and like a dream; I prostrate to the mirror that is like an illusion and like a dream.
May the assembly, who are like illusions and like dreams, all awaken to the mind that is like an illusion and like a dream, and may they all become Buddhas who are like illusions and like dreams.
I prostrate to the true essence of the teaching in this realm, vast and unimpeded, pervading all lands as numerous as grains of sand.

In accordance with the inverted perceptions of sentient beings, there is nothing they seek that is not obtained. Although it manifests in thirty-two forms according to their bodies, the phrases of the Dharma taught are but a single sound.
This sound does not arise from the faculty of the tongue, nor does it enter through the faculty of the ear; such is the nature of the six sense bases.
It is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished; therefore, those who invoke my name attain liberation. I too have realized this gate of liberation, which is no different from that of Avalokiteśvara.
Both difference and non-difference are also quiescent and extinguished, and there is neither quiescence nor one who is extinguished.
Therefore, I am identical to this Avalokiteśvara, and all sentient beings likewise realize this.

The ordinary mind is pure like water; the Sage’s transformation is perfect like the moon. A single reflection falls upon a thousand waves; high and low alike are clear and transparent. Originally, it is neither defiled nor pure;
how could one further discuss its waxing or waning? It is one and the same inconceivable reality—how can one engage in deluded discrimination?
I contemplate the Honored One Avalokiteśvara, whose essence and function both transcend all bounds. Within these oysters and clams, he encompasses lands as numerous as motes of dust;

in the space of a finger-snap, there are asaṃkhyeya eons. A great trichiliocosm fits within a single hair, and its robes and caps can be clearly counted—by whom were these necklaces and ornaments fashioned?
Wishing to use the mind as a metaphor for a pearl, he took his own body as the tongue to fully open the gate of perfect penetration, enabling the removal of the knots of affliction.

According to the capacities of beings, he preached the thirty-two methods, each one with blazing intensity. Yet, when the speaker’s words were cut off and the listener’s mental activity ceased, true realization was attained.
The Great Being is ever-present before us; with its cool clarity, it washes away the scorching heat (like the image of a clam or oyster).

It is profoundly still and unmoving, its substance like empty space. It enters along with all elevations and depressions; sense organs and objects merge into one another. When it is within the ear, what is there to observe?

In deep valleys, sounds echo back as responses; though they are before one's eyes, what need is there to listen? When spring blossoms unfurl their colors to illuminate the thickets, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all proclaim wondrous wisdom;
metal, stone, strings, and bamboo instruments all perform the discourse of universal penetration. Thus, I pay homage with my head to the image of the Tathāgata.
His eyebrows arch like the bow of Śakra; he possesses a śakrābhilagna head, pure jewel-like eyes, and mūdrā-arms, each numbering eighty-four thousand.
There is nothing he seeks that he cannot obtain. Whether sentient beings are walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they are constantly within his embrace.
This fresh grape leaf is entirely due to illusory delusion that reveals its full efficacy.
I observe that within the three realms of dust and toil, sentient beings are in turmoil; their own nature is not clear, being obstructed by craving and desire.

They are submerged in the ocean of suffering, following the waves of consciousness. From kalpa to kalpa, they discard the false only to grasp at the false again. Therefore, the Great Being Wenshi, by means of...
Compassion and skillful means serve as a lotus-leaf boat; having emerged, one places it upon the further shore.
There, one suddenly realizes one's own nature and seeks no further outward. Avalokiteśvara is you, and you are Avalokiteśvara.

Those who invoke his name share the merit of sixty-two billion bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Yet, in responding to the capacities of sentient beings, he differs from the thirty-two manifestations that preach the Dharma in various lands.
The Dharma-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories; there is no place where it does not manifest.
Without feeling there is no response. As I contemplate this image, it is like the moon in the sky; though its orb is one, its light pervades the hundred rivers.

Through emptiness awakening to emptiness, and through the awakening of emptiness becoming empty, layer upon layer of illusions are extinguished, and in every thought-moment the Way is perfected. It encompasses the eighty-four thousand [dharmas].
The thousand gates of the *pāramitās* constitute a single universal gate (*samantamukha*); there is no gate to be opened.

This is the inconceivable wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), which constitutes a single sagely wisdom; there is no wisdom to be defined. To scoop up the moon from amidst a mass of fierce flames, and for the waves to overturn at the summit of Mount Sumeru.
A single invocation of his name eradicates immeasurable suffering; a single sight of his form bestows immeasurable bliss.

Without stirring his countenance or spirit, he suddenly manifests throughout the ten directions; universally employing compassion and wisdom, he dwells eternally within the five turbidities. He hears what cannot be heard and awakens to what cannot be awakened.
The moon is bright across the vast sky as a single stone sheds its clouds; the wind rises over the great plains as the tides recede from the four oceans.
Seated in meditation upon a flat rock, the mind has no object of focus. Responding mysteriously to ten thousand occasions, how can the Way be discussed?

It can cause the suffering to find joy, the obscured to find clarity, the premature to attain longevity, and the dead to return to life. Listen to the forms and images of the ten directions and observe the entirety of the realm...
The sound is majestic and vast; indeed, it is beyond the reach of naming.

In every thought-moment, he gives rise to loving-kindness and exercises compassion, so that every person may leave suffering behind and attain happiness. With a single glance or a single prostration, all together realize the eternally abiding Dharma-body.
Whether saintly or ordinary, all are led to achieve Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Having come from immeasurable kalpas in the past, [the moon...]
It cannot be fished from the surging waves;

it is within the eyes, the ears, and the nose. Whether in the small chiliocosm, the medium dichiliocosm, or the great trichiliocosm, whenever a single sentient being suffers, they receive the compassionate pity of the Great Being.
Water is on earth and the moon is in the sky, yet the true essence stands majestically right before one’s eyes.
The moon in the heavens and the moon in the water—alike through antiquity and today, both waxing and waning. This very gate of universal penetration has never required a word of explanation.
In the vast, boundless ocean floats a single lotus leaf; though empty space may come to an end, the fragrance never ceases.
The Holy Teacher has nothing to say; the youth has nothing to hear. The green mountains are simply green mountains; the white clouds are simply white clouds.
Having sifted through all twenty-five modes of perfect penetration, Mañjuśrī’s eloquence is but a vain flurry.
A single scroll of the Universal Gate Chapter: vertically and horizontally it rests upon the tip of the brush; throughout its entire body there is no image. The paper is filled with black ants;
empty space collapses and Mount Sumeru shatters. Having delivered all sentient beings, his vow does not cease.

The Great Being is the father of all sentient beings; sentient beings are the children of the Great Being. As a father feels the greatest compassion for his child, how could he not give rise to loving-kindness and pity?
Upon a seat of fragrant grass and with branches of green willow, this is precisely the time to completely transcend the eight difficulties.
The response-body that accords with types takes this very body as its tongue; this gate of perfect penetration speaks incessantly and fervently.
It is able to hear with the eyes, and its sound is without interruption—majestic and sublime, eternally abiding and never extinguished.
The basket does not see the fish; the entire body is eyes. If the eyes were to see, it would be like a fish falling into the basket.
When seeing and non-seeing are both transcended, and hearing and non-hearing are extinguished—excellent, O Mahāsattva! You constantly manifest within this Sahā world.
Awakened, the sky is vast and open; the moon of the mind is solitary and full. Sitting in repose, unmoving, its radiance is boundless.
Narrow, it is but a single hair; broad, it encompasses the great chiliocosm. Roll up the painting, and the true body manifests before you.
Manifesting in the form of a celestial maiden, she gathers the minds of sentient beings; like a blue lotus, she emits a great mass of fire that cools their feverish afflictions.
Both of these are empty. I prostrate to her compassion, which does not depart from this very place.
Entering through hearing, one then contemplates and practices. The liberation of sentient beings is not sought outwardly.
A single speck of dust upon the great earth, a single bubble in the vast ocean—the true essence is unmoving, yet its manifestations pervade everywhere.
The countenance of perfect penetration is difficult to depict; it is right here before you, how very clear!
When the wind moves the myriad leaves of the green willows, at dawn come the two or three calls of the yellow birds.
By the power of wondrous wisdom, sounds reach the eyes and forms reach the ears; though they fill the void, not a trace remains.
Even when layers upon layers of clouds obscure the body above, they appear before one in an instant, fundamentally never separated.
The vow of compassion is as heavy as a mountain; the dust of karma and worldly toil is as deep as the sea.
Selling fish at the crossroads, the mind that protects life is itself the mind that kills.
At the side of the Vajra-stone, Sudhana visited; compassion was inevitably provided as his guide. Simply say:
what is present before one cannot be spoken of; it is like a single bright moon in a cold pond.
Perfect penetration does not permit leaving the mundane world; the Way resides within ordinary daily activities. A few strokes of pale mist enshroud the emerald trees;
a single flying waterfall descends the green mountains.
How can one grasp the reflection of the moon in water? One need not pole the lotus-boat beneath one's feet.
Holding up the rosary of one hundred and eight beads—when has one ever sought sentient beings outside of the Buddha?
Through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one realizes compassion, wisdom, and vows. This body is fundamentally empty, yet there is no land where it does not appear:
a white moon disc radiating light within the azure void, with a golden face from which a jade-like *ūrṇā* protrudes.
The people of this Sahā world possess great karmic conditions; it requires only a single invocation of the name for it to manifest before them.
But who is it that moves their mouths right now? You must go ask the Immortal in White Robes.
Clearly discerning, awakening, and contemplating, one leaves behind the sense organs and their objects; universally delivering the deluded multitudes from the wheel of suffering.
One must believe that within the midst of blazing sounds and forms, the unchanging Suchness manifests its entire body.

The whale emerges from the sea, tossing the waves; the *huānguǒ* parrot arrives from the void. From within its mouth, the pure flask murmurs incessantly, proclaiming that the Perfect Penetration leads all toward Sudhana.

When seeing forms, the mind first manifests; when hearing sounds, the Way is already revealed. Your compassionate countenance is like the single orb of the moon; beholding and prostrating before it brings refreshing clarity.
The rocks reveal coral trees; the mountains contain amethyst clouds. In the void, there is speech beyond speech; upon the great earth, there is hearing beyond hearing.
After the rain, the azure sky is clear; clouds stretch across, heavy with purple mist. Suddenly I behold the wondrous form: the entire sea is filled with lotuses. Waves strike the gray cliffs;
the wind blows through the purple bamboo grove. Two parrots fly in, facing one another as they speak of the Mind-Only.
Encountering suffering, one rescues from suffering; following the currents, one enters the flow.

Across the boundless ocean of lands, a single-leaf lotus boat sails through a marketplace where fish are sold and the stench of rot fills the roads. Sentient beings are easy to deliver, but false teachings are difficult to support.
Praise to the Bodhisattva Cintāmaṇicakravartin:
Homage to the Great Being, the King of the Wish-Fulfilling Wheel! Fundamentally, there is not a single dharma; he pervades the ten directions.

Therefore, for one who recites the mantra, body and mind are peaceful and blissful even before the sound is uttered; for one who gazes upon the sacred image, movement and stillness are [tranquil] even before the eyes are raised.

Auspiciousness! Accomplishing ten thousand virtues and extinguishing a thousand calamities, I now take the waters of the four great oceans as milk, the five Sumeru mountains as incense, the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees as implements of offering, and the sun, moon, and stars as the light of lamps and candles.
The worlds are unspeakable in number; space cannot be measured. Together with all sentient beings...

They shall be born together and practice the Dharma in unison, making offerings according to the teachings until the very end of future kalpas, thereby adorning and purifying the Bodhisattva’s site of enlightenment.
Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha has manifested a body of compassion since time immemorial; dwelling in the hells as if visiting a garden, he causes all sentient beings to be forever liberated.
The Wheel of Suffering: when a single precious jewel is lifted up, it illuminates the darkness; when the six-ringed golden staff is moved, it increases majestic power.
Those who uphold its name shall escape the retribution of birth and death; those who behold its image shall realize the cause of Nirvana.
The inconceivable power of great vows; for future beings across the boundless ocean of lands.
Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into Vimalakīrti’s Illness;
a eulogy on the Dharma-gate of Non-duality, free from discrimination. Thirty-two people probe the moon in the water; the youth Mañjuśrī is fundamentally non-existent.
It is said: "Yet it is Vimalakīrti who is truly loquacious. The creation of this painting was not accidental; its intent lies in both speech and silence.
Contemplating that which precedes heaven, the flower falls to the ground, brushed away by the hand. All phenomena listen as the lion’s roar resounds."
The Great Being Mañjuśrī praises the mountain-jade for its brilliance; his turning of the jewel is unhindered. He assists the King of Emptiness and proclaims the supreme meaning.

That which is the fundamental ignorance of sentient beings is the subtle wisdom of discernment of all Buddhas. At times he holds a thousand bowls; at times he manifests five topknots; or he provides instruction...
He guides the sixteen princes as the Dharma Master Wondrous Light; or he exhorts six thousand bhikṣus at the eastern edge of the City of Enlightenment.
There, the Elephant King turns in circles and the Lion performs his playful dance. In every place is the World of Golden Color; in every place is Mañjuśrī.
Directly speaking, people do not understand; the void further extends its golden arm.
The Layman Vimalakīrti accommodated thirty-two thousand lion thrones without leaving his room of ten feet square; yet, for that single moment of silence,
he was called an "old man of many words."
Maitreya Bodhisattva praised [the world] for five hundred and sixty million years before finally descending to be born among humans. Not dwelling within the Heaven of Contentment,
his body and mind remain at ease wherever they go.

Praise for the Tooth Relic of a Pratyekabuddha Presented to Cheng, the Librarian of Japan, by a Boy upon His Arrival in Wu. While on his way to Japan, Cheng the Librarian encountered a young boy who offered him the tooth relic of a pratyekabuddha. Having obtained it, he treasured it and requested a eulogy.
The eulogy says: [The eulogy follows.]

There was a sentient being who appeared in a world where no Buddha dwelt. Having previously received the prediction of becoming a Pratyekabuddha in past kalpas, he attained realization through the blooming of flowers and the falling of leaves;

his mind merged with the essence of reality, and by contemplating these causes and conditions, he suddenly transcended to a higher state. Within the triple world, he was like a bird escaping from a cage.

Although he did not preach the Dharma, he manifested supernatural powers: he rubbed the sun and moon with his hands and lay his body across the void, performing eighteen such transformations to enlighten the ignorant masses.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he emitted the fire of samādhi, spontaneously dissolving his physical frame until only a skeleton remained.
The wondrous śarīra fell in various grains, clustering like pearls and dropping one by one. The Venerable Dao-ren obtained one of its large teeth;
it was as hard as vajra and as pure as a lotus flower. It could not be crushed by mortars or pestles, and was as flawless as jade or snow.

I prostrate twice with my head to the ground. Might there not be some small measure of good fortune? I have composed these words of praise to look up to his lofty footsteps; may their subtle influence permeate the Dharma-realm, purifying the eyes and mind.

May spiritual beings provide protection and guardianship, so that the entrustment is never forgotten. If people can maintain reverence and faith, there shall be no one who does not give rise to merit.
*Fó rì pǔ zhào huì biàn chǔ shí chán shī yù lù*, Scroll Thirteenth. Phonetic Transcriptions:
Tián (dú jiān qiè) Diāo (dīng yāo qiè) Shǔn (shí yǔn qiè) Dié (tú yè qiè) Zhì (chú shì qiè) Yīn (yú shēn qiè) Xié (xié)

(xū yè qiè) gāi (gǔ tái qiè) jùn (qí yǐn qiè) yíng (yú chéng qiè) hōu (huǒ hòu qiè) zhī (qí zhī èr yīn) fàn (fú fàn qiè) huǐ (huī guǐ qiè) cuò (zǔ guò qiè) huǎn (hù bǎn qiè) gé (gǔ hé qiè) láo (lù gāo qiè) bí (pí yīn) fú (fú niú qiè)
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huibian Chushi, “The Sun of the Buddha Shining Universally,” Volume Fourteen, Part Two:
Verses and Eulogies of Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Compiled by Attendants Wensheng, Zhenglong, and others.
Praise of the First of the Sixteen Great Arhats,
the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja of Aparagoyānī Island.

Possessing the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, you are a most excellent field of merit for humans and devas. By making offerings to you, one can summon superior fruits;

by spreading out a seat, one may verify the freshness of the flowers upon it. Within the palace of the Dragon King, there abound rare delicacies; in the continent of Goḍānīya, there exists a great affinity.
The waters of the ocean were churned to produce the flavor of ambrosia; through this, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is brought to fulfillment in this heart.
The second was the Venerable Kanakavatsa, a Great Being of Kaśmīra who resided among the cliffs and beneath trees;
his dwelling was even more serene and empty. He came at times to benefit sentient beings, first forgetting his own food, seeking only what was necessary to sustain his body and desiring nothing else.
When he listened to the Dharma, a blue dragon would place the alms-bowl within his mouth; a white deer would run about, holding flowers in its mouth.
On the steps and ledges, the bright moonlight of the long night is as clear as if washed away. Sitting, I listen to a śrāmaṇera reciting Sanskrit texts.
On the third terrace is Pūrvavideha-dvīpa; the Venerable Kanakavatsa dwells eternally in Pūrvavideha.
As I sit here, I see only the dust rising from the ocean; crossing the river, I divide myself into three.
A beast, yet at the end it may manifest the auspicious sign of a single qilin. How fleeting is the long duration of time in the heavens; how hurried is the brevity of an eon in the world.
In the emptiness of nature, every thought-moment is free from craving and desire. Cherish this well, and cast yourself entirely away from those in the burning house.
The fourth position is the North Kuru continent, the venerable Sūpīṇḍa, within a great trichiliocosm of worlds.

It is commonly said that the Buddha-dharma does not exist here; the garments from the kalpa-trees are not prized by the heart, and since one is satiated by the long-grained rice, what need is there for it?
Yet, provided that the hearts of those receiving transformation are subdued, how could one worry about being lost in a foreign land?
Tujū. This Way circulates throughout the four continents; the fruits of the karma of sentient beings are easily withered and decayed.
In the fifth position, the Venerable Nāgārjuna of Jambudvīpa was manifest in the world and transcended it;
whether wandering through marketplaces or dwelling in the mountains, he has come of his own accord to rest his mind at Yandang.

For a long time he has been away, returning from preaching the Dharma in the Dragon Palace. Gigantic boulders burst open, scattering clouds in fragments; from the high cliffs, waterfalls cascade down with a murmuring roar.
Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—there is nothing that is not meditative concentration. Who would say that his clear nights and bright days are ever idle?
The Sixth: Venerable Bhadra of Dvāravatī Island. Dvāravatī Island spans eight hundred *li*;
the billowing ocean waves fill the sky, parting the cloud-capped peaks. Sentient beings, with their conceptual thoughts, err at every turn;
The Great Being, being without mind, is at peace everywhere. Nearby, stream waters wind through red agate; In the sparse forest, snow sprinkles upon the azure.
Lánggān (Lapis Lazuli). Flowers scattered by the various devas form a great accumulation; morning and evening, the wind comes to sweep the stone altar.
The Venerable Kālika of Saṃkha-dvīpa, to whom the Tathāgata entrusted his charge, shall never forget it.
How could he ever conceal his benefit for beings in secret? He will dwell long in the world and never depart.

Disenchanted, even a brief sojourn in the heavens is no hindrance. With coarse robes, a patched bowl, and the necessities of life, one dwells in vast wildernesses and deep mountains—the sacred sites of the Path.
Free and at ease, one is like a lion’s cub, indifferent to the seasonal shifts of heat and cold.
The eighth is the Venerable Pralambaśālavatīra, who dwells on the Island of the Sages (Ṛṣidvīpa) in Pralamba.
He causes all who possess consciousness to emerge from the river of craving; his exquisite flavor of bliss is like that produced by the Snowy Mountains.
How marvelous! The Fire-Sage’s radiant *puṇḍarīka* flowers bloom; from the dragon palace, waters surge upon the ground before his steps, and clouds from Vulture Peak connect with his doorway.
The outer slopes; how much more so for a place of Chan where people do not go? When gathering flowers, one sees deer and elk passing by.
At the ninth station, in Mount Gandhamādana, Venerable Śubhaka dwells.

In the mountains of Gandhamādana, the waters and rocks are wondrous. In every movement—turning, pacing, bowing, or rising—his four deportments are such that body and mind have shed away all idle husks.
Bǐ. Speech and silence have always been the wondrous dhāraṇī; the fine grass naturally exudes a fragrant scent. The distant mountains stretch infinitely with their variegated azure peaks;
as the devas offer ambrosia at noon, it is precisely the time for the city guardian to beg for alms.
The tenth is the Venerable Aṭavaka of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, in the palace of Śakra, Lord of the Thirty-three.
With a shaven head and square-cut robes, he dwells therein. His golden bowl contains *sudhā* rice;
by day his mind is like the emptiness of Prajñā. Having forever escaped the wheel of suffering, he must benefit sentient beings. His practice ascends to the precious abode.
Exerting effort, he had previously received the prediction of bodhi; yet he still awaited the full maturation of the power of adornment.

Upon completing the eleventh stage, Pilang Guzhou, the Venerable Rāhula—Pilang Gu being the name of the ocean-island—traversed back and forth with unimpeded supernatural powers, for his true mind was fundamentally free from birth.
Extinction. Since when has the Great Way required reliance on proof or cultivation? The illusory man of Western India brandishes a fly-whisk; the immortal of the Upper Realm burns ox-head incense.
Six times a day they chant salutations to the golden image; the formless must be sought through that which possesses form.
The twelfth: Venerable Kanadeva on Mount Bandhuka. Mount Bandhuka pierces the void; white clouds veil its emerald clarity.
His name is ranked among the five hundred śrāvakas; his Way covers the three thousandfold world system.
As he rises from meditative concentration, the moon’s shadow slants upon the golden hall; after the midday meal, incense curls through the jade pavilion.
The furnace wind sometimes enters the *kuṇḍikā* for bathing; one must believe that even a śrāmaṇera possesses such supernatural powers.
The thirteenth location is Mount Pṛthuśṛṅga (Guǎxié), where the Venerable Aniruddha resided.
The mountain is named Pṛthuśṛṅga because its fame was heard everywhere. Within it lies a separate world-system of its own, where rain-dragons listen to the lectures and heavenly flowers fall.

Dampness; wild deer rely on the warmth of the grass at the meditation steps. Myriad transformations all emerge from the signless; throughout the ten voids, there exists only that which is provisionally named.
When this principle is clearly realized, one transcends birth and death; what need is there to seek elsewhere for the gate of liberation?
The fourteenth is the Venerable Vanavāsi, who may dwell among the mountains;

his name signifies that he can abide upon the eternal peaks. Whether sitting, reclining, or walking according to the occasion, though his body belongs to illusion, he must cultivate that very illusion.

Having realized the fruit of non-arising, he delivers sentient beings. As the rhinoceros-horn handle is frequently shaken, petals fall; as he attempts to unfold the precious scripture, the moon [appears].
Lunming (Wheel Radiance). Since the five fetters were extinguished, afflictions and bodhi have been entirely equal and level.

In the fifteenth stage, at Vulture Peak Mountain, the Venerable Āśvaghosa—after the Tathāgata had already passed away—resided with fifteen hundred dragon-elephants; his concentration and wisdom were perfectly radiant, like the sun.
The moon; body and mind pure like a lotus. Extraordinary birds and strange beasts come to surround it. Auspicious mists and propitious clouds unfurl and roll back.
In this place, from time to time, the sounds of bells and chanting arise, solemn as when the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma.
The sixteenth is the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka, who dwells among the Great Beings on Mount Cakravāḍa.
His bright pearl is free of flaws and his jade is without blemish. By day he recites the thousand-line verses of the Prajñāpāramitā;
from heaven rain falls in four colors of *māndārava* flowers. The sound of the *gandī* bell reaches afar as the monks perform their *poṣadha*; the thick smoke of incense perfumes the Buddha.
The *kāṣāya* robe—white oxen may naturally suffice alongside sheep and deer. First leading children to drive small carriages:

the Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, praised [him] as one who from the beginningless vast kalpas has never uttered a single word. Who says that only after five thousand years did he finally open his lips?
There are those who speak and those who do not speak. For now, do not slander the patriarchs. Breaking chopsticks to stir the great ocean;
using a lamp-wick to prop up Mount Sumeru. The mouth does not move the tongue; the feet do not cross the threshold. For fifty years, he sat in meditation upon a single couch.

He is the ninth patriarch of the Chan gate throughout the three thousandfold world-system. The Buddhas are not the Way; parents are not kin. Whether in mind or in conduct, what is false and what is true? Atop the mountain peak...
Turning over white waves, red dust rises from the bottom of the well.
A cloth bag praises the flowery avenues and willow lanes as it passes through them at will; even the tiger’s den and the demon’s palace cannot hinder it. Suddenly, upon its back, it rubs itself once.
The Eye—this nearly startles Master Jiang Mahā!
The black staff moves back and forth, prodding; though the cloth bag is light, he refuses to cast it aside.
The inexhaustible, layered ocean of the Flower Treasury—all is wrapped within a single belly.
A person waiting at the crossroads does not realize their face is covered in dust; layered with scraps of broken paper, they wrap up dry excrement—every time it is picked up, it is fresh once more.
Leaning on his cloth bag, he dozes off; in hundreds of thousands of millions of years, it is but a single moment.
There is no such monk in the Sahā world, and there is no such Buddha in the assembly of the Dragon Flower.
Hanshan and Shide praised Lichou:
"Before he had even reached Guoqing, who could have recognized Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra? With his three-inch tongue, he carelessly leaked the secret;
what skill does he have but to act like a wind-crazed madman?"
The great ocean of perfect enlightenment is the monastery; when one arrives there, where have the holy and the ordinary ever existed?
Two *dhūtas* clap their hands high, letting people say they are too ragged.
Is there no one within Guoqing Temple? They speak only of the poverty of Hanshan and Shide.
With broom and dustpan always in hand, it is a pity that even the pure grounds grow dust.
Gazing afar toward the southeast, a mass of purple qi gathers; Tumbling clouds and pouring rain become increasingly majestic. The countenances of the sages and worthies are clearly present;
Do not say that this person has gone and will not return.

The Great Master of Wisdom’s eyebrows were adorned with eight colors; his eyes shone with double pupils. Since the Dharma is fundamentally unobtainable, how could his eloquence ever be exhausted? The Great Void is beyond all signs.
The blazing sun stands at its zenith; the silver ground is the Buddha-cave, and the jade spring is the divine craft. Tongschi received the precepts and inherited the tradition through consecration.
Like a fragrant elephant in the river of dhyāna and a great dragon in the ocean of teaching, one gazes up and looks toward him—reaching as high as heaven and as deep as the earth.

His fame and his reality are not like the chirping of a mouse or the empty cry of a bird. This is what is called the Patriarch Nāgārjuna, whose school flourished in the North (Qi) and whose teacher was in the South.
The illusory form of Chan Master Yue Linghui.

National Teacher Qingliang praised that ignorance is fundamentally empty and the dharma-realm is like an illusion; who, then, is Samantabhadra? His vows and practices are perfected; the traces of his ten stages are like bird footprints.

The second is the *Juebo* (Awakening Wave) Preface: "Ordinary beings and sages are equal; delusion and enlightenment share the same flock. I bow my head to the Cool and Pure One, whose wisdom penetrates and illuminates the principles of reality.

He expounds the Vairocana-garbha Sūtra and is called a true son of the Buddha. Like a thousand dragons sending forth waves, he flows with compassion across the four seas; his Ten Great Vows are sovereign."
The portrait of the Seventh Imperial Gate Master appears before us; with fly-whisk in hand, he dwells eternally in the world, imperishable within the great void.

Master Bodhidharma’s encomium first distinguishes that the precious jewel is not worth even half a character; next, his refutation of the six schools lacks any definitive core. Having come from South India, [he has brought this teaching].
He entered the land of Zhendan and again confronted the King of Liang, yet once more claimed he did not recognize him. He stayed at Shaolin for nine years, facing a wall.
How laughable is Shen Guang—obviously a thief! When it came to "settling the mind," he could not find his mind;
look at what "extraordinary" feat this was—it could not avoid such a great mess. Meeting Song Yun beyond the Pamir Mountains, his worn-out sandals remain to this day.
A single boat on the Yangtze River; a single flower upon the great earth. Vast and open, there is no sage. Wherever you encounter him, tell me:
who is he? It is Xiangzhi’s father and son; it is Lord Shen Guang.
Who says he knocked out his front teeth? He was beaten to death and buried deep in a pit.
It was simply because King Liang was not clever enough to let him escape and enter the court of the Wei dynasty.
At that time, had I manifested divine light, my three prostrations would have been nothing but a feigned surrender.
I stood to one side to watch the seam of his opening mouth, then stepped forward and toppled the entangling pillar.
At Shaolin, he sat in cold meditation through many springs; his nostrils still rest upon his upper lip.
It is simply because his local accent could not be changed that people called him a Brahmin.
Twenty-eight donkeys from the Western Heaven trampled it to pieces; China alone possesses it. The descendants of later generations are mostly stubborn and perverse;
each one is more forceful than the last, their beaks as sharp as a spearhead.
For three years he traversed the sea by the power of his supernormal faculties; on a single reed raft floating down the river, demonic monsters abounded.
One might think that at the very end he could block them all, yet as before, he could do nothing against Song Yun.

The sixteen patriarchs painted by Indra: having heard the Venerable Man’s request for encomiums, I praise the First Patriarch—his front teeth were easy to conceal behind his lips, yet his beard-hairs were difficult to hide beneath his chin. After Shen Guang’s three prostrations, the single peak of Xiongeri rose high.
The Sixth Patriarch gave rise to the discourse on the wind and the banner; its transmission has never ceased. If someone comes to question me, I say: "Six ears do not conspire together.
Ox-head...
Sitting upon a flat stone, how many times have I seen spring arrive? The hundred birds leave no trace; mountain flowers fall and bloom again.
The Governor of Niaoke is named Juyi; the Chan Master’s title is Niaoke. When we meet, do not speak of perilous heights; here lies a single expanse of fine mountains and rivers.
Nanyue asked, "What is the seal of Caoxi? It leaves people at a loss for words; Simply because it is free from defilement, It breaks through ten thousand layers of barriers. — Mazu.
Polishing a brick will not produce a mirror; sitting in meditation will not produce a Buddha. A clay ox fights until its horns break; one tries to pick out bones from empty space.
Baizhang suffered a headache for his efforts—it was not the patriarch’s true intent. Day after day upon the rivers and lakes, wild ducks fly about in confusion.
Master Nanquan of Zhaozhou had such a child as this: he thoroughly exposed the story of Mount Tai, yet upon his return, no one knew him.
Xuefeng.
Rolling the wooden ball before the assembly, he brandishes the "tortoise-nose" staff facing the sun. Clearly revealing his innermost heart, each stroke covers heaven and earth.
Xuansha cast away his fishing boat and climbed Mount Feiyuan; touching his own toes, he attained realization on the spot.
Yunmen beat the Buddha to give to the dog to eat; only by knowing gratitude can one repay it. Later, the old master Zhenjing again sought to "smoke out" Yunmen;
Ciming...
From within an antique chest, he brings forth all manner of things. The white gold returns to the aged mother; looking upon it, one’s very marrow turns cold.
Yangqi kicks out a donkey that has but three legs; it never shifts a single step, yet it tramples the streets of Chang’an.
White clouds atop Yunmen’s “Shang Daren” (The Superior Person); white clouds on Mount Qiu, all alone. From this, they transform into three thousand; the pure breeze comes without ceasing.
— Yuanwu.
How wondrous, to recognize the sound! It has intention yet lacks sentiment. A single expanse of emerald crags gathers; idly, one pours forth one’s very liver and gall.
Great Wisdom splits open the head of Huashan Chan; he is a profound grievance for the monastic disciples. The bamboo whisk is cast from raw iron; a spark of flint flashes against the blue sky.
The various sages depicted by Indra hear the Superior Man’s request to praise him as he sits in profound stillness within the mountain cave;
though his lips move incessantly, he speaks only that there is no dharma to be taught— how can one contend with such falling flowers?
Fenggan dwelt among the monks in the temple; he would cross the mountain ahead while riding a tiger. When Governor Lüqiu arrived, he said, "You are Amitābha.
— Hanshan.
He does not dwell in the realm of Wondrous Joy; he does not yearn for Mount Qingliang. Each and every one seeks to become a Buddha, yet they lose out to this Daoist’s leisure.
Shide originally picked up [something] at the start, and thus he took that as his name. If you wish to understand this meaning, there is neither birth nor non-birth.
Master Bao hangs a knife, a ruler, and a staff from his head; from time to time he wanders through the marketplaces. This Bodhisattva son of the Xiao family speaks only of causes and conditions.
His sack—
Wandering aimlessly, my straw sandals wear thin; I have long endured sleeping within a cloth bag. The robes and bowl remain in the celestial palace—when will I return?
Lanzan’s fire for roasting yams in the hearth does not reach the azure heavens. For what reason do the lords of the world so frequently dispatch imperial messengers to summon him?
The boatman sets out at dawn when sky and water join; He returns at dusk when the moon fills his boat. If the scaled dragon is not encountered, When will he ever cease casting his line?
—Eulogy for Master Zhaozhou.
I visited Nanquan early on; having realized the ordinary Way, my debt from traveling has been repaid.

As the years of dwelling in the mountains grow old, I preach the Dharma according to circumstances without deliberation. Answering Zen questions as they come, why labor over seeking them out? An ancient Buddha returns once more.
The host of demons is completely swept away. The cypress tree before the courtyard—beaten by the wind and struck by the rain, its dense foliage filling the eyes.

"The dog has no Buddha-nature"—shining like snow upon a drawn blade, it kills with reckless ease. To this day, its Way spreads through heaven and earth; it is not merely a story told among Yan and Zhao.
Eulogy for Master Yunmen: For three days he waited at Muzhou’s gate; his staff was broken and his feet were lame. When Xuefeng asked him a single question, he fell silent and bowed his head.

Within the assembly of Lingshu, he was the eye of the human and celestial realms; within the Great Tang, he was the sworn enemy of the patch-robed monks. To employ him is like using a cart to cross a river.
Treading over and piercing through, he carves a hollow dwelling within the void; because of a dried-up dung-stick, he raises spears and halberds upon level ground.
Finding the path, he blocks the path; looking at the tower, he strikes the tower. If it were Master Zhenjing, seeing you, he would surely crush you to death.
But let us ask the master painter: for what reason did he paint him?
Eulogy for Great Master Linji:
With the gallop of a dragon and the stride of a tiger, with a horse’s jaw and a donkey’s jowls, he was thrice personally struck out by Huangbo within his room;
at Dayu’s ribs, three punches were enough to set him free. At that time, the old woman’s heart was far too earnest; this madman has caused a great stir.
Come back! Before you can continue the Buddha-patriarchs' life-force of wisdom, you have already conceived the calamity of the Zen school. A painful blow like rain falling on a bright day;
a scorching shout like thunder in the blue sky. Once the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is utterly extinguished, not a speck of dust remains throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system.
Eulogy for the Patriarch Yangqi:
From the beginning, he never knew how to speak of Chan. He simply followed the custom of wrapping hemp in paper.

He sat firmly beneath the cloud-canopy of Yangqi, yet he flaunted the "chestnut thorn" and the "golden circle. This single turning of the public case deceives the great assembly; this three-legged donkey leaps up into the heavens.

Bearing the heavy burden of Compassionate Wisdom, I rejoice that the white clouds have laid down their shoulders. There are no secret formulas for the immortals; father and son do not transmit them to one another.
Master Wuzu praised Elder Deng:
he possessed much *dharmaprīti*, cherished the *Cintāmaṇi-dhāraṇī*, and was accustomed to chanting "La-la-li. He bit through the bitter iron.
*Kai*. This is actually a poem about the cockscomb flower. To bring it up is truly terrifying. Who would believe that a white-bellied tiger has a nine-tailed spine?
It spreads the world out as a chessboard and writes the meaning of the Patriarchs across the void. Fair-skinned beauties and elegant young gentlemen see gods and see ghosts;
they speak of things and speak of principles. Truly, it is not true, yet it is not false—above heaven and below earth.
Knowing the subtle signs, the subtle signs. Zen Master Yuanwu praised [this]:
"At the crowing of the cock, he flew up onto the balustrade; suddenly, he dropped his sack. Opening his mouth and moving his tongue, he revealed this very sound."
Cutting through iron and severing nails, he brings forth the lower section. He manifests the seal of the mind, uncarved and unadorned, utterly transcending verbal explanation.

He upholds the vehicle of the fundamental division, which from the outset is without orientation or opposition. He contains Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed and casts the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters.

Seven times he was magnificently exalted; nine times he personally presented himself before the Emperor. If one speaks of the circulation of the True Eye, it shall continue until the end of the future.
*Tu!*—Praise for the Patriarch Dahui.
In the chamber of Zhantang, he leaped about, his mouth full of Chan talk; beneath the words of Foguo, he overturned everything and changed his course from the very beginning.
Awakening is itself without awakening; speaking is itself without speaking. The refined gold in the furnace and bellows sends sparks flying;
the black-lacquered bamboo staff roars like thunder and flashes like lightning. The lion crouches on the ground and bellows; the jackal’s head splits asunder.

For eighteen years, he has roamed freely through Heng and Mei; the Zhao jade was originally without flaw. Returning from thousands of miles of rivers and lands, the fresh ginger has not lost its pungency.
Ascending once more to Mount Lingxiao, he again enacted Linji’s shout. Xiaoshijia said, "One person points south; the edict is enforced throughout Wu and Yue.
This too is nothing more than taking a tortoise and turning it into a turtle.
Yuanmoan of Japan painted the twenty-two patriarchs and requested encomiums for them. For the First Patriarch:
For three years, winter and summer, he crossed the vast deep; He encountered a monk with hair in the Xiao family. When asked, "Who is it facing me? he said, "Not so."
"Śikṣānanda, for whose sake did you toil so hard to reach Jinling?
Fortunately, the Second Patriarch was a truly magnificent man; yet he came to Shaoshi to receive such 'smearing and plastering. Nevertheless, having prostrated himself, he knew shame."
Shame! I have sought for a lifetime, yet not even one arm of my own mother can I find.
The Third Patriarch held his staff across his chest and said, "O sinner, from where does your sin arise? You must know its cause. He did not even inquire about the monk who had come from afar.
Worldly convention: A single phrase, free from self-interest, reaches the fundamental truth.
For thirty autumns, the Fourth Patriarch’s side did not touch his mat; he never had a mind for the Dharma to comply with people's requests. On the road to Huangmei, he encountered a child.
Child, our enemies of the past have met once more.

Even the relationship between the Fifth Patriarch and his disciple was but a matter of circumstance. Clearly, this Way has been spread throughout the human world; as for the subsequent legacy, upon whom shall it rely?
Case: Lush green pines fill the four mountains;
how many monks from the Huangmei assembly of the Sixth Patriarch were there? All at once let go—Neng of Lingnan. To this day, atop Mount Dayu...
Stone. Year after year, the spring wind grows the creeping vines.
What thing from Nanyue comes so majestically? No one recognizes it; they give rise to doubt and suspicion. A flash of lightning, a spark on stone—distinguishing the black and white.
Plainly: the eye of this boundless life of toil suddenly opens wide.
Mazu’s “Mind is Buddha” was a constant babble; “Neither mind nor Buddha” became increasingly unbearable. The eighty-four patriarchs’ various gateways—
Separate! When has there ever been a single one who was a fellow practitioner?
Baizhang’s wild duck flew high and landed on a distant sandbar; he detested being pinched by others until his nose ached. To contemplate such a thing is utterly tasteless.
The flavor: neither laughter nor weeping can be formed.
Huangbo’s great capacity and great function manifest the family style; he sits and cuts off heaven and earth—this old man alone. All descendants of later generations possess [this].
"Listen! How can ten individuals in five pairs be deaf?

The True Person of No Rank (Wuwei Zhenren) of Linji is right before your face. You masters are much like those who toy with their own spirits; at the time of death, you will extinguish the True Dharma."
The Eye—how could it stop at darkening the three thousand seas and mountains?
Xinghua scatters real pearls within the purple silk curtain. Today, he has clearly been verified; he speaks with self-knowledge, yet his practice does not match his words.
"It is attained. He spoke further: "Do you still recognize this old monk?
Nanyuan established the pivot of the discourse with the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching; everyone present is merely deceiving themselves. From the tip of the staff, Mahesvara emerges.
The Eye. Entrust it to all quarters to be scrutinized in detail.
The Heart-Seal and Iron Ox Mechanism of the Patriarch Fengxue have already been repositioned upon the brow; facing the array, one cannot capture or release.
It is so. It makes people laugh at Lupei for all eternity.

Shoushan has a mouth—what harm is there in reciting the Lotus Sutra? Without cause, he continues the ancestral lineage like hemp seeds; by the side of the King of Chu’s city, the river flows eastward.
Water once left its mark upon the teeth of people of the time.
Yangshan’s ten wisdoms are gathered in a single phrase of Tongzhen. Fish and dragons lock their doors at Fenzhou; tonight, the wind and frost are felt all the more keenly.
Tight! Even Buddhas and Patriarchs would shrink their heads upon hearing this name.
Ciming held his sword crosswise over a basin of water; his straw sandals were cast to the ground and his staff stood at the gate. The Lion of Xihe roared with ferocity.
Truly so. Those who come must be taught how to lose their very souls.

Had Yangqi not been moved by the solemn sound of the drum in the hall, how could Ciming have emerged for the evening instruction? After he took up residence, he plowed his fields to earn his own food.
Having eaten, he then thought: "The old Gautama speaks of dreams;
White Cloud wishes to know the tonsure-master of Cha-ling. One must return on the night of the New Year’s Eve—the spring breeze upon a single blade of grass."
It turns. How many know of the jade halls and crystal towers?
The Fifth Patriarch’s iron sour plums are flaunted before people; he brings forth a single flower like a cock’s comb. This has always been the words of my late master.
Rudely cast aside the bow and the forge to establish my livelihood;
Yuanwu’s golden duck has extinguished its incense within the brocade curtains. All elegance resides in that single crow of the cock; now, everywhere one encounters the Shao.
Awakened! Wild birds and mountain flowers no longer cause delusion.

In the wondrous joy of neither-back-nor-front, one tests the student; with a three-foot bamboo staff, there is no distinction between the distant and the intimate. To whom can this story be entrusted these days?
Case: Exposed to the sun and buffeted by the wind, yet another spring has passed.
My late master, the Venerable Yuansou of Jizhao at Mount Jing, praised this portrait of the Compassionate Honored One, saying:
"The gate of extinction is fundamentally non-existent; right and wrong are utterly eradicated; Buddhas and patriarchs are swallowed whole. Zangyun is the son who carries on the family legacy."
The fourth-generation descendant of Miaoxi, he wielded the bamboo whisk of Shoushan to fully uphold the orthodox command.
He blinded the eyes atop the Mahesvara deity and utterly dispelled the profound darkness. For twenty years at Tiantong Jing Mountain, he wrapped mud-clods in cotton and enveloped boulders in brocade.
Within the seventeen hundred halls, his blows fell like raindrops and his shouts crashed like thunder, overturning mountains and seas and shaking the very foundations of the world.
Heaven and Earth. A single phrase that cuts off the secure barrier: beneath the fragrant incense burner sits an iron Kunlun.

Regarding the Chan Master Jinweng’s eulogy stating that the Patriarch Hu Daomo was not the true ancestor—what need is there to count these withered Zen practitioners? If it were not for the one who would exterminate his own clan, who else could succeed to the lineage?
A gate as vast as the heavens: stones stand from within the void; throughout the entire world there is no obstruction. Fire burns within water; the great earth has not a single inch of soil.
This describes its essence. Who would discuss birth and death, coming and going? When it functions, it does not depart from sound, form, voice, and language.
It is both nature and appearance; it is perfectly square and perfectly round. Be clear and direct; realize it right before you.
I received this karmic instruction from my former teacher, the Venerable Master Netung of Tien-ning, who praised it thus:

"The substance of the Great Way is vast; the empty hall echoes in response. His countenance is present now as humans and devas meet. With his tattered straw sandals, he traveled through fifty-four prefectures and districts;
with his coarse sitting mat, he paid homage at the inconceivable ancestral pagodas. The miasma of the South Sea was heavy."

How profound! The clouds over the Northern Mountains gather in layered folds. Having already accomplished the great matter of the wandering monk’s life and having fully encountered the venerable elders of all quarters, he cleared away the thorns and brambles to establish a jeweled monastery, and transformed those who lived as butchers and wine-sellers so that they might cultivate pure karma.
The wondrousness of the direct transmission of the single lineage cannot be described by words; his heart for providing silent benefit and hidden aid is as natural as space itself.
Circling around. Summer after summer, year after year. One must recognize the descendants of Tianxiang; let us look at the flowers and leaves of Shaolin.
He himself titled Linji as his primary study under Huangbo, who struck him with a fist beneath the ribs at Dayu. Xuefeng was a successor of Deshan. In...
Attaining the Way at the Aoshan Inn may cause one’s fragrance to flow for a thousand ages, yet it cannot avoid falling back into the weeds once more.
Beholding this physical frame, what kind of eyes and brains does it possess? Upon entering the gate, who can ascend to the hall? A three-foot bamboo whisk sweeps like a flash of lightning.
Question: From what does this humble physical form arise? A vast ocean from a single bubble; a great cloud in the void. Originally it has no substance;
it cannot be captured by brush and ink. To raise the pen is already an error; it is presented face-to-face. Burn the writing tablet! I wish to speak of practice.
Fifty years spent in monasteries, three thousand *li* traveled on foot; meeting Pòzhuò Duò, he was thoroughly enlightened by Yīsù Jué.
With white hair, he gazes upon clouds and mountains; this body follows the grain for its nourishment. Last night, when the wind and rain passed, the gourd fell from the wall.

To the very top and to the very bottom; through to the bone and through to the marrow. Essence does not depart from function, and function does not depart from essence. To describe it by force of words, there is originally nothing comparable.
For fifty years they have been forged into a single whole; yet were one to deliberate upon them, they would be separated by three thousand miles.
Taking empty space as one’s mouth and the myriad phenomena as one’s tongue, one fully upholds a single phrase and speaks it constantly throughout the six periods of the day.
Setting aside Deshan’s staff and casting away Linji’s shout—extraordinary! To fish for the moon within a furnace of blazing flames.
Having a mouth but no tongue, one remains thrice-sealed and does not speak. The pillar and the lantern preach for him. *Vandana*, I hope you are well.
A gentleman may be eight [in stature]; he rubs his forehead as he watches the fish, burning incense to sacrifice to the otters.
"Sun-face, Moon-face; Suzhou, Changzhou—these have no basis whatsoever, yet they possess their own origins. Performing somersaults atop the banner-pole of a Buddhist temple;
building a breath-ball in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
The Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished by the blind donkey; the wondrous mind of Prajñā is the totality of emptiness. That which the Buddhas and Patriarchs have transmitted is precisely this:
throughout worlds as numerous as grains of sand, they shake the wind of the school.
Rising from sleep within the Wambao Ward, the drums sound outside the Chongtian Gate. Picking up a flake of snow from a red furnace, it is midday and yet strikes the third watch.
This is the portrait of Master Guding; Elder Lin of Xiangfu Temple requests a eulogy.

The Fourth sat upon the site of enlightenment. From birth, he was solitary and steadfast—a master with the true eye, a sage-artisan who transcends the mundane. He shattered the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials into their wholeness;
through one suppression and one exaltation, divergent paths were made to return to the source. He transmitted the lamp of the patriarchs and stilled the disputes of the six schools.
His body was not a body, his marks were not marks; Heaven commanded him to be held aloft upon a thousand peaks.
Portrait of Chan Master Xingzhong of Chongbao Temple in Shaoxing. At the request of Elder Ming of Shangcheng, I offer this eulogy:

With the wisdom of a single hair-tip, he measures the entirety of the empty Dharma-realm; wearing the authentic seal of literary art upon his elbow, demons and heretics have no path by which to spy upon him.
Grasping a black lacquer bamboo whisk in his palm, Buddhas and patriarchs willingly yield ground to him. The mountains of Huai...
