To the west of the [Yellow] River and to the east of the Zhe River, he occupies the monasteries of the third dhyāna and subdues all eminent masters. He is like the autumn moon reflected in a river;
it does not ascend from below, nor does it descend from above. Like the spring breeze fanning the trees, the leaves naturally turn red and the flowers naturally bloom.
How virtuous is this supreme vehicle! It is as if it already exists, yet I shall describe and clarify it, so that I may not bring shame upon the patriarchs of the Xi family.
Portrait of Chan Master Xibai. Invited by Elder Wenzhang of Jetavana Monastery to provide a eulogy:
His realization transcends past and present; his learning encompasses both the inner and outer paths. Like a white-tusked incense elephant, he tramples and cuts across the stream;
like a golden-maned lion, he roars as he crouches upon the earth. His spiritual function may be called peerless; his literary compositions are but his playful sport. Blue sky.
In broad daylight, he released the auspicious radiance of the ancient Buddhas; amidst the red dust of the bustling marketplace, he revealed the ancestral intent of Nanhu.
It was enough to cause the great ocean’s waves to surge and Mount Sumeru to shatter into pieces. Shaolin did not recognize it, and Caoxi did not understand it;
yet, Zhenjingci’s Way grew ever loftier, laughing at those of all quarters who take progress as retreat. This is the direct transmission of Guding and the sixth generation of Miaoxi.
Also. *The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huibian Chushi, "The Sun of the Buddha Shining Universally," Volume Fourteen,
Pronunciation Guide*.
Bèng (bǐ zhèng qiè), pù (pú bào qiè), chán (shì shān qiè), bǐ (bǔ lǚ qiè), yī (yú yǐ qiè), nǐ (yú qǐ qiè), lú (dāo hú qiè), hù (hú gǔ qiè), kē (kǔ hé qiè), jìliàng (upper:

jù jì qiè; lower: liáng jiǎng qiè), lán (lì qiè, three times), sān (suǒ jīn qiè), jiào (gǔ xiào qiè), chuǎi (chū wěi qiè), yǎn (yú jiǎn qiè), duò lì (upper: tú luò qiè; lower: lì de qiè), xiè (xiān yè qiè).

Là (lì dá qiè) | Cuì (cāng kuì qiè) | Zhuó (dīng jué qiè) | Hǎn (hú zhǎn qiè) | Āo (áo yīn) | Zhǒu (zhāng qiè liǔ) | Cù (qī liù qiè) | Tà (tuó háp qiè) *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fúrì Pǔzhào Huìbiàn Chǔshí, Volume Fifteen*
Compiled by the Dharma-attendant attendants, Shancheng and others,
for the instruction of Chief Seat Jue.
Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as companions? If you awaken here, the business of a lifetime of study is finished.
Simply eat when hungry and drink when thirsty; sit at leisure and sleep when weary. Though one passes through millions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it is like the snap of a finger.
What more need be said of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? Even beasts, donkeys, horses, jars, basins, hairpins, and bracelets are all [the same].
When brought together and melted into a single gold, ghee, curd, and clarified butter are all stirred into one flavor—unmoving and unchanging, without beginning or end.
This is called the "ever-abiding Dharma-body for enjoyment," the Pure Land of Mind-only. Thus, whether in the bustling markets of the red dust world or amidst withered wood and cold ashes;
whether in the midst of adversity or favor, moving freely in all directions, contracting or expanding, appearing or disappearing—how could there be any further restriction or hindrance? Forever.
This is truly what is called "not only have I alone now attained realization; the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical.

This refers to the instructions of the former Elder Yangqi, who demonstrated and pointed out how to let go of the diamond ring and cast away the thorny jujube fruit—those who can swallow and leap over these are the ones who succeed.
Indeed, there are many; yet those who cannot leap over it are also not few. Now that we are increasingly distant from the Sage, those who raise this discourse grow ever rarer.
It requires a person of great power to accomplish a matter of great power. One must reflect with vast clarity within oneself; it is not a matter of seeking elsewhere.
Only then will one know that one’s own self is the diamond circle (*vajramaṇḍala*)—who else would you have leap over? One’s own self is the chestnut nut (*kapittha*).
Thorny burrs! Who else is there to swallow them? Take it for granted that the old man Yangqi will be defeated without even being examined.

Since Elder Shiban calls himself an "elder," he has appeared in the world to act for the sake of others; this is comparable to using a golden scalpel to scrape away cataracts from the eyes—it is no small matter. If...
To wound the blade or offend the hand inevitably results in the gouging out of one's eyes. How perilous and precarious! There is not even the space of a hair between life and death;
how can one indulge in the "blind bag" of ignorance, wagging their three-inch tongue to speak empty falsehoods and deceive others? Look at this Jia Shan: when he first resided at Jingkou Temple...
Although he had achieved his own realization, there was still leakage when it came to the point of "letting the hands hang down. Later, he went to Huating to see Chuangzi.
When Chuangzi said to him, "It is three inches away from the hook; why do you not speak? he replied, "I cannot speak. Chuangzi then struck him once with an oar across the mouth.
"The silk line at the tip of the pole is for you to play with; not disturbing the clear waves, its meaning is naturally distinct.
At this, he attained great penetration. Therefore it is said: "To study Chan, one must first attain awakening; having awakened, one must then meet a true person.
If you do not meet such a person, you will merely become a fabricated Chan practitioner, preaching a blind form of Chan that ruins people's children wherever you go. However...
One's own fundamental principle must be upright; one’s practice must be clear and lucid. Whether the monastery grounds are large or small, leave them entirely outside of your concerns.
Under Linji, Fengxue and Shoushan never gathered three hundred or five hundred followers, yet their Way has traveled throughout the world until now.
As the saying goes: "The mountain does not need to be high; it becomes famous because there is an immortal upon it."
This school demonstrates that the Head Seat Hong did not say:
"Śākyamuni did not appear in the world; Bodhidharma did not come from the West. Sentient beings have straight noses and horizontal eyes; the world is bright by day and dark by night;
honey is sweet and gall is bitter; cranes are white and crows are black; wind is cool without waiting for the moon; fire is hot without waiting for the sun."
And yet it is hot. Each and every instance is a completed kōan; at every turn, it is one’s own fundamental livelihood.
What can be called this school? What is the face of this school? Even Shitou and Nanyue cannot open their mouths; Linji and Deshan can only stand by with hands in sleeves.
To gather hundreds of thousands of millions of thunders into a single shout—what is that but the sound of a hot bowl clinking? It binds infinite emptiness.
Empty-handed, he brandishes a single staff. It is like a sharp arrow piercing through the thick weeds. Utterly naked, there is nothing to take hold of; stark and bare, there is nothing to grasp.
He calls the Bodhisattvas "slaves" and regards the Śrāvakas as "maidservants. He bows loftily to Śākyamuni and does not prostrate before Maitreya.

Even if one acts in such a manner, it still does not accord with this school. If you understand how to raise one to clarify three, weighing the situation with the precision of a scale, and grasping the meaning before a word is spoken—only then will you be ready.

To know before they have even raised their voices—such a caliber is extraordinary. Even if one possesses a slight degree of correspondence with this, such individuals are difficult to find within the lineage of this school;

we admit only those of superior talent, regardless of whether they are dull-witted or not. If one lacks such an eye for selecting Buddhas, what would it avail even in a thousand years? May the Head Seat exert himself.
The Master of the Treasury, Guan,
points out that the Yellow-Faced Old Man entered deep into the Snowy Mountains and sat in cold stillness for six years, consuming nothing but a single grain of hemp and a single grain of wheat,

yet he did not consider this to be suffering. Suddenly, on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, at the hour of Zi (midnight), looking up at the morning star, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
He sighed and said: "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata;
yet, because of their deluded thoughts and attachments, they fail to realize it. I shall instruct them in the Noble Path to cause them to leave behind all attachments.

For this reason, there arose the teachings of the partial and the perfect, the provisional and the full, which filled every corner of the world. Yet even so, these did not fully satisfy his original intention, until finally at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

The Master [Bodhidharma] held up a flower to show the assembly; only then was the ultimate matter of his final days completed. This all came from the accumulation of practice over kalpas of vast eons;

truly, it was not easy. Therefore, it is said in the teachings: "Within the ocean of my Dharma, there is not a single word or a single phrase that was not sought by relinquishing the rank of a Cakravartin King, nor was it obtained by relinquishing all that one possesses."
There is. That which is sought and attained is called the Unsurpassed Dharma Jewel. It is bestowed with both hands upon others;
you should yourself receive it upon the crown of your head and uphold it, never again giving rise to contempt or negligence. Tianning once had a question:

"Tell me, is that which was attained at Mount Snowy the same as or different from that which was transmitted at Vulture Peak? If you say they are the same, one is Teaching (Jiao) and one is Chan. If...
The Parting from the Way. There is neither beginning nor end. Try turning a word of response and see.
Verses compiled by one attendant, Wenbin, and others.
Send the Venerable Zhi to Jiangxi to utter a word where wisdom does not reach:
"A cast-iron hammer has been eaten by worms. May those who travel north, south, east, and west to study the Way not tread upon the path of non-arising.
On the path of non-arising, thorns are many; if you seek the Buddha with the mind, you will only find more confusion.
He becomes a demon. He idly stretches out his two legs and takes a nap, letting the days and months pass like a flying shuttle. Who cares about heaven? Who cares about earth?

To speak of the wondrous and discuss the profound is merely to dally with the "stinking air" of rice and gruel. Mazu produced eighty-four disciples; when questioned, there was none who did not understand.
Even if one were as capable as Guizong, it would still be like a blind donkey following the great crowd. Such is the case.
Now, what a fine time of peace! Who would debate the two characters of "Buddha-Dharma"? Before the hall, the green grass is a fathom deep;
often, glue and pitch grow from the corners of one's mouth. Cast aside Deshan’s staff; there is no need for Linji’s shout.
When it is cold, heaven and earth are cold throughout; when it is hot, heaven and earth are hot throughout. If you wish to walk, walk; if you wish to rest, rest. Be careful not to—
Hesitating, he guards the tracks of the way.
To the silent retreat of Chief Seat Yuan—silence, silence, silence!
What unsurpassed Bodhi can be attained? Having attained that which is unattainable, one returns home. A mistaken recognition of the boundary.
The fence marks the boundary; one ascends the hall and enters the chamber to behold the person. Whether speaking or remaining silent, neither is the truth. Even this very statement is not accepted;
were there even a hair’s breadth of it, it would be mere dust. Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout are the skillful arrangements of the ancestral gateways.
When will the son cease inheriting his father’s trade? It is much like calling a tortoise a turtle. Not so!
As it was said regarding the entrusting of mountains and rivers: day and night they blaze forth without ceasing. Among them, one phrase is especially direct;
all people throughout the great earth must remain tongue-tied. When Mowan heard this, he laughed heartily: "What can the hundred birds carrying flowers do for me?"
I show you good meditators:
do not think of good, do not think of evil. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you bind yourselves empty-handed. Think of good, and think of evil as well;
thus the old monk makes these twelve periods his own. When asked about the nature of good and evil, they manifest in thousands of variations—reversal and compliance, vertical and horizontal.
It is simply because one does not recognize the true master that one lacks skillful means when facing critical moments. Good teacher, good teacher, listen to my words:
from antiquity until now, there has been no sage or worthy one. To don robes and eat food—this very thing is it. Otherwise, go and study the "five flavors" of Chan practiced in various quarters.
Seeing off Chief Seat Yue of Zhongzhu as he travels to Jiangxi:
"Branch after branch of coral supports the moon; The impulse to go north, south, east, and west is difficult to restrain.

Whether one reaches the destination five thousand li away, Or whether the eighty-four [disciples] have attained realization— Last night the osmanthus drifted with celestial fragrance; This meaning is clear and difficult to..."
Concealment. What dharma was ultimately taught in the celestial palaces? To this day, the twin ravines flow with surging waters.

One may go, or one may stay. The qilin does not wear golden chains; the straw sandals’ ropes have snapped as the path through the clouds deepens. Picking up tortoise hair, he threads it through his ears.
Sent to Chan Master Nuo of Fuzhou: Revisit the Lord of Tiantong; stay alert!
Old and decrepit Ruian calls out his own name and answers himself. A snake swallowing a turtle’s head, smoke issues from its mouth;
a tiger biting a great beast, horns sprout upon its head. Do you understand? Do you know? Within the Great Tang Empire, there is no Chan.
The Master said: "Linglong Yanzhu was seventy-four; he was the foremost branch of the *utpala* flower.
Do you know as you depart on this journey? Do not lightly tread upon the straw sandals; ahead lies yet another highest peak—not only is Flying Ape Ridge difficult to cross."
A Text for the Offering of the Sandalwood Image by Abbot Lang:
The physical form of the Holy Master Tathāgata Mañjuśrī is neither sound nor form. Maudgalyāyana exhausted his supernatural powers in vain;

though he traveled back and forth to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven many times, the artisan merely carved fine sandalwood. At that time, the thirty-two craftsmen all claimed they were carving the Brahma-voice itself.
It cannot be obtained. Since it is the Brahma-sound, even if one carves it, how can it be of any benefit if it does not resemble it perfectly?
Lately, it has wandered among humanity; whether north, south, east, or west, one may view it at will. Yet they do not recognize the true form of the Tathāgata.

There is no place in the human world where sandalwood is not found. Who does not possess the body of the Tathāgata? Yet they carry their bags and shoulder their satchels, wandering in vain. This remains unresolved.
People listen to a single word, yet who among them here and now moves their own mouth? The mind is not the Buddha, and the Buddha is not the mind.
Among the myriad bodhisattvas on Mount Qingliang, where can one find the flowing water and falling blossoms?
Seeing Attendant Gui off as he returns to Mount Lingyin in Tiantai.
Attendant Gui’s physical presence and spirit were exceptionally refined and elegant. Upon entering, he requested a verse for his departure.
I wrote it according to his whim, alternating between short and long lines. One line was short: "A gnat’s eye cannot contain it. One line—
Long! Pervading the realm of empty space, it cannot be measured. The National Preceptor called out three times, laying bare his liver and gall.
The Attendant responded three times, casting off the frost and ice. The ancient Buddha Zhaozhou spoke even more words; he wrote characters in the dark, yet their brilliance shone forth.
Take this as a parting gift and remember it well; when you reach other lands, do not misrepresent it. Your home is at Chicheng, deep among a thousand peaks. Last night, the wood...
Leaves rustle in the wind and rain.
I bid farewell to Zen practitioner Zan as he travels to Mount Tiantai and Mount Yan.
O Son of the Bodhisattvas, a hundred years of life pass in the snap of a finger; there is not even the leisure to clip one’s nails, let alone seek [the Way].
I have gazed upon the mountains and played by the waters; yet though there are these mountains and waters, what fault do they possess? In every land and at every dust mote, all is delightful.

When one raises their head and encounters that which belongs to oneself, only then does one know: "It is because of me that you receive my prostration. I have heard that among the many peaks of Tiantai, five hundred sages dwell;
I have also heard that Juṇa was at Yandang, sitting and watching the snowy cascades fly across the clear sky.
Green vines climb straight up the cold pine trees; where flowers fall and birds cry, the monkeys hang. Before the mountain lies the foundation of an ancient temple;
even until now, no one dwells there. Where no one dwells, one should not travel; let it be that for ten thousand ages green moss grows.
Rather than scolding the Buddhas and Patriarchs atop a solitary peak, why not tread upon the crossroads?
Dust and dirt.

Sending the attendant Xian to travel to Siming to study the Buddha was like being possessed by a demon; practicing Chan was like being obstructed by Chan. Neither studying nor practicing, he has brought this physical vessel to naught.
A guest beneath the gate of the Patriarchs—how noble and resolute his spirit! He moves the boat that ferries others across, fully repaying the debt of his travels.
Departing, he simply departs; the path lies beyond the red dust of the world. Arriving, he simply arrives; his eyes are covered by his pair of eyebrows.

No matter how many layers of barriers there may be, an iron whip shall shatter them all. All things are simply ordinary; do not mistake this ordinariness for an ordinary understanding. As Zen student Sheng departs to travel to Jinling: Before Bodhidharma came to the Eastern Land, flecks of white cloud drifted across the blue sky. Now that Bodhidharma has come to the Eastern Land— [The verse continues: The Great Way is vast and wide, yet few can traverse it. The true path is straight and level, yet few can walk upon it. If you wish to see the ancient Buddha, look at the mountain peaks. If you wish to meet the Patriarch, look at the flowing water. Do not seek it in the scriptures or in words; Do not seek it in the mind or in consciousness. If you can see through these two gates, Then you will see the face of the old man. If you can hear through these two ears, Then you will hear the sound of the wind. If you can understand this, Then you will be a person of the Way. If you cannot understand this, Then you are a person of delusion. If you can pass through the ten thousand-layered gates, An iron whip shall strike them all to pieces. All things are simply ordinary; Do not take "ordinary" to mean ordinary. If you wish to see the ancient Buddha, look at the mountain peaks. If you wish to meet the Patriarch, look at the flowing water. Do not seek it in the scriptures or in words; Do not seek it in the mind or in consciousness. If you can see through these two gates, Then you will see the face of the old man. If you can hear through these two ears, Then you will hear the sound of the wind. If you can understand this, Then you will be a person of the Way. If you cannot understand this, Then you are a person of delusion. If you can pass through the ten thousand-layered gates, An iron whip shall strike them all to pieces. All things are simply ordinary; Do not take "ordinary" to mean ordinary. Later, yellow birds chirp in pairs among the green willows. How many autumns have passed since Lord Xiao became Emperor? The ordination of monks and the building of temples—how leisurely and drawn out it was!
Golden scales pass through the net, yet fail to pass through the net; alas, three times the hook was cast in vain. The official road is rugged and impassable;
for descendants of later generations, it becomes a thicket of thorns. A small quail can only skim the ground in flight; the great Peng bird is but in vain.
There are wings suspended from the heavens; from the north and south of the Chang Jiang to the west and east of Zhejiang, a single flower with five petals meets the autumn wind.
In deep mountains there are no people, and the vast marshes are silent; one sees only foxes and hares nesting among the mugwort and tamarisk.
In years past, a single sandal was left behind—having neither head nor tail. Now it is cast away upon a heap of refuse, yet it wins a pure breeze that never ceases.
Ascending to Chan, ascending to Chan—what is this for? From afar he ascends Mount Feng from Fengshan; with coarse and exhausted integrity, he possesses the "eye on the crown of the head.
He understands and laughs at our Master for coming here in such a special manner.
Seeing off Chan Master Xian of Nengren on his journey to Jinling:
Have you not seen how the Stupa of Tianxi rises higher and higher? Looking down, the ocean of worlds appears like dust motes and hairs.
Tower shadows are seen in every household; tower shadows pass through every home. In every single house there is a stupa—reach out your hand...
Shadows cannot ultimately escape being cast. The house does not move, nor does the stupa shift; it is not far from the earth, nor distant from the heavens.
Dongjiang Shouzuo has gone eastward along the river; his iron staff flies across the sky, unable to be detained. Even within the City of Stone, such a one is not common.
In the guest house of Yuezhou, not even one person remains. In one place, neither departing nor staying, neither coming nor going;
the monk’s conduct is free from even a speck of dust. Once the rain has passed, the cold penetrates the bones; the peaks along the river gather in a mass of emerald green.
In the style of Master Nanchu, I compose this verse to see off Secretary Mei as he departs for Tiantong to pay homage to the Buddha-Dharma at Mount Putuo and to the Chan Patriarchs.
What is the Chan of words and letters? With a single stroke, it is erased—broad daylight under a clear blue sky.
It makes the elders of Hunan laugh to death. Deeply engraved in large, formal characters, the Layman of Vairāṣṭra is nowhere to be seen.
He fusses and fumbles, striking small pellets with partiality; yet when questioned by others, he is left speechless, his mouth closed.

Zen, Zen! How did Ling-shih Shuji’s record come to be circulated? "The moon over the bamboo produces cold whistles; the wind through the pines enters the night lute. Since you are so skilled at riding the sound...
Covering over form—what prevents one from speaking of the wondrous and discoursing on the profound? Within the Cave of the Tide-Sound, strike the golden lamp; atop Mount Taibai, ride the iron boat.
To send off the Chan practitioner Yin.
Seals on ink, seals on water, seals on emptiness. Layer upon layer of brocade seams right before one’s eyes. For a sharp-witted monk, what need is there to grasp at them?
North, south, east, and west—there is no handle, yet there is no front or back. Listen and you do not hear; look and you do not see.

An adept who penetrates all quarters knows the shifts of the occasion; let the moss grow freely over the ancient hall. Penetrating the green eyes without blinking—the hand that illuminates all things.
Better to be empty. Refined gold from a great furnace, every step of his southern journey transcends Vairocana.
Sending off the Venerable Head Cook Yuanmei:

"This mind is Buddha" and "Neither mind nor Buddha"—his discernment was as precise as weighing a grain on a scale, yet his teaching remained as uniform as a single brushstroke. Amidst the mountains of Daming, [he stood].
Suddenly they meet: the ears stand erect and the hair hangs in disarray. Vinaya Master Kebin has emerged victorious in the Dharma-battle;

the fragrance of the steamed rice perfumes the vast void. Neither non-existent nor existent, yet not non-existent—black, black, bright, bright, three, eight, nine. Fortunately, he is a cub of the golden-maned lion;
his spirit as he travels to study the Way pierces the Ox and Dipper constellations.

Regarding the old stories from various quarters that the Chan practitioner Xiang has brought forth, no one has ever raised them before. One who raises them must have their eyebrows standing straight up. Wooden horses, pairs upon pair, travel with the moon;
clay oxen, couple after couple, dance before the wind. From Min to Zhejiang, who has gone on pilgrimage? Right here and now, it is simply rest.
Hesitation. "The porridge has been eaten; go wash the bowls. This was once brought up by the ancient Buddha Zhaozhou.

When the Chief Seat of Yansheng Monastery was being sent back to Japan, the chief seats of both halls simultaneously let out a shout. At that time, Linji was truly loquacious. Those who have transmitted this story know how many there are.
The year. As before, the hull of the ship is made of *bin* iron. In the past, I rode upon a raft to travel to the Great Tang; now, clutching my double-layered robe, I return to Fusang.
Upon arriving home, I bring forth the phrase of host and guest: "The needle-eyed fish swallows the Golden-Winged King."
Master Longhe, Director of the Pure Compassion Monastery, employs skillful means to request once more the "Rhinoceros Fan" of his attendant. Before the gate of Yongming lies a single lake;
suddenly, a mani jewel leaps forth. Both fan and jewel are cast away—no donkey is needed to cure the illness.
Carrying medicine. What a fine five-colored qilin soaring through the sky! How could it be bound by golden cords?
Vividly rolling, brilliantly manifest—boundless pure breezes fill the vast expanse.
I bid farewell to the Abbot Jing of Tianning;
what sutra is he looking at? What meaning does that sutra explain? From afar, he has come ten thousand li from Wanshi-Fusang; from nearby, he parts with the twin cypresses of Siming.
He bows his head in greeting and joins his palms with earnest devotion; every detail is luminous and wondrous, every aspect is natural and true.
It does no harm to lift up your sitting mat; let me first give you some tea to moisten your lips. You have traveled throughout the Great Tang without finding the Buddha-dharma;
it is an iron Kunlun beneath a golden incense burner.

Seeing Master Guan off as he returns to his hometown, I say one thing and then another: from of old, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have had no secret formula. If you ask further, "To whom was the transmission at Vulture Peak entrusted?"—the entanglements will inevitably sprout new shoots.
When a man of the Way lets go of the mind that chases after things, in that very moment, he is vast and empty, transcending antiquity.
Now, soaring directly upward on the *fúyáo* wind for ninety thousand li— the Great Peng is no ordinary bird—
it has sent forth the "Single Holy Arrow" of Drum Mountain to the Abbot Baoben Xi, shooting it deep into the nine-layered city. Yet, Old Fu has lightly seized it...

Abiding. Xuefeng could not help but provide commentary from the very beginning. He thought of the grandmotherly heart of the ancient masters: they would pick up tiles and rubble, intending for them to become gold.
Later people merely follow along with sounds and forms; though they travel thousands of miles in search, it is all in vain. Recognize the True Buddha within yourself;
otherwise, even those with blue eyes and yellow heads will treat you with utter contempt.
I am sending five thousand-plus volumes of the Great Canon (Tripitaka) to Wei, the Abbot of Zhongzhu. Every single volume speaks of one’s own mind; it is not merely language or written characters.
To laboriously search for it upon paper is in vain. There is a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in Central India whose two eyes are as clear as the azure autumn waters. In his leisure time...
I see him gazing at the clouds and mountains; as soon as he sees a monk approach, he turns his back to the wall. This is the intent of the Patriarchs of the Tathāgata-dhyāna school.
Does the Librarian understand it? When he was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, fragrant flowers drifted to fill the ground before the steps.

I send Zen practitioner Chanren to the east and west of the Yangtze, the north and south of the Huai. A single ancient road is as straight as a string. Upon leaving the gate, green waters wind around green mountains.
On his feet, the hemp sandals sprout two wings; the Unranked True Person has nowhere to be found. Autumn is high, and fallen leaves drift down the mountain.
Lín: "Whether one who travels to consult masters possesses the eye or not, here in the Dharma Hall the green grass grows deep.
When old masters see such a person, they mostly point and comment, or else they overturn the meditation seat for him."
What object did you bring, Zen practitioner, to come here like this? A shrimp swallows the moon; an iron saw dances the *Santai* dance.

Upon the tip of the staff and beneath the soles of the sandals, a single clap of thunder stirs up a pure breeze. When meeting, there is no need for verbal prolixity; one simply treads upon the— [The text ends abruptly.]
It is not one's own possession. It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, its shadow sinking into the cold water;
having penetrated the patriarchs' barrier before the triggering mechanism, one sits and beholds a thousand flowers blooming upon the tip of the pestle.
Sending Zen person Yun back to Mount Yang:
A small Śākyamuni, a great Buddha of Chan. Buried deep beneath four whips of rattan, he is a fine son who props up heaven and supports the earth.
If one were willing to learn like a fox, one would remain attached to its den; who, then, does not have the eye of wisdom at the crown of their head?

Everyone possesses the efficacious talisman behind the elbow. Why, then, do you wallow in such confusion, waiting for further instructions? It is right here, it is right here—yet you have already traveled a hundred thousand *li* across the shifting sands.
If you encounter a true知音 (one who understands), show it to them; why wait to ask about the price of rice in Luling?
To the Chan practitioner Xixi:
Within the hollow of a lotus fiber, the world is vast; the great Peng bird knocks down the moon from the edge of the sky.

When this mountain monk awakens in the middle of the night, to whom can he speak of this boundless meaning? Ten or five pairs of traveling companions—wandering the quarters without anything to bring back.
A square eye. When Deshan, clutching his staff, visited Guishan, how much entanglement was cut through!
Two mouths with not a single tongue; a thousand carts on the same track. A Daoist riding a cow backward; a tortoise chewing raw iron.
To move the gourd and plant it upon a stone; the earthen ox drips its entire body of blood.

When sending off Zen practitioner Yi, one must not cite one thing while citing two. Having brushed past the Third Capital (Chang’an) and the Fourth River (Kaifeng), what difficulty is there in turning heaven and earth upside down?
It is as easy as turning stones into gold. Without seeking or grasping, and free from all taboos, when Lord Zhang drinks, Lord Li gets drunk. At the summit of the solitary peak—
Taking office with sovereign mastery, he plays freely at the gates of the bustling market. Right before one’s eyes, he pierces through the solid core of the mind;
he presses down a gourd upon the water until it sinks. With staff slung across his shoulders for thousands of miles, the blue sky and bright sun are drenched in rain.

As I see off the Japanese Head Librarian of the Eastern Collection on his journey to Mount Tai and Mount Yan, east and west of the mountain range, there is a single phrase that no one can bring forth.

Suddenly, if one stumbles upon it and speaks it, the five hundred venerable ones will all raise their brows; the water flows beneath the ravines, clouds rise from the mountain peaks, and the green pines rustle.
White stones gleam and flash; Piṇḍola comes and goes, and Nāgakumāra appears here and there.
Even if one were to dedicate oneself to the vehicle of the Tathāgata, it would still be nothing but old, rotten vines. This separate transmission outside the teachings is brought forth once more:
beneath the ocean floor a thousand fathoms deep, a golden lamp is struck to light.
Sending off the Venerable Kōng of Mount Jing:
Moss and dust at the bottom of the well; a carp upon the mountain peak. Everyone sits and listens to the water by the incense burner.

Three ascents and nine arrivals, yet he remains unawakened. Who says there are "skin and marrow" at Shaoshi? To take this matter and measure it with the mind is in vain; The mountains and rivers have grown long for you.
Proclaiming it far and wide, the void opens its mouth and laughs without end; the pillar and the lantern vie with one another to emit light.
When Xinghua struck Kebin, the monastic community was like a boiling cauldron. One must be a golden-maned lion cub to let out a roar that shakes the earth.

I sent attendant Xun to study with the Second Patriarch Songyue Weng for the settling of the mind and the Third Patriarch for the repentance of transgressions; it was like a seamless iron hammer, resembling the "gourd-seal" mark.
"Simply because my grandfather practiced deception, the calamity has not ceased to afflict his descendants. I pick it up from a heap of refuse and cast it into Lake Dongting.
There is a monk from Fusang who loves to prattle with his lips; I have kicked him in the dark and pulled him up in the light.
The mountain monk claps his hands and laughs aloud: what principle is this, after all?"
To discuss reward is to shatter the bright moon pearl of the black dragon; to discuss punishment is to strike out the five-colored marrow of the phoenix.
Reward is precisely punishment, and punishment is precisely reward. Go see Old Man Songyue; he will surely have a skillful means for you.
Sent by me, Attendant Yue, to pay homage to the Patriarchs in Jiangxi:
there is only the true moon; there is neither the "not" nor the "is. The discourse at Vulture Peak was never uttered; Caoxi’s finger was likewise empty.
I went to see Master Mazu. He was like a winnowing basket moon: perfectly round without a seam; vast and open, encompassing beginning and end.
Among the eighty-four patriarchs, Guizong was the most outstanding; all other spiritual friends remain merely within the realm of light and shadow.
The self is not him; he is precisely the self. When light and shadow have vanished, the waters of the West River are sucked dry.
Sending off Chan practitioner Yi on a journey to Mount Tai and Mount Yan:
In years past there was an old man named Lüqiu; failing to recognize Fenggan, he needlessly lamented. Hanshan and Shide ran wild with their eccentricity.
Mad! He ran into the deep forest, where there was no place to seek him. Yongjia went specifically to visit Caoxi; he circled the meditation seat, shook his staff, and displayed his majestic demeanor.
The pine wind and river moon remain just as they were before. Those who awaken do so of themselves; those who are deluded remain deluded.
Yet, there is neither delusion nor awakening. A swift falcon does not strike at a rabbit by the fence. Ten thousand miles of cloudless sky, the ocean moon rises high—head and tail are one.
The Road to Heaven.
Attendant Chè is sent to pay homage at Potalaka and visit his teacher;
to behold the Precious One of Bodai, whether encountered or not. Ten thousand miles and a thousand leagues within the perfect radiance—will he see his parents of this life?
Seeing them, they meet face-to-face in every movement and stillness, in coming and going. To leave one’s teacher too early has been ridiculed since antiquity;
who today can claim self-awakening without a teacher? Look at Linji meeting Huangbo: he was a true disciple who surpassed his master.
Cheshan was a fine red-fin carp; even vermilion sand cannot compare to him. With a single clap of thunder, he flew up into the heavens—frogs and earthworms!
The earthworm vainly clings to its surroundings.
I bid farewell to the Zen practitioner Zhe, who carries his staff to visit his master. Along with this letter to Master Zhongmo:
At seventy-eight years of age, the teacher who wields his staff— His eyes are like dots of lacquer, his eyebrows like snow; He clearly brings forth Subhūti from a painting.
Tí. Sitting, he listens to the solitary ape’s cry as the moon sets; in the deep mountains and ancient temple, the sky is bitterly cold.
Leaves a foot thick are piled before his couch; the hearth fire burns while the curtain remains unrolled. His *kāṣāya* robe is black like the smoke from the brazier.

When a guest arrives, he fears only that the smoke might escape—how can he help it? The mountain forests do not hide him well enough. His reputation for the Way resounds through the rivers and lakes; carrying his book-case and staff...
The sack is certainly not one; returning east from a thousand li away, you have frequently sent word. Your father, after all, still possesses a sense of home.
Even with the wondrous spiritual powers of Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, why must you laboriously present these "perfect circles"?
Sending Attendant Ming back to Mount Dongshan and Mount Nanping;
among the five hundred followers, there are great spiritual powers and wondrous applications. How pitiable is the toil of Piṇḍola!
There is no time when he does not attend the offerings at the donors' gates. Now, let the attendant return with his alms bowl; even on his eyelids, he has no concern for length.
Long eyebrows. He asks where Chan Master Qushan is; against the wind, he further seeks the rhinoceros calf. How can the rhinoceros calf be depicted?
Wang Wei’s brushwork and colors are thin; the mist and rain of West Lake obscure it in vain. When the sun rises over the eastern mountains, its head and horns are revealed.
On the sixth day of the first month, Master Cheng sent Zhe, the Abbot, to visit the Teacher. At last, spring has arrived; the myriad flowers and hundred grasses all display their vital spirit.

The staff of Shoushan is lively and agile, striking the wind and beating the rain, truly startling the world. Chan Master Zhe has obtained it and does not employ it recklessly; when the occasion arises, he can kill or give life at will.
Seizing and releasing—Dongshan’s five ranks dare to be displayed; Linji’s three mysteries need not be flaunted.

Usually kept by one's bedside, they are directly made into enemies of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. With the eye atop the head illuminating the great thousandfold world, what arising and ceasing is there?
It is like bubbles floating on the water. One solid stroke shatters the snow of Yuanhu; a single point opens the moon over Mount Jingqiao. To you, Master...
It is truly difficult to remain steady; that "surpassing the teacher" is no empty boast. Yet, because of leaning on the staff, I thought of Mount Shou;
suddenly, I turned back again, following the spring wind home.
Sending off the Zen practitioner Jun to pay homage to the Patriarchs:
the Buddha-dharma does not fear being ruined; let it fill the ditches and ravines as it pleases, spreading vast and boundless across heaven and earth until no one can speak of it.
Now, what harm is there in raising it up? It is far superior to making offerings by burning *fengxiang* incense. One great matter.
The teachings of the Tibetan tradition are but idle paper; I grasp them with my hand to wipe away a sore. Though China is vast, there is no other path:
the Seven and the Two-and-Thirty gaze face-to-face. The colt tramples all under heaven; Prajñātāra’s words of restful sleep have ceased.
A Gift to Master Zhiyu for Reciting Sutras and Gathering Firewood:
What a fine embodiment of the Vajra! It is vast and open, with neither surface nor interior; from the beginning, it has never accepted a single speck of dust.
But how, ultimately, can one wash it? Since one does not wash the body, nor does one wash the dust—where there are no traces, one must most certainly avoid hiding oneself.
Yet he comes to sit amidst the heap of sounds and forms; when flowers bloom on a withered tree, it is a spring of its own kind.

In days of yore, the Medicine King burned his two arms; his single thought of the Way’s heart never regressed. The majestic true body suddenly manifests before one, yet later people do not realize the intent behind the burning of the body.
Do the seven fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra consist of many words? They simply take this very thing to transform the donors. At all times, beat the drum.
He invited the monks for a bath, so as not to let the cauldrons grow cold on a fireless hearth.
He sent Shishuang back to the State Preceptor’s residence at Haimen.
"The rising sun shines first upon the east; when lost, the sky is overcast and the nature-ground is dark, but upon awakening, the day breaks."
The light of the mind shines forth. When jade is in the mountain, the trees are moistened; when pearls sink in the abyss, the river becomes beautiful.
With the numinous talisman behind the elbow, one sweeps away the Buddhas and Patriarchs; with the eye of wisdom at the crown of the head, one opens the way for humans and devas.
When the wind whistles, the precious flower seat speaks without speaking; where it is cold and still, the hall of withered wood meditates without meditating. He draws it forth from his sleeve.
An object from the Tang Dynasty: a string threading together rabbit horns and tortoise hair.
Sent to Zen practitioner Peng as he returns to his home village:
one, two, three, four, five. Licorice is sweet; yellow bitter gourd is bitter. Once, in the kingdom of Silla, I ascended the hall; now, in the Great Tang...
Before the drum has been struck within the kingdom—five, four, three, two, one—it is as black as lacquer and as bright as the sun.
A shepherdess by the seashore, a *jué-ma* riverbank’s stone of longing for her husband. The most wondrous among the wondrous, the most profound among the profound.
A ready-made koan, under the bright sun and blue sky, above heaven and below earth. Three fingers, seven horses; Śākyamuni and Maitreya are empty.
A name—no one knows who gave it. A single drop of water from the great ocean; a mountain an inch high like Mount Sumeru.
If you let go of the mind, every place is home.

The Japanese master who sent the Abbot back to his home country was truly joyful; he did not shrink from the myriad li of the whale-waves, sacrificing his life for the sake of the Dharma as he reached the South.
How many such renunciants are there today? One who truly practices Chan belongs to the lineage of Chan; their secret realization silently accords with the truth. Furthermore—
How extraordinary! From of old, Buddhas and patriarchs have been one's natural enemies; yet who would be willing to recognize mountains and rivers as their own self?
These five thousand scrolls of words upon paper—how laughable, like a foolish fly that drills on and on without ceasing. One’s own precious treasury contains not a single thing;
all the people in the great world cannot lift it up. If you can lift it up, then go back home: the east wind enters the seasonal laws and the plum blossoms bloom.
Sending off Zen Master Shizang of Tianning to return to Jingguang:
Old Man Yongjia was mistaken to go wandering on foot; he was called "One-Night Enlightenment" by others. Caoxi was merely a woodcutter;
how could he have ever understood the practice of studying the Buddha-dharma? The three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand practices—once pressed, the pure wind suddenly [arises].
Dissolving and melting away, I have happenstance composed these words, yet they are called "True Treasures of the East" (Zhendan jing).

Washing mud with mud is not clever; adding feet to a painted snake is a vain labor. Look at these two approaches—they are both utterly incorrect. How can students thereby transcend birth and death? Within the Tathāgatagarbha there has never been a pearl;
for ten thousand ages, a hollow name has hung upon people's lips and teeth. This is the posthumous title for Chan.
With his mouth swallowing all directions, he asks me with great earnestness about Pure Light: whether there is a pearl or not, he demands an answer.
The old man of Yongjia must be in a hurry; tell him what the present age is like—do not linger over the pines and wind, nor the rivers and moon.
As the *yintuowei* (in-charge of the assembly) sees off those who visit their kin, each person has their own karmic affinity (*shengyuan*). A swift horse requires but a single whip.

If Bodhidharma had not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch had not gone to the Western Heaven, where would the Way-person’s karmic affinity lie? Across ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains, they come and go as they please. Coming and going.
Never separated by even a speck of dust, the whole body is revealed in its majesty throughout daily life.
Covering heaven and earth, spanning from antiquity to the present, it is neither the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye nor the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana.

"The Buddhas are not my teachers"—a tiger with horns emerges from the wild weeds. "My parents are not my kin"—the celestial qilin snaps the golden chains. Stepping out the door, one follows each stride.
A pure breeze arises; it sweeps for thousands and tens of thousands of miles with a whistling sound.
It carries the Chan practitioner Ze, whose divine blade carves away the raw jade of Mount Jing. Though he is but a youth, he is well-suited for refinement. Upon the Terrace of the Phoenix—
The young phoenix, its wings unfurled, laughs at the cloud-swallowing Peng bird’s slowness. Everywhere it goes, nothing can contain it; if you wish to know the disciple, observe the master.
At Mount Nanyue, polishing a tile will never produce a mirror; striking the ox was the very sickness of that time.

A colt tramples the people of the world to death—only those with the true eye can distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox. Those who have attained the Way throughout antiquity and today are as numerous as clouds and smoke. Above.

Human life is short; one should strive diligently. Simply exhaust your ordinary sentiments, for there is no saintly understanding. Eat when hungry and drink when thirsty, following conditions as they arise.

As the Abbot Xing departs for Jinling, the spring mountains are green and the spring waters are lush. One branch, two branches—plum blossoms are blooming. Ten li, five li—the winding paths through the villages.
Cloud shadows gather and disperse over the stone city; the crowing of roosters breaks off and continues at the thatched inn.

One may try to depict it, yet cannot finish the depiction; one may try to paint it, yet cannot complete the painting. Having exhausted all five thousand and forty-eight volumes, not a single word remains capable of appraisal.
The Daoist laughs at me for opening my mouth in vain; adding a point to an arrow-tip only results in leakage. Turning one’s back on the Dharma Hall, one puts on straw sandals and enters the well.
With a deep well and a short rope, one will ultimately find it difficult to draw water.

Those who send their minds toward meditation think that the mind is not the Buddha; they know it is not the Way. Whether north, south, east, or west, where can one seek it? It is rare, exceedingly rare.
There is even less; the events of two thousand years are but empty rumors. With a three-inch tongue, one sweeps through chaos at will.
A shrimp is caught amidst billowing waves of wheat; a blade of grass is plucked from the flames of a red furnace.
Sending off Master Jiao, the Librarian of Jiangshan:
Zhongshan is like a coiling dragon; Shicheng is like a crouching tiger. Face-to-face presentation—there is no further evasion or mediation.
I laugh at that talkative old Gautama, who "rides on two" and "rides on three. Since the capacities of sentient beings are unequal, they often [fall into error]. Like jade...
The axis-staff piled upon the lapis lazuli case; the Daoist’s point of view is naturally distinct.
Departing from the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, the iron net is suddenly rolled up and the vast ocean dries up; coral branches branch out, supporting the moon.

Sending off Venerable Yuan, the Single Source of All Spirits: we provisionally name him "Buddha. The spring rain falls in mist, the spring breeze sweeps softly. The pear blossoms are pale white, the willows are a deep green;
the mountains and rivers before our eyes appear as if drawn in a painting. The skull-remains constantly interact with the world; the nostrils touch and rub against it.

The Family Tradition: If you understand it, it is like a snake swallowing a turtle’s nose; if you do not understand it, it is like a tiger biting a great beast. Whether you understand or do not understand, why such a desperate urgency?
Where the practitioner walks, fire burns through ice; atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak, they stand alone on one foot.
Master Sen sends forth his praise from atop the bell tower; he grows vegetables beneath his bed. A fierce tiger sits blocking the road; the ocean at Chicken Island has no lid.
Master Sen comes from the east; how grand and resolute is his spirit! Opening his mouth, he swallows Buddhas and patriarchs, showing no concern for the obstruction of his teeth.
Regarding these extraordinary words from all quarters, there is not a single thought of attachment; only one who is the person of old can clearly understand this "downloading.
I, this mountain monk, am instead pleased with him, and at dawn or dusk, I shall entrust him with the bowl and satchel.
To the Zen practitioner Ji: The foundational ground is already present; there is no need for contrivance. Grasp it directly—what a fine way of life! When cold, wear clothes; when hungry, eat.
The holy life is established and what was to be done is accomplished. If you pollute your breast with intellectual understanding, you will be like an elephant drowning.
The mud grows deeper and deeper; you must seek out and consult a virtuous teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*). Amidst the mist and waters of a hundred cities, you shall meet one who understands.
This mountain monk briefly provides a skillful means: I have traveled throughout Chu, Yue, Ou, and Wu. Beneath my straw rain-hat, the pure breeze is known only to myself;
atop my staff, the bright moon is seen by no one.

I transmit to Venerable Administrator Fu the secret instructions not passed down by the Buddhas and Patriarchs. They are leaked everywhere at the tips of the hundred grasses. The Sea God, enraged, seizes his coral whip;
the Lamp-King of Mount Sumeru suffers beyond measure. Suddenly startled, he rises from the peaks of Mount Cangbian and flees into the breast of Master Fu.

Within the sleeve, a single blow from the golden hammer shatters everything into a hundred fragments; they scatter as seventy-two blue lotuses. Thrown before one’s face, the person fails to perceive them;
try once more to shake out your skirt and robe and look! A fierce tiger rests upon the crag, its hundred-step aura majestic;
its gaze is brilliant like flashing lightning. Yet I recall the traveler beneath Mount Daxiong; on a narrow path we met, and he was struck by my staff.
The General of Supreme Victory sits in emerald oil; let the fierce warriors offer their strategies.
To see off the Chan practitioner Ning as he pays homage to the Patriarchs:
the green mountains and white bones are not the Patriarch himself. He knows nothing of what has passed beneath his feet; even if he were to find a gāthā, what would it matter?
To employ it is to rush through clouds and across waters in vain. As for asafetida, there is no "real"; as for mercury, there is no "false.

It is fundamentally and spontaneously complete; intellectual understanding is but a weary labor. Changqing rushed out the door of the Sangha Hall; having rolled up the curtain, he saw the whole world.
Sent off by Zen practitioner Xing, form does not reach the ear; how can sound touch the eye? O keen and sharp patch-robed monk, you must strictly avoid carrying a single board.
To go on like this is still short of one more blow. To outshine the past and cut off the future—vulgar masters miss it even before they raise their eyebrows. Pick it up!
Once it has arisen, it immediately becomes a stagnant commodity. Among the three thousand disciples at Mengchang’s gate, when one examines them closely, not half a single one remains.

As I see off the Chan master Qing for Jiushang—departing from the region of Zhejiang to reach Jiangxi in the distance—I have a device to present directly before you: the boat passes through Poyang Lake.
Waves within the lake; yet one comes to gaze upon the Five Elders’ Peak. Is it stillness? Is it movement? Try to discern and distinguish them. Both mind and environment alike wither away.
A meal of *harā* rice and a stew of old bones—according to the family’s wealth or lack thereof, this is the lifelong fulfillment of the Master.
How can those who gallop north and south in pursuit fail to see that the original radiance is right before their faces, while they turn their backs like walls?
I send off Chan Master Ji along the Way, the Way, the Way. Upon the flames of the red furnace is but a single blade of grass. Zen, Zen, Zen! In the river, every boat is made of wood.
Having entered the world, he meets no one who takes him up; I bitterly urge him to travel on foot. Within his robes lies a bright pearl; day and night—
The radiance blazes forth; when it meets, it meets immediately. Be careful not to hesitate. The walls, the tiles, and the rubble are all those who understand.
Have you not seen the butcher Guang'e? His karmic consciousness had no basis at all. When he cast down the butcher’s knife from his hand, he said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas."
The matter of the Chan school for the Abbot Zhizang is like an iron wall; even if one exhausts all supernatural powers, one cannot enter it.
When he brandishes the "Blow-off-Blade" sword, West India and this land are dripping with blood. How could Tianning surpass the various quarters? Ordinary and holy beings dwell together in eternity.
In the realm of Quiescent Light, each has their own life’s journey, lacking nothing at all. The great trichiliocosm is gathered into a single hair-tip;
the pearl within the Tathāgata-garbha is presented for the mountain monk to behold. With a sweep of his sleeves, he departs the gate; like a thunderclap and a flash of lightning.
How could a pack of jackals ever do anything against the clay-carved golden-maned lion?
Sending Master Zhuzang back to Guangnan:
A bright pearl from the ocean depths is now being kneaded into mud and tossed onto a heap of refuse, yet its value has increased tenfold.
Thus you repay my inverted desire; whether you find joy or not, whether you are satisfied or not—it is all within yourself.
A wondrous marvel within the house: the celestial wheel is turned and the terrestrial axis is rotated. *Lara liri larali*.
What is there in this separate transmission outside the teachings? One doubt resolved, another doubt arises.
A verse for sending Zen practitioner Fang back to Yangshan:
"It is like a room with six windows; monkeys inside and outside call to one another. Suddenly, one falls asleep, and two find themselves seeing each other.
Yangshan has personally come to Zhongyi; upon the pure ground, even motes of dust fly. A Great Man!

This fellow is a hand that kills or gives life; wherever he encounters someone, he strikes like a thunderclap in the blue sky. He adds a little where there is much, and subtracts a little where there is little.
Whether right or wrong is irrelevant; face-to-face, it is three thousand miles away.
Sending off Zen Practitioner Fu back to Min:
Xuan Sha did not emerge from Fei Juan Ridge; he took the entire great earth and made it into a sesame cake.
Two clay figures glare with wide eyes—one agrees, one does not. Autumn arrives and the chrysanthemums turn yellow; the toad puts on its brocade trousers. The monastic groves.
A bustling, vast expanse; throughout the entire realm, there is no concealment. Licorice is sweet, yellow bitter is bitter; five times five makes twenty-five from the start.
Every person has their nostrils reaching up to their upper lip; every cat catches mice.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Dushan as he journeys to pay homage at Wutai:
within Mount Wutai dwells Mañjuśrī, who sits firmly severing the world of Qingliang. Though the kalpa-fires have blazed forth many times, they ultimately cannot burn him so that he is destroyed.
Raising one's head, one immediately beholds his gathered body-radiance; this ancient site of practice lies to the south, north, east, and west—a sharp sword.
Clearly cutting through self and other; how vast and boundless is the world beneath heaven!

If the Old Man of Oxherding should happen to meet him, he steps forward with palms joined and lightly seizes him. "Three before and three after"—returning to the South, there is no place for questioning.

Sending off Chan practitioner Dao: "Four-seven, twenty-three—no transmission and no reception. Each and every one faces south and gazes at the Northern Dipper. Upon the top of the banner pole, the lotus heart looks upward;
the wind stirs the groves as the lion roars. Truth does not conceal falsehood, nor does crookedness hide the straight. The staff holds its head high."
The straw sandals sprout wings; refined gold of a hundred smeltings does not change its color. Where Sudhana travels, there are no thorns;
Dongping smashed the mirror of Guishan. Linji was not yet a "white-handed thief."

To those Chan practitioners who wish to recognize the "true person of no station": ordinarily he is seldom joyful and often wrathful; when night falls and he sleeps soundly for one watch, upon waking there is nowhere for him to hide his body.
Having finished eating gruel, he washes his bowl and departs—how very clear! Do not be muddled and confused. To gather up the entire great earth...
Not an inch of soil. Nanquan does not beat the drum of Yanguan.
Sending off Zen practitioner Xing:

the ancestral masters of the past have posted their talismans at the Gate of Ghosts; their descendants through the generations undergo a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, yet they still revile Śākyamuni and treat him with arrogance.

Maitreya, as for the place where the diamond takes up the mud, those within the house know it well; whether it be beautiful, it does not contribute a single hair’s breadth, and whether it be ugly, it does not contribute a single hair’s breadth.

To drive an iron stake into empty space and to roll waves upon level ground—your mind is frantic and your mouth is clamorous, yet you do not realize that within the treasury of our King there is no such blade.
To the departing monk Mi: Your entire body is eyes, yet you do not see yourself. When scolded, you become angry; when praised, you rejoice. Aha-ha! What a fine elder brother!
Those who recognize kindness are few; those who betray it are many. The green mountains by the river do not change; the white sun at the edge of the sky remains as it is.
Like a shuttle: amidst the clamor of the world, there is profound stillness. You must attain liberation right where you are, so as not to be entangled by the dust of worldly toil.
What need is there to concern yourself with the five flavors of Chan from all quarters? Let the dustpan and broom sweep everything from the very beginning.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huibian Chushi, "The Sun of the Buddha Shining Universally," Volume Fifteen Phonetic Transcriptions:
Bēi (pǐ mí qiè) Guā (gǔ huá qiè) Náo (rú zhāo qiè) Chī (chǒu zhī qiè) Yàn (wū jiàn qiè) Là (lì hé qiè) Lè (lì)

(Liè gē qiè) Dēng (Duō dèng qiè) Zàn (Zǐ dàn qiè) Bó (Bù gé qiè) Guì (Gǔ huì qiè) Biè (Yú liè qiè) Biāo (Biāo yīn) Xià (Hū jià qiè) Chī (Chī zhī qiè) Jīn (Wǔ jīn qiè) Biàn (Pí yàn qiè) Dá (Dīng dá qiè) *The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Furi Puzhao Hui Bian Chushi, Volume Sixteen*
Verses for the Two Attendants, compiled by Wenbin and others,
sent to Chief Seat Quan upon his return to Yangshan.
Mount Sumeru strikes the drum of empty space; the myriad phenomena and the vast array of forms dance in unison.
This startles the old master Nanquan, who falls prostrate; Shushan loses the daughter of the Cao family. When wide, it pervades the Dharma-realm; where narrow, not even a needle can pass.
A short rope of four or five feet reaches down a well of ten thousand fathoms. Do not say that Yangshan’s era is distant; in the celestial palace, they are currently preaching the *Mahāyāna*.
Mahāyāna. One does not know who the striker of the gavel is. Upon awakening from a dream, one merely blinks in vain. The essence of the Great Way is vast;
it is neither good nor evil. To transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness is the study that leaves behind the paths of sage and ordinary being.
It is like seeking tortoise hair upon the back of an iron ox, or cutting rabbit horns from the waist of a stone woman.
Seeing off Zen Practitioner Zong back to Xuefeng:
Heaven and earth share the same root; the myriad things and I are one body. What a fine, liberated monk! Be careful not to sit here.
Do not admire the various sages; do not prize your own spiritual brilliance. Untie the glue and remove the bonds; pull out the wedges and extract the nails.
Turning over on Wushan Ridge; looking at the eyes, one faces Wangzhou Pavilion. Remember this upon arriving home: "Inquire with earnest greetings;
may Master Zeng have ten thousand blessings. Three wooden balls roll away, terrifying the blind shaven-headed monks who wander the world.
Seeing off Chan Master Pu as he returns to Min:
The green mountains are green and the white clouds are white. If you wish to recognize the "one thread," it is two five-hundred-pieces. This is the famous variety of lychee from Fuzhou.
For the most part, they are swallowed whole by the *hu-lun* (the "gobbler"). Xuan Sha struck him so that his toes were broken, causing his entire body to break into a cold sweat.

As for those currently called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*), they merely press sand to extract oil while interacting with beings and benefiting living things; they discern the truth before one has even stepped through the gate.
Why wait until one has ascended the throne of the Lamp-King to seek a true companion throughout the five lakes and four seas? A single melody of the "Yangchun" lacks its harmony.
Renhe sent Zen practitioner Songyi to pay homage at Putuo and prostrate before the Great Being of Putuo.
This very sound of speech is it. To thus receive the resonance and inherit the void—how is this?
Transcending birth and death: the dull-witted bird flies against the wind; three thousand li in a single day. Iron trees bloom at night;
by morning they have already borne fruit. One awakens in Aparagoyānī in the west, while walking in meditation in Pūrvavideha in the east.
In Jambudvīpa in the south the drum is beaten; in Uttarakuru in the north the lute is plucked. Tell me, what tune is this? When you listen, yet there is no sound.
When the First Patriarch saw a monk arriving, he simply faced the wall; when the wall was broken down by others, it became a scene of total disorder. At Shoushan, the gate opens toward the south;
everything is already complete, which is truly effortless. If you wish to sit, you sit; if you wish to walk, you walk. It is like leveling the ground.
They dig deep trenches and pits. Sentient beings are themselves the Buddhas; the Buddhas are themselves sentient beings.

Without departing from a single thought-moment, they penetrate from beginning to end. Vast and boundless, pervading the earth and filling the heavens, yet people often leave the waves to seek the water.

To send off Chan Practitioner Ke: "The mind itself is Buddha; the Way is without mind. Unawares, one’s whole body enters the wild weeds. The speech of the ancients is clumsy and today’s people laugh at them;
yet the ancients laughed at the cleverness of today’s people. Those born later and growing up late should shun cleverness; they must first lower their heads and learn.
An old hand. Yet I recall Nanquan’s fine words: "I want him to remain dull-witted throughout his life.
The third and the first, the middle nine and the lower seven. The four oceans flow into the Eastern Sea; this is the Prajñāpāramitā.
Regarding the Chan practitioner Songli:
the Tathāgata had no Chan; the Patriarchs had no intent. They were like withered trees, stones, lumps of clay, and clods of earth.
Since the old barbarian said he did not know, the wood-seller also said he did not understand. Niaoke never left the bird’s nest; Dandi [simply] struck the ground once.
Growing up and striking the earth, leaping out from the vast net of the heavens—such a one is called a monk who has accomplished his task.
Taking another step beyond the hundred-foot pole: in Shoushan’s hand lies the black staff.
Having sent off the Chan practitioner:
the Buddhas of the past have already passed away; the Buddhas of the future have not yet been born; in the present interval, there is no Buddha.
For now, let us set aside the story of Tianning. What excellence does Tianning possess? "The karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, having no fundamental basis. Kunming.
The sword was lost within the pond; yet one retrieved it from the West River. Picked up, it is once more an iron caltrop;
blown hither and thither by the wind. The Son of Heaven of Fusang laughs aloud; eyebrows of a foot and two inches hang down over his chin.

Seeing off the Chan practitioner Xing for Jiangxiang, the autumn rain falls incessantly; the autumn wind whistles and howls. Now there, now here; parting for a moment, then reuniting. On the far side of the Xiang River, wild geese first arrive;
the fisherman’s song pierces the clouds with its mournful flute-like melody. Furthermore, reeds drift like snow against the layered distant mountains.
Unfolding a screen of layered brocade—how lamentable, this "lacquer bucket" that is never satisfied! To call this the realm of *tathatā* (True Suchness) is for you, O *ācārya*, to be truly pitiable;
do not establish intellectual interpretations within the School of the Patriarchs.

To see off Meditation Master Kuang: The Buddhas of the three ages do not know it exists; The great earth, mountains, and rivers run upside down. The tabby cat and the white ox, however, do know it exists;
A red lotus root bursts forth from the midst of fire. In the morning one looks to the southeast, in the evening to the northwest; Like scattered pearls upon a platter, there is nothing to grasp.
Traces of his presence: on the long continuous bed he eats his fill; sitting, reclining, or walking, he exerts no effort. To speak of the wondrous and discuss the profound is itself folly.
For one who has left the household life, there is originally nothing to do. In Jiangxi and Hunan, they proceed in this manner;
there is no need to further question the Vairocana Master.

Sent off to visit his parents, this Chan practitioner contemplates the state prior to birth: the wooden horse chasing the wind vanishes like smoke. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he has remained unawakened, regardless of the shifting cycles of cold and heat.
Ten thousand years are but a single thought; a single thought encompasses ten thousand years. Such is the wondrous function of spiritual power; the Great Way is void and profound.
Atop his head is Maheśvara; along the way, traveling companions shoulder to shoulder—all together they illuminate this very matter:
the golden crow emerges from the eastern sea.
When the Chan practitioner Jing sent away his rope bed, it ran off and entered a loquat tree; Mount Sumeru leaped up and ascended into the heavens. To study the "dead word" is to miss the mark;
to study the "living word" is to transcend the sands of the Ganges. Where there is nothing said, it is the lion’s roar; where something is said, it is the howl of a jackal.
Severing both ends, striking the bridge of the nose, opening the eight characters, and piercing the eyes:
the water buffalo grazes on sweet grass, wandering freely and at will along the byways.
The place where the Chan practitioner Senghua, a man of genuine practice, walks: thousands and ten thousands cannot hold him back. He roams freely through Xiangnan and Tanci;
his staff, one *xun* long, is cast from raw iron. Wherever he goes, he unravels the needle from the dry bone and chants amidst the withered autumn wind. Autumn winds howl and whistling.
Cloud-shrouded skies. In every direction there are virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); one must discern between dragons and snakes, so seek them out.
Have you not seen how the weary Zhaozhou, at eighty years of age, was still in a hurry to travel from place to place for the sake of study?
And have you not seen how Mazu’s single shout at Daxiong Peak left Baizhang deaf for three days?
A Parting Verse for Chan Master Gong of Zhongzhu as He Returns to Eastern Zhejiang:
Recently you came from Zhongzhu, yet now you are heading toward Siming. The Linglong Rock meets the Yujing Peak; these are all places where you have traveled with ease.
At Damei, "the mind is the Buddha"; at Putuo, "hearing and practicing what is heard. At Yuelin, there is but one [Buddha].
The hemp sack. Five hundred bhikṣus at Tiantai. Hanshanzi coming and going on Mount Huading. Nuona sitting and cutting off the Dragon Spring.
The entire Tripitaka is but a tangle of vines; everything else is merely a bowl falling from a hill. Fire is originally without fire.
Those who rely on words are in a state of confusion. From atop Mount Aoshan Inn, I call out to my elder brother: "On the head of the Huangbo tree grows honeyed fruit.
Sent by the attendant Tiantong Zheng to undertake a second visit for further study.
When Niaoke blew on a cloth-hair, the attendant was immediately enlightened. This intimate verse from Tiandong requires no further commentary or annotation.
As the weather grows increasingly cold in the tenth month, cross the Xixing ferry early; though we gaze at one another across a thousand li, we travel the great road back and forth.
When entering the room for the second audience, one must take care with the clenched fist of wrath.
When seeing off the attendant, bow to Putuo;
let the eyes listen to sounds and the ears observe forms. Amidst the clear and cold clouds, a thunderclap flies forth—this is the gate of sovereign perfect penetration.
How many patch-robed monks know the ultimate point? In years past, before emerging from the rising sun, he personally beheld the Holy Master at Potalaka.
Returning once more to seek him in the depths of the ocean mountains, he saw [the Master] atop Mount Sumeru, wearing Mount Sumeru upon his head.
Sending off the rector Ying to pay homage at Putuo, and striking Kebin at Xinghua;
he was fined and expelled from the monastery. Examine these old stories from all quarters again and again with careful scrutiny.
Who with ears would not hear? Who with eyes would not see? A pillar hangs a lantern; the mountain gate faces the Buddha hall.
Dragging his staff crosswise, he goes off and winds around the Qín River. He strikes his own toes, and his whole body breaks into a cold sweat.
The person atop Mount Potalaka faces you directly day and night. *Du!* You who have come from Goryeo, O Zen practitioner, to pay homage to the one on Mount Potalaka—what do you take to be the Way?
Be most careful not to seek it laboriously in the external realm; to seek it externally is but a vain exertion.
Divine! This very mind-jewel is ever luminous. The waters of Wu are azure; the mountains of Yue are green. Three clouds, four clouds; a bird, one call, two calls.
The Tathāgatas of the three ages cannot lift it up; the patriarchs of successive generations find it difficult to open their beaks.
If you wish to see the House-to-House Avalokiteśvara, it is clearly because of me that you may pay homage to him.
I, the student, send Zen practitioner Jun to the region east of Zhejiang to pay his respects and study.
Traveling through mountains and admiring the waters—Master Yunmen said, "Things do not arise in isolation. From here, go to the region east of Zhejiang.
Seeking out whom? With a seven-foot black staff slung over his shoulder, he first ascended Mount Yujia to pay homage to the Śarīra, then proceeded to Potalaka to consult the Holy Master.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven; seven, six, five, four, three, two, one.
A preeminent monk among the forest of monasteries—why must he seek it elsewhere from others?
Seeing off Chief Seat Ying of Mount Jingshan as he returns to Lingxiao Peak in Ningbo:
The Mahāyāna Dharma has been clearly elucidated and broken through; The hundred negations and four propositions are all transcended. Who can harmonize with this "White Snow" and "Yangchun"?

It reaches the point where one leaps from the Hanshen Pavilion straight up to the Brahma Heaven. —Sōtō (Dongpo) *Note: The character [跳-兆+孛] is a variant or scribal error for "leap/jump" (pǐ). The text refers to the famous encounter between the Chan master Dahui Zonggao and the layman Su Shi (Dongpo), who was so inspired by the Master’s teaching that he leapt from the Hanshen Pavilion to the top of Mount Tiantai.*
The pond swallows Mount Siming; suddenly, riding backward upon the Buddha hall, he strides out the gate. On the Go-board Rock, let the moss-stains remain as they are.
Do you not see? Hanshan returned too early; for ten years he has forgotten the path by which he came.
And do you not see the Old Man Mingjue, nowhere to be found? The spring of the Ten Continents has ended and the flowers wither away; the coral groves bask in the bright sun.

Gao! When you sent Chief Seat Ju to travel through Tai and Wen to discuss sitting in meditation with Yin Guang for kalpas, it was still no more than "securing the mooring ropes before letting go of the boat. Wenshu’s spending the summer retreats in three places is very much like this.

The price is set by the vast heavens. For men of outstanding talent and spiritual lineage, going and staying are matters of free choice: one may travel to Mount Tandan in the morning and proceed to Mount Luofu in the evening.
Once the Dharma has been preached in the celestial palaces, one who understands such matters simply lets them be. Every person is Śākyamuni and Maitreya; every individual is Hanshan and Shide.
Having roamed throughout Tiantai and Yandang, and having swept across mountain cities and coastal lands, their nostrils have always been [straight].
The great head hangs down. Do not say that meeting face-to-face means one does not know the other.
Sending off Attendant Fu for Maitreya Buddha in Xinchang, Zhejiang:
his feet do not leave the ground as he runs; at midnight he passes through the Fusang tree; facing south, he gazes at the Big Dipper.
Returning to Mount Tiantai and Yandang, I again visited Mount Qingliang and Potalaka. There I encountered Hanshan clapping his hands and listened as Shide sang aloud:
"A-he-he, A-he-he! As before, I sit cross-legged within the hall; there is no need to toil across ten thousand li over the waves of the whale-sea."

The Head Seat Xiansong paid his respects at Yuyang and Bodai, where [the teaching] transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations. Who among those of the Mahāyāna Dharma could be its true recipient? It was able to make the "Silent Son" (Śāriputra) hang his head in shame.
It can cause my Way to radiate its brilliance. Throughout the eastern Zhejiang and western regions, explore at will. Among these, who has realized it and who has not?
If you truly recognize the person of original nature, the myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences are all swept away. The Dharma-body originally possesses no *śarīra*;

it is through skillful means that it manifests to subdue the hosts of demons. The Great Beings of hearing and contemplation respond to every dust mote and world-system, yet in the end, they have never [departed].
Kubodha, you vainly claim that the stone at Fangguang Temple is too vast for ordinary beings of shallow capacity to reach.

Yet, though its jade halls and crystal palaces dwell amidst colored clouds, what is there to value when viewed with the True Eye? With a hand pointing to the tea in the Duanhua Pavilion, he was the first to discern the flowers within the cup.
How many people mistake hemp for rope, and further, recognize that rope as a snake? [He] turned his back...

Having returned from Tiantai to wander through Yandang, how could the Venerable Nanquan have left behind nothing but his image? Great Dragon Pond and Little Dragon Pond—cascading snow and overturning clouds for thousands of myriad fathoms.
Throughout the entire realm of dust and sand, it is one and the same sky; everything is vividly clear before one’s eyes.
Before even taking a step, one has already traversed it all. Who can afford to waste their straw sandals on this?

Sending off Bao-tuo Ding, the Rector: Mountains of Eastern Zhejiang, waters of Western Zhejiang; the five lakes and four seas are all one's own self. A bright moon is held high upon the head of the staff;
cold clouds are trodden haphazardly upon the soles of the straw sandals. Those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure; they must penetrate the truth atop the Bao-tuo Rock.
People say it is truly extraordinary, surpassing both form and sound. A single branch of peach blossoms in an ancient cave in springtime; this journey meanders toward Tianyu.
On and on, the *udumbara* flowers and distant mountains turn green. Send my regards to the two venerable elders; as you leave the gate, I cannot help but give you these final instructions.
To send off Chan practitioner Shun, along with a note for his teacher:
In Suzhou there is one, and in Changzhou there is one. Two by two does not make a pair; three by three is likewise not nine.
If there were a single phrase that reached you, my tongue would fall out; if there were not a single phrase that reached you, my mouth would be silenced. O sharp-witted monk!
To know while not knowing—your teacher himself is truly a master of the True School. Why do you abandon the sweet peach tree and instead spend all your time climbing the mountain to pluck sour pears?
*Sent to Chan Master Wannian upon his return to Japan.*
Ten thousand years in a single thought; a single thought for ten thousand years. It is not at Mount Tiantai or Mount Wuyi, nor is it in the East Land or the West Heaven (India).
If you realize this, the wind blows and the grass bows; if you do not realize it, paper wraps the hemp.
