Verses on the Four Attendants, compiled by Wenbin and others;
Mingzhen Verses, twenty-eight stanzas in total.
I possess a single *maṇi* jewel, buried within the field of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Yesterday, I extracted it from the mud, and its radiance illuminated boundlessly.
There is nothing that is not known by its intent; it is ever-present in our daily lives. Who in this world does not possess this treasure?
Yet, being mired in delusion and not yet liberated from the entanglements of the *āvaraṇas*, one is fettered by the karmic retribution of birth and death, whether as a human or a deva.
Once one encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), is this not indeed a great causal condition?
(1) These very words, sounds, forms, and colors are neither sense organs, nor sense objects, nor consciousness. Śākyamuni personally beheld Dīpaṃkara;
thus he was named "The Capable One" and "Tranquil Silence. He leveled his own field, thoroughly clearing away the rubble, thorns, and briars; the radiance of his body pervades everywhere.

How could there be only ten voids? They may even number in the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions. To attain Buddhahood in a single thought, one need not doubt the manifold methods; how could the scope of transformative influence ever be exhausted?
Although these are called the adornments of wondrous practice, they ultimately lead back to non-attainment. (The second item, right).

Everything one encounters is none other than this Way; do not discriminate between the refined and the coarse, or the great and the small. Sentient beings and Buddhas—what difference is there? All are created by one's own mind.
By cultivating goodness, one is reborn in heaven by transformation, enjoying rare and wondrous treasures;

by committing evil, one falls into hell, surrounded by iron beds and copper pillars. When the karmic retribution of one’s sins manifests at the moment of death, it is only then that one regrets not having practiced earlier.
Awakening is affliction; delusion is awakening. (The three on the right). The Chan Master does not rely on extensive knowledge;
he eats when hungry and drinks when thirsty according to the occasion. To employ the mind by means of the mind is a great error. To cultivate the Way while remaining within the Way is pitiable.
Searching for it internally and externally, it is not seen; even in the middle, there is not a hair’s breadth of it to be found. Sentient beings seek it elsewhere.
Wisdom. How do the Buddhas differ from the ignorant? It is like a single piece of gold fashioned into various vessels—a jar, a basin, a hairpin, a bracelet, or a ring.
Their essential nature fundamentally undergoes no change, yet it is subjected to a thousand uses through the hammering of the furnace. (The above four).
Greed, anger, and delusion are called the three poisons. These three poisons arise from the one mind; yet fundamentally, the three poisons are empty and quiescent.

From this moment, the three poisons subside into stillness, and one suddenly attains the adamantine true body. One hears directly the perfect voice of the Great Awakened One, clearly realizing that there is neither arising nor ceasing.
To those who understand, this is neither ancient nor modern; for the wise, it is the ultimate reality manifest before them, while the foolish seek it outwardly.
Deluded emotions create karma that is difficult to sever, like an elephant sinking into mud that becomes ever deeper. (The fifth point on the right).

Contemplating the mind while sitting constantly to practice meditative concentration, one desires to realize it directly in this very life, attaining the eternally abiding Dharmakāya and being worthy of continuing the Tathāgata’s life of wisdom.
If, however, one sinks into emptiness or stagnates in quiescence, one falls into the dhyāna-disease of the two vehicles; the clear pool does not permit this.
A coiled dragon—how could a great elephant roam the rabbit’s path? At every place one wanders freely and finds joy; one thoroughly clarifies the true nature of oneself.
Within this, there is neither confusion nor fixity; above this, there is neither the ordinary nor the sage. (Sixth)

The Dharma is beyond words and letters; yet people instead become attached to words and letters. Even if one is diligent in the Tripitaka, how does that compare to directly cutting through to the root?
To wander about counting the strokes of characters is to fail to awaken; to recite scriptures repeatedly only causes one to grow increasingly muddled.

The ground of the mind is fundamentally devoid of a single thing; it is like a clear sky, utterly free from the traces of dust. Why do you create obstacles for yourself, following after the six sense organs day and night?
In a single thought, all that exists is emptied; there is no door for demons or heretics to peer through.
(7) Long ago, the Great Being Vimalakīrti manifested illness within the city of Vaiśālī. Thirty-two Bodhisattvas each discoursed upon the profound principle of non-duality.
When Mañjuśrī questioned Vimalakīrti, Vimalakīrti remained in silence alone. Now, for those at the stage of ordinary beings...
Ordinary people, having not yet studied the Samādhi of Sound, rashly pass judgment on public cases (gong'an) and recklessly revile the sages and saints.
Unless one has attained realization of one's own mind, such frivolous talk regarding Prajñā will bring about sin. (8)

Monks of the Final Dharma do not yield; they mostly engage in anger, strife, and contention. Having left the home life in reliance upon the Great Precepts, one must take the Six Principles of Harmony as one's supreme ideal.
Arhats have profoundly realized non-arising and have never opposed others. How excellent!
The shaven head and the square robe are the very image of the Buddhas of the future. With a mind that is serene and level within, there is no one in the world who does not rely upon them.
Do not give rise to even a single thought of the fire of anger; its blazing intensity is difficult to turn back as it consumes the plains.

(9) The karmic consciousness of sentient beings is vast and boundless; within their hearts, all is like boiling water. They merely follow sounds and pursue forms—by what means can they reflect inwardly and return the light?
To investigate Zen and realize one’s own nature is like a long-traveling guest returning home; after kalpas of wandering, one is finally gathered back.

One should maintain mindfulness; one should maintain mindfulness that encompasses the ten directions. When encountering objects or meeting conditions, remain unchanging. Put on clothes and eat meals as usual.
Through this, ignorance is extinguished, and the feverish afflictions naturally become cool and refreshing. (The tenth.)
Failing to comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this is termed ignorance (*avidyā*). I observe that ignorance has no intrinsic nature;
it neither abides, nor ceases, nor arises. The Bodhisattva transcends both principle and phenomena, while the Śrāvaka is terrified by forms and sounds.
One dwells in the carefree Land of Bliss, while the other remains in the deep pit of liberation. Departing from these two extremes, the Middle Way is brilliantly pure and luminous.
Moving freely among humans and devas, one extensively delivers sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (11).
The numinous void is originally formless; there is no need to sever delusive thoughts. Delusive thoughts are themselves the true mind—why must one be divided into two?
When ice melts, it becomes water, warm and gentle; when water freezes, it becomes ice, hard and cold. Thus it is with turbid and evil sentient beings...
They can be transformed. The pure Buddhas are worthy of veneration. The fundamental nature of all Buddhas and sentient beings—how could it be like external objects that wax and wane?
In a single instant upon the Vajra Seat, they forever sever all prior influences and traces. (12)

The Dharma-body has no visible boundaries or surface; in daily life, when has it ever been lacking? Whether in speech or silence, movement or stillness, in all actions and deeds, one naturally accords with the Way without deliberate intent.
Yet, should there be even a hair’s breadth of attachment or obstruction, one will immediately be ensnared by demonic realms.

The great ocean universally receives the hundred rivers, and Mount Sumeru is composed of the four precious substances; yet, in the end, none can escape impermanence—your mere self-display of vastness and loftiness is but in vain.
Once one awakens to the wondrous principle of true emptiness, both nirvana and birth-and-death are fully understood (13).

Sentient beings are originally and inherently Buddhas, yet they willingly fall into the den of ignorance. If one awakens to the fact that ignorance is fundamentally empty, one will transcend saṃsāra from this point on.
It is like a single bright lamp that can shatter a dark room of a thousand years; it definitively resolves greed and anger.

The essential nature [of phenomena] is like flowers in the sky or a mirage; they are not real. You must simply resolve to investigate with determination; you must not follow your own whims or succumb to negligence.
Only the Zen school possesses the direct shortcut; there is no other essential method for entering the Way. (14)
The Buddha’s mouth has never uttered a word; how could the Dharma-body have birth or extinction? It is only because he conformed to the ways of the world that we see a myriad of differences.
He minutely distinguished the causes and effects of ordinary beings and extensively set forth the essential instructions of all the sages.

The gates of the profound mystery were opened one by one, and the nets of the teachings were established layer upon layer. Finally, he held up a flower to show the assembly, completely discarding all expedient means for directness alone.
For example, it is like ten *hu* of donkey’s milk being scattered over a single drop of lion’s blood (15).
There are many foolish people in the world who follow after sounds and forms, drifting along with them; they do not realize that the myriad phenomena all arise from the transformations of the mind.
Thus they fall into the sea of worldly toil, unable to escape the snares of Māra. The sheep-cart is precisely this.
An ox-cart. How does my face differ from the Buddha’s face? Turn your head directly downward and it is there; there is no need for me to labor my mouth in exhortation.
Once you cast off this skin-sack, you will escape the tribunal of Lord Yanluo. (16)
Though as small as a firefly’s flame, it can burn down the great earth and its forests; do not allow a single thought of anger to arise, for it will extinguish the boundless mind of the Way.
Buddhas and Patriarchs cause people to protect themselves, guarding against the encroachment of external realms. What difference is there between sentient beings and the Buddha?
To cast aside True Suchness and seek elsewhere is to let forth that which covers heaven and earth—a reality that is fundamentally neither ancient nor modern.
Know that the efficacy of Prajñā is such that an iron ship entering the sea does not sink (17).
To realize the Way, there is nothing superior to self-awakening; in Zen practice, do not seek elsewhere. To instead search for the Buddha outside the mind is like trying to extract oil from sand.
Even the yakṣa Yaśoda laughed at this; he once cast away his mirror to search for his own head. White clouds stretch for a thousand miles.
Ten thousand miles away. Before the autumn, after the autumn—the yellow leaves. If you wish to resolve it, resolve it this very moment; if you do not cease, on what day will you ever cease?
Clapping hands and singing aloud, I return home, riding backward upon the white ox of the open field. (18)

The sages and saints who have attained the Way throughout past and present should contemplate that there is neither cultivation nor realization. Both afflictions and bodhi are extinguished; both nirvana and birth-and-death are equally pure.
Unmoved by the winds of external objects, they constantly abide in the samādhi of the *nāga*. Their response to Buddhas is as perfect as the great void;
when facing circumstances, they are as limpid as a clear mirror. Majestic in both the mundane and supramundane realms, they manifest the Dharma-kings’ teachings wherever they may be.
All ordinary beings are fundamentally the same; they do not depart from the essence and nature of the Dharma-realm (19).

When the deluded turn away from evil toward good, the path of the Buddha grows ever more distant as they seek it. Let go of body and mind and rest; in a single moment, both good and evil are cast aside.
One need not think of the bliss of heaven, nor need one fear the torments of hell. What a wondrous state of natural spontaneity!
The Buddhas of antiquity fill the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm. Since there is neither birth nor death, neither coming nor going, how could there be right or wrong, long or short?
The nature-ground is naturally level and smooth; what use is there to eliminate or sever the afflictions of worldly toil? (Twenty)

The Dharma King has appeared in the world; through skillful means he speaks of emptiness to shatter attachment to existence. That which exists must ultimately return to non-existence—this is the holy lion’s roar.
Adorned with the jade-like brow-hair and golden marks, his entry into *nirvāṇa* will not be long.

When the time comes for heaven and earth to collapse, who will distinguish between the rich and the poor, the beautiful and the ugly? Pitiable are the deluded followers of external paths, who falsely cling to the longevity of Brahmā.
When eighty thousand great kalpas have ended, it is difficult to avoid the cycle of rebirth.
(Verse 21) Where can one escape birth and death? How many people realize the true void? The true void has no form or appearance;
yet you further ask about south, north, west, and east. If even a hair’s breadth of deluded thought arises, every point becomes obstructed and impassable; to cling to it is inevitably to fall.
The deviant path—letting it go does not exempt one from obscurity and delusion. When body and mind are suddenly and directly liberated, one is like a bird soaring freely out of its cage.
If there is no illness, what need is there to take medicine? Ignorance and wisdom are both fused as one. (22)
No matter how many preferences and aversions you may entertain, they are like bubbles floating upon the water. As bubbles arise and vanish, they cannot be stopped;
as thoughts go out and come back, they never cease. You must exert yourself to awaken with fierce mindfulness. Turn the light inward and seek nothing else.
An empty room with no owner—when it collapses, what need is there to rebuild? When hungry, take up the bowl and eat; when sleepy, use a block of stone as a pillow.
Happy throughout the twelve periods of the day; who can be like me, free from sorrow?

(Verse 23) A phantom conjures a great mansion, where gardens, groves, flowers, and fruits vie for freshness. Within it, men and women are arrayed; carriages and horses come and go, bustling with activity.
They take pleasure in shouting and dancing, indulging in license and wild abandon according to the occasion. [Yet all is but] the bones and skeletons of birth and death.

The earth is filled; weddings and the sounds of flutes and songs abound before one's eyes. The foolish grasp at these as being truly existent, unaware that they are produced by illusionary transformations.
In the end, not a single thing exists; when the clouds disperse, it is once again the clear blue sky. (24)
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without fabrication; it is neither internal, external, nor intermediate. Why need one laboriously loathe sounds and forms?

Sensory objects and faculties are likewise unrelated. To sever afflictions (*kleśa*) is to move further away [from the truth]; to seek the realization of *bodhi* is already difficult. Where there is thought, one sinks into birth and death;
through non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), one spontaneously accords with *nirvāṇa*. Both paths are obstacles; the Middle Way is yet separated by mountains and rivers.
Shatter the mirror to meet [the self]. Body and mind are thus empty and at ease.
(25) To awaken is to seek awakening within delusion; delusion arises from within awakening. Bound by these two dharmas, when will one be liberated to achieve Bodhi?
Buddhas and patriarchs have never given any indication; it is only through folly and madness that conceptualizations arise. Ordinary people remain attached to them.
Do not abandon [them]. Those with nihilistic views deceive themselves from the outset; the wise do not seek liberation. A single word can shatter a multitude of doubts.
Greed and anger are themselves the Great Way. Turning one's back on the Heart-King, whom would one ask? (26)

Dīpaṃkara bestowed the prophecy upon Śākyamuni, who realized that within the Dharma there is absolutely nothing to be attained. I observe the heavens and the human realm, yet I do not see Maitreya of the future.
How strange are these beings of the turbid and evil age; they behold the Buddha before their eyes yet fail to recognize him. Why need one turn one’s head or twist one’s brain?

One should simply ride upon sound and encompass form, delivering sentient beings throughout all time until the end of the future, manifesting hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of emanations.
Now, the Dragon Flower [Bodhi] is revealed; all people in the world cannot fathom it.

(27) If you wish to recognize your own precious treasury, it constantly emits light throughout the six periods of the day. It is originally neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it is never separate from sitting, lying, or walking.
It is the marrow of the Tathāgatas of the three ages and the eyes of the patriarchs of successive generations. It is very much like [the moon’s reflection] in water.
The moon’s reflection is just like the indigo dye within the pigment; it is vividly beyond grasping or rejecting, and ultimately difficult to discuss in terms of destruction or formation.
In every place it encounters conditions, it brings benefit; in every speck of dust, it delivers those whose minds are lost. (28)
The Dharma Master Shōdai Tokugen lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and composed eighteen verses, which he sent [to me], saying:
"To attain the Way, one must extensively deliver sentient beings; to deliver sentient beings, one must necessarily clarify the nature-mind. In Jambudvīpa, there is a Brahmā."
Dharani. In the hells there is no passion; Ānanda emerged from it only after being ensnared by Māra’s net. Mañjuśrī arrived to protect the Dharma when the boat was about to sink.
That much learning is not to be considered extraordinary; what matters is the diligent practice cultivated over vast eons.
From the external reaches of empty space to the internal physical body, nothing at all exists outside the truth of this mind. A floating bubble is insufficient to exhaust the vastness of the ocean;

one must discard the pointing finger and recognize the lunar orb. The mind that conditions itself to hear the Dharma is not the fundamental nature; the true master of the pavilion is surely not a passing traveler.
Detached from sound and form, there is no discrimination—this is like planting flowers upon a rock or dust at the bottom of a well.
Hands open and hands closed, jewel-light flies forth; looking back to the left and right, who is this? One must believe that where this head moves, it does not hinder the state of total stillness.
When the mind is enlightened and nature is seen, there is no expanding or contracting; when one recognizes objects and follows the stream, it is but deluded cognition.
These are the true words of the Unsurpassed Dharma King; how could they be like the false and deceptive teachings of Maskarī Gośālī?
The nature of King Prasenajit has never changed; seeing the Ganges in old age is as if seeing it in youth. There is no need to grieve over the fading years or white hair;

floating clouds will eventually disperse into the blue sky. Those who came from the distant past—where are they now? Those who departed to become desolate mounds—their bones have already been cast away.
When the fires of the kalpa blaze forth and not a single thing remains, it is clearly the state before one's parents were even born.
Investigating the mind through the seven locations, the mind is found to be non-existent; analyzing the seeing through the eight returns, the source of seeing is revealed to be originally void.

The thousandfold secret locks are split open, and a single round, luminous pearl bursts forth. From this point on, the intellectual understandings of both sages and ordinary beings are severed; what birth and death, or the constraints of emotion and nature, can there be?
When the pivot-phrase is raised, those who truly understand it are few; let it remain as a model for the world.
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, views, and consciousness—pervading the entire dharma-realm, they are primordially perfect. One should know that the true meaning is beyond words;

it is not a matter of false calculations regarding causes, conditions, or spontaneity. Arising and ceasing have no source, for the essence is eternally abiding. Those who are coarse and superficial do not awaken to what this sutra explains:
which sentient being is not destined to become a Buddha? This serves as the condition for their deliverance in the future.
The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are the Tathāgatagarbha; within a single hair-tip, the ten directions are transparently revealed.

The great earth never assists in its manifestation, yet empty space, as if possessing a mouth, proclaims it of itself. Sentient beings do not maintain the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā), while all Buddhas dwell in the Constant Light of Quiescence.
What can obstruct birth, death, coming, and going? Like a bird flying through the vast blue sky, there is no end to its flight.
When awakened awareness clearly perceives that difference is ultimately identical, then the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are seen to be empty.

When the mind of Yaśoda’s son naturally subsides from its madness, the spell of the Mātanga girl can no longer ensnare him. This directly severs fundamental ignorance, thereby bringing one into communion with the wondrous principle of the Tathāgata.
All conditioned phenomena throughout the three periods of time possess cessation; yet the ten directions of space, being beginningless, are certainly without end.

When the six meanings arise within the perfect stillness, the one vanishes entirely and the six are melted away. Detaching from sensory clinging, the mind is inwardly stilled and is no longer existent;

as laborious activity arises before the sense-objects, their nature is fundamentally empty. Moving freely through rising and sinking like a fish escaping the net, going or staying without hindrance like a crane leaving its cage—how can one describe the mutual functioning of each faculty? It is exactly the same as untying the knots in the flowered cloth.
How excellent are these twenty-five methods of perfect penetration! Each was cultivated through diligent practice without stagnating in emptiness.

Although there are differences in the gateways to the Dharma entered, the realization of the original nature of the mind-ground is the same. Contemplating the words of Samantabhadra, one finds them even more profound;

selecting among them, Avalokiteśvara’s faculty of hearing is most acute. By the riverbank, green willows have just been washed by the rain; the song of several yellow birds resonates through the spring breeze.

Cut off lust, eliminate killing, and further abstain from theft; one cannot attain Buddhahood by seeking it through false speech. If these four precepts are maintained without defilement, all demonic affairs and obstacles will cease.
Once the site of practice is established and the mind and body are pure, the divine mantras are proclaimed throughout the oceans of lands.
Immeasurable Vajra-holders come to protect the Dharma; may they take their vajras and shatter the heads of evil Māras.

The eighty-four thousand inverted perceptions serve as the causes for the twelve classes of beings. When the wondrous, luminous nature of awareness is awakened, the false and floating mind is itself the fundamental reality.
Whether dragon, ghost, celestial immortal, or human—whether with a red fleshly usnīṣa, feathers, scales, or a purple-gold body—who can sit in stillness and contemplate them?
Within, without, and in between, they are utterly free from even a speck of dust.

Sentient beings of the three realms dwell in reliance upon food; by forever abandoning wine and meat and severing the mind of lust, the karma of mutual birth and mutual killing ceases to exist, so that external objects and demons shall never again invade.
Engraving [the precepts] upon the bones and marking them upon the flesh, one upholds the pure precepts; wherever one looks, one beholds the Buddha and hears the profound sound.
Like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli, a single radiance of glory illuminates all from antiquity to the present.
Wisdom first shines forth as the habits of desire dry up; the stages proceed from the forty-fourth mind toward peace.

Belief in the initial Middle Way is the nature of pure truth; like a consecration, it is like a king entrusting his kingdom to his heir. Beneficial conduct delivers sentient beings with an ever-expanding mind; turning from the True back toward the mundane, how vast is the Path!
To ascend to the Ten Stages, one must apply preparatory practice (*prayoga*); the practices and awakenings are layered, yet each is also singular.
I have heard that hell originally does not exist; when the ten habitual practices are completed, the six retributions arrive.

If one turns evil thoughts into the merit of teaching others to become Buddhas, the mountain of blades will, upon a single shout, become a golden terrace. Not craving the pleasures and amusements of the heavens, one is willing to avoid the womb of human love and desire.
One’s original nature as Amitābha is constantly manifest; a single lotus flower awaits the time to bloom.

The ten classes originally stem from the ten ghosts; when their lives end and retribution is exhausted, they are reborn as humans. The ten types of immortals merely differ in the length of their lifespans;

within the three realms, none escape the body of birth and death. Even those dwelling at the Peak of Existence in the Heaven of Ultimate Form, or Great Arhats who have emerged from the mundane dust, though they exhaust the great Way of emptiness and find no place of return, cannot yet avoid beginning again and entering the cycle of rebirth.
In an instant, the five aggregates and ten dhyānas were dissolved; in fifteen layers, the evil māras were successively shattered.
With eyes of clarity, one need not fear the obstruction of darkness; how can solid ice withstand boiling water? When the mind itself is awakened, it is no different from attaining sainthood;
like water flowing evenly, how could there be separate waves? Reaching even unto Bodhi without the slightest lack—everyone praises Ānanda!
The essence of the five aggregates has always been empty; these five layers of delusive thought must be eliminated. They do not depart from the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment;

one must recognize the source from which they first arise. Suffering through the permeation of many kalpas beyond counting, once the six sense organs function interchangeably, all is extinguished without remainder.
Even if one were to fill the void with precious offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, such merit would not equal that of one who propagates this sutra.
I show these nine verses for all practitioners of dhyāna:
what has been transmitted through four sevens and two threes? Clearly, the Buddhas and Patriarchs are one's own kinsmen turned enemies.
What is brought forth is nothing at all; it is pierced through by a single word. Yet you still seek awakening and understanding with the mind; there is no need to search for it elsewhere.
The root source: day is bright, night is dark—this is but an ordinary matter. The wind bells at the corner of the eaves chime all the more busily.
It is entirely because one has obscured one’s own mind that one merely wanders aimlessly, seeking outward. Failing to recognize the painted rooster, one calls it a phoenix;
mistaking yellow leaves for gold, one seeks out a master, traversing mountains and rivers from afar, following after sensory objects and yielding to circumstances for years on end.
Deep in the moonlight, if someone asks, you must say to them: "In whose house is there no Avalokiteśvara?
Now, to speak in vain of the "Ordinary Age"—no one can bring forth this story in its entirety.
When did Linji ever see Huangbo? Zhaozhou never even reached Nanquan. A wooden horse chasing the wind goes like lightning; a mud ox entering the sea has departed.
Like smoke; the boat moors atop Mount Sumeru. A single pole thrusts through the sky reflected in the water.
Standing alone in peril, yet intimate in application—how many fail to realize they have missed the person on the other side! Even the Master could not avoid casting out the realm of the mechanism;
the student must be made to discern host and guest. A hot shout and a wrathful fist vanish like lightning; heaven and earth are entirely filled.
Raising the dust. Indeed, if one can transcend all boundaries in every instance, one is like a divine colt with ten shadows that grinds the colors of the qilin.

To prattle on while chanting the Way is certainly not the truth; to silently respond to the opportune moment is likewise not intimate. Yet, it is the mountains, rivers, and the great earth that speak;
to laboriously set forth written words and spoken language is in vain. Do not boast of "wonderful" when striking the seat or raising the whisk; to cluster brocade and pile up flowers is but a waste.
A fresh quarrel! One can trust that such a thing does not exist in our school.

Clearly failing to recognize the person of original nature—this is precisely the moment when trees wither and leaves fall. When the golden wind is revealed, how many truly know it? Before entering the profound gate, it is difficult to open one's mouth;
from the beginning, those of great awakening have no teacher. To spread out your handkerchief for the sake of traveling to study is in vain; even the flash of lightning is deemed too slow.
Reflect deeply. Fifty-three people in the furnace, heated and forged into a single child, Sudhana.
Not removing delusive thoughts, not removing the Real—this too is like painting a lunar disc with cinnabar.
How many can accept this in their very being? How many try to settle the mind by force? Hanshan has directly forgotten the path of coming; he drags his cloth bag along, filled to the brim.

The eye-dust: in both the mundane and supramundane worlds, there is constant joy. While others compete over things, self, and others, regarding them as distant or intimate, Ruiyan calls out to himself, "O Master!
When mouth and heart disagree, the Way is not one; though brought from a thousand miles away, it must be ground to powder.

Placing the whole platter forth, it is entirely empty space; chasing sounds and pursuing forms, the tortoise falls into the net. Having attained the meaning, one forgets the words—the crane [soars free].
Freed from the cage, why must one ascend the hall to seek instruction? Within the present moment, there is no dharma that is not perfectly penetrating.
In daily life, when things are clearly manifest, whom do you ask? To discuss the profound and explain the subtle is merely to display much knowledge;

yet, moment after moment, there is truly no ceasing consciousness. In every thought, when has there ever been a time of dwelling? If you were to urge sentient beings to cultivate concentration and wisdom, you would only cause the Buddhas to arise [from their state].
Foolishness! Five pairs and ten items are difficult to swallow and penetrate. One fashions a golden ring for oneself and uses chestnut shells.
Among the monks who have read the Tripitaka, they seek six verses;
yet the characters do not form words, and the eight phrases are not right. Throughout heaven and across the earth, those who understand are rare. A wild lion has just opened its mouth.
The mouth—fierce Nātha instantly loses his majesty; the three apertures and the perfect pearl are attained in a single word. The Dharma-realm of the ten directions returns before one’s eyes.
You, Elder Brother, are permitted to understand the Buddha-dhyāna; now return to me the upward-turning pivot of our school.
The matter transmitted outside the teachings—how could one be so slow to grasp it before a single word is spoken? As soon as you seek wondrous enlightenment, the mind becomes clouded;

failing to penetrate the profound barrier, the eyes are covered in rheum. When the Buddha’s name is brought up, one must rinse one's mouth; when the Zen seat is overturned, there is no room for a teacher.
Why need one mention the partial, the perfect, the half, or the full? All are but empty fists used to deceive small children.
Old papers have long rested upon my desk; within them lies a *maṇi* jewel illuminating the great thousandfold world. It reveals everything clearly, yet people do not understand;
it marks the essential meaning plainly, yet that meaning is difficult to proclaim. How can one speak of it from a cowpen or a horse stable? How can the Dragon Palace in the Sea-treasury express it?
A single phrase encompasses immeasurable meanings: the Jambu tree stands on the southern shore of the sea.
Seeking the mind and not finding it, the mind is at peace. Why, then, do Chan practitioners find it so difficult? From antiquity to the present, there have been countless varieties;
changing heads and faces in a hundred thousand ways. One must teach the rabbit to leave its burrow and further compel the eel to climb the bamboo pole.
If one’s own spiritual platform remains unawakened, the Tripitaka serves only others for their viewing.
Held up, he asks again: "What sutra is this? The precious treasury is clear and bright, its doors unbarred at night. The pillar extends its brow as the ten thousand phenomena speak;
Mount Sumeru joins his palms as the vast void listens. Yunmen suddenly thrusts out his staff; Bazhang points aimlessly at the pure pitcher.
He pulls back the three eyes atop his head— I know you still harbor a lingering sense of cleverness.
The mind is the banner of the wondrous Dharma, luminous and radiant; its illumination of past and present is surely not in vain. Frozen ants on the steps vainly search for their burrows;
foolish flies striking at paper have not yet pierced through the window. The Great Master Bodhidharma is but a wheel crushed underfoot;
Śākyamuni Buddha is merely a tangle of vines. In our daily lives, we simply remain in this state of ease; even Māra and the heterodox teachers could be brought to submission thereby.

Nine Poems on Sending Off a Monk to Dwell in a Hermitage The gate of dwelling in the hermitage stands wide open as vast as the heavens; I raise my fist to greet those who come and go. Through skillful means, I allow others to present their lacquer bowls;
In leisure, casting the line, I catch the yellow bear. Whether window or wall, the mind manifests everywhere; Neither saint nor ordinary person—this is the Dharma.
Fahai, you cannot remain within the station of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; let the golden hall be left for the moss to grow.
When I sat in meditation in my wooden hut during the Great Sui dynasty, how could I have ever devised clever answers? I took a snake upon my staff and cast it into a fierce fire;
I took a straw sandal in my hand and covered a tortoise. Whether in right concentration or false concentration, I cause all deep doubts to be suddenly severed.
Cut off all doubt. In the East or in the West, there are no Buddhas or Patriarchs. To speak of Chan is not to move one's lips or skin. Even with a house full of gold, the eyes remain closed.
Dwelling in the mountains is surely not a matter of great stupidity. When the rice in the bowl is scarce, one must eat the parched grain;
when the clothing on the body is thin, paper can be cut to make it. At sunrise, the practitioner goes out to hoe the earth; at nightfall, the youth lights the lamp.
The lamp is lit. You must know that the Buddha-dharma has no high or low; only upon awakening can one nurture the sacred embryo. Thick white clouds deeply protect the seclusion of the green cliffs;
the manifested way of life spares one from seeking outside. A single patchwork robe is worn upon the body for now; a three-bay thatched hut merely covers the head.
Amidst the long pines and a fragment of stone, there is leisure and nothing to do; with plain rice and coarse tea, one is fully satisfied.
He immediately stopped. He brought forth a long-handled ladle for scooping from the stream.

Where there is no elegance, he is elegant nonetheless. For a long time, this man of old dwelt in a mountain cave; he encountered a laywoman who had come to burn down his hermitage. At the crossroads of the street, there is neither front nor back;
yet on the summit of the solitary peak, things are truly perplexing. Gathering withered wood at the break of dawn, he returns at evening, rushing through the fierce [wind].

The tiger has passed. This alone is the wondrous application of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*). When a visitor inevitably asks, "How is it? he has wandered through the Zen groves and now dwells in a hermitage.
As he departs to bid me farewell, his words are murmured and indistinct. To wield the brush and write a verse—is this not a mistake?
To stifle one's voice and swallow one's words is even more unbearably pathetic. Since all phenomena are empty, how many have truly realized this? Ten out of ten have missed the mark—ask!
The first three [generations]. The ancients acted out of profound compassion for the Buddha; they did not weary of entering the bustling monasteries within city walls.
When the Fourth Patriarch visited Lanrong that year, they suddenly met beneath Mount Niutou. Through a single word, one realizes one's nature and only then does one achieve the Way;
when the hundred birds offer flowers, their tracks vanish. One need not fear the howling of wolves through the eternal night, as one passes the time long-roasting firewood.

Deep winter; the flowing springs and layered peaks speak clearly. To lead the stream of Chan practitioners to this school, one must stand within the shadow of the green mountains, at the side of the mattock.
Seeking people for the sake of the Dharma is truly pitiable. Striking the ground was never intended as a casual strike;
grinding a tile is indeed a chaotic grinding of tiles. One must simply cause the bottom of the bucket to fall away along with the wall, and seize the head-rope all at once.
The nose is pulled; he hands over the true seed-grass that extinguishes the barbarian. Everyone should clearly grasp it before birth; what doubt is there in piercing clouds and crossing waters?
Turning the head and looking back—who is this? Within a grain of millet, the world is spread out;
inside a hole as thin as lotus fiber, Mount Sumeru hangs suspended. A single thatch roof is not exchanged for a thousand houses; once full, one can forget ten thousand things.
An eon of famine. If one asks what the state of dwelling in the mountains is like: "Every person’s nostrils are large and their heads hang low.

[This concludes] the eight verses on the Huayan Assembly for my friends, written amidst the great snow before Mount Zhengjue: "The morning star shines at night, and all under heaven is red. The Tathāgata’s True Eye has already struck [the mark]."
Lost! Jueyuan speaks of liberation from the very beginning; he intends to serve as a model for all time, past and present.

He directly causes both the ordinary and the sagely to transcend all entanglements, yet the vast and grand gateway remains as it was. How could this require the hidden lash or the secret refinement of effort?
The sutras of the great trichiliocosm reside within a single mote of dust; when it is split open, they are returned to those of transcendent capacity.

Sentient beings without beginning shall all attain Buddhahood; the primordial great fruit is never separate from the cause. Bubbles arise and bubbles perish within the layered seas; flowers fall and flowers bloom upon every tree in spring.
One may trustfully enter the desolate fields without discrimination; grasping them sideways or using them inverted, they are all wondrous treasures.
The seven characters of the title are most clear; already ten thousand leagues separate us from the Western Heaven. Without unrolling the crimson silk binding, one first attains realization;

what need is there to laboriously present the jade-encased scroll? Flower branches, cluster by cluster, distinguish red and white; mountain streams, line after line, alternate between turbid and clear.
Everything before the eyes is none other than the true Dharma-realm, encompassing all that is sentient and insentient.
The Great Vairocana, whose sound and form encompass all—what a pity that this man lacks the spirit of a true hero! To have traveled in vain to Lantian in search of beautiful jade;
who would have known he was carrying pearls wrapped in a cloth bag? How could there be need for many words from the mouth?
Originally, not a single character exists within the sutras. Casting aside the leftover soup and rancid rice, Zhaozhou hangs his gourd on the eastern wall.
In a single kṣaṇa, the Way is realized; there is not a single dharma upon which one can set the mind. The ten directions and the entire dharma-realm manifest from the mind;
the great earth, mountains, and rivers are as level as the palm of a hand. Red fruit ripens upon the branches of iron trees; white hair grows beneath the chin of the clay ox.
Clearly pointing out the path that reaches through the heavens, one travels freely to the south, north, east, and west.
The fifty-three gates of knowledge are all contained within the tip of a single needle. When the mind accords with principle, there is no difficult matter;
when one’s feet do not touch the dust, that is universal study. At the valley mouth, the yellow oriole sings its "a-ta"; beneath the eaves, the purple swallow warbles its "ni-nan.
How does one ultimately enter the mysterious gate? The Way says: it comes from Sichuan in a leaking basket.
Maitreya comforts Sudhana with earnest sincerity; with a single snap of his fingers, the gate of the pavilion opens.
Body and mind are both relinquished at this very moment—whence, then, do these sensory realms arise? A thunderbolt strikes across the bright blue sky;
dust swirls through the vast white day. Behold the handless man who waves his sleeves; upon the stone, the lotus grows according to its nature.
Though the words are many, their meaning is one and the same. It is the very marrow of sentient beings and the heart-liver of the Buddhas.
Why trouble yourself reading through opened volumes of scripture? Just look where the incense smoke rises. A swift hawk ever thinks of soaring beyond the void; a foolish fly only drills into paper.
Even if you could lecture until the heavenly flowers fall, if you do not penetrate this principle, it is all in vain.

Four Poems on Sending a Monk to Shu In the fifty-four prefectures and districts of Western Sichuan, The splendor of the scenery is so vast it cannot be contained. With a single umbrella and a single bundle, he departs on his pilgrimage;
May he wander as he pleases among the fine mountains and fine waters. In years past, the Great Being resided at Zhaojue; Who today shall receive him?
The supreme flow: the eight thousand *yojanas* of the path are as close as a span; it is no different from the eaves of one's own house.
Go on, go on to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra; do not mistake *duḥūla* cotton for the real. On the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, inquiry and consultation take place;

within the void, the principal and the attendants of Wondrous Virtue are complete. Tilting the ear, one hears only the manifestation of the Bodhisattva; turning the body, one still beholds the elephant.
The King has returned; do not seek it elsewhere in triviality. The secret meaning is clearly present within you. This journey must reach the house of Da Sui;
take care of the turtle-nosed snake in the pond. Ten or five pairs have all missed the mark; the seventeen hundred [monks] were in vain with their circumlocutions.
When awakened, the mountains and rivers of the great earth are narrow; when lost, one wanders the roads of a foreign land.
The road is long; if there is even the slightest trace [of obstruction], it must be cleared away, lest people say you are plucking willow blossoms.
The Great Image of Jiazhou reaches the blue clouds, yet this is still but a minor manifestation of the Tathāgata’s body.

The true essence encompasses all of empty space and cannot be fully contained—by what cause can the fleshly eyes of sentient beings perceive it? Wherever conditions meet, one encounters Maitreya; though speechless, he turns the Dharma wheel with resonant clarity.
The Wheel of Dharma. Joining the palms and bowing the head, one performs three prostrations and rises; only then does one realize that the entirely provisional is the entirely real.
Sweet and bitter bamboo shoots from the Jianji Hermitage on Mount Lu, and light and salty pickled vegetables from Guizong Monastery—Mount Lu’s true countenance is now clearly revealed.
Lù: "The patch-robed monk’s body and mind are especially deluded. Autumn arrives and yellow leaves fall from the tree-tops; deep in the night, white monkeys cry atop the peaks.
If you seek the profound and the wondrous while practicing Zen, ten thousand miles of shifting sands lie even further to the west."

Entrusting the mallet and clappers to the Zen Master at the Gate of the Eastern Sea by the Twin Trees: the robe and bowl remain forever in the Tuṣita Palace; two *tao* trees serve as the Buddha-work, while a three-foot bamboo staff displays spiritual power. Upon the ridge of the Clay Ox, he swallows the yellow calf; before the Stone Tiger Mountain, he bites— ...the white rabbit. The great matter is already settled; what further need is there for words? The thousand sages and ten thousand saints have all passed through here; they have all been struck by this one blow. If you can understand it thus, you will see that the Buddhas of the three times and the patriarchs of the nine schools are all within this single sound. If you cannot yet understand, listen to this verse: The Twin Trees stand firm, the East Sea flows on; The mallet and clappers are handed to the old monk. The robe and bowl remain long in Tuṣita; Two *tao* trees perform the Buddha-work. A three-foot bamboo staff unfolds divine powers; On the ridge of the Clay Ox, he swallows the yellow calf. Great Tiger! I have a family letter with nowhere to send it. A golden knife cuts through the vast void; send it to the old dhūta on Mount Qiányán Fúlóng at Shèngshòu.
As I turn my thoughts, I find the karma-consciousness of ignorance grows ever more abundant. It is truly laughable that the ancients would wield their staffs [in such a manner].
"Ho! This turns out to be raising arms and brandishing weapons on level ground. I transmit a single spell of wisdom; I have written out a song of lifelong joy.
Having retired from affairs, I am usually too lazy to speak; let him at the stone mortar recite the *Mahā*. "
In mourning for Daoxuan of Mount Jiao: I lived in Qiantang for two years; Several times we traveled together by lake boat. At Zhangjiasi Temple, spring was at its height;
By the Yangtze River, the moon repeatedly reached its fullness. I only hoped that the kōan of my late master would be resolved; Now all call him the Son of Silent Illumination.
Sun Hyeon: Who would have known that in the blink of an eye, a thousand autumns would pass? Tears drench these verses of *gāthā* and *canyou*.
Lamenting for the Master Brother of the Stone Chamber at Jiangxin, who has been there for years—why does he not answer his call today? The eighty thousand afflictions are but empty and vast.
Sweeping away! The ocean of three thousand lands is cold and translucent; it uproots the world’s foundationless trees and extinguishes the lamp of the human realm that never knows night.
This final radiance is impossible to conceal: within the fierce fires of a red furnace, ice forms.

Congratulations on the Great Vehicle Dharma being proclaimed by Chief Seat Yong of Mount Jing-shan! Five topknots towering and lofty, piercing the heavens; with a single shout, empty space is reduced to dust.
Once again he raises the ancient karmic conditions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; clearly, a sword is suspended between his brows. How could one wait for the gourd to fall from the earth?
Turning upward, he suppresses the assembly of dragons and elephants filling the hall; only then do they know that the Dharma community possesses such heroes and sages.
To the monks, four verses:
"It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. With a single blow, the Patriarch shattered the heavy barrier. Taking one's own mind to further grasp the mind...
Recognizing it, one who has no hand reaches out again with a hand. Gold dust needlessly increases the cataracts; the sword’s edge descends directly to sever dullness and stubbornness.
Pity those who linger in phrases and rely on words; they even claim that the ordinary lies between speech and silence.
It is not the banner, nor is it the wind; the deluded person needlessly falls into a snare. Zhang Liang’s schemes for stabilizing the state are but a deception;
Li Jing’s boasts of his prowess in cleaving through battle lines are in vain. The ten-shadowed divine steed still obstructs the Way; the nine-tufted auspicious phoenix does not depart from the void.
If you wish now to recognize the purport of Caoxi, take a step toward the West and yet head toward the East.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; why does Zhaozhou alone say it is non-existent? Zhaozhou skillfully wields the "blow-off-hair" sword;
the patch-robed monks cast themselves entirely into the trap for the hare. Beyond the gate the snow is deep and human tracks are few; at the ferry-head the wind is fierce and the waves are coarse.
If one seeks further mysterious understanding in the presence of reality, one will laugh oneself to tears—the blue-eyed barbarian of the Western Heaven.
All sentient beings lack Buddha-nature; yet every skull resounds with the dragon’s cry. Dongping knew how to shatter the mirror of Guishan;
the Old Man Pang once strummed the zither of Mazu. Through vast eons, there has been no front or back; the ancients truly possessed sublime wisdom and resonance.
Yet even the foolish child speaks of a path beyond words, turning level ground into a thicket of thorns.
Answering the Verses of Master Fuci: Three Poems on Sending Off Chan Master Yi A single breath turns the entire Great Canon;
Yet he returns to hide his body within a single peck-measure. He stirs open the fierce flames of the red furnace, And draws forth the cool, white lunar disc.
Presented face-to-face, the whole body is revealed; In the end, it does not go beyond this.

The Master’s mind was true; his words were all transcendent and sublime. How many people have merely picked up the leftovers and licked their fingers! With a single breath he turned the entire Great Canon;

in a speck of dust or a pore, the ocean of lands reveals his whole body. He clearly realized the principle of non-arising within one's own nature and was able to turn the True Wheel of the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
He split open the three phrases to reveal the profound and the essential, cutting off both extremes to eliminate all falsehood.
Harmony and Truth. The wild mechanism is much like the stone of Lantian; it mistakenly kills the man who bends his bow to shoot the tiger.
With a single breath, he turns the entire Great Canon; the golden-maned lion knows how to turn its body. Saints and commoners suddenly appear in the mirror of the high platform;
demons and heretics fly crosswise on the glowing iron wheel. As soon as one enters the realm of language, it is all delusion; following after sounds and forms, one immediately...
Deviant from the truth. Now I recall the old man of Changting, waiting for someone at the crossroads.
From the *Zongjing Lu*, the ten kinds of non-obstruction in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these ten verses are shown to the monks as the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*).
The true nature is identical in all, yet lands differ in appearance; vast, empty, and pure is the Great Vairocana. Fragrance clings to the thousand-layered petals of the lotus;
reflections appear as five-colored mani jewels. The myriad phenomena of the dharma-realm have never truly existed, yet the proclamation of the fundamental vehicle is not non-existent either.
Relying on this, do not further debate mind and objects; thorns have always been the level path.

In the empty space where formation and destruction are unimpeded, Buddha-lands dissolve and then form again; like bubbles and flowers upon water, they vanish and then arise once more. Why need one debate their substance or function, or argue over self and other?
There is no need to compare the roots and objects for deficiency or fullness. The three thousand lands transform according to the mind; the light of the two-eighths moon follows [the observer].
Waiting for the dawn. From antiquity to the present, hands have turned over like the palms of one's own hands. How many times, one knows, has the Yellow River become clear?
Whether vast or narrow, there is no obstruction;

one must know that breadth and narrowness do not hinder the form. The distinction between sage and ordinary person, delusion and awakening, resides within the spiritual mind. All manner of waters enter into both the square and the round.
Vessels: Of one kind, empty, according to the size of the jar. Whether Bodhisattvas, devas, or humans, or asuras, mosquitoes, or gnats, they drink from the vast ocean;
by the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), which is inherently equal, shifting from narrow to wide is simply peace itself.
The four, the one, and the many are unimpeded;
ten voids are squeezed together within a single hair-tip. A hundred billion hair-tips encompass the oceans of lands. Refreshing breezes perfume the grasses and trees;
the vast, boundless great ocean gathers all rivers and streams. Colored threads directly thread through bright pearls; golden images are all adorned with jewels.
Gather the mirror. Examine closely the point where appearances merge before you; let all return to the single square inch of the mind and seek nothing else.

Within a single thought-moment, the five marks are unimpeded and the myriad dharmas are perfectly realized. Sentient beings and the world are entirely encompassed within it, like the light of a pearl, whether large or small.
They appear in various colors—red, white, blue, and yellow—but one ultimately does not know where they arise. Only now do I believe they are originally empty.
How can one understand this single phrase of everyday life? When the sun rises in the west, it sets in the east at night.
The six subtle, unobstructed, and winding paths can all be followed one by one; reaching the most profound and remote depths, they surely shift and transform.

At the place where a bee swallows a drop of honey as fine as a hair’s tip, when an ant passes through a nine-curved pearl, when a great ocean is hidden within the pore of a mustard seed, and when [the world] is placed inside the hollow of a lotus fiber—[all these are encompassed].

Mount Sumeru and a wildfire arise like fireflies; even the wise understand this through such metaphors. The seven [realms] manifest and conceal without obstruction, amidst a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, occurring spontaneously.
They do not fall into the extremes of high or low, nor of defilement or purity. The sacred state is precisely the mundane, and the mundane is precisely the sacred.

The Sage is perfect when appearing incomplete and complete when appearing deficient; its patterns and details are like freshly sprouted bamboo shoots, and its cause and effect are as if an unopened lotus bud.
This belongs solely to one’s own mind and is not an external object; whether in shade or in sun, it is equally the original sky.

The eightfold manifestation is unimpeded: within a single atom, a single land, and a single Tathāgata; there is nothing not encompassed across all lands and all atoms. Before the palace of Śakra, nets of pearls are woven;
within the palace of Brahmā, mirrors face the terraces. When the wind ceases, the great waters swallow the stars; when the sun shines upon the fragrant pond, the lotuses bloom.
The calyx opens; this very thing envelops empty space. How wondrous is its numinous clarity and vast penetration!

The body of Śākyamuni within the Great Flower Treasury Ocean, where the nine lords and their retinues are unimpeded, is adorned by its entourage everywhere in truth. Behold the jade-like radiance of the arrayed constellations.

The rabbit [in the moon]. The wealth and nobility of all kings belong to the Golden Wheel; the surging waves of rivers and streams are nothing but water; the blooming flowers of grasses and trees are all spring.
When the ten *pāramitās* are fulfilled in a single thought-moment, who here is "I" and who is "another"?
In the water of the thirteenth generation, the gourd sinks when pressed down; neither coming nor going, it is not even now. Empty flowers fall in confusion as they follow the flowing stream;
a stone shoot newly emerges from the distant forest. Cease using such words to discuss the wondrous Way; with what else could one compare it?
True Mind. Old Man Yongming is too talkative; I surpass him with my deep bowl of tea by the western window.
This verse on dispersing the numinous and becoming a sage while dwelling in the mountains:

Like the Treasure Keeper seeking harmony, because a monk asked me about the meaning of the West, I spoke of my years of mountain dwelling. Rest from clinging within the ranks of Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The feet: for ordinary fools, let us follow along shoulder to shoulder. Three rooms of a house hidden in a mountain valley; ten thousand trees of pine blossoms reflecting upon the stone spring.
Since the vast kalpas of the past, nothing has changed; Ānanda remains as before, in the presence of the World-Honored One.

Entrusted to the Venerable Fuzhong of Tiantong, atop Mount Changgeng amidst the white clouds: Holding forth the mandate from the West, he smiles as he unfolds his countenance. Layer upon layer of crags and peaks encircle the master’s chamber;
Ten thousand pine trees surround the gates of the Chan cloister. Who took away that gold and jade in years gone by? Today, Tianlong ought to join him.
I see him off on his return. This aged man is just like one who peers at a leopard through a bamboo tube, occasionally catching glimpses of its spotted markings.
I send this to Master Huigou of Daci;
from Lingyan he has moved again to Huayan, and counting these stations, it is exactly three times he has reached Ciyun. My longing for my native land stretches a thousand miles.

A Barrier. You shall shoulder the Buddha-dharma upon one shoulder alone. Who can approach the golden-haired lion crouching on the ground? The jade whisk stirs the wind as you discourse without weariness.
Grasping hands, we do not yet know where this place is—on a late autumn day, the cool moon rises from the southeast.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huibian Chushi, “The Sun of the Buddha Shining Universally,” Volume Eighteen.
