(Xiàn yīn) Yū (yú qù qiè) Tú (tú yīn) Zhà (zhī jiā qiè) Miè (mí ruì qiè) Zhù (zhī shù qiè) Táo (tú lì qiè) Yìng (yú zhēng qiè) Bāo (bó jiāo qiè) Zhuī (dīng huí qiè) Shì (shén ěr qiè) The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huìbiàn Chǔshí,
"The Buddha-Sun Shining Universally," Scroll Nineteenth.
Gāthā Verses on the Five Attendants, compiled by Wenbin and others;
the Fourfold Selection.

The person is taken away, but the scene is not; at dawn, when the sun has risen three times its height, a thousand gates are silent. Peach blossoms grow on tree after tree near the front pond, yet the fair lady does not appear to come and reflect her image therein.
The scenery is taken away, but not the person; a jade whip and golden stirrups reward the waning spring. Where do the thousands of reds and ten-thousands of purples go?
Suddenly a wind arises and sweeps them up as dust.
Both person and environment are utterly swept away; a vast, long serpent encircles the crescent moon. Who dares to confront its tip, that Great Axe?
It shall surely cause the tracks of men to vanish for ten thousand *li*.

Neither person nor environment can be taken away; above, below, and in the four cardinal directions, spring seems to be poured forth. The Sage Ruler hangs his robes [without laboring], and sun and moon shine bright;
the General lets loose his horse, and heaven and earth are vast.
In summary:
A single set of withered bones forms the teeth; two thin slabs of skin serve as the ears. Last night at the third watch, the ox was lost;
when dawn broke, the fire was lost.
The four categories of guest and host, and the guest among guests: fish eyes shall become priceless jewels; the blind Persian comes to strike a bargain—same ailment, same poverty.
The guest within the host: east and west are not distinguished as he mumbles on, never letting the staff in his hand depart.
He mistakes the lantern for a pillar.
The host within the guest: virtue is never solitary; it must have its neighbor. In the jade palace and crystal towers there is no thatch of weeds; who knows?
This is one from the Imperial Capital;
the Lord among Lords. When the Great Function manifests, all rules and regulations vanish. A single drop of blood from a golden-maned lion scatters ten bushels of milk from a donkey.
General Verse:
What gate does not turn toward this gate? An iron caltrop from within a furnace of ten thousand smeltings. It is not that I, this mountain monk, am fond of pointing and commenting;
everyone should cherish their own two eyebrows.

A single shout of the fourfold roar is like a vajra sword; when it is brandished across the face, it is difficult to evade. Whether it be Buddhas, patriarchs, or celestial demons, should there be even the slightest trace of existence, it must be struck down with painful severity.
A single shout is like a lion crouching on the ground; wild foxes from ancient tombs die upon encountering it.
If one is a cub of the golden-maned lion, he will stretch out his four paws and shake his two ears.
A single shout is like a probing pole or a blade of grass in the shadow; who among those who enter it understands it, and who does not? The blue-eyed barbarian raises his iron whip;
through the Yumen Pass, he penetrates the road to Chang’an.
A single shout does not function as a single shout; the Yellow River in the tenth month freezes solid to its very bottom.
A tiny fox trots along with its tail wagging; this time, do not be falsely alarmed.
The First of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials:
What transmission is there from Śākyamuni to Maitreya? Coming and going between the human realm and the heavens, the ancient well lies vast and empty as one fills it with snow.

The second mystery: never having opened one's mouth, it exists prior to words. Though one may personally seize it like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint, one’s nostrils are still pierced by me.
The third mystery: a monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing over its head. It was only because he snapped the golden lock that he could take hold of the mind.
Hanging from the tree of the liver—this is the primary requirement. There is nothing at all extraordinary or mysterious about it: I have never eaten a meal and my belly remains empty;
I have not drunk tea for a long time and my lips and tongue are parched.
The second essential point: A student outside the gate comes to report that Master Wuyou has become the top graduate (Zhuangyuan).
Zixu hears this and laughs heartily.
The third essential point: It is precisely because of compassion that he descends into the weeds; neither "I" nor "he"—how truly marvelous! The eye of a gnat.
With mountains and rivers encircling it within;
the verse on the essential principle of Mount Shou says:
"The Gentleman’s clumsiness is not clumsy; his essence is as clear as ice and snow. On his back he draws a rabbit-horn bow, shooting down the moon at the edge of heaven."
The daughter’s skill is neither skillful nor unskillful; one is old, the other is not. Having mounted the water buffalo, do not let it enter the weeds.

This is the first of the three precepts of Fenyang; Buddhas and patriarchs have long since transcended them. Do not speak of the time before birth; cease discussing the severance of the path of the mind.
The Second Secret: Who distinguishes between movement and stillness? A fan made of tortoise hair fans a mud ox; a single drop of blood. The Third Secret:
Jiangnan and the two Zhejiang provinces; in spring, ten thousand trees in bloom; in winter, a thousand crags covered in snow.
The ten wisdoms are identical to the truth;
even those of superior capacity enter together. The swift falcon cannot overtake [the prey]; the barrier of Fenglin is shattered.
Standing upon the water wearing boots, with whom does he roar in unison? Facing south, he gazes at the Big Dipper. The monkey worries as it scratches its head; the dog runs about shaking its mouth.
How can one share in life and death? The path beyond is slippery. Pan Lang rides his donkey backward; the Brahmin wears his socks inside out.
Who shares in gain and loss? The judge’s pen in his hand. Cold water soaking a winter melon. Everyone is muddying the waters together.
What is identical and complete? Like a thief entering an empty house, he picks up river-gold, yet it is actually jade from Lantian.
What is identical and all-pervasive? A gnat swallows a tiger; the boatman sails down to Yangzhou; throughout the great earth, there is not a single inch of soil.
Who can share in true wisdom? There is neither "is" nor "is not. Xuefeng once rolled the ball; Juzhi likewise raised his finger.
Who could truly be said to have studied together with them? Yet here you are, speaking at random. Bitter gourds are bitter from root to tip; sweet melons are sweet from stem to end.
That which is the same as the Great Matter: the mountain shape, the staff. Northerners do not look at each other’s noses; Southerners do not look at each other’s ears.
What thing shares this single substance? Three times nine is twenty-seven. Every year is a good year; every day is a good day.
The Three Barriers of Huanglong:
"What is my hand like compared to the Buddha’s hand? Two by two, three by three—nine times nine. Lord Li falls drunk in the street;
it was originally Lord Zhang drinking wine."
"What are my feet like? They are like donkey's feet. Here, one cannot step upon them; with eyes closed, one leaps across the Yellow River.
Throughout the entire world, the red sun blazes brilliantly.
Every person has their own karmic affinity (*jīnyuán*); who comes after and who comes before is unknown. Zhaozhou traveled on foot even at eighty years of age—how truly marvelous! (Xiānglán).
It is found only in the *Yuchuan* (Fisherman’s Boat).
It records that when the Elder Wuji was sent to Goryeo by Gaoli, he himself said that he had traveled through Goryeo.
Recently, people have been saying that he resided at Huairan; it is unknown how many disciples were under his guidance.
The assembly: three times three before and three times three after.
Gazing at the flying waterfall from Five-Crown Mountain, there lies below a cold pool, a sea ten thousand fathoms deep. It is said that a divine dragon has descended there for a long time;
its entire body enters a bowl as large as a needle.
The relics of the True Body have no fixed location; the Eastern Land and the Western Heaven are but one family.
One cannot see the temple of Tongdu at Yanyang, where divine light once long encircled the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*.
I have heard that there are Five Terraces at Jiangling, where a branch from the Radiant Stone has been sent. The Great Being Mañjuśrī appears clearly;
do not say that the clouds of delusion cannot be swept away.
I raise my whip upon the singing sands; countless lutes vibrate their strings of their own accord.
For three hundred li, everything is one color—roses—completely wrapping the mountains and rivers in brocade and embroidery.
The Vajra mountain has twelve thousand peaks; far and near, high and low, each is different.
On which peak can I find a place to settle, so that in years to come I may bind my hut and dwell within it?
A thousand layers of dark chambers, ten thousand years of ice— To call this "lapis lazuli" is but a provisional name. It does not obstruct the eyes of brothers seeing one another;
At midnight in Fusang, the sun’s orb shines bright.
A Verse on the Ten Oxherds of Liangshan:
Seeking the ox, he travels to the ends of the earth, searching everywhere; He enters directly into the depths of ten thousand layers of misty peaks. Having resolved this very day and tomorrow—
On a sunny day, by the green willow embankment, one hears the warbling of orioles.
Traces are seen along the roads to the east, west, south, and north; are these not surely the imprints left by treading? Look closely, however, and there are none.
This very person: from this moment forth, do not doubt him.
Seeing the ox across the wall, one recognizes its horns and hears its voice; after the rain, the grass before the village is lush and green. A pair of eyes, black and lustrous.
The Vinaya: The color of the hair on his entire body is difficult to paint;

though he has obtained the ox, the nostrils of the distant heavens must be pierced for him. Only when the golden cord rots will it be removed; henceforth, there is no need to distinguish between black and white.
He said: "Mixing mud with water, we dwell together for now.
Tending cattle has long been my unrestrained life. Mountains and clouds fill my eyes; dust fills my eyes. Today, I am finally able to perceive the touch."
Pure. Willingly tending the crops, one might inadvertently encroach upon another's land;

yet riding the ox back home, with the distant ridge of the front slope barely a few feet away, it is my own home. Layer upon layer, the spring mountains are draped in evening clouds. What a fine moment for returning!
My son, a single hook of the new moon hangs from the eaves.
The ox is lost, yet the man remains;
through a thousand layers of clouds and trees, ten thousand folds of mountains. Lying prostrate or sleeping sideways, I am free to be at ease. This scene cannot be captured within a painting.
It is attained. Who says the body remains within the painted image?

When both man and ox have vanished, one turns back and tramples through the vast void. Once a single point is penetrated, every place is penetrated; throughout the earth and under heaven, there is no shadow.
Traces. Who knows who will understand and establish our school?

Returning to the root and restoring the source, each and every faculty possesses its own efficacy. Hearing sounds and seeing forms, one is neither blind nor deaf; from dawn to dusk, all is simply the ordinary.
As for this matter: having awakened from sleep, the ocean sun is as red as three bamboo poles.

Entering the marketplace with hands hanging down, the precious and the cherished are completely cast aside; coming thus, it is clearly like the beak of a crow and the gills of a fish—illuminating heaven and mirroring earth, truly marvelous.
Extraordinary! It causes the eyes of all weary beings to open wide.
The Verse on the Twelve Hours:
At the Hour of the Rat, the great earth is pitch black; there is no need to wait to examine it with the True Eye—the pillow suddenly falls away.
The earth, Mount Sumeru, collapses; the oceans dry up.

At the hour of the Ox (2–4 a.m.), near and far, all is as silent as the crowing of a cock. Ten thousand thoughts and a thousand reflections prevent sleep from coming. Though the body remains within the world, it finds no rest.
Then, one puts on clothes and descends the steps to walk.

At the hour of the tiger (3–5 AM), who among them is a person at leisure? Noble and base, wise and foolish, all are for the sake of this body. Merely preoccupied with eating and sleeping, they cannot be roused;
even their slaves and servants grow resentful.
At the hour of the Rabbit, the sun’s orb gradually rises high; it has already run several times before the steps.
The nostrils and eyes are as busy as if drilling, yet they heed not a thousand things—save for the eyebrows.
At the hour of the Dragon, one cannot help but prepare food by boiling and frying; the fire sputters, the wood smolders, and smoke fills the hearth.
Four alms bowls, three of them broken; a pair of spoons and chopsticks, incomplete.
How wondrous is the activity of the hour of the snake! The gates stand firm while guests come and go; they sit together to drink tea and see each other off.
The empty sky opens its mouth and laughs heartily.
At the hour of noon, the crimson sun stands precisely in the center; the five-colored maṇi jewels shine across the great void. When all are smashed to pieces, not a single thing remains;
yet it is still red, white, blue, and crimson.
In the hour of Wei, the tree shadows pass to the west of the window; face-to-face presentation leaves one utterly bewildered. From beginningless kalpas, it has been uninterrupted;
for what reason today is there such a gap between clouds and mud?
How many moments of light have passed in a single day? Already the evening shadows of the mulberry and willow trees encroach upon us. Shake off your lethargy and do not succumb to sleep;
the crows and sparrows are already chirping through the groves.
At the hour of You, the crimson sun sinks behind the western mountains; The thatched cottage and wooden gate are closed early. A few old crows perch atop the pine treetops;
They fly away at dawn and do not return until nightfall.

At the hour of the Dog (7–9 p.m.), when there is no business, do not open the door. Lie quietly; all is vast and silent, the four walls shrouded in darkness. There is a natural radiance that cannot be seen;
when it is seen, birth and death can no longer swallow you.
At the hour of Hai, one washes the feet and ascends the bed to sleep; born in this great Jambudvīpa, how pitiable! Before long, the day breaks again;
one knows not in what year rest will finally come.
Sending off Master Xuan to pay homage to the Patriarchs:
The pearl has never been strung; the jade has never been polished. This whole-and-round phrase is free from all ambiguity.
Seeking the sacred bones in Jiangxi with such urgency— Yet it is like ripples upon a windless sea.
When the Venerable Xing, the Rector,
was proclaiming the Ten Epithets within the Dharma Hall, the Venerable Ānanda also raised his eyebrows; turning around to pay his respects,
he departed the hall, inadvertently overturning the jade dais pool.
Seeing off a practitioner of Zen returning to the Seven Min Regions:
Xuan Sha did not cross Flying Vulture Ridge. The billions of mountains and rivers rest upon the tip of his staff; if you return to your home province, you must verify this for yourself.
When the scale-weight reaches the well, it suddenly floats.
Seeing off Abbot Sui as he returns to Lingyin:

From of old, Buddhas and Patriarchs have shattered the profound barrier; Ten thousand treatises and a thousand sutras are difficult to bring to the mouth. Before the tongue moves, all has already been revealed:
The moon over White Lotus Peak shines cold upon the people.
Farewell, Zen practitioner Xian!

What is so extraordinary about the sages and worthies? Their nostrils have always been tucked over their upper lips. If you give rise to even a hair’s breadth of views regarding increase or decrease, know that you are not one of those within the ranks.
Seeing off Zen Practitioner Ying:
A noble monk of rare spirit has long been unheard of. With one phrase facing the sun, jade and stone are distinguished.
Without lightly airing his straw sandals, the red trees of Mount Wu meet the clouds of Mount Yue.

Sent off, Attendant Xuan, to study the Way and investigate the profound mysteries as an eminent monk. With a single staff across a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters, from beginning to end you shall not fall into the traps of others.
Only on that day will you be worthy to carry on the ancestral lamp.
Sending off the Abbot Ding of Huqiu:

A sleeping tiger is originally a great beast; turning over and leaping out from amidst the thicket, it devours both the ordinary and the holy, and only then does one see the true pulse of Yangqi flow through.
Sent to Attendant Chang of Yüquan:
His cotton trousers are bright red and his paper robes are fresh; he does not depict Mañjuśrī or Samantabhadra. Having shaken himself free, not even a speck of dust remains;
how could he allow pure understanding to defile the field of the mind?
Seeing off Attendant Shun to Huqiu:
White clouds fly down beside the Sword Pond; a new paper robe covers a square of jade. The shadow of the pagoda suddenly stands inverted;
for his sake, I suspend my brush to write this outline.
Sending a question to the Chan practitioner:
beneath Mount Fenghuang he has established a camp; hoisting his banner and slaying his generals, he rarely encounters an opponent.
Even if he can emerge from the "Long Snake" formation, he still wears a ten-thousand-jin bell upon his head.
The Record of Mount Jingshan relates that a carp was born with a single horn. Suddenly it leaped up into the blue heavens;
Chan Master Juzhi could find no trace of it, yet he pierced the nostrils of the Dragon King.

When seeing off the Chan practitioner Yong, it would have been better to depart before he had even said goodbye. You must take blank paper and ask others for [their calligraphy]. Fengshan has not yet had the leisure to respond;
for now, listen to the sound of the pines and raise the *huatou*.
Sending off Chan Practitioner Chang:
A single sheet of cold clouds stretches across the sea. The man of the Way is now sailing his iron boat.
At nightfall, pearls emerge from the dragon palace; boundless radiance stirs the earth.
Seeing off Zen Master Xing for Tiantai:
The autumn wind whistles, the leaves flutter. He heads toward Tiantai to cross the Stone Bridge.
With a single step, it must be split in two; The era of Putong is here today.
Thanking someone for sending charcoal,
I light it as evening falls until the hearth glows red. A decrepit and incompetent old man, sickly and frail,
I am reminded of the ancient saying that "the will to live remains," for even in the month of December, there is a spring breeze.

Sitting cross-legged by the earthen stove at night, I sit motionless as the last leaves burn out. The young monk sleeps soundly and does not answer when called. The great trichiliocosm is empty and void; there is neither Buddha nor patriarch.
An old insect turns over and extinguishes the lamp in the night shrine.

Sending off a Chan practitioner who leaves the forest only to enter another: crossing waters and piercing clouds, the path grows ever deeper. Who would say that foreign lands are fundamentally not separated?
With every step of his straw sandals, he treads upon gold.
Seeing Zen Practitioner Ri off on a journey to Nanyue:
Nanyue soars high, piercing the great void; What will it truly be like for the man of the Way to go alone? An old monkey cries out from deep within the clouds;
Dew drips from the pine needles as the moon first rises.
Seeing off Zen Practitioner Ming on his journey to Tiantai:
The five hundred śrāvakas did not remain on the mountain; Why be confined to either heaven or the human realm? A single cup of yellow tea water suffices;
Having made the offering, one returns once more by the old path.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Zhi on his journey to Nanyue:
The ancient road winds far and long, back and forth; White clouds gather coldly in heaps all day long. The Venerable Banzhou has no place to be found;
Only secluded flowers upon the rocks open in the dew.
Seeing off Chan Master Yi to Suzhou:
A single glance at Lake Dongting reveals waters vast and boundless; the path ahead stretches far as the field of vision widens. The red sedges and white water lilies mark the very best of autumn;
one knows not who there might be holding a fishing rod.
The moon-hare has its form, and the cassia tree has its branches; how does this compare to the time before light and shadow had even arisen?
Throughout antiquity and today, countless have gazed upon the moon, yet only Master Nanquan Wang is truly permitted [to do so].
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Qing on his journey:
the snow has melted and the roots of the sedge turn green again. In the secluded chamber, the embers glow and the empty bottles rattle. How many mountains of Wu and peaks of Yue are there?
What effort could possibly reach the ancestral temple?
I hear the cuckoo calling, calling, one cry after another; Yet I laugh at the traveler who does not understand its song. Where is the old hometown? I have not yet returned.
White clouds vainly lock away the green of the wild mountains.

Having seen off the monk Sengji, the dew still wets the tall pines, not yet dry at dawn. With sincere courtesy, I see him off as he descends the lower ridges. Should anyone ask about matters of mountain dwelling on the road ahead, simply say:
"Since winter arrived, the tenth month has been cold."
In response to the monks' request for further instruction, Master Wuzu Yan showed them this:

"The peonies bloom everywhere throughout the city; one cannot help but scatter dust and sand upon meeting people. When he picks up the cypress tree in front of the courtyard, Zhaozhou’s gate is as far away as the ends of the earth."
Entrusting this to the Imperial Commissioner, Duke Wang Xiu Yongzhizhi, who points directly toward the southeast; the hundred prefectures follow the wind, all gazing upward with awe.
I long admire the late Prime Minister Pei, who was able to penetrate the meaning within Huangbo’s words.
This matter is presented face-to-face for the occasion; do not ask about the Patriarch’s intent in terms of east or west.
When a high official’s brushstroke weighs as much as a mountain, who says there is another ladder to ascend to heaven?
A Gift to the Chan Practitioner of Nanyue Mountain, who formerly built a thatched hut to dwell upon the mountain peak. Having lived there for many years, he has become estranged from the world.
He once cast a single line upon the thousand peaks and caught a fish with golden scales and green fins.
Entrusting this to my fellow practitioners, try taking a measure of empty space. Empty space turns out to be no more than a single thread long.
When that single thread is snapped and its weight is measured, a barefoot Persian is running through the Great Tang.
The Patriarch left behind a single sandal; who travels between the East and the West?
Having cast it into Lake Dongting, he causes dust to rise from the vast ocean.
The fisherman hooks his catch upon the boat; there, Sanlang bows in thanks. He remains hidden deep within the reeds, resting his head high on his green straw cloak and singing a song.
Unaware that upon the back of his floating hut lies the biting frost.
On account of the snow, he addresses the assembly:
"Flakes of snow fly through the vast expanse of space; The green mountains before one's eyes are rarely seen. Even now, they have not vanished from this Chan courtyard;
Five pairs and ten individuals do not know where to return."

The Junior Minister Dao Tong visited me while riding in the radiant light of his falcon-bannered carriage; in the past, I once nurtured him when he was but a youth. Today, the mountains of "self" and "other" were shouted down by me.
I recall our meeting again in the Hall of Inspection; this is now the third time in Heco City.
The Patriarch’s intent is clear at the tips of the hundred grasses; the long river has flowed eastward since ancient times. You must know that this thing is not another thing;
whether sitting, lying, walking, or standing, you need seek it nowhere else.
On a Cold Night, Sent to a Friend:
I wish to ask after your well-being, yet not a single word remains. The sky is cold and the night is chill as I sit by the hearth.
Reflecting thus on the traveler before Mount Xiong’er, In vain there stand two slender cassia trees.
In response to the rhyme, I answer Master Mengtang of Guoqing:
From the beginning, the eye has never seen its own nostrils; in the East and the West, there is no patriarch. This eighty-year-old monk’s head is white as snow;
let the meditation cushions and Zen boards be as they happen to be.
The devas and humans rain down *māndārava* flowers day after day; why do you, O Empty-Born One, sit in silence? The old Chan master is dreamless, with both hatred and love exhausted;
he sings a new melody to the "Qu" tune, harmonizing with the songs of the Mo Yao people.
In response to Master Chucái of Dōngshān:
"In the past, I and you both studied under Jìngwǔ; rarely does a disciple surpass his teacher.
Amidst the vast expanse of the seventeen hundred [cases], I recall instead the time of 'Great Peace and No Affairs.'"
The alms bowl is overturned over the four continents; the staff horizontally swallows the Teacher of all Buddhas.
Without using even a fraction of strength from the wrist, releasing and gathering it both occur as the occasion demands.

Answer: "Miaoyuan, Head Seat Xuanshu, said that Yangguang did not receive [the robe] from Ananda. How can one handle the old man who continues the flame and links the fragrance? 'The same breeze blows over a thousand li'—this is a single phrase;
the fisherman dances his oars, the rustic sings."
I would give Faheng thirty blows for taking this public case to slander his former master. Fortunately, in silent illumination there is no transmission;
who remembers the moment the mallet was raised and the whisk held aloft?
Answer: My fellow practitioner from the West Hall, Jiong, has sent me a wondrous gāthā. Regardless of how it may be, the white clouds and the springtime have never known such a melody;
every time I strike the rhythm, I sing it once more.
Inscription on the Painting of Chuanzi and Jia Shan:
A single stroke of the oar—Heaven and Water are one. Three inches away from the hook—Water and Heaven are joined. Jia Shan did not know how to withdraw his body;
He still waited for Huating to overturn the boat.
Dongshan said, "Even to say directly that 'originally there is not a single thing' does not yet qualify one for his robe and bowl.
The verse says:
"The host in hand weighs high and low; In bargaining and deliberating, all is uneven. Truly, no one can offer the price."
[The Master] counted them. Gold and white jade were as cheap as mud.
A monk offered ninety-six turns of speech, the last of which said: "Even if you bring it here, he will not accept it. The verse says:
When one path is open, every path is open; who can distinguish south from north or east from west? The spring breeze pays no heed to differences in local dialects;
everywhere the peach blossoms are as red as ever.

To transmit the Dharma to another is to reach the point where there is no longer anything to transmit; this is the true transmission. Though the Great Dharma weighs as much as ten thousand *jin*, it hangs from a single strand.
When the person concerned does not expend even a fraction of effort, the blazing, radiant light fills the field of vision before them.

Sengshun has come from afar to visit the venerable masters of all quarters; his straw sandals have not trodden in vain upon the dust. In deep villages and ancient monasteries there is nothing extraordinary—how shameful that a man of such high attainment must come but once.
Sending Chan Master Qiong to Tiantai:
To cast an iron ox within a furnace of a hundred refinements; a jeweled tower appears upon a single blade of grass.
Fenggan claps his hands and Hanshan laughs; who like him has attained such freedom?
As you, Chan practitioner Yin, depart for Jiangxi to pay homage to the Patriarchs:
a hundred billion Mount Sumerus fit within your sandal-bag; boundless lands are contained within your alms-bowl pouch.
If you possess the eye of one who travels to study, all the successive patriarchs will together bow before you.

As this very time marks the completion of the nine-month summer retreat for the Zen practitioner Yuan, the flower-bag has blossomed branch after branch. Go as you please to the east, west, south, or north;
how many will recognize the divine light upon the crown of your head?
Sending off Zen practitioner Jing on his pilgrimage:
Nine times he reached Dongshan, his two eyes azure; three times he ascended Touzi, his two eyebrows arched. Outside every house lies a path leading through the night;
do not travel where the ancients have trod.
Seeing off a practitioner bound for Mount Wutai:
The first friend among the hundred cities is Mañjuśrī. Your pilgrimage to visit the various quarters will not have been in vain. Do not ask whether Mount Qingliang is far or near;
wherever there is affinity, you shall encounter him.
Sending off the Chan practitioner De to Mount Nanyue:
The staff he holds transforms into a dragon; It swallows up heaven and earth, leaving no trace. If someone asks, you must say to them:
"The Ten-Thousand-Year Pine stands on Mount Zhurong."
As the Guest Master Fuku is sent to Jiangxi, who is the host and who is the guest?
One step upon entering the gate is already known beforehand. The colt has trampled countless people to death;
only Guizong’s eyes are like his eyebrows.
The attendant sent to the provincial capital to visit his mother seeks the stem of a flower in the sky at the moment of its birth; he must seek the source of the sun’s brilliance amidst the waves.
It is not that his attachment to worldly love is heavy upon leaving home, but rather that his dreams and soul linger most often in his native land.
Sending An Chanren to visit Tiandong:
Who says that the gourd is not sour? A patch-robed monk with eyes—how could he be deceived?
Looking out at the long pines for twenty li, his heart grows cold before his feet have even crossed the gate.
Seeing off the departing Chan practitioner, I employ the rhyme of Jiangshan;
he once dwelt upon Dulong Peak. The master Bao’s knife and ruler should be brought forth; once brought forth, they shall be presented for this mountain monk to examine.
For what reason does he keep them hidden in his bag and refuse to open it?
Sending off the Zen practitioner Qin to pay homage at the White Stupa and the Sandalwood Image:
A piece of purple sandalwood from Mount Wutai, wrapped in gold, is called the six-foot body of the Tathāgata.
If you truly wish to know the real from the false, go and ask Mañjuśrī atop Mount Wutai.
Ten Verses on Seeing off a Person to Bow at Potalaka The Great Being stands clearly at the perilous pass; Amidst black winds and amidst the waves.
If one can cast oneself in and turn back out, The tide reaches the sandbar and the sun rises over the mountain.
Layer upon layer of green trees hang like hair reaching her shoulders; Patches of crimson clouds cover her skirt down to her feet. With palms joined, she bows forward and offers her greetings;
The sound is heard all at once throughout the great trichiliocosm.
The sea splashes millions of miles of shimmering silver; the mountains heap two or three layers of dense green.
If you wish to know the profound signs of the Great Being, listen to the bells at dawn and dusk.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all share the same name; they utter a single sound that becomes ten million sounds. Their tongues are worn away and their mouths silenced;
where the green mountains end, white clouds stretch across the sky.
An Avalokiteśvara resides at the gate of the face; extending a blaze of light, it illuminates heaven and earth. A morning breeze blows him onto the Paṇḍaka Rock;
gazing east toward Fusang, all is suddenly darkened.
Avalokiteśvara bears Amitābha upon his crown; how could the Dharma of the mind ever weary of being polished? Do not say that the holy and the ordinary are far apart;
you must know that the great ocean is fundamentally one with its waves.
Myriad kinds and a thousand variations reside within the single mind. One seeks Avalokiteśvara atop Mount Potalaka;
yet even if one perceives him with perfect clarity, as before, clouds shroud the Purple Bamboo Grove.
The Superior One sets forth for the South; the Great Being has already emitted light from between his brows. Take note of the successive layers of their mutual abiding:
the ocean tide pushes the sun up toward the Fusang tree.

At the fifth watch, the sun rises like molten gold over the sea; from ten thousand miles away, the morning comes with snow rolling over the sands. With a single thought of faith, one knows this is all delusion;
the Universal Gate is never separated by even a hair’s breadth from the ends of the earth.
Potalaka Rock is but a heap of stones; the sound of the tide reaches it twice each day. Do not say that Avalokiteśvara never appears;
it is the height of the mountains and the vastness of the sea that deceive people into coming.
The gate of the Great Immortal of the Western Lands is distinct from that of Zhutang; throughout antiquity and the present, how many have been able to ascend?
Beyond the fences of the yellow-headed and blue-eyed, it is to the talented monks who enter the inner chamber that we must yield.
An iron wall, a thousand fathoms high; steep crags of towering majesty. All forged from pure, unyielding steel. The blue-eyed barbarian monk cannot see through them;
the spring wind day by day embroiders the azure moss.
The mind of friendship is most difficult to know; it is like iron walls and silver mountains reaching a hundred thousand fathoms.
When both paths of birth and death are thoroughly discerned, every stone, great and small, is pure gold.
Entering the Jewel Mountain empty-handed, one departs empty-handed; heaps of gold and jade are brilliantly clear.
At ease, one picks up a blade of grass, which shall never be exhausted throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes.

The pivot of the non-abiding wheel turns incessantly; seeing it should be difficult. The platter rolls the pearl, and the pearl rolls upon the platter. Yet one still marvels that the platter and pearl leave traces behind.
As the evening clouds fly away, the azure sky is cold.
The waters at the foot of King Chu’s city flow eastward; they will not cease until they reach the vast blue ocean. Yet, upon arrival, how could they ever distinguish "you" from "me"?
All waves alike surge against the heavens.
Flowing forth from the breast, it covers heaven and earth; small as a single drop, vast and boundless.
Clearly knowing this is not the business of another, yet these very waves swell the hundred rivers.

The great void, within and without, is empty and devoid of a single thing; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all encompassed therein. Treading upon and overturning the sea of existence, the dust of worldly toil is stilled;
shattering the city of *śūnyatā*, the kalpas of time are eternal.
Master Yu’an has always dwelt in his three-bay thatched hut; Through many springs, birds have brought flowers in their beaks.
Though the bottom of the door and the gateway have been changed, The person of old remains, unchanged as ever.
The Great Sūtra says that the mouth of Śākyamuni is narrow; the Prajñā and Avataṃsaka are but minor empty fabrications.
One might think that the Nirvāṇa encompasses everything, yet the two characters "Mahā" have not even been opened.
The great fool employs skillful means; those who employ the clumsy are rare. The mind is like wood or stone, utterly devoid of knowledge; yet within it there is a place of clarity.
This state of bewilderment is fundamentally not delusion.
The endless succession of patriarchs has transmitted only this; the Buddhas hand it over to one another in the same way.
Though the waves of the sea may dry up and Mount Sumeru crumble, one does not see the empty sky ever decay.
Mountingsan stands firm and constant amidst the white clouds; it is no mere "Flying Peak" of minor stature.
Though the Vairambha winds have overturned seas and mountains many times, they have never so much as stirred a single pine tree.
At the single strike of the fragrant bamboo, Xiangyan forgot all knowing; the great earth sinks level at this very moment.
Beating through rain and knocking against wind, there are thousands upon ten thousands—yet all are but green branches enduring the cold of winter.
In spring, the eastern breeze blows vast and wide as the waters murmur on. Not a thousand mountains nor ten thousand hills can obstruct them.
If one recognizes where their source arises, let the falling flower petals drift freely among the world of men.
The old man of plum trees observes the southern branches and then the northern ones; let his two temples turn as white as silk.
When illusory flowers have utterly perished, the reality remains—this is precisely the time when the green leaves bear fruit.
There is no meaning, World-Honored One; what dharma could possibly be proclaimed? Kāśyapa has never concealed anything from the beginning. For now, simply till the fields and eat your fill of rice;
preach of Zen with great flourish as you please in all directions.

Hidden in the wilds of Mount Yuanqiao and the Square Vase, it grows deeper and deeper. A single hue of white clouds covers the jade grove; from of old, it has never been separated from those of this age.
Yet one laughs at people coming from afar to seek it upon the sea.
Dao Lin originally used speech to manifest the wordless; he abides neither in the middle nor in the two extremes.
Thorns and sandalwood are both cut away, lest branches and leaves provoke the winds and smoke.
Do not attempt to cut rabbit horns from the waist of a barren woman, nor scrape tortoise hair from the back of an iron ox. Suddenly the thatched hut sheds its lapis lazuli tiles;
in the ancient well, the weeds and dust rise ten fathoms high.
Though the Way-mountain is mindless, it still stands behind a further barrier; only upon encountering its steep precipices does one know the difficulty of reaching the summit.
If one were to ask what was accomplished during those six years, frozen clouds lock it deep within, and the snow falls vast and white.
Zhu Yin dwells in the Five Indies, far removed from the dust of the world; he sees only the blue sky and no people. Ultimately, he hides his body with no trace remaining;
yet where there is no trace, do not hide your body.
The True Lineage overturns the seas and mountains, shaking heaven and earth; throughout the south, north, east, and west, this Way is honored.
Linji and Deshan had neither staff nor shout—did they not know what to entrust to their descendants?
The great net encompasses the four seas, gathering all within a single cast; there is no need to cast the hook for the giant tortoise again.
Behold where the myriad eyes are spread wide—within them lie infinite fish and dragons.
In the emerald courtyard, through the years of cold, its color remains ever green. It was once illuminated by divine light until dawn.
Though three feet of snow may pile up at the steps, the gate of the Patriarch’s school has never been closed.
The sword-hilt is gripped; its blade is as chilling as frost. When brandished, who would dare stand before it? I release for you the Master within;
even a million demonic armies are utterly subdued.

A thousand billion Mount Sumerus are crushed into fine powder; worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are kneaded back into form. Within the hollow of a lotus fiber, one pushes against the red sun;
a vast expanse of mountains and rivers becomes as flat as the palm of a hand.
From where does this numinous, empty, and luminous single point arise? It exists solely within the midst of ordinary daily activities. Ultimately, it is difficult to deceive Pao-t’uo;
he simply joined clay and tiles with empty space.
A separate peak rises steeply, piercing the azure heavens; its precipitous cliffs and hanging crags have a path for climbing.
Do not say that the mountain terrain here is perilous; ahead lies yet another, highest tier.
Where form and appearance exist beyond the elephant, one falls into the mundane dust; where there is neither appearance nor form, that is not yet the truth.
Not remaining within the boundaries of heaven and earth—how many clear chimes for a single man at leisure!
Without deviation, from the center one reaches the right; from the right, one deviates toward the center. If you examine this closely, you will find yourself attached to both sides.
Sweep away these two extremes entirely, and a single bright moon hangs in the midst of heaven.
The first moment this mind is raised becomes the second; it is tranquil and unmoving, yet not something external. You must know that the Buddha-dharma is not a great deal:
when you sit and cut off heaven and earth, you will see the Truth every day.
Shi’an sets aside the single deceptive move; upon entering the gate, do not ask whether it is east or west.
Solely holding up an empty fist, he sits grandly in the hall, shaking the ancestral wind.
In ancient times, Tianran rode upon a holy monk; Master Ma used skillful means to bestow a name. Every person is fully endowed with such a body;
it is not something created through causes and conditions.
The Mirror Hall was cast from the very beginning as nothing but refined copper; only when it reflects do we realize its original emptiness.
With walls of white silver and tiles of pure gold—tell me, who dwells within?
Furthermore, the first phrase of returning to the root and reverting to the source is exactly like when the primordial chaos had not yet been divided. Clearly, one is counted as ten million;
from those ten million, one returns once more to the One above.

Miscellaneous Writings (including the Water and Land Assembly Seated Discourses, Biographies, and Epitaphs),
compiled by Attendant Zhongduan, Zhengcan, and others;
appended to the colophon of the Master’s Blood-Script Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
As for the eternally abiding true mind, by lifting up a single speck of dust, every speck of dust is suddenly manifested.
As for its inconceivable and wondrous virtue, by practicing a single deed, every deed is fully revealed. It is like all colors relying upon space, or like a thousand waves surrounding the sea.

From the initial stage of faith, there is no station that it does not pervade; until one reaches the site of enlightenment, how could the fundamental essence differ? Yet sentient beings are deluded by their false thoughts.

Not knowing this, people falsely take the delusory to be the enlightened truth. The Buddhas, illuminating the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), thus proclaimed the Mysterious and established the doctrine.
Its phenomena transcend the secondary traces of the Reward and Transformation bodies; its principle cuts off the common talk of ordinary beings and sages.

It blazes forth through past and present; things and self interpenetrate. This is the great purport of the *Avataṃsaka*, the head and foremost of all scriptures. May it lead bhikṣus to awakening and entry.
Realizing the ten dharma realms, one enters the gate of profound mystery. Nature and appearance are extinguished yet not non-existent; body and mind are manifested yet not existent.

Drawing blood for ink to transcribe this sutra, at the moment the brush touches the paper one personally beholds Samantabhadra; at the place where a finger snaps, one has already participated with Maitreya.
Seeking it through accumulated kalpas is never enough; gaining even half a verse leaves one more than satisfied. One should cause divine beings...
Protecting and upholding [the Dharma], he extensively brings benefit to the world.
He has inscribed the Lotus Sūtra in blood;
its profound principles are empty and transcendent, and the True Vehicle is serene and still. To contemplate it is to be without contemplation; nectar drenches his heart. To maintain it—

It is held fast; a golden seal seals its mouth. This is why the emanated Buddhas assemble and the Many-Treasures Stūpa arrives, so that those far and near may turn toward it together, and all across past and present may be united by it.
It is the model for the Dharma-giving of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, and the cause for the awakening and entry of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions.

Though one may labor in vain through kalpas of realization and cultivation, perfection is attained in a single kṣaṇa. Yet, while bells and drums are not the essence of ritual music, the instruments cannot be dispensed with;
and while written words are not the ultimate of the *zong* (the fundamental vehicle), the script cannot be absent.
One catches the fish by means of the trap, and observes the moon by means of the finger. Long ago, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his body before the Buddha Śubhavyūha; and Śākyamuni...
The Venerable Asita, by means of this non-substantial body, realized the Dharma of eternal constancy.
The Bhikṣu Dehui of Huilangye, with the light of wisdom, drew blood to transcribe this sutra, vowing to propagate this Way until the end of his life.
As exquisite patterns were spread from the tip of a hair, all the devas showered flowers; as molten gold flowed across the paper, the great earth shook in response. It was like this:
As the oil flows in succession, the lamp does not go out; as the branches and bark are uninterrupted, the tree flourishes. Be careful of the end as you were of the beginning.
There is not much more to the Buddha-dharma; it is difficult for anyone to attain it in its long-term endurance. Exert yourselves!
This King of Sutras is most venerable; its secret treasury is profound and its ultimate truth transcends all names and speech. Yet, through skillful means, it enables one’s awakening and entry.
Since the Tathāgata first expounded it beyond the thousand-year period, and until Kumārajīva’s second translation, this work has been formed into seven fascicles.

To receive, uphold, read, and recite it is like drinking from the ocean—its boundlessness is inexhaustible; to copy and circulate it is like measuring space—it is never-ending. It brings hidden benefit.
The hidden benefits are profound; their wondrous functions are as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Rejoicing and extolling them, one finds the divine efficacy beyond measure.

Now there was a bhikṣu named Weide, whose sincere devotion pierced the sun and whose pure discipline harbored frost-like purity. He reflected that the conditions for attaining liberation could not be fulfilled without a teacher, and that to reach the ultimate limit of repaying kindness, what else could he rely upon but the Buddha?
Thus, he gave rise to the gathering clouds of practice and refined his mind-ground, shedding tears from his ten fingers.
With blood, he completed the seven fascicles of this scripture to repay his teacher’s kindness and to requite the Buddha’s grace. Considering such a resolve, how could it be considered a minor cause?
All you who share my same stream should offer your praise.

In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is said that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous, remaining unchanging throughout all time; fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous, being such as it is both in delusion and enlightenment.
It is likened to empty space, yet is not empty; it manifests all phenomena, yet is not a phenomenon itself. It transcends hearing and seeing, differing from them.

Causes and conditions interweave their radiance in a pervasive net, filling all directions with purity. The Buddhas of the ten directions collectively proclaim the profound essence of the definitive meaning;
all sentient beings fully possess the true body of perfect penetration. It is only because they are disturbed by adventitious dust that they fail to realize the brilliant clarity of daily life.
Bound by ears and eyes, who can understand how to ride upon sound and cover over form? As long as the sense organs and their objects remain unliberated, how can one [attain freedom]?
Ceasing mental activity and forgetting external conditions, one falls into the cage of emotional thoughts and is moved by the karmic retribution of rising and sinking.
It is like a diseased eye seeing halos around a bright lamp, or like bubbles and flowers arising from the great ocean. Outside, there are the mountains, rivers, and worlds;

within, they are divided into the realms of ghosts, animals, humans, and devas. These are fundamentally formed by the weaving of delusions and appear solely through the exhaustion of staring; the four and three realms wind and turn about one another.
The twelve wheels revolve: birth and death, death and birth; existence and non-existence, non-existence and existence.
One must directly sever craving and desire here and now, returning to the state of a *puruṣadamyasārathi* (the tamer of men). From this day forth, may we swiftly reach Bodhi.

Teach me, your disciple of much learning, to transcend the realm of the five aggregates and to thoroughly purify the ten kinds of *dhyāna*. If one can proclaim this mantra-heart, then one may subdue all heterodox paths.
Benefiting others and benefiting oneself, in both the mundane and supramundane realms, may you realize the Immovable Honored One and attain supreme enlightenment.

The śrāmaṇera Zhizu of Weichengzhao, in his youth, practiced asceticism with a keen resolve for the gate of dhyāna. Possessing a mind like the *śūkarakalpa* (adamantine), he transcribed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
With single-minded devotion focused upon its forms, he completed ten fascicles. He vowed to uphold it throughout his life and commissioned this record.
I have merely composed this brief account to provide a general outline; I am deeply ashamed that it remains so crude and neglected.
Regarding the title of this scroll depicting the Sixteen Arhats:

in Sanskrit, they are called *Arhat*. This is translated here as "Slayer of Thieves," "Worthy of Offerings," and "Non-arising. As these three meanings are contained within the term, [it is thus rendered in] the Eastern Land...

It is not translated [into Chinese]. "Arhat" (Killer of Thieves) means killing the thief of ignorance. "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings) means being worthy of offerings from the heavens and the human realm.
"Arhat" (Unborn) means realizing self-nature nirvana; it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning, and even now it is not extinguished. The *Prajñāpāramitā* says:

"When the five fetters of the higher realms are severed and forever exhausted, one is called an Arhat. These five higher fetters are: first, craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), which refers to form...

1. Craving for the realm (*dhātu-tṛṣṇā*). 2. Craving for the two formless realms (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*), namely craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). 3. Ignorance (*avidyā*), namely the lack of clarity in the mind.
4. Restlessness (*auddhatya*), namely mental agitation. 5. Pride (*māna*), namely the mind’s self-exaltation. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

"The superior grade of the ten wholesome paths of action is practiced with wisdom [yet remains inferior] because the mind is narrow and base, because of fear of the three realms, because of the absence of great compassion, and because it is understood through the voice of another as a śrāvaka."

Because they have reached their end, they are called the Śrāvaka-yāna. Regarding these Arhats, only the Buddha alone can reprimand them, causing them to practice with ceaseless diligence until they perfect the fruit of Buddhahood. Other lesser beings should not treat them with contempt;

rather, they should respectfully make offerings to them to seek merit, for they serve as a bridge and ferry across both the mundane and supramundane worlds. As an external text says: "A journey of a thousand li begins with a single step."
At the base [of this work], it is said: "A nine-storied terrace begins with a mound of earth—is this not so?

Regarding the Record of the Image of Great Compassion: the Thousand Hands and Eyes of Great Compassion is the manifested body of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. We reverently contemplate the Bodhisattva, who, because of...
Regarding the practices and vows of the stages (*bhūmi*), that which can be described has already been fully recorded in the various sūtras.
As for his divine power and sagely virtue, which manifest in a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, they are truly beyond the reach of thought or calculation.
Suppose there were someone who took ten billion Mount Sumerus as brushes, ten billion great oceans as ink, and ten billion Sahā worlds as...

On paper: from this day forth, until the end of the future, I shall write it extensively, write it specially, and write it repeatedly—not merely writing it once—but shall gather it together throughout hundreds of thousands of nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sands) eons, through unspeakably unspeakable revolutions of time.

I have not yet been able to write even one part of it. Furthermore, suppose there were a person who took all the empty spaces of the ten directions, the lands of all Buddhas, and all rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, grasses, trees, and forests, and reduced them entirely to fine dust. From each and every grain of dust, they would manifest immeasurable bodies;

from each and every body, they would possess immeasurable tongues; and from each and every tongue, they would exercise immeasurable powers of eloquence. Beginning from this very day, until the end of the future...
From the future limit, whether taught openly or secretly, day and night without interruption, they shall praise it with hymns;
yet even within hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Ganges-sands, through unspeakably unspeakable cycles of eons, they would not have expounded even a single fraction of it.
Although there are many, that which is venerated is called "the One. The One is all; all is the One. It is so minute that it has no interior;

it is so vast that it has no exterior. If this is so, then even if one were to fashion an image using a single pellet of earth, a single finger-length of wood, or a single *zhu* of gold, how would this differ from the body of a hundred million trichiliocosm worlds?

I was seated [in that position]. In the autumn of the fourth year of the Zhizheng era, I came to preside over Shoushan. The following year, I deliberated with the assembly on the construction of the Wanfo Baogé (Precious Pavilion of the Ten Thousand Buddhas).
The year after that, the pavilion was completed. And the year after that, I obtained the financial support of the venerable elder bhikṣu Ruochin.
A statue of Great Compassion was fashioned, and its construction was completed the following year. Alas!
The Dharma-body is truly beyond calculation; yet now it manifests in a small form, specifically a body sixteen feet tall.
It has twenty-one faces, one thousand and eight arms, and its eyes are equal in number to its arms, with one additional eye for each face. Each of its forty-two hands...
There are various supports. Light radiates from the throne, which in turn supports the feet.

From the stone beneath the feet to the transformation Buddha atop the head, the height is forty feet and some odd inches. The wood used is *nán* and paulownia; the lacquer is vermilion; the gold is pure gold.
The sunlight is on the left; the moonlight is on the right. The Dragon Girl Sudhana and the Great Power of the Heavenly General Wei are stationed in attendance in succession.
Upon suddenly opening the door and gazing out, it is dazzlingly bright, as if seven mountains of gold were emerging from the sea and standing firm before one.
How great is this spirit of giving! It truly cannot be measured by material things. Now, I specifically mark those who have offered their faith.
It was merely ten thousand *míng* of cash; yet how difficult it must have been! I have often marveled at Qínzhī’s accumulation of wealth:

he practiced frugality not for his own sake, having already lavishly adorned the Buddha images in the Great Hall, yet now exerting all his strength to create this image as well. People spoke of him incessantly.
Qin alone was humble and did not boast. Such a person intended to serve as a warning for those who would come after;
thus he composed this work. Those who follow should likewise provide an account of him, lest they fail to do so.

If there were neither composition nor account, then even though this record exists, who would not have had such a record? But if there is both composition and account, then even without this record, who [would not remember]?
There is this record; it could not fail to be recorded. Written in the spring of the ninth year of the Zhizheng era, when the dragon was in the year Jichou (1349), by the abbot Fanqi.
A Verse on the Reconstructed Jewel Stupa of the True-Body Relics of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Whenever the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world, they invariably manifest eight kinds of signs:

from their initial descent of the spirit and birth, through their renunciation and cultivation of the Way, their subduing of Māra and attainment of Buddhahood, their turning of the Wheel of Dharma, until finally their entry into Nirvāṇa.
He shall shatter his body of purple-gold into eighty-four thousand *śarīra* relics, causing devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits to construct stupas for their worship;

thus their sins will be extinguished and merit produced, leading ultimately to Bodhi. My original teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata—here translated as "The Capable One" (*Nengren*) and "Tranquil Silence" (*Jimo*)—is currently the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa.
While dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, he serves as the Great Being Vajragarbha (*Huming Dashi*).

The World-Honored One, having fulfilled his requirements and completed four thousand years as a candidate for Buddhahood (*kṣānti*), at the arrival of the time, descended to be born in Kapilavastu, into the palace of King Śuddhodana.
Mounting the sun-elephant, he entered the womb of Queen Māyā. When ten months were complete, he was born from her right side.
This occurred in the land of Eastern Zhendan (China), in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin, on the eighth day of the fourth month.
On the eighth day of the second month in the forty-second year, he traveled through the four gates and leaped over the city wall to leave the household life; at that time, he was nineteen years old.

He tested various heterodox methods and subdued the non-Buddhists. On the eighth day of the second month in the third year of King Mu’s reign—the *guīwèi* year—he attained enlightenment as the morning star appeared.
For the sake of the five men, including Kauṇḍinya, he turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. All...
He realized the fruit of the Way and dwelt in the world preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years. Later, he addressed his chief disciple, Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I have [entrusted] to you the pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the true mark which is markless, and this subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate."
"I entrust this to you. You shall protect and uphold it, and you must also command Ānanda to act as his deputy in the propagation of the teachings, ensuring they do not cease.
Furthermore, I entrust this golden-threaded *saṃghāṭī* robe to be transmitted to Maitreya.

Having finished these instructions, he passed away peacefully at the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River, between the twin *śāla* trees, lying on his right side with his feet stacked one upon the other. This was the fifty-second year of King Shu.
In the year of Wuchen (Ren-shen), on the fifteenth day of the second month, the cremation fire was extinguished.
The eight kings divided the *śarīra* relics among themselves and returned to their respective countries to erect stupas, vying with one another to preserve them for worship.

One hundred years after his parinirvāṇa, there was a king named Aśoka—translated here as "Without Sorrow"—who took all the *śarīra* relics from the various stupas, numbering eighty-four thousand grains, and fashioned eighty-four thousand [stupas].
Regarding the stūpa at the village of Jambū where there were one hundred million households, Venerable Yaśas dispatched a spirit to suppress it with a single stūpa.
According to Master Daoxuan’s *Gantong lu*, there were thirteen stūpas in China;

among those venerated by Liu Sahe, only that at Ayuwang Temple in Mingzhou possessed particularly magnificent radiance from its śarīra, such that prayers offered with utmost sincerity would certainly be fulfilled.

This clearly manifests the power of spiritual resonance. Fan Qi’s place of birth was Xiangshan. He entered the monastic order at the age of nine and immediately heard that the construction of a stupa brings the greatest merit;

thus, he often felt this deeply within his heart. On the third day of the second month in the first year of the Tianli era, the Wuchen year (1338), while serving as the abbot of Tiantong Yongzuo Chan Temple in Haian Prefecture at the age of thirty-four, he began the construction of the Thousand Buddhas Hall in the Renshen year (1352).

In the second year of the Yuantong era, the year of Jiaxu, he dreamed that the Dragon King presented him with treasures; consequently, he solicited contributions for the pagoda, and offerings arrived daily.
Later, in the spring of the second year of the Zhizhi era, the year of Bingzi, the dragon manifested its coiling form within his chamber, complete with all five colors.
Those from the four quarters came to view it, and after two months, it departed. When the pagoda was completed, it returned once more, appearing and disappearing.
It was not one [image]. To this day, it is worshipped as the Dream-Realized Dragon King (*Svapnāntara-nāgarāja*). In the summer, the foundation for the stūpa was laid.
On the twenty-third day of the ninth month in the third year, the *dingchou* year, at the hour of the rat, construction of the stūpa began. By the *xinsi* year, the work was completed.

It consists of seven stories and eight sides, reaching a height of twenty-four *zhang*. Its adornments are magnificent and exquisite; all who behold it are filled with joy. Twelve years passed thereafter.
During the outbreak of war, in the autumn of the Jihai year, the precious vase was lost; its value was calculated at two hundred taels of silver.

At that time, having retired from affairs at Tianning Monastery in Jiahe, he lived in seclusion in a hermitage. When the community requested that he resume leadership of the monastery, he then had a brass precious vase cast and retrieved it.

In the twenty-fourth year of the Zhi Zheng era, on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in the autumn of the Jiachen year, we venerated the stupa with a ritual offering of a water jar, whereupon the heavens rained down precious flowers.
In the seventh month of the following year, the Yisi year, the plastering was finally completed. Thus, from the Dingchou year to the Yisi year— [End of Text]

It has now been twenty-nine years since then. At the age of seventy, Fan Qi gazed upon [the image], circumambulated it, and with great joy and exultation, prostrated himself one hundred times and spoke this verse:
The relics of the Tathāgata are boundless; not merely eighty-four thousand in number,
stupas erected in the heavens and on earth exceed the sands of the Ganges in count—
made of gold, silver, pearls, and lapis lazuli, as well as musaragalva, amber, and agate.

Whether using beryl, crystal, and the like, or various types of black aloeswood and red sandalwood, exquisitely adorned with diverse carvings and engravings—the wondrous fruit obtained is inconceivable.
Or perhaps one offers a single flower or a single incense; or even simply bows the head and joins the fingers and toes.
Some circumambulate once and perform one prostration; there are none who do not sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Some sprinkle fragrant water upon the ground, some grind scented mud to coat the walls, and some burn oil lamps to create radiant light.
There is none among them whose wisdom regarding the Buddha is not perfected.
Since Śākyamuni’s parinirvāṇa long ago, his stūpa has been the foremost field of merit.
Its base is as broad as a jujube leaf, its pinnacle as fine as a needle;
yet its shadow rises majestically to the Brahma-world, entering it with the same equanimity as empty space, never departing from the dust, the crevices, or the pores of a mustard seed.
I now erect this great stūpa, wherein resides the true body of a former Buddha;
vast, expansive, and magnificent, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.
All Tathāgatas dwell within it, and there are no great Bodhisattvas or Śrāvakas who do not come together to receive these offerings.
The eight classes of devas and nāgas all revere and protect him; All who possess eyes gaze upon him.
A bright moon-jewel is placed upon his crown; His belly is filled with the mantras of the precious casket.
At night, silver lamps shoot toward the stars; Flowers bloom in full blaze upon the king of celestial trees.
The eight-sided wind chimes produce wondrous sounds, Surrounded by seven tiers of railings;
Universally bringing benefit to all sentient beings, Their merit is as lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru,
And like the great ocean that receives a hundred rivers, They shall remain forever, through all eternity.
May I, together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, equally attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Vedic Honored Deity Praises the Four Terraces of Mount Sumeru. To the south is Deva; beneath him is the General named Veda, whose rank is that of a Youthful One (Kumārabhūta).
Protect my China! Wearing helmet and chain mail, wielding the vajra to subdue Māra—O Twenty-eight Divisions and Thirty-two Generals, most virtuous among generals, upon whom Śakra relies:
when I sit, you rise; when I turn my back, you face me; protect the good and ward off evil.

Accumulating merit and practicing cultivation, the bhikṣus of the final age will receive the precepts incompletely; in their daily activities—whether rising, sitting, eating, or resting—they truly rely upon the Honored Celestial Beings.
Like a lame person obtaining a staff, or one crossing water obtaining a boat, they receive the Buddha’s entrustment, and their vows are as boundless as the ocean.

by imperial decree, he ascended the seat at the Zhongtian Temple on Mount Jiangshan during the Water and Land Assembly.

The Master said: "In the pure realm of True Suchness, when all is extinguished, nothing at all remains. Yet, by following conditions of defilement or purity, it subsequently forms the ten dharma-realms.
As for these 'dharma-realms,' they are the mind of sentient beings. The mind of sentient beings is the Buddha-mind. How magnificent is this mind!
Formless and signless, it pervades the ten directions; spanning from antiquity to the present, it encompasses all existence. It exists only..."
Within the realm of sentient beings, there is a consistently defiled function called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Within the realm of the Buddhas, there is a consistently pure function called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Both ignorance and Buddha-nature are empty. Yet, sentient beings do not realize this emptiness;
deluded by ignorance, from immeasurable kalpas until the present life, they give rise [to afflictions] through body, speech, and mind.
Greed, anger, and delusion. Those whose conduct is dominated by greed number twenty-one thousand; those whose conduct is dominated by anger number twenty-one thousand;
those whose conduct is dominated by delusion number twenty-one thousand; and those whose conduct is characterized by equal proportions of all three number twenty-one thousand.
Together, they create eighty-four thousand afflictions and karmas, whereby they encounter royal punishment in life and fall into hell after death, remaining there for many kalpas.
There is no time for emergence. An ancient worthy said: "All bitter fruits are experienced because of karma; once experienced, they return to nothingness. What suffering is there?
Have you not seen that the *Cittarāja-mudrā* by Master Fu of the Liang Dynasty says: "Contemplate the King of the Mind, subtle and wondrous, difficult to fathom.
Formless and signless, it possesses great spiritual power. It can extinguish a thousand calamities and accomplish..."
Regarding the myriad virtues: although their essential nature is empty, they are able to bestow the Dharma-Principle. When observed, they have no form; when called upon, they produce sound.

They act as the generals of the Dharma; the precepts of the mind transmit the scriptures. It is like the taste of salt in water or the presence of blue pigment within lacquer—their existence is certain, yet their forms are not seen.
Furthermore, it is said: "If you wish to seek Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing. Although the nature of the mind is empty...
The essence of greed and anger is real; enter this Dharma-gate and you shall sit upright and attain Buddhahood. [He] raises a whisk and says:

"Do you see? The World-Honored One Amitāyus is right now upon the tip of this whisk, emitting a great radiance that universally illumines the ten directions, filling all of empty space and the entire Dharma-realm—unspeakably, unspeakably, and yet again unspeakably vast."
As many as there are atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems— ten billion suns and moons, ten billion sets of four continents,
ten billion great oceans, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion celestial palaces of the desire realm, ten billion celestial palaces of the form realm,
and ten billion celestial palaces of the formless realm— within each and every one of these worlds, among the heavens...
Within each of these palaces there are bodhisattvas surrounded by assemblies as vast as the ocean, who preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, each in a different manner:
through sudden or gradual teachings; through direct or expedient teachings; through vertical or horizontal explanations; and through clear or concealed discourses.
Whatever they teach, it all speaks of this very mind. What principle is not perfected therein? What phenomenon is not fully contained?
What single speck of dust is not encompassed? What single world-system is not included? If you can see this point, then those who have not yet crossed over shall be made to cross;

those who have not yet attained liberation shall be made to be liberated; those who have not yet reached the other shore shall be made to reach the other shore; and those who have not yet realized nirvana shall be made to realize it.
May they attain nirvana;
thus shall the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace be fully repaid at once. Should this not yet be so, I shall add further commentary.
(He strikes the whisk and says: Do you hear? If you hear here, then all of you have your ears within a single sound, and that single sound is universal.

This spread throughout the ears of all people. This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara’s Dharma-door of Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*). When drums are struck simultaneously in ten directions, they are heard at once in ten places;
this is the reality of perfection (*yuan-zhen-shi*). One hears sounds through a wall, and they can be heard both far and near;
this is the reality of penetration (*tong-zhen-shi*). Since sound does not exist, it is not extinguished; since sound exists, it is not born. These two—birth and extinction—...
The detachment from conditions is eternal and true. Therefore, the Buddhas attain it here and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Bodhisattvas attain it here and bring the six perfections and myriad practices to fulfillment.
Pratyekabuddhas attain it here and penetrate the clear understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination. Śrāvakas attain it here and realize the three knowledges and six supernormal powers.
They realize the eight liberations. The devas attain this and transcend the ten stages. Humanity attains this and becomes fully endowed with all virtues.
The asuras attain this and forever sever arrogance. Those in the hells attain this and are all liberated from the wheel of suffering.
Even the hungry ghosts, animals, and all beings of the four modes of birth and nine categories—[attain this]. One...
All sentient beings who attain this will, without exception, awaken to the Buddha within their own minds and realize the Buddha within their own minds.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended.
Since the mind cannot be apprehended, the Buddha cannot be apprehended, nor can the Bodhisattva be apprehended. Only...
Awakening is also unattainable. Śrāvakas are also unattainable. The devas are also unattainable.
Human beings are also unattainable. Asuras are also unattainable. Pretas, animals, and all sentient beings of the four modes of birth and nine categories are likewise unattainable.
Even this "unattainability" is itself unattainable. —Master Yongjia.
The Way: clearly seeing that there is not a single thing; neither person nor Buddha exists. The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean;
all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. Thus, the Second Patriarch, Shen Guang, visited the First Patriarch Bodhidharma and said, "My mind is not at peace;
I beg the Master to grant me peace of mind. The First Patriarch replied, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall give it to you."

Anshou said, "The mind sought cannot be found. The First Patriarch said, "I have finished settling your mind for you," and with his whisk, he drew a single stroke, saying, "This cuts through the tangle.
At this very moment, when the fruit is fulfilled and the work is complete—how do you express it in a single phrase?
"With this profound mind, I serve all lands; this is what is called repaying [the debt]."
Regarding the grace of the state:

We reverently acknowledge that Your Majesty, the Emperor, is heroic, martial, benevolent, and sagacious. Having unified the realm within the seas, You nourish the myriad people as Your own children, extending Your care to the nine tribes and eight barbarian peoples.
There were none who did not submit as guests. Consequently, they ascended mountains on ladders to present tribute and crossed the seas to offer precious rarities.
In the first year [of his reign], he issued a general amnesty for all under heaven, bestowing the grace of leniency upon all. Even the innocent and the wronged were granted deliverance;

silver and silk were specially bestowed, and the Shanshi Yuan (Bureau of Goodness) was commanded to construct the *Mingyang Shuilu* (Water-Land Rite for the Living and the Dead) at Jiangshan Chansi Temple.

For one full day and night of the Great Fast, various Buddhist rites were performed therein. Offerings were made to the Buddhas, worthies, sages, the deities of heaven and earth, and the spirits and ghosts of the three realms.

Furthermore, the monk Fan Qi was summoned to proclaim the Dharma of the School of Mind. May all the merit and virtue thus accumulated serve to deliver those of the four modes of birth and six paths of existence;
may all the innocent and the wronged be entirely liberated from the dark realms and reborn in the Buddha-lands.
They achieve enlightenment; their aspirations are like wish-fulfilling jewels. They shatter the cavern of ignorance and sever the root of birth and death with the sword of wisdom.
By means of the Great Dharma, they awaken to the mind; they proceed to the Land of Bliss to behold the Buddha.

Furthermore, it is recounted that Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty invited the Great Being (Fu Dashi) to expound the sutras. When the Great Being ascended the seat, he struck once with his fly-whisk, and Master Bao [said]: "The Bodhi..."
Sakyamuni said to the Emperor, "Your Majesty, do you understand? The Emperor remained silent. The Bodhisattva said, "The Great Being has finished preaching the sutra.
The Master [Zhaozhou] added, "Today, by the Imperial Grace, this humble monk Fanqi has been permitted to ascend this seat to proclaim the First Noble Truth. May all who are deluded universally..."

The flowing stream is the same as the Buddha-way. That which the Old Man Śākyamuni could not fully exhaust in forty-nine years—the subtle and great Dharma-gates—has all been revealed at once by Master Fu. But tell me, where does the crux lie?
