On the thirteenth day of the third month in the second year of the Hongwu era, by imperial decree, the Master ascended the seat at the Water and Land Assembly in Jiangshan Chan Temple.
The Master said: "The Dharma-thunder resounds and the Dharma-drum is struck; the clouds of compassion spread and the nectar of immortality is sprinkled. Now, this Dharma-thunder...
The drum has already been shaken; the Dharma drum has already been struck; the clouds of compassion have already spread; the nectar of immortality has already been sprinkled.
But tell me, what Dharma does this mountain monk preach? Does he preach the Dharma for the Śrāvaka vehicle? Does he preach the Dharma for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle?
Does he preach the Dharma for the Bodhisattva vehicle? Does he preach the Dharma for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Speak!

Is it directed toward the realm of ordinary beings? Within the teaching, within the middle way, and within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is no dharma named "directed toward the Śrāvaka vehicle," "directed toward the Pratyekabuddha vehicle," "directed toward the Bodhisattva vehicle," or "directed toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)."

There is no dharma called "tending toward the realm of ordinary beings," nor is there any dharma called "tending toward defilement" or "tending toward purity," or "tending toward saṃsāra" or "tending toward nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are non-dual, just like space, whether in the past, future, or present.
It cannot be sought and found; yet it is not that space does not exist. To speak according to reality, the very negation of space is already like driving in a stake.
Yunmen’s fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens and strikes Indra’s nostrils;
a blow from the carp of the Eastern Sea causes rain to pour down like an overturned basin. How will you all deal with this?
"How do you understand this? After a long silence, he said: "Without giving rise to even the slightest thought of cultivation or study, one is eternally sovereign within the light of formlessness.
He further said: "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing. What is it?
Having spoken thus with clarity, what more need be explained or annotated? This matter does not reside in words; ten pairs and five groups—[this is how it is made].
A Gathering of Language. How bitter! How tragic! Master Xiangyan said: "It is like a person climbing a tree with neither hand grasping a branch nor foot treading upon one.
Suddenly, someone below the tree asks, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
If he answers him, he loses his body and life; if he does not answer him, he violates what was asked. To answer is right; not to answer is right."
This is so. Master Dahuì said: "The Chan of my school is like a mass of fire. If you touch it, it will burn you to death;
if you turn your back on it, it will freeze you to death. It is just as Master Yongjia had these two lines:
'What is the point of giving a ladder to a thief? 'It is not difficult to see one's form in a mirror. [In] the water...

Seizing the moon—how can it be grasped? It is as level as a mirror’s surface, yet as perilous as a precipice. At the place where the Vajra takes up the mud, there is one who is a person of my own house.
To further provide you with another ancient saying: The Fourth Patriarch of our school, the Venerable Upagupta, once had a clansman renounce the world.
One night, he went to stay at the Tian Temple. Thereupon, the Patriarch composed [this verse]:
Through skillful means, he transformed himself into a yakṣa who carried a dead man on his shoulder. Another yakṣa arrived empty-handed, and the two spirits began to dispute.
One said, "I am the one who brought this dead man. The second said, "I am the one who brought this dead man.
The first spirit said, "I have witnesses; this person saw me when I was carrying the dead man here."
The man thought to himself, "I shall certainly die now; I must speak words of truth. After speaking, he said to the latter ghost:
"This dead man was brought here by the former ghost; it is not yours. The latter ghost became greatly enraged and tore off one of his arms.
The former ghost then reattached the dead man's arm as it was before. The latter ghost again tore off another arm, and the former ghost tore off yet another.

The arm of the dead man was restored to its place. Then the latter ghost pulled out both his legs, and the former ghost completely replaced them with the legs of the dead man, restoring them as they were originally.
Thus, the two ghosts together ate the freshly pulled flesh and immediately departed.
This son of noble family has attained sudden and great enlightenment.
Today, the Sage Emperor universally delivers those in the dark realms by commanding me, the monk Fanqi, to preach the Dharma and deliver all these sons of the Buddha.
It is my hope that beneath a single word, they shall be completely resolved and free from doubt, realizing that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind, thereby accomplishing wisdom.
The body does not depend on another for awakening; it is like suddenly waking from a dream, or like a lotus flower opening.

When the Fifth Patriarch, Master Yuan, acted on behalf [of the student] by joining both hands together to form the beak of a pigeon and saying, "Gu-gu-qua," the Master (Xuedou) comments:

Biography of the Monk Chushi:
His name was Fanqi; his style name was Chushi; his childhood name was Tanyao. He was a native of Xiangshan in Mingzhou and belonged to the Zhu clan.
His father, Gao, was fond of goodness and possessed hidden virtues. His mother, Zhang, served the Buddha with the utmost reverence.
On the day of Ding-si in the sixth month of the year Bing-shen, the second year of the Yuanzhen era of the Great Yuan, she dreamed that the sun fell into her breast and gave birth to the Master.
While the Master was still in his swaddling clothes, a divine monk came to see him and said to his father, "This child is a Buddha. In the future..."
"You shall surely uphold the Buddha-dharma and illuminate this turbid age. Because of this, his clan and village community named him Tan Yao. At the age of four, he lost both his father and mother;
he was raised by his grandmother, Lady Wang, who orally transmitted the *Analects* to him. He was immediately able to recite it from memory.
When someone asked which passage he preferred in the book, he replied at once: "The gentleman finds his analogy in righteousness (*yi*). Six.

At the age of six, he was adept at composing rhymed couplets; at seven, he could write large characters. Having read the *Odes* and the *Documents*, he never forgot them upon a single glance, and the entire district hailed him as a prodigy.
At nine, he traveled to Xizhe, where he followed Master Ne’weng Mu of Tianting Monastery in Haiyan to receive instruction in the classics.
He subsequently relied upon his paternal great-uncle, Master Jin’weng Xun, at Chong’en Monastery in Lake County. Zhao Wenmin...
The Duke, whose ancestral tombs were at Chong’en, frequently traveled there; each time he saw the Master, he marveled at him.

He purchased a monastic certificate for him, and through the courtesy of Elder Neng, he received ordination. At the age of sixteen, at Zhaokong Temple in Hangzhou, he received full precepts and became a bhikṣu.

At that time, his literary talent was brilliant and flourishing, and his reputation was widely renowned; the eminent masters of the famous mountains throughout the two provinces of Zhejiang vied with one another [to seek his instruction].
He wished to invite Xu Gu Ling of Jingshan, Yun Wai Xiu of Tiantong, and Hui Ji Xi of Jingci to his assembly;
each of them had several hundred eminent disciples (dragon-elephants), yet they all praised him highly. At the age of twenty, Jin’eng moved to Daochang.
He was appointed as his attendant. Subsequently, he was also entrusted with the keys to the storehouse. One day, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage:

"When seeing depends on conditions and clarity is the cause, darkness results in the absence of vision; yet when clarity arises spontaneously, then all appearances of darkness can never again obscure it."
Consequently, he attained a realization. From then on, as he read both Buddhist and secular classics, it was as if they were familiar from past habit;

yet, regarding the ultimate point of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he still encountered obstructions. When Master Yuansou Yuan of Mount Jing took up residence there, his reputation for the Way was preeminent throughout the land.
The Master went to visit him and immediately asked: "What is the meaning of 'Speech issues forth without sound; form exists before things'?"
The old man suddenly said, "Words are uttered but are not sound; form appears but is not substance. Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
As the Master prepared to offer a reply, the old man let out a thunderous roar of a shout (*huì*). The Master was left stunned and withdrew.

Later, when Emperor Yingzong issued an edict for calligraphers to go to the capital to transcribe the Great Tripitaka in gold, the Master was selected among them. He took his leave of the old man and departed. Upon arriving at the scriptorium, he...
In the Wanbao Ward, near the Chongtian Gate, one night after waking from sleep, he heard the drums sounding atop a decorated pavilion.
Suddenly and completely awakened, he saw through to the very core of Jingshan’s way of guiding people. He composed a verse, saying: "Outside the Chongtian Gate, the drums roll on and on;
Suddenly, the void collapses upon the earth. Picking up a flake of snow from the red furnace— It turns out to be the Yellow River."
"June Ice. This was indeed the eleventh day of the first month of the *jiǎzǐ* year. That year, he returned to the East and once again attended upon Yuansou at Mount Jing.
Yuansou welcomed him with a smile and said, "I am glad that you have successfully completed your great task.

From then on, their teacher-disciple relationship reached a state of definitive resolution, and the karmic conditions between master and disciple were as clear as a spreading mist. Yuansou subsequently appointed him as the second seat (*duìzuò*), and he [the Master] studied...
Many sought his counsel and instruction. Before long, by imperial decree of the Xuanzheng Yuan, he was appointed to succeed to the abbacy at Fuzhen Monastery in Haiyan Prefecture.

There, he offered a single incense stick in homage to Yuanseu, who was the fifth-generation successor of Miaoxi. In the Wuchen year of the Tianli era, he moved to Tianning Monastery in the same prefecture.
In the Yihai year of the Zhiyuan era, he moved to Baoguo Monastery in Hangzhou. In the Jia申 year of the Zhizheng era, he moved to [Jia]... Monastery.

He awakened to the fundamental enlightenment of Xingjun. In the year Dinghai, the Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title "Chan Master Furi Puzhao Hui bian" (Sun of the Buddha Universally Shining, Wisdom and Eloquence).

In Dingyou, he moved to Tianning Temple in the same prefecture. In Jihai, harboring the intent to retire from public life, he noted that Tianning in Haiyan possessed the splendor of both sea and mountains;
he consequently constructed a residence on the western side of the temple and styled himself the "Elder of the Western Studio."
In the year Gui-mao, the temple master Zu-guang passed away. The District Magistrate urged Master Qiang to once again take charge of the temple affairs.
In the year Wu-shen, he recommended his foremost disciple in the Dharma, Jing-huan, to succeed him, while he himself returned to grow old in the Western Chamber.
The Imperial Ming has begun its auspicious reign and unified the realm under the four seas.
The Son of Heaven reflected that generals and ministers might perish on the battlefield, and commoners might die by the sword;

it was therefore fitting to establish a memorial service according to the teachings of Śākyamuni to rescue and deliver them. Accordingly, on the eleventh day of the ninth month of the first year of Hongwu, he issued a summons.
The Master preached the Dharma at Jiangshan. The court officials reported his teachings to the Emperor, who was greatly pleased.
In the third month of the following year, he again summoned the Master to Jiangshan to preach the Dharma, following the precedent of the first year.
Upon hearing his account, the Emperor was again greatly pleased; on the fifteenth day,
he granted him a banquet below Wénlóu and personally received him with inquiries of courtesy and comfort.
An imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Tianjie Temple. On the tenth day, when it was time for his departure, silver from the Inner Treasury was bestowed upon him as a gift.

Furthermore, in the autumn of the following year, the Sovereign, considering that the principles of ghosts and spirits are profoundly mysterious, felt that the Buddha must surely have established definitive teachings on the matter, and thus deemed it appropriate to summon his disciples.
I once inquired about this with Master Shi De. Consequently, sixteen individuals were summoned from both sides of the Zhe River;
myself, the Master, and Master Mengtang E were among them. On the twelfth day of the seventh month, we arrived at Tianjie Monastery and stayed in the abbot’s quarters.
The Emperor commanded an official of the Ministry of Rites to offer his congratulations and further ordered an official of the Ministry of Provisions to bestow firewood, rice, and other items.
He then instructed that the questions posed be investigated thoroughly and presented for discussion on the day of the fast. However, on the twenty-second day, the Master manifested slight illness.
Nevertheless, when compared with various masters who cite sutras and treatises to discern the subtleties of this principle, [his understanding] remains self-evident.

On the twenty-sixth day, he suddenly requested a bath and changed his robes. Sitting in the full lotus posture, he wrote a verse: "The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death.
A wooden horse neighs in the night; the sun rises in the west. Setting down his brush, he said to Mengtang, "Elder brother, I am going. Tang...
[The official] asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going to the West. The official said, "There is a Buddha in the West; is there no Buddha in the East?
The Master then let out a thunderous shout and passed away. The official of the Ministry of Rites reported the Master's final verse to the throne.
The Emperor lamented for him for a long time. Song Gong Jingliao and Wei Gong Dapu, both Hanlin Academicians, were his spiritual friends outside the secular world;
they were particularly moved by grief. For four days while the body was enshrined in the coffin, the countenance became increasingly radiant and lustrous.
Monastics and laypeople alike came to pay their respects, as if attending the *parinirvāṇa* of a Buddha. The abbot of Tianjie Temple, Chan Master Bai’an Jin, was the disciple of Guding Ming.
The Upādhyāya was the foremost successor to the Dharma and a younger brother in the Master’s spiritual lineage.

He performed every funeral rite with the utmost propriety and, together with others, invited various masters to offer the Dharma as a funeral offering. At that time, it was customary to prohibit cremation.
Out of respect for his teacher, the Emperor specially established the precedent of cremation for members of the Sangha. On that day, the heavens were clear and serene;

more than a thousand people accompanied the funeral procession. Among the remains after the cremation, the teeth, the root of the tongue, and the rosary remained unburnt. Five-colored śarīra relics were scattered profusely over the skeletal remains.
The disciple Wensheng, who had come to study under him, took the skeletal remains and the items that had not been consumed by fire back to the sea.
On the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month, [Master] Yan was interred in the West Chamber and a stupa was erected for him. Throughout his life, the Master saved sentient beings;
he performed Buddhist services through both words and writing. His *Recorded Sayings in Six Assemblies* have long been carved into woodblocks and circulated.

Furthermore, there are the *Pure Land Verses*, the *Verses on Maitreya’s Rebirth Above*, the *Collection from the Northern Tour*, the *Fengshan Collection*, and the *Xizhai Collection*. Additionally, there are [his] harmonized...

The *Verses on the Three Sages of Tiantai*, the *Mountain Dweller’s Verses* by Chan Master Yongming Shou, the poems of Tao Qian, and the poems of Lin Bu—altogether comprising several volumes—are all circulated in the world.
Wherever the Master resides, donors gather like clouds; whatever he undertakes to construct, they provide for.
In a mere instant, the work was successfully completed at Tianning Temple in Haiyan.

A great Vairocana Pavilion was constructed, and cast-bronze images of Vairocana Buddha, the Thousand Buddhas, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Great Compassionate Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Bodhisattva were fashioned.

These images were arranged in upper and lower tiers, their marks and features exceptionally sublime. Furthermore, a seven-story jeweled pagoda was built, reaching a height of two hundred and forty *chi*.
The remaining cubits were completed, but the stupa suddenly became tilted and was on the verge of collapsing. The Master, fearing this, offered prayers to the Buddha.
One night, there was a great wind and rain, and the people of the prefecture heard a voice from the air saying, "Go quickly to Tianning to save the stupa!

The next day, the stupa was as upright as it had been before. When the Master returned, however, the stupa had been nearly destroyed by military conflict, and the precious vase at its summit was lost.

The Master further collected donations to repair and restore it. At that time, Jinghuan served as the administrative secretary of Mount Jing; he provided the funds to cast precious vases to replace the damaged ones.

On the day the vases were offered, heavenly flowers rained down profusely and a wondrous fragrance filled the air. The local people gathered to witness the event, marveling and sighing in admiration without end.
He constructed a great pavilion at Benjue Temple, the upper level of which was dedicated to the ten thousand Buddhas, while the lower level was dedicated to...
The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion was enshrined by a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Stage. The magnificence of this majestic image was perhaps unsurpassed in the region west of the Zhe River.
As for the Master’s character, his stature was short and small, yet his aspirations and capacity were vast and great. He embodied non-action, while his spiritual responses were unfathomable.
His vigorous activities were entirely directed toward revealing the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) to others, so as to lead them to awakening and realization.
And so it ends. Therefore, although there may be the beauty of construction and the richness of eloquent discourse, in reality, there is neither making nor speaking.
It is like spring to the flower, or the moon to the water; what can be described are merely their shadows, colors, and fragrances.
The influence of the transformation of the Way extends throughout the world, both within and beyond the seas; scholars in Goryeo and Japan, in particular—
I admire him deeply. His secular age was seventy-five, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka-vaṣa) was sixty-three.

He ordained several dozen people, and several dozen succeeded his Dharma. Jing-huan and Wen-sheng, intending to seek out and take leave of a great calligrapher of the present age to inscribe his stupa, so as to manifest it for future students, requested me to record his life and deeds. I, at first...
While at Mount Jing, he was in profound accord with the Master. Furthermore, they both received the Dharma from Master Yuansou.

Subsequently, as he traveled back and forth between East and West Zhejiang, he came to know the Master’s life and conduct in great detail. Upon the Master’s passing, he personally witnessed the efficacy of his radiant light.
Thus, he could not decline the task. However, due to his own failing health and the fact that his records were numerous yet meager, he nevertheless composed these words.

The gentleman may find something to examine herein. Written on an auspicious day in the ninth month of the Gengxu year of the Hongwu era by his dharma-brother Zhiren, formerly resident at Chongbao Chan Temple in Shaoxing Prefecture.
Preface to the Stele Inscription for Chan Master Furi Puzhao Hui-bian.

In the first year of the Hongwu era, when the Emperor ascended the throne, he dwelt in serene majesty and took pity upon the four seas, where the contending armies had caused many generals, soldiers, and commoners to perish by untimely deaths;
their spirits having no refuge, none but the World-Honored Buddha was sufficient [to provide salvation].
He delivered them across [to liberation].
In the ninth month of autumn, an imperial decree was issued for more than ten eminent monks from Jiangnan to hold a Great Dharma Assembly at Jianzhong Chan Temple on Mount Jiang.
At that time, Chan Master Chushi was indeed among their ranks. When the Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, he did so to inspire and uplift humans, devas, dragons, and ghosts.
The Emperor listened. When the ceremony was concluded, a close attendant entered to report this;
the Emperor was greatly pleased. In the third month of the spring of the second year, he again followed the precedent of the first year, summoning the Master to preach the Dharma as before.
A banquet was bestowed beneath the Wénlóu Hall, where the Emperor personally received [the teachings].
The Emperor consulted him. Upon his return, the Inner Treasury was opened and white silver was bestowed as a gift.

In the autumn of the third year, the Emperor, considering that the manifestations of ghosts and spirits are subtle and difficult to fathom, believed that the lost scriptures must contain clear explanations.
He thus carefully selected a monk who had mastered the teachings of the Tripiṭaka to question him. The Master, along with Mengtang E and Xingzhong Ren, [was summoned].
...and so forth.
They were summoned and arrived, being lodged at Daecheongye Temple.

The Sovereign commanded the Office of Rites to provide them with hospitality. Subsequently, they cited and relied upon the sūtras and śāstras to compose a treatise, which was then about to be submitted.

In the morning, he presented his memorial. Suddenly, the Master manifested a slight illness. After four days had passed, he urged those around him to prepare a bath. He changed his robes, took up his brush, and wrote a verse:
"The true nature is perfectly luminous; Fundamentally, it is without birth or extinction. The wooden horse neighs in the night; The sun rises in the west."
Having finished writing, he said to Mengtang, "Brother, I am about to depart. Mengtang asked, "Where will you go? The Master replied, "To the West.
Mengtang asked, "If there is a Buddha in the West, is there no Buddha in the East?
The Master let out a single, stern shout and passed away peacefully. This was on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month. [Recorded by] the Abbot of Tianjie.
Xibai Jin was the adopted son of Master Famen. In attending to the funeral arrangements, he observed every ritual propriety without exception. At that time, there was a prohibition against cremation;
the Ministry of Rites reported this matter to the Emperor.
The Emperor specially decreed that his teachings be followed. Following the cremation, his teeth, jaw, tongue, and rosary remained entirely intact.
Relics adhered to the remaining bones, clustering like beads.
His disciple, Wensheng, took the bones and the unburnt remains back to Haian, where he selected the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month to construct a stupa.

He was buried at Tianning Yongzuo Chan Temple. After the burial, his successor in the Dharma, the chief disciple Jinghuan, together with Wensheng, came to request an inscription based on the biography of Master Ren composed by [his] disciple.
Master Ren was widely versed in both Buddhist and secular classics; his prose was concise yet profound, possessing the style of the Western Han dynasty.
His words may be trusted as being true and not deceptive. Having carefully examined the biography, [I find that] the Master’s name was...
Fanchi was his name; Chushi was his courtesy name. His childhood name was Tanyao. He was a native of Xiangshan in Mingzhou, surnamed Zhu.
His father was Gao and his mother was Zhang. Zhang dreamed that the sun fell into her bosom when he was born.
While the Master was still in his swaddling clothes, a divine monk rubbed the crown of his head and said, "This is a Buddha-sun. In the future, he shall be able to illuminate the dark alleys."
People named him Tan Yao because of this. At the age of seven, his spiritual nature was exceptionally sharp; upon reading a book, he immediately grasped its general meaning.
When asked what kind of words he preferred, he replied at once: "The gentleman finds his analogy in righteousness.
As for composing verses and imitating calligraphy, he far surpassed his peers. Far and near, he was hailed as a "wonder-child," and at nine years of age, he renounced secular life.
He entered the Yongzuo era and received the scriptures from Master Nüweng Mu. He subsequently relied upon Master Jinweng Xun at Chong’en Temple on Lake Hongzhou;
Master Xun was his ancestral uncle. Duke Zhao Wei recognized the Master’s potential and purchased a *sengjie* (monastic certificate) for him, enabling him to undergo tonsure and become a śramaṇa.
He later proceeded to Zhaokai Temple in Hangzhou to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). At that time, he was already...

At the age of sixteen, when Master Xun moved to reside at Daochang Monastery, the Master served as his attendant. Not long after, he was appointed to oversee the library. While reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, upon reaching the passage:
"When seeing arises from conditions and clarity is the cause, darkness becomes a place where there is no seeing," he had a sudden realization.

He subsequently perused a vast array of texts without relying on a teacher’s instruction; the meaning of the words and phrases opened up to him spontaneously. Nevertheless, he remained stuck on the level of names and conceptual characteristics.
Unable to cast off his entanglements, he heard that Master Yuansou Duan was propagating the Way at Shuangjing. The Master went there to inquire, saying, "When speech is uttered, it is not sound;
when form appears, it is not an object—what is the meaning of this? Yuansou then used the Master’s own words to interrogate him in return.
The Master was just about to formulate a response when the old man scolded him and sent him out. From then on, a multitude of doubts clogged his chest like a boulder pressed against it.
Later, during the reign of Emperor Yuan Yingzong, an imperial decree was issued to grind gold into powder to serve as ink for copying the Great Canon (Tripitaka).

The authorities, noting that the Master was skilled in calligraphy, selected him to go to the capital of Yan. One night, hearing the drums strike at the West City Tower, he broke into a sweat as if pouring.
It rained. [Wuming] struck the desk and laughed, saying, "Today, the nostrils of Mount Jing have fallen into my hands.
He then composed a verse containing the lines: "Picking up a single snowflake from a red furnace / Is indeed ice on the Yellow River in the sixth month.
He then turned back toward the east and re-entered Shuangjing. When Yuansou saw that the Master’s countenance was full and radiant, he said, "The secret transmission of the West..."
Master Yi said, "My son has already attained it. He immediately assigned him the second seat and remarked that the Great Dharma of Miaoxi was entirely present within the Master.
Whenever anyone came to seek instruction or pose questions, he frequently charged the Master with resolving their doubts. This was during the Yuantai period of the Ziding era.
The Xingxuanyuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) had long been aware of the Master’s reputation and commanded him to take up residence at Fuzhen Monastery in Haiyan.

Subsequently, he was promoted to the abbacy of Yongzuo. As Yongzuo was the site where the Master had received his monastic precepts, he constructed a Great Treasure Pavilion (*Mahāratnakūṭa*) and cast a thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa in bronze.
Furthermore, he commissioned images of Vairocana, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara.
All the images were placed within it. He further constructed a seven-storied stūpa, over two hundred and forty feet in height.
When the work was nearly complete, the structure threatened to lean. The Master prayed for it, and that night there was a great rain and wind.

The local inhabitants heard spirits conversing with one another, saying, "The Tian-ning Stūpa is leaning; go quickly to save it! By dawn, the stūpa was exactly as it had been before. It was then moved.

At Baoguo Temple in Hangzhou, he renovated Benjue Temple in Jiaxing and further constructed a nine-bay Wufogé (Ten Thousand Buddhas Pavilion), which was so magnificent and grand that it appeared as if a celestial palace had descended to the human world.
The Imperial Preceptor, admiring his religious practice, bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Furi Puzhao Huidian.
The name "Furi" (Sun of the Buddha) was quite consistent with the prophecies of the divine monks of former days.

Those who understand him differ from this view. When the position at Baen-sa Temple became vacant due to its reputation for repaying parental kindness and filial piety, everyone agreed that Baen-sa was a preeminent monastery in the entire province and that none but the Master could occupy it.
The Master reluctantly complied with the public request and went there, but soon thereafter he withdrew to live in seclusion at Yongcho-sa.

He constructed Xizhai (West Chamber) as his plan for a final resting place. In the *guimao* year of the Zhizheng era, the local magistrate urged the Master to take charge of the affairs of the temple.
At that time, the stupa had been destroyed by war; the Master rebuilt it. Later, Jinghuan succeeded him, and the Master returned once more to live out his old age in Xizhai.
As for the Master’s character, he was short of stature, yet his spiritual presence was refined and lucid. He upheld and elucidated the True Dharma.

Flowing forth in torrents and spreading in vast waves, there was no knowing where it would end. In every place he presided over, both monastics and laypeople looked up to him with devotion, like waters returning to their valleys.
In the space of a single finger-snap, halls and towers sprang up, soaring to pierce the clouds; yet one never saw the Master exert any effort.
The gentleman remarked: "The Master moves with sovereign ease, responding to things without leaving a trace—like mountains and rivers giving rise to clouds."
Like thunder coiling and lightning flashing, his divine power was withdrawn; all became silent and still.
Consequently, from within—Yan, Qi, Qin, and Chu—to without—Japan and Goryeo—all sought counsel on the essentials of the mind and hurried to his seat.

Having obtained even a single word from the Master, they would frame it in silk and store it away, regarding it as no less precious than a ceremonial jade tablet. The Master may truly be called one who brings no shame to the descendants of Miaoxi.
Thus it was. The Master’s secular age was seventy-five, and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-lakṣa*) was sixty-three. Those who attained the Dharma numbered several dozen;
those who received ordination numbered several dozen. As for the skillful applications of his preaching, they are seen in the *Recorded Sayings* of the six assemblies.
As for his playful mastery of the brush and ink, they are seen in his compositions for the Three Sages of Tiantai, as well as for Yongming Yanshou, Tao Qian, Lin Buzhou, and others.
He composed the *Pure Land Verses*, the *Verses on Maitreya’s Ascent*, and the *Three Collections of the Western斋 (Zhai) from North of Feng Mountain*.

Altogether, these amount to several volumes, all of which have been transmitted to the world. For a long time I have admired the Master’s Way, and recently I had the opportunity to hold his hand by the Hulong River, where we conversed on the profound mysteries (*xuan*).
Consequently, I presented him with a single volume of my remaining discourses to seek his correction. Upon reading it, the Master...
He sighed and said, "I did not expect that what the Confucian scholars have produced would reach such a level. You must protect and uphold it well. The Master was skilled at guiding others;
by inferring from this single instance, one can gain a general understanding [of his teachings]. When he heard of the Master’s passing, he [consulted] Mr. Wei of the National History.
His grief was such that he could not overcome it. Master Wei also deeply understood the Teacher. The inscription reads:
"The profound instructions of the Great Mirror have been transmitted for over ten generations; Miaoxi arose and kicked open the banquet of dragons and elephants.
Like a great general stationed at the center of the line, ten thousand iron-clad soldiers wear their quivers and scabbards."
Whoever touches him finds their life’s hair suspended; who among five generations could match his sage-like excellence?
The Buddha-sun rises from the vast ocean, its crimson flames flickering across center and periphery;
wherever its radiance reaches, there is no darkness or obscurity. I recall when he first flew with his mendicant staff to Northern Yan.
In the vermilion tower, the painted drums are entwined with golden stars; With one strike, the three realms are all vast and open.
Within the fire, a pure lotus is newly spread; Its deep blue color contains the void, severed from all entanglements.
From this point, a hundred-fathom spring gushes from the mouth, Washing away the five turbidities and leaving behind all stench and impurity.
Within lie the various states of China, and without, the land of Chaoxian; The throngs who come are shoulder to shoulder.
To show them the true aspect is no empty word; Stupas and temples blaze forth across famous mountains and rivers.
One Buddha can transform into ten thousand and a thousand; When the myriad things are gathered back into the One, the Way is complete.
Unrecognized, he was falsely accused of having worldly attachments;
by imperial decree, a palace messenger arrived to proclaim the mandate. At Zhongshan he preached the Dharma, transcending all worldly entanglements;
ten thousand people looked up to him with devotion as he folded his two hands. One morning he entered nirvana, like a cicada shedding its shell.
In the West, a mere snap of the fingers brings him before us;
White jade pavilions and lapis lazuli fields, with golden bells and precious trees proclaiming the true teaching. The Master has departed, yet his spirit does not migrate;
In the serene light, he is eternally settled, beyond partiality or fullness. I compose this eulogy to be engraved upon the green stone stele.
Brilliant, radiant, and majestic, his legacy shall endure for years to come.
Hanlin Academician, Vice Minister of the Second Grade, Compiler of Imperial Edicts, concurrently serving as... [Editor].
